author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Deer Hunting
body:
The deer hunt has proved one of our most successful games.

The deer is a dummy, best made with a wire frame, on which soft hay is wrapped till it is of proper size and shape, then all is covered with open burlap. A few touches of white and black make it very realistic.

If time does not admit of a well-finished deer, one can be made of a sack stuffed with hay, decorated at one end with a smaller sack for head and neck, and set on four thin sticks.

The side of the deer is marked with a large oval, and over the heart is a smaller one.

Bows and arrows only are used to shoot this deer.

A pocketful of corn, peas, or other large grain is now needed for scent. The boy who is the deer for the first hunt takes the dummy under his arm and runs off, getting ten minutes' start, or until he comes back and shouts "ready!" He leaves a trail of corn, dropping two or three grains for every yard and making the trail as crooked as he likes, playing such tricks as a deer would do to baffle his pursuers. Then he hides the deer in any place he fancies, but not among rocks or on the top of a ridge, because in one case many arrows would be broken, and in the other, lost.

The hunters now hunt for this deer just as for a real deer, either following the trail or watching the woods ahead; the best hunters combine the two. If at any time the trail is quite lost the one in charge shouts: "Lost Trail!" After that the one who finds the trail scores two. Anyone giving a false alarm by shouting "Deer" is fined five.

Thus they go till some one finds the deer. He shouts: "_Deer!_" and scores ten for finding it. The others shout: "_Second_," "_Third_," etc., in order of seeing it, but they do not score.

The finder must shoot at the deer with his bow and arrow from the very spot whence he saw it. If he misses, the second hunter may step up five paces, and have his shot. If he misses, the third one goes five, and so on till some one hits the deer, or until the ten-yard limit is reached. If the finder is within ten yards on sighting the deer, and misses his shot, the other hunters go back to the ten-yard limit. Once the deer is hit, all the shooting must be from the exact spot whence the successful shot was fired.

A shot in the big oval is a body wound; that scores five. A shot outside that is a scratch; that scores two. A shot in the small oval or heart is a heart wound; it scores ten, and ends the hunt. Arrows which do not stick do not count, unless it can be proved that they passed right through, in which case they take the highest score that they pierced.

If all the arrows are used, and none in the heart, the deer escapes, and the boy who was deer scores twenty-five.

The one who found the dummy is deer for the next hunt. A clever deer can add greatly to the excitement of the game.

Originally we used paper for scent, but found it bad. It littered the woods; yesterday's trail was confused with that of to-day, etc. Corn proved better, because the birds and the squirrels kept it cleaned up from day to day, and thus the ground was always ready for a fresh start. But the best of all is the hoof mark for the shoe. These iron hoof marks are fast to a pair of shoes, and leave a trail much like a real deer. This has several advantages. It gives the hunter a chance to tell where the trail doubled, and which way the deer was going, It is more realistic, and the boy who can follow this skillfully can follow a living deer. In actual practice it is found well to use a little corn with this on the hard places, a plan quite consistent with realism, as every hunter will recall.

It is strictly forbidden to any hunter to stand in front of the firing line; all must be back of the line on which the shooter stands.

There is no limit to the situations and curious combinations in this hunt. The deer may be left standing or lying. There is no law why it should not be hidden behind a solid tree trunk. The game develops as one follows it. After it has been played for some time with the iron hoof mark as above, the boys grow so skilful on the trail that we can dispense with even the corn. The iron mark like a deer hoof leaves a very realistic "slot" or track, which the more skilful boys readily follow through the woods. A hunt is usually for three, five, or more deer, according to agreement and the result is reckoned by points on the whole chase.
summary: The deer hunt has proved one of our most successful games. The deer is a dummy, best made with a wire frame, on which soft hay is wrapped till it is of proper size and shape, then all is covered with open burlap. A few touches of white and black make it very…

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: The Bear Hunt
body:
This is played by half a dozen or more boys. Each has a club about the size and shape of a baseball club, but made of straw tied around two or three switches and tightly sewn up in burlap.--One big fellow is selected for the bear. He has a school bag tightly strapped on his back, and in that a toy balloon fully blown up. This is his heart. On his neck is a bear-claw necklace of wooden beads and claws. (See cut.)

He has three dens about one hundred yards apart in a triangle. While in his den the bear is safe. If the den is a tree or rock, he is safe while touching it. He is obliged to come out when the chief hunter counts one hundred, and must go the rounds of the three till the hunt is settled.

The object of the hunters is to break the balloon or heart; that is, to kill the bear. He must drop dead when the heart bursts. The hunter who kills him claims the necklace.

But the bear also has a club for defence. Each hunter must wear a hat, and once the bear knocks a hunter's hat off, that one is dead and out of this hunt. He must drop where his hat falls.

Tackling of any kind is forbidden.

The bear wins by killing or putting to flight all the hunters. In this case he keeps the necklace.

The savageness of these big bears is indescribable. Many lives are lost in each hunt, and it has several times happened that the whole party of hunters has been exterminated by some monster of unusual ferocity.

This game has also been developed into a play.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Spearing the Great Sturgeon
body:
This water game is exceedingly popular and is especially good for public exhibition, being spectacular and full of amusement and excitement.

The outfit needed is:

(1) A sturgeon roughly formed of soft wood; it should be about three feet long and nearly a foot thick at the head. It may be made realistic, or a small log pointed at both ends will serve.

(2) Two spears with six-inch steel heads and wooden handles (about three feet long). The points should be sharp, but not the barbs. Sometimes the barbs are omitted altogether. Each head should have an eye to which is attached twenty feet of one-quarter inch rope. On each rope, six feet from the spearhead, is a fathom mark made by tying on a rag or cord.

(3) Two boats with crews. Each crew consists of a spearman, who is captain, and one or two oarsmen or paddlers, of whom the after one is the pilot. All should be expert swimmers or else wear life-belts during the game.

The Game.--Each boat has a base or harbor; this is usually part of the shore opposite that of the enemy; or it obviates all danger of collision if the boats start from the same side. The sturgeon is left by the referee's canoe at a point midway between the bases. At the word "Go!" each boat leaves its base and, making for the sturgeon, tries to spear it, then drag it by the line to his base. When both get their spears into it the contest becomes a tug of war until one of the spears pulls out.

The sturgeon is landed when the prow of the boat that has it in tow touches its proper base, even though the spear of the enemy is then in the fish: or it is landed when the fish itself touches base. The boats change bases after each heat.

Matches are usually for one, three, or five sturgeon. Points are counted only for the landing of the fish, but the referee may give the decision on a foul or a succession of fouls, or the delinquent may be set back one or more boat lengths.

Sometimes the game is played in canoes or boats, with one man as spearman and crew.

_Rules_.--It is _not allowable_ to push the sturgeon into a new position with the spear or paddle before striking.

It is _allowable_ to pull the sturgeon under the boat or pass it around by using the line after spearing.

It is _allowable_ to lay hands on the other boat to prevent a collision, but otherwise it is forbidden to touch the other boat or crew or paddle or spear or line, or to lay hands on the fish, or to touch it with the paddle or oar, or touch your own spear while it is in the fish, or to tie the line around the fish except so far as this may be accidentally done in spearing.

It is _allowable_ to dislodge the enemy's spear by throwing your own over it. The purpose of the barbs is to assist in this.

It is _allowable_ to run on to the sturgeon with the boat.

_It is absolutely forbidden to throw the spear over the other boat or over the heads of your crew_.

In towing the sturgeon the fathom mark must be over the gunwale--at least six feet of line should be out when the fish is in tow. It is not a foul to have less, but the spearman must at once let it out if the umpire or the other crew cries "fathom!"

The spearman is allowed to drop the spear and use the paddle or oar at will, but not to resign his spear to another of the crew. The spearman must be in his boat when the spear is thrown.

If the boat is upset the referee's canoe helps them to right. Each crew must accept the backset of its accidents.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Tilting In The Water
body:
For this we usually have two boats or war canoes manned by four men each. These are a spearman, who is also a captain, a pilot, and two oarsmen.

The spearman is armed with a light pole or bamboo eight or ten feet long, with a soft pad on the end. Sometimes this is further provided with a hook. This is a forked branch with limbs a foot long; one is lashed to the bamboo, the other projecting out a foot, and slightly backward. The end of the spear and the fork are now thoroughly padded with burlap to the shape of a duck's head and bill. And it must be cased in waterproof, to keep it from getting wet and heavy. The object of the hook is to change suddenly from pushing, and to pull the enemy by hooking round his neck. Each boat should have a quarter-deck or raised platform at one end, on which the spearman stands.

The battle is fought in rounds and by points.

To put your opponent back into the canoe with one foot counts you five; two feet, ten. If he loses his spear you count five (excepting when he is put overboard). If you put him down on one knee on the fighting deck, you count five; two knees, ten. If you put him overboard it counts twenty-five. One hundred points is a round.

A battle is for one or more rounds, as agreed on. It is forbidden to hook or strike below the belt. The umpire may dock for fouls.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Canoe Tag
body:
Any number of canoes or boats may engage in this. A rubber cushion, a hot-water bag full of air, any rubber football, or a cotton bag with a lot of corks in it is needed. The game is to tag the other canoe by throwing this into it.

The rules are as in ordinary cross-tag.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Scouting
body:
Scouts are sent out in pairs or singly. A number of points are marked on the map at equal distances from camp, and the scouts draw straws to see where each goes. If one place is obviously hard, the scout is allowed a fair number of points as handicap. All set out at same time, go direct, and return as soon as possible.

Points are thus allowed:

Last back, zero for travelling.

The others count one for each minute they are ahead of the last.

Points up to one hundred are allowed for their story on return.

Sometimes we allow ten points for each turtle they have seen; ten for each owl seen and properly named; five for each hawk, and one each for other wild birds; also two for a cat one for a dog.

No information is given the scout; he is told to go to such a point and do so and so, but is fined points if he hesitates or asks how or why, etc.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: The Game of Quicksight
body:
Make two boards about a foot square, divide each into twenty-five squares; get ten nuts and ten pebbles. Give to one player one board, five nuts, and five pebbles. He places these on the squares in any pattern he fancies, and when ready the other player is allowed to see it for five seconds. Then it is covered up, and from the memory of what he saw the second player must reproduce the pattern on his own board. He counts one for each that was right, and takes off one for each that was wrong. They take turn and turn about.

This game is a wonderful developer of the power to see and memorize quickly.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Farsight, or Spot the Rabbit
body: Take two six-inch squares of stiff white pasteboard or whitened wood. On each of these draw an outline rabbit, one an exact duplicate of the other. Make twenty round black wafers or spots, each half an inch across. Let one player stick a few of these on one rabbit-board and set it up in full light. The other, beginning at one hundred yards, draws near till he can see the spots well enough to reproduce the pattern on the other which he carries. If he can do it at seventy-five yards he has wonderful eyes. Down even to seventy (done three times out of five), he counts high honor; from seventy to sixty counts honor. Below that does not count at all.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Pole-star
body:
Each competitor is given a long straight stick in daytime, and told to lay it due north and south. In doing this he may guide himself by sun, moss, or anything he can find in nature--anything, indeed, except a compass.

The direction is checked by a good compass corrected for the locality. The one who comes nearest wins.

It is optional with the judges whether the use of a timepiece is to be allowed.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Rabbit Hunt
body:
The game of rabbit hunting is suited for two hunters in limited grounds.

Three little sacks of brown burlap, each about eight inches by twelve, are stuffed with hay.

At any given place in the woods the two hunters stand in a ten-foot circle with their bows and arrows. One boy is blindfolded; the other, without leaving the circle, throws the rabbits into good hiding places on the ground. Then the second hunter has to find the rabbits and shoot them without leaving the circle. The lowest number of points wins, as in golf. If the hunter has to leave the circle he gets one point for every step he takes outside. After he sees the rabbit he must keep to that spot and shoot till it is hit once. One shot kills it, no matter where struck. For every shot he misses he gets five points.

After his first shot at each rabbit the hider takes alternate shots with him.

If it is the hider who kills the rabbit, the hunter adds ten points to his score. If the hunter hits it, he takes ten off his score.

If the hunter fails to find all the rabbits, he scores twenty-five for each one he gives up.

The hider cannot score at all. He can only help his friend into trouble. Next time the two change places.

A match is usually for two brace of rabbits.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Hostile Spy
body: Hanging from the totem pole is a red or yellow horse-tail. This is the grand medicine scalp of the band. The hostile spy has to steal it. The leader goes around on the morning of the day and whispers to the various braves, "Look out--there's a spy in camp." At length he gets secretly near the one he has selected for spy and whispers, "Look out, there's a spy in camp, and you are it." He gives him at the same time some bright-coloured badge, that he must wear as soon as he has secured the medicine scalp. He must not hide the scalp on his person, but keep it in view. He has all day till sunset to get away with it. If he gets across the river or other limit, with warriors in close pursuit, they give him ten arrow heads (two and one half cents each), or other ransom agreed on. If he gets away safely and hides it, he can come back and claim fifteen arrow heads from the council as ransom for the scalp. If he is caught, he pays his captor ten arrow heads ransom for his life.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: The Man-Hunt
body:
This is played with a scout and ten or more hostiles, or hounds, according to the country, more when it is rough or wooded.

The scout is given a letter addressed to the "Military Commandant" (usually the lady of the house that he gets to) of any given place a mile or two away. He is told to take the letter to anyone of three given houses, and get it endorsed, with the hour when he arrived, then return to the starting-point within a certain time.

The hostiles are sent to a point half-way, and let go by a starter at the same time as the scout leaves the camp. They are to intercept him.

If they catch him before he delivers the letter he must ransom his life by paying each two arrow heads (or other forfeit) and his captor keeps the letter as a trophy. If he gets through, but is caught on the road back, he pays half as much for his life. If he gets through, but is over time, it is a draw. If he gets through successfully on time he claims three arrow heads from each hostile and keeps the letter as a trophy.

They may not follow him into the house (that is, the fort), but may surround it at one hundred yards distance. They do not know which three houses he is free to enter, but they do know that these are within certain limits.

The scout should wear a conspicuous badge (hat, shirt, coat, or feather), and may ride a wheel or go in a wagon, etc., as long as his badge is clearly visible.

To "tag" the scout is not to capture. "The blockade to be binding must be effectual."

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Hunt the Coon
body:
This is an in-door game, founded on the familiar "Hunt the Thimble."

We use a little dummy coon; either make it or turn a ready-made toy rabbit into one by adding tail and black mask, and cropping the ears.

All the players but one go out of the room. That one places the coon anywhere in sight, high or low, but in plain view; all come in and seek. The first to find it, sits down silently, and scores one. Each sits down, on seeing it, giving no clue to the others.

The first to score three coons is winner, usually. Sometimes we play till everyone but one has a coon; that one is the booby. The others are first, second, etc.

Sometimes each is given his number in order of finding it.

Then, after seven or eight coons, these numbers are added up, and the lowest is winner. If no coon is available use a thimble.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Spear Fights
body:
This is an in-door game with out-door weapons. The soft-headed, eight foot spears of the tilting-match are used. The contestants stand on barrels eight feet apart. Each tries to put the other off his barrel. It is well to have a catcher behind each player to save him if he falls.

Games are for seven, eleven, or thirteen points.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Navajo Feather Dance
body: An eagle feather hung on a horse-hair, so as to stand upright, is worked by a hidden operator, so as to dance and caper. The dancer has to imitate all its motions. A marionette may be used. It is a great fun-maker.
summary: An eagle feather hung on a horse-hair, so as to stand upright, is worked by a hidden operator, so as to dance and caper. The dancer has to imitate all its motions. A marionette may be used. It is a great fun-maker.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Feather Football or Feather Blow
body:
This is an in-door, wet-weather game.

The players hold a blanket on the knees or on the table. A soft feather is put in the middle. As many may play as can get near. They may be in sides, two or four or each for himself. At the signal, "Go!" each tries to blow the feather off the blanket at the enemy's side, and so count one for himself.

A game is usually best out of seven, eleven, or thirteen.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Cock-Fighting
body:
Get two stout sticks, each two feet long (broomsticks will do). Pad each of these on the end with a ball of rag. These are the spurs. Make an eight-foot ring. The two rivals are on their hunkers, each with a stick through behind his knees, his hands clasped in front of the knees, and the arms under the ends of the spurs.

Now they close; each aiming to upset the other, to make him lose his spurs, or to put him out of the ring, any of which ends that round and scores one for the victor. If both fall, or lose a spur, or go out together, it is a draw. Battle is for seven, eleven, or thirteen rounds.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Hand-Wrestling
body:
This is a jiujitsu game, introduced by Dr. L. H. Gulick. The two contestants stand right toe to right toe, each right hand clasped, left feet braced, left hand free. At the word, "Go!" each tries to unbalance the other: that is, make him lift or move one of his feet. A lift or a shift ends the round.

Battles are for best out of five, seven, eleven, or thirteen rounds.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Badger-Pulling
body:
The two contestants, on hands and knees, face each other.

A strong belt or strap is buckled into one great loop that passes round the head of each: that is, crosses his nape. Half-way between them is a dead line. The one who pulls the other over this line is winner.

The contestant can at any time end the bout by lowering his head so the strap slips off; but this counts one against him.

Game is best out of five, seven, eleven, or thirteen points.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Poison
body:
This is an ancient game. A circle about three feet across is drawn on the ground. The players, holding hands, make a ring around this, and try to make one of the number step into the poison circle. He can evade it by side-stepping, by jumping over, or by dragging another fellow into it.

First to make the misstep is "it" for the time or for next game.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Hat-Ball
body:
When I was among the Chepewyan Indians of Great Slave Lake, in 1907, I made myself popular with the young men, as well as boys, by teaching them the old game of hat-ball.

The players (about a dozen) put their hats in a row near a house, fence, or log (hollows up). A dead line is drawn ten feet from the hats; all must stand outside of that. The one who is "it" begins by throwing a soft ball into one of the hats. If he misses the hat, a chip is put into his own, and he tries over. As soon as he drops the ball into a hat, the owner runs to get the ball; all the rest run away. The owner must not follow beyond the dead line, but must throw the ball at some one. If he hits him, a chip goes into that person's hat; if not, a chip goes into his own.

As soon as some one has five chips, he wins the booby prize: that is, he must hold his hand out steady against the wall, and each player has five shots at it with the ball, as he stands on the dead line.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Duck-on-a-Rock
body:
This is a good old grandfather game.

Each player has a large, smooth, roundish stone, about five or six inches through. This is his duck. He keeps it permanently.

Toe rock is any low bowlder, block, stump, bump, or hillock on level ground. A dead line is drawn through the rock, and another parallel, fifteen feet away, for a firing line.

The fellow who is "it," or "keeper," perches his duck on the rock. The others stand at the firing line and throw their ducks at his. They must not pick them up or touch them with their hands when they are beyond the dead line. If one does, then the keeper can tag him (unless he reaches the firing line), and send him to do duty as keeper at the rock.

But they can coax their ducks with their feet, up to the dead line, not beyond, then watch for a chance to dodge back to the firing line, where they are safe at all times.

If the duck is knocked off by anyone in fair firing, the keeper is powerless till he has replaced it. Meantime, most of the players have secured their ducks and got back safely to the firing line.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Road-side Cribbage
body:
This is a game we often play in the train, to pass the time pleasantly.

Sometimes one party takes the right side of the road, with the windows there, and the other the left. Sometimes all players sit on the same side.

The game is, whoever is first to see certain things agreed on scores so many points.

Thus: A crow or a cow counts 1 A cat 2 A hawk 3 An owl 4 A sheep 5 A goat 6 A horse 7

The winner is the one who first gets twenty-five or fifty points, as agreed.

When afoot, one naturally takes other things for points, as certain trees, flowers, etc.
summary: This is a game we often play in the train, to pass the time pleasantly. Sometimes one party takes the right side of the road, with the windows there, and the other the left. Sometimes all players sit on the same side. The game is, whoever is first to see…

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Chalk the Arrow
body:
This is usually played in the city streets, one player running and trying to keep out of sight of the others who follow. The runner is given time to disappear around the first corner before the others start after him, and at every corner he turns he marks (with chalk) an arrow pointing in the direction he takes. Those pursuing follow by the arrow, the first one seeing him being the runner for the next time.

This may also be played by having any number run and only one follow, the first becoming "it" for the next time.
summary: This is usually played in the city streets, one player running and trying to keep out of sight of the others who follow. The runner is given time to disappear around the first corner before the others start after him, and at every corner he turns he marks…

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Dodge Ball
body:
Of any number of players, half of that number form a circle, while the other half stand inside of the ring (centre) facing outward. Now, the game for those in the centre is to dodge the ball which is thrown by any of those forming the circle with the intention of striking the centre ones out. Every time a member is struck he is dead, and takes his place among those of the circle. Now he has a chance to throw at those remaining in the centre. This arrangement keeps all taking part busy. Only one is out at a time. This being kept up until finally only one is left. He is hailed the king. For next round, players exchange places, i. e., those who were in the centre now form the circle.

Note: If the touch is preceded by a bound of the ball it does not count.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Prisoner's Base
body: Goals are marked off at both ends of the playground, the players divided into two equal divisions, occupying the two goals. About ten paces to the right of each goal is a prison. A player advances toward the opposite goal, when one from that goal starts out to catch him. He retreats, and one from his side runs to his rescue by trying to catch the pursuer--who in turn is succored by one from his side, and so on. Every player may catch anyone from the opposite side who has been out of goal longer than he has. Any player caught is conducted to the prison by his captor and must remain there until rescued by some one from his side, who touches him with the hand. The one who does this is subject to being caught like any other player.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Throwing the Spear
body:
The game is an old Greek and Persian pastime. "Throw the spear and speak the truth," was a national maxim of the Persians that we may copy with advantage.

The apparatus required is some light spears and an archery target. The spears should vary from five to six feet in length; the point should be shod with a steel tip, having a socket into which the wooden handle is fitted, and made fast by small screws passing through holes in the sides of the metal, and then into the wood itself. The wood, for about a foot above the barb, should be about three quarters of an inch in diameter, and from thence gradually taper to about a quarter of an inch in thickness until the end of the spear is reached.

Some spears are fitted with feathers, like an arrow, but these are not necessary to obtain a good throw, and soon get dismantled in continually falling upon the ground. Any ordinary target will serve. It may be an archery target, a sack full of straw, or a sod bank.

The object of the contest is to hit the target from a given mark, the firing line. Whoever throws nearest to the centre of the target the greatest number of times out of six shots is hailed the winner.

The best form for throwing is with the left foot forward, the leg perfectly straight, body well back, its weight resting on the right leg. Now extend the left arm forward, in a line with the shoulder, and over the left leg; poise the spear horizontally in the right hand, holding at the centre of gravity by the forefinger and thumb. Bring the right arm backward until the hand is behind the right shoulder.

Now, inclining the point of the spear slightly upward, make your cast, bringing the right arm forward, followed by the right side of the body, the right leg forward and the left arm backward. Count yourself fortunate if you even hit the target in the first few attempts, but practice will make a wonderful difference. The distance should be mutually agreed upon, but fifty feet for a boy of fifteen and one hundred feet for an adult will be found about right.

To "throw the javelin" is another phase of this pastime. The javelin is four to five feet in length, three quarters of an inch in thickness, and fitted with a barbed end, slightly heavier than the spear end. The "object of the game" is to throw the javelin as far as possible but not at a target; instead, the javelin must stick into the ground.

In throwing the javelin, hold it in the right hand, the left leg and hand being advanced; the barb and arm at this point should be at the rear. Then, describing a semicircle with the arm over the right shoulder, and leaning well to the rear, hurl the weapon as far as possible forward.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Follow My Leader
body: With a large number of boys this can be made a very effective display, and is easy to do at a jog trot, and occasional "knee-up" with musical accompaniment. It also can be done at night, each boy carrying a Chinese lantern on top of his staff. If in a building all lights, of course, would be turned down. A usual fault is that the exercise is kept on too long, till it wearies both audience and performers.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Unprepared Plays
body:
Give the plot of a short, simple, play and assign to each player his part, with an outline of what he has to do and say, and then let them act it, making up the required conversation as they go along.

This develops the power of imagination and expression on points kept in the mind, and is a valuable means of education.

It is well before starting to act a play in this way to be a little less ambitious, and to make two or three players merely carry out a conversation on given topics leading up to a given point, using their own words and imaginations in doing so.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: The Treasure Hunt
body:
The treasure hunt needs observation and skill in tracking, and practically any number can take part in it.

Several ways of playing the game are given below.

1. The treasure is hidden and the scouts know what the treasure is; they are given the first clew, and from this all the others can be traced. Such clews might be (a) written on a gate post: "Go west and examine third gate on north side of stream"; (b) on that gate, scout's sign pointing to notice board on which is written, "Strike south by south-east telegraph post, No. 28," and so on. The clews should be so worded as to need some skill to understand, and the various points should be difficult of access from one another. This method might be used as a patrol competition, starting off patrols at ten-minute intervals, and at one particular clew there might be different orders for each patrol, to prevent the patrols behind from following the first.

2. The clews may be bits of colored wood tied to gates, hedges, etc., at about three-yard intervals, leading in a certain direction, and when these clews come to the end it should be known that the treasure is hidden within so many feet. To prevent this degenerating into a mere game of follow my leader, several tracks might be laid working up to the same point, and false tracks could be laid, which only lead back again to the original.

3. Each competitor or patrol might be given a description of the way--each perhaps of a slightly different way; the description should make it necessary to go to each spot in turn; and prevent any "cutting" in the following way: "Go to the tallest tree in a certain field, from there go one hundred yards north, and then walk straight toward a church tower which will be on your left," etc. All the descriptions should lead by an equal journey to a certain spot where the treasure is hidden. The first to arrive at that spot should not let the others know it is the spot, but should search for the treasure in as casual a manner as possible.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Will-o'-the-Wisp
body:
This game should take place across country at night. Two scouts set off in a given direction with a lighted bull's-eye lantern. After two minutes have passed the patrol or troop starts in pursuit.

The lantern bearer must show his light at least every minute concealing it for the rest of the time. The two scouts take turns in carrying the light, and so may relieve each other in difficulties, but either may be captured. The scout without the light can often mingle with the pursuers without being recognized and relieve his friend when he is being hard pressed. They should arrange certain calls or signals between themselves.
summary: This game should take place across country at night. Two scouts set off in a given direction with a lighted bull's-eye lantern. After two minutes have passed the patrol or troop starts in pursuit. The lantern bearer must show his light at least every minute…

similarActivities.author: Zygmunt Wyrobek
similarActivities.note: Both variants describe a night pursuit of scouts who pass a lantern between them and reveal its light at fixed intervals.

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Treasure Island
body: A treasure is known to be hidden upon a certain island or bit of shore marked off, and the man who hid it leaves a map with clews for finding it (compass, directions, tide marks, etc.). This map is hidden somewhere near the landing-place; the patrols come in turn to look for it--they have to row from a certain distance, land, find the map, and finally discover the treasure. They should be careful to leave no foot tracks, etc., near the treasure, because then the patrols that follow them will easily find it. The map and treasure are to be hidden afresh for the next patrol when they have been found. The patrol wins which returns to the starting place with the treasure in the shortest time. (This can be played on the river, the patrols having to row across the river to find the treasure.)

author: Ernest Thompson Seton
publisher: Doubleday, Page & Company for the Boy Scouts of America
title: Horse and Rider Tourney
body: In playing this game it is necessary to have a soft, velvety piece of grass, or if in doors, in the gymnasium, cover the floor with regular gymnasium mats. It requires four boys to play the game, two being horses and the other two riders. The riders mount their horses and dash at each other with great caution, striving to get a good hold of each other in such a way as to compel the opponent to dismount. This can be done either by dragging him from his mount or by making the horse and rider lose their balance so as to throw them off their feet. A great deal of sport can be gotten out of this game, and boys become very skilful after a little practice.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Kim's Game
body:
The patrol leader should prepare a collection of small objects, such as various penknives, fabric samples, pencils, pens, stones (rocks or minerals), booklets, and so on.

For beginners (in the first few games), only 15 objects are arranged, while for those more practiced, 20—30. After placing the objects not too close to one another on a table, they are covered with a cloth.

Then, the scouts are instructed to sit around the table so that each can see well, and the cloth is lifted for 1 minutes, after which the objects are covered again. Instead of watching a clock, one may count aloud at a moderate pace to 60.

Afterward, each scout must prepare a list of the remembered objects or recite them in a whisper to the patrol leader, who notes them down with marks on a previously prepared name list.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Morgana's Game
body:
Scouts are instructed to approach any of the shop windows, to which one scout has simultaneously been assigned as the judge.

The judge ensures that the scouts look at the display for only one minute, after which the scouts return to camp and write down the names of the objects they noticed and remembered. Points (marked as strokes) are awarded for the greatest number of items.

A more challenging variation of the game follows:

The judge or instructor, or the patrol leader, walks with their patrol and stops in turn in front of the windows of six shop displays, spending 1/2 minutes at each. Then, each participant writes down the names of the objects observed at each display (or only at one of them, designated by the patrol leader), and the one who lists the most wins and receives points (strokes).

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Hearing Exercise
body:
A selected scout sits on a stool with eyes blindfolded. The area chosen for this game must be covered with dry twigs, leaves, gravel, and pebbles. A second scout, approaching cautiously from a distance of 90 meters, must traverse this space in 1½ minutes and touch the seated scout before being heard. Naturally, before the game, the selected scout is required to give their word of honor to adhere to the truth.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Scent Exercises
body:
Prepare a certain number (for beginners 7, later always more—up to 15) of paper cones or dark little bottles (10 grams) and place in each one an item with a distinct scent, such as: a piece of onion, roasted coffee, rose petals, anise, orange peel, cloves, violet flowers, etc., or pour in different liquids like: kerosene, turpentine, ether, etc. Arrange these items in a single row, a few feet apart from one another, and instruct each participant to walk along the table, sniffing each tube (or vial) for 5 seconds. Then give each person one minute to write down from memory, in order, all the scents they encountered.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Eyesight Exercise
body:
The following game excellently develops sharpness of vision. After handing each scout a card divided into 12 small squares (or a sheet from a grid notebook), they are instructed to move several hundred meters away (starting from 100), toward the shorter wall of the room. The judge then takes a large card (stretched on a drawing board) or a white cardboard, divided into 12 squares, each with sides at least 3 inches long, or if indoors, 1¹/₂ to 2 inches. Next, the judge pins black cardboard circles, each half an inch in diameter, in any of the 6 squares and turns the card so everyone can see it clearly. Then, everyone slowly approaches, and once they can clearly distinguish the marked pattern, they copy it onto their own cards. The winner is the one who accurately reproduces it from the greatest distance from the judge.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Campfire Race
body:
When setting up camp, especially after prolonged strenuous games, it is possible to keep the weary in a state of nervous tension through the stimulus of competition. It suffices to promise a certain number of marks to the entire patrol that, in the shortest time, gathers kindling, arranges it, and lights a campfire, using the fewest matches for this purpose.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Expedition for Plants
body:
Exercises sharpness of sight, trains in identifying plants, and enriches memory, or rather reinforces the memorization of botanical names.

Scouts may be instructed individually or in pairs, by bicycle or on foot, to go in any direction they choose and bring back certain specified (rarer in the given area) plant species. For example, 10 tree branches, or 10 wildflowers, or 10 poisonous plants. When selecting plants, one should use a handbook describing the geographical distribution of plants in our country.

The patrol leader or judge will award points for the fastest return with the requested plant.

title: Scout Postal Service (on Foot or by Wheels)
body:
(on foot or by wheels).

Setup at a distance of 100—500 metres (on wheels 2—3 times farther). Each patrol leader arranges their own patrol as for a relay race with flags.

Transmitting a dispatch over a longer distance may be carried out by several teams. The team leader is then responsible for ensuring that the dispatch does not experience any delay in their sector.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Tracking Footprints
body:
One patrol should sit so that the soles of their boots are clearly visible. The second patrol is given 3 minutes for observation. Then, the first patrol is allowed to leave, except for one scout who is instructed to take several steps on soft ground, prepared specifically for this purpose. Afterward, the scouts of the 2 patrol are called back and, based on observing the boots, must guess whose footprint it is. Naturally, the second patrol does not know which scouts were sent home and who remained to make the footprint. A good exercise in winter.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Drawing the Track
body:
After leading your patrol outside the town and showing them a certain track, offer a reward for the best and most accurate drawing of the imprint (track) of the left (right) foot. Scouts may follow the track for a short distance until they reach ground where the tracks are most clearly imprinted.

A variation of this game will be drawing horse hoof tracks, including measurements of stride length and (based on these) identifying the horse's gait—whether it walked at a walk, trotted, or galloped.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Approaching the Guard
body:
The instructor sends various scouts in different directions, half a kilometer away from him. Then, he waves a flag to signal the start of the game. At this point, all scouts drop to the ground and, hiding behind bushes or ground irregularities, now creeping stealthily, now crawling, approach him ever closer. When the instructor gives the second signal with the flag, everyone stands up, approaches him, and delivers a report. In the meantime—that is, between the first and second flag signals—the instructor performs brief movements, such as sitting, kneeling, looking through binoculars, removing his hat, waving his hat, wiping sweat from his brow, sneezing, walking in circles, counting on his fingers, shading his eyes with his hand, clapping his hands, etc. The scouts must observe, remember, and later recount all these movements to him upon their return. Additionally, the instructor carefully scans all directions, and if he spots any of the scouts, he notes 2 minus marks against them. During the report, the scout who correctly lists all the judge’s movements in order and crawled the closest receives 3 marks. To save time, scouts can be given cards on which they write down the observed movements under their names.

A variation of this game is: **Approaching the Game (Wildlife Stalking).**

The instructor takes the role of the game (animal), while the scouts move 100 steps away from him, drop to the ground (preferably on undulating terrain or sparsely covered with bushes), and, crawling, try to get as close to him as possible without being seen. If the instructor spots any of them, he orders that scout to stand up and cease playing. After some time, he gives a signal with a bugle or a call, everyone stands up, and the one who crawled the closest unnoticed wins and receives marks.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: What Length?
body:
A good camp exercise is the task of recording answers to questions about lengths and heights, for example:

1. How tall am I in my hat? When sitting on a stool? When sitting on the ground? When lying on my back?

When lying ready to shoot? In a straddle? In a lunge? In a squat? And so on.

2. What is the length of the camp table? What is the height of a nearby house? What is the height of a given landmark tree? And so on.

The winner is the one who provides the greatest number of measurements, most closely approximating the truth.

A more challenging variation of this game is estimating distances. For this purpose, several scouts of equal height are sent out from the camp. All are ordered to walk in a straight line and count their steps. The judge positions them and records the number of steps for each station. Meanwhile, those remaining in the camp estimate the distance, and the instructor records their guesses. Upon the judge’s return, the winner is the one whose numbers most closely match the truth.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Finding North
body:
In this exercise, individual scouts are positioned at a distance of 30 meters from one another and instructed to place their staff on the ground in the direction where they have found north—or south—without the aid of tools, then step back 6 paces. The judge then compares the marked directions with a compass, and whoever comes closest to the actual truth wins. This game should be repeated both by day and by night.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Map Reading
body:
A judge or patrol leader takes the patrol to a foreign town or an unfamiliar area where they wish to gather certain details. There, they show the scouts a map of the area and assign each one a destination to reach. While outlining the route on the map, they simultaneously list churches, taverns, manor houses, streams, bridges, statues, distinctive (orientation) trees, and other features that the scout should encounter and observe along the way. Each scout is given a specific distance to cover and a certain number of points to note.

Afterward, the scouts set out, and upon their return, the instructor or patrol leader receives their reports. The winner is the one who brings back the most accurate report in the shortest time.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Near and Far
body:
The patrol leader guides their unit in patrol formation through the town or surrounding area. Having prepared beforehand lists of objects for the Scouts to observe, they distribute these lists at the moment of departure and instruct the Scouts to mark with strokes each time someone spots an item on their list.

The patrol leader compiles the list of objects to train the Scouts in observing both near and distant distances simultaneously, and to break the habit of Scouts—trained in tracking—of focusing solely on the ground beneath their feet. Example list of objects: a broken window, a damaged chimney top, a matchstick, a button, a dog’s track, a bird’s track, a tower, an orientation tree, a statue, the number of birds flying, what kinds of birds, a lame horse, a horse’s track, the horse’s gait, etc. The most observations marked with strokes wins.

For variety, this game can be modified so that the Scouts are only required to observe and remember their observations, while the patrol leader alone notes them down. Later, through clever and even cross-questioning, the patrol leader determines which Scout in the patrol has the keenest observational sense. Initially, observations are made over a distance of 2 kilometers, later gradually extending to longer multi-mile excursions. Example questions: What sound reached your ears as we left the town? From which direction was the wind blowing? How was the smoke rising? How many carriages were coming toward us, and how many were behind us? What was the inscription on the statue? How many geese were swimming? How many roosters were crowing? From which direction were the crows flying? etc.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Finding the Thimble
body:
The patrol leader asks their patrol to leave the troop room for a few minutes, while they themselves place a thimble, ring, coin, piece of paper, or any small object in a visible spot, though not too conspicuous. The patrol is then called back to search. Whoever spots the hidden object sits down without even giving away its location with their gaze. After some time, the patrol leader asks one of those seated to point out the spot to the rest of the searchers. The winner is the one who saw the thimble first, and in the next game, they take charge of hiding the thimble.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Outline of the Immediate Camp Vicinity (Croquis)
body:
When a troop establishes a camp anywhere, it dispatches scouts with notebooks to gather an outline of the surrounding area within a radius of 2 kilometers. It is possible to send 4 patrols in 4 directions, ideally guided by the compass rose. The patrol leader sketches, while the scouts measure distances by pacing and time, and bring back details such as: road bends, terrain undulations, distances, railways, rivers, ravines, gullies, embankments, dikes, ponds, landmark trees, houses, statues, boundary posts, and mounds.

The patrol that produces the best outline or chart in the shortest time wins, earning a certain number of marks.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Signal Game
body:
This is an excellent exercise for Morse code signals. The troop, or unit, is divided into **3** parts, or only **3** patrols are designated for this game. Part A may be the smallest but must consist of the best signalers (e.g., **3** scouts from Patrol A).

Part C must be the largest (Patrol C plus the remainder of Patrol A). The game lasts **2** hours.

First, Unit A sets out and chooses a position on a high hill, tree, tower, or rooftop, depending on where there is the best view of the desired distance or a limited area with a radius of **1/2**—**1** km, depending on whether the terrain is open or concealed. This unit (A) takes with it Morse flags (or Semaphore flags) or any other signaling apparatus (whistles, trumpets, etc.).

Next, Unit B (Patrol B) sets out and attempts to hide within the agreed boundaries of the area, aiming to deceive the watchful eyes of the signalers (A). It appears and disappears in various places, striving to mislead the enemy observing its movements. It should be dressed in khaki colors, as this facilitates the difficult task of concealment. Once it finally occupies a well-hidden position, it is no longer permitted to change its location.

**15** minutes after B, Unit C sets out, guided by the signals from Unit A reporting the position occupied by B. It endeavors to approach unseen and surround the hiding place of Unit B. If Unit B is surrounded, it is considered captured, and C wins. However, if more scouts from Unit B escape

(which is permitted from the moment encirclement is detected) than are surrounded, then B wins.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: The Spider and the Fly
body:
An area of one square kilometer, whose boundaries are marked out in the terrain (or only on a map), designated for the web. Urban terrain is just as suitable for the game as terrain outside the city. One hour is sufficient for a single game.

The entire patrol, or only half the patrol drawn as the fly, sets off and seeks a comfortable hiding place. The second patrol, or the other half, departs a quarter of an hour later as the spider in search of the fly. Each patrol is accompanied by an impartial judge.

The spider may scatter but must report to the patrol leader if any trace of the fly is discovered. If the spider does not find the fly within an hour, the fly wins. The fly records the names of those scouts from the spider patrol whom it saw. Similarly, the spider records the names of those scouts from the fly patrol whom it spots, along with the location of their hiding place. For these reports, the judges distribute points at the end of the game.

Both sides should have colored badges for easy distinction. Hilly or undulating terrain is also suitable for this game.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Cossack Maneuver in the Steppe
body:
(Encounter with a Tatar).

This game is an excellent school for stalking and has the added advantage of requiring no equipment and no large gathering. It suffices with 2 patrols, 2 pairs of scouts, or even 2 scouts. The terrain can be city streets just as well as undulating plains overgrown with bushes outside the city, roads with ditches and avenues, ravines, forest paths, and the like. The principle of this game is to spot the opponent without being spotted oneself.

Both sides set out (at the same time, as enforced by the judges) from two opposite points, 2 kilometers apart, and as they advance toward each other, they take advantage of ground unevenness, trees, and bushes to conceal themselves. In this way, they stealthily crawl or sneak forward, striving not to expose themselves while straining their eyes to spot the opponent. They may also use ruses, such as climbing a tree or sneaking in a wagon, but they must not disguise themselves. Patrols may scatter, but they must maintain constant communication with their patrol leader, whether through signals, visual contact, or messages, because a patrol only achieves and counts a victory if the patrol leader announces in the agreed manner—for example, by raising a small flag and giving a whistle signal—that his party has spotted the opponents. For this reason, before every bend or ravine, or generally wherever the terrain hinders communication with the patrol leader, the scattered patrol should regroup.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Cossack Maneuver in the Trenches
body:
A game that excellently sharpens visual acuity while also training in the art of stealth.

Each Scout participating in this game has a number composed of 3 digits sewn onto the front of their hat. The length of the digits should be at least 3 inches so that they can be easily distinguished from a distance of 100 meters.

The entire troop then divides as follows:

Two or three platoons (or 2—3 patrols if only 1/2 troops are taking part in the game) march 300 meters away from the camp with the order to return to the camp by stealthily creeping in—first crouching, then crawling—so that the defending garrison left behind in the camp’s trenches does not spot the approaching attack. If the terrain makes the defenders’ task easier than the attackers’, then only 1 platoon, or 1 patrol, remains in the camp for defense. Each side is assigned an impartial judge.

As the attacking side approaches, the garrison, under good cover to remain unseen, observes the attackers’ movements and attempts to read the opponents’ numbers. As long as the enemy’s numbers are not distinguishable, they are considered beyond firing range.

The closer the attackers come, the more carefully they must ensure they do not expose themselves above cover (a rock, bush, etc.) and make it easier for the defenders to read their numbers. A good Scout should also not forget, in their eagerness, that while creeping, they must only look from the side of the cover. It is forbidden to turn the hat so the numbers face sideways or backward, or to cover the numbers with a hand. When the garrison or the attackers are able to read the numbers, they call them out loudly, and the judges record them. When they are within 50 meters of each other (or of the camp), the judges from both sides loudly announce the numbers they have recorded, and their owners must withdraw from the game.

When the attack commander believes their unit has approached so closely that further concealment is impossible, they give the signal to charge, especially if the terrain is open, and the defenders then try to read as many numbers as possible aloud. When the attack comes within 10 paces of the camp, the judges signal that no more numbers may be read. The judges then read out the numbers recorded just before and during the charge across open ground. Those whose numbers are read withdraw from the game and are properly counted as casualties.

If the attack reaches the camp in numbers equal to the garrison (after counting casualties on both sides), victory is theirs. If they arrive in fewer numbers than the garrison, the garrison wins.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Fox Hunt for the Cat
body:
A terrain is chosen, preferably hilly, covering an area of 5 kilometres square if the entire day is to be devoted to this game. If only a few hours are available, the space should be significantly smaller. The boundaries of this square must be clearly defined, described, and understood by every Scout before the game begins, preferably a day in advance. The following day, early in the morning, 4 Scouts set out in the role of hares. They are easily recognised by a red sash, neckerchief, or armband fastened to their arm. They may go together or separately and hide as they please, but once a hiding place is chosen, it may not be changed.

An hour after the hares, the rest, numbering 16 (2 patrols), set out on the hunt. The hunters may also proceed together, singly, or in pairs in whatever direction they deem appropriate. Experience has shown, however, that hares are best hidden singly, while hunters are most effective when working in pairs. To distinguish hunters from ordinary people, they wear an armband or neckerchief of a different colour from that of the hares.

The game consists in the hunters tracking the hare by its traces (tracking irons, coloured paper, confetti, peas, corn, etc.), and once tracked, catching up to and capturing it. A hare is considered caught when a hunter touches it with their hand. This is a very lively and varied game, which trains both sides in hiding, stalking, tracking, and getting to know the area. A set evening hour, announced to all, ends the game, and the judges award points to the winners based on whether a hare was caught or the greatest number of discarded traces (confetti, peas, etc.) was collected.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Collecting Cotton
body:
Prepare pieces of cotton or yarn each 1 feet (30 cm) long. The type may be the cheapest, as long as the color is not bright (khaki is best).

Use these pieces to mark a path as an instructor through pastures, forests, rocky areas, or generally less frequented places. Avoid cultivated fields unless they are your property or you have permission from the owners. Do not simply throw the cotton on the ground; instead, attach it to trees, fences, bushes, and low-hanging branches, spaced 20 paces apart.

Then, send out 1 or 2 patrols to collect all the pieces of cotton and reach the end of the marked path as quickly as possible. When a scout participating in the game spots a piece of yarn, they announce it by calling out their patrol’s name so that both patrols can more easily orient themselves in the search. Apart from the instance of finding a trail, no other shouts are allowed. Each patrol gathers the found yarn into the hands of their patrol leader, and the leader whose patrol has collected the greater number of cotton pieces by the end of the game wins.

This game gives the instructor an opportunity to identify the most skilled trackers. If the trails are skillfully laid out, the scouts of the winning patrol deserve an additional mark for their cleverness. This method of tracking has the advantage over tracking irons in that it teaches scouts to pay close attention not only to the ground but to all directions.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: The Escape of a Siberian. (Lion Hunt)
body:
(Lion Hunt).

A Scout, playing the role of an escaping Siberian, runs in any direction through the snow, where tracks are clearly visible, until he finds a suitable hiding place in which to conceal himself. The rest of the patrol sets out 20 minutes later, following his tracks until they reach his hiding place. When they approach within a snowball’s throw, the hidden Siberian aims snowballs at them, and every Scout hit steps out of the game. The pursuers also try to hit the Siberian with snowballs. The Siberian is allowed to take refuge in a tree, and must be hit 3 times before he is considered dead.

In summer, the game changes in that the Siberian attaches tracking irons and fills his pockets with corn or peas, so that on rocky or muddy terrain, where tracks disappear, he can mark his trail by dropping a grain or pea at every step. Snowballs are replaced either with pine cones or tennis balls.

Due to excessive similarity, the Lion Hunt is not presented as a separate game.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Scout Race with Reconnaissance
body:
The patrol leader positions individuals or small groups at three different points. These people are dressed differently and hold various objects, such as sticks, newspapers, etc. To distinguish them from bystanders and passersby, the aforementioned participants adopt special postures, such as kneeling or sitting cross-legged.

The points are located 400—1500 steps away from the "start." Every half minute, the patrol leader sends out one scout. The scout runs to the nearest group, memorizes their appearance and posture, and, after receiving information from the judge stationed there about the direction (according to the compass or sun) in which the next group is located, continues running. After circling all 3 points, the scout returns to the "start." After completing the circuit, each scout submits a report to the patrol leader, answering the following questions:

1. How many were in the group?
2. How were they dressed, and how could they be distinguished from bystanders?
3. What was their position in relation to a nearby landmark in the area?
4. What was the distance from their own position?
For each accurate and complete description of a group, 5 marks are awarded (15 for 3 groups). For every 10 seconds exceeding the winning circuit time, 1 mark is deducted. For errors and omissions, 1 or only 1/2 marks are also deducted.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Catch the Thief
body:
The troop leader or instructor hangs a red scarf in a visible place in the camp or the troop room. Then, they walk around to all the scouts busy with their tasks and whisper into each one’s ear: “A thief is in the camp” (or “in the room”). To one of them, they say: “A thief is in the camp—you are the one,” and name a distant location about one kilometer away, such as Jordan Park, etc. The chosen thief must, within the next **3** hours, snatch the scarf, wrap it around their neck, and flee in the direction indicated above. None of the others know who the thief is, when they will steal, or where they will run. Everyone only knows one thing: the disappearance of the red scarf is the alarm signal, the moment the theft has occurred, and the scout with the red scarf around their neck is the target of a general chase. All activities cease, and everyone except the guards, patrol members, and crew sets off in pursuit as quickly as possible. Whoever tears the scarf from the thief—or even just a piece of it—wins. But if the thief reaches the finish line with the scarf, they win.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Following the Guide's Trail in the City
body:
Exercises similar to the Siberian scout in the forest. A scout sent ahead as a guide has pockets filled with grains, peas, nutshells, or paper: "confetti." Every few steps, they mark their trail on the ground. They may also use a piece of chalk to draw signs on walls, sidewalks, lampposts, and trees.

The patrol following must collect all the traces and erase all the signs. If the guide has to move to an area where the traces they have on hand would disappear, they leave a note beforehand, marked in the scouting manner, indicating the direction of further travel. The purpose of this game is not tag but a detailed description of the route taken following the guide's trail. The best description wins points.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Expedition to the Pole
body:
Each patrol taking part in this expedition, having equipped themselves with sledges, loads them with food, cooking utensils, sheepskin coats, shovels, and the like, and in turns, all scouts pull them forward in pairs. Ahead, **2** scouts proceed for some **2** kilometers before the supply train and mark the route, sometimes with the tracks of their boots, sometimes with various signs.

The rest pull behind them, read the signs, and upon arriving at the site, build huts from snow using shovels, with sticks serving as supports and brushwood to reinforce the walls and roof.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: The Round-Up in the City
body:
A scout known for cunning, agility, and guile is chosen as the fugitive (smuggler). The starting point for the fugitive should be a location 2 kilometers away from the camp (scout headquarters). If possible, the starting point should be one from which the greatest number of roads lead to the camp. The game is to last one hour, assuming this time is sufficient for the fugitive to return to the camp.

The fugitive sets off from the "start" precisely at the designated time, which is also known to the opponents. It is better if a judge is appointed to ensure the start is punctual.

The remaining scouts hide along all the roads, straining their eyes to recognize the fugitive, who approaches the scout headquarters in any disguise. The rule must be observed that no ambush may be set within a radius of 300 paces from the start or finish.

The fugitive, however, is not allowed to disguise themselves in women’s clothing, nor use a cab, tram, or cart. They are also forbidden from entering a shop to hide if enemies are already close by. Whoever recognizes the fugitive calmly approaches them, greets them with the agreed-upon password, and accompanies them to the scout headquarters. Any scuffling or fleeing is strictly prohibited.

After one hour, everyone returns to the camp, and the winner receives marks.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Cuckoos
body:
Cuckoos are birds surrounded by extraordinary sympathy among us. They deserve this widespread sympathy—and even our gratitude—not because they herald spring, but because they protect our forests from destruction. Hairy caterpillars, which devastate woodland trees, roam unpunished, devouring the needles of spruces and firs, for no bird eats these prickly, bristling larvae. Only the cuckoo has developed a taste for these caterpillars, and they have become its exclusive food. As a large bird, it must spend the entire day foraging in the forest to satisfy its hunger. Thus, it has no time to build its own nest or incubate its eggs. Instead, it lays its eggs in the nests of wagtails and other songbirds. From time to time, after the young have hatched, it visits its offspring and likely brings them a delicacy—a hairy caterpillar—to accustom them to the food Providence has destined for cuckoos.

The setting for this game consists of selected exits and intersections of 3—6 streets arranged to form a circle. At each exit or intersection, circles with a radius of 9 steps (nests) are drawn. A scout stands in the circle as the nest-keeper, or young cuckoo, while 2 fledglings, or wagtails, stand outside the circle’s perimeter. The number of nests should not exceed 6, so two or three patrols may participate in the game. If 3 patrols join, one patrol suffices for the cuckoos, and 2 for the wagtails. Cuckoos wear red badges, while wagtails wear blue ones.

The game of cuckoos involves the old cuckoo mother visiting her young cuckoos in their nests, while the quarrelsome wagtails defend the nests against her entry. To signal her success in reaching the nest and feeding her chick a treat, she must take the red badge. If she fails—that is, if the wagtails touch her before she jumps into the nest—the wagtails take the young cuckoo’s badge. (The mother cuckoo also wears a red badge.) Wagtails may only strike the cuckoo outside the circle’s perimeter, i.e., the nest; inside the nest, the cuckoo is safe. Wagtails may not hide in shops or hallways but must remain on the street. After each attack on a nest, successful or not, the wagtails and the young cuckoo report to the judge, while the old cuckoo attempts to reach the next nest. The side that collects the most red badges and delivers them to the judge wins.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Snow Fortress
body:
This game involves two patrols.

One patrol builds a snow fortress according to their own ideas, with possibilities including embrasures—whether round (a redoubt), four-sided (a bastion), or a zigzagging bastion. Once the fortress is completed, the patrol that built it becomes its garrison and prepares for defense, gathering a full supply of snowballs as ammunition.

The second patrol acts as the enemy, launching an attack on the fortress and aiming snowballs at its defenders. The defenders likewise attempt to hit the attackers with snowballs. Any scout struck by a snowball is considered "dead" and withdraws from the game. The number of attackers should generally be 2 times greater than the defenders. After a quarter of an hour, the attack ends, and victory is awarded to the side that, after counting the casualties on both sides, has a greater number of survivors than the opposing side.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Crooked Things
body:
A patrol exercise in the city. The entire patrol walks forward in single file, a few paces apart, one behind the other along one side of the street, then returns along the other side to the starting point. During this walk, each Scout pays close attention to all directions, and if anyone spots any irregularities, defects, crooked things, or incorrect arrangements, they immediately note everything down on a piece of paper. This could be a slanting shop sign, a poster stuck crookedly or crumpled, a broken window, overturned items in shop displays, and so on. Irregularities in moving vehicles are not taken into account at all, as they escape the final control of the judge. The one who spots the most crooked things collects marks. This game excellently trains the power of observation.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Skrzetuski of Zbaraż
body:
The objective of this game is to deliver an important letter, document, or message to a besieged city or fortress. Potocki of Kaniów wrote a letter on the shaved head of his hajduk. When the hair grew back, he sent this unusual letter, and the recipient, in order to read it, had to take up a razor and first shave the messenger’s head.

A Scout chosen as Skrzetuski attaches a sash or scarf to his arm, 60 cm long, and upon reaching the destination, must still have this insignia in the same place. The besieged fortress may be represented at will by a location, house, tree, or judge standing at a designated position. The distance the messenger must cover is approximately 4 km.

The enemy knows the direction (goal) and the exact time the messenger sets out and may prepare an ambush to capture him, but they are not allowed to see the departing messenger. They also may not cross the boundary line set for the besieged, located 300 yards (i.e., 270 meters) from the commander’s headquarters. These boundaries should be marked beforehand with visible trees, mounds, a road, or a river. As proof of capture, the enemy must unfasten and take the sash (insignia) from the messenger’s arm. The messenger is allowed to disguise himself, but not as a woman; he may hide in a wagon, etc. The game can take place in the field or in the city. However, even in disguise, he must still wear his insignia on his arm.

The game lasts at most 10 hours, which should be sufficient time for the messenger to deliver the dispatch and return with a reply.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Two Couriers with Dispatches
body:
A game in which 2 patrols, or 2 troops, compete for superiority. The patrols stand at a distance of 4 kilometers from each other. The troop instructor or referee is positioned at an equal distance (2 km) from the patrols, in a town at the junction of 2 streets, or on an outing in the middle of a forest. At the appointed time, couriers from opposite sides set off simultaneously and punctually.

The task of the remaining scouts in each patrol is to skillfully place obstacles in the way of the opposing courier so that he cannot deliver the letter. To this end, they lie in wait for him in an ambush along the route he is most likely to take to reach his destination. However, they must leave 200 meters from the start and 200 meters before the finish line free. A captured courier may be held, and his letter taken from him, but it is forbidden to struggle with him, let alone strike him. Simply touching the courier during pursuit by opponents already signifies that he has been caught.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Allied Forces Junction
body:
The troop is divided into platoons, or into 4 equal parts. The first platoon proceeds to a chosen location, at least 1 kilometer distant. The second platoon moves in the opposite direction, also a kilometer away. The rest of the troop remains in the same place as the united army.

Platoon 1 and 2 represent allied armies at war with the main army that separates them. The task of both allied armies is to join their forces without coming into contact with the enemy, which is 2 times stronger in numbers. To this end, they dispatch scout armies and messengers with dispatches to ascertain the enemy's position and to communicate with each other. If the allies succeed in joining their forces without encountering the common enemy, they are the victors.

The enemy army's (platoons 3 and 4) objective is to prevent the allies from joining by disrupting communication, capturing messengers and scouts, surrounding or ambushing, and taking one of the allies prisoner. If, after the allotted time, the obstacles set for the allies prove ineffective, the allied side also has a claim to victory.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Linking Up with the Cut-Off Detachment
body:
This is a variation of the above game and provides excellent practice in stealthy movement.

A detachment of scythemen has been cut off from its main army by enemy guards. After confirming this fact, it sends a courier with a dispatch to the main camp of its army. The scythemen’s courier encounters Kraków scouts along the way, who have just pitched their tents and set up camp between the main army and the cut-off detachment of scythemen.

The courier holds a brief consultation with the troop leader and patrol leaders, during which he describes the critical situation of the scythemen and asks for their swift assistance. Scout honour compels them to help, but to do so, they demand further details from the courier about the position of the cut-off detachment.

They learn that this cut-off detachment is only 2 kilometres away from their camp, and for better clarity, the courier sketches a rough outline (croquis) of the scythemen’s position and the enemy guard posts, which have wedged themselves between the scouts and the scythemen like a wedge.

The scouts’ task is to slip through, sneak past, or outflank the enemy guards to reach the cut-off detachment of scythemen without being noticed by the enemy during this manoeuvre.

The cut-off detachment of scythemen should be positioned on a distant, elevated hill, clearly visible. If there are not enough scouts, the judge may represent the cut-off detachment on the hill.

The enemy guard posts are to be stationed along the main road or highway connecting the scouts’ camp with the scythemen’s detachment on the hill, and red flags, visible from a distance, make it easy to orient oneself regarding their placement. If the enemy spots any of the sneaking scouts, they should record their name and signal with a whistle in an agreed manner for them to withdraw from the game. If the enemy can name the patrol to which the spotted scout belongs, that entire patrol should withdraw from the game.

This game requires a high degree of scouting discipline, so that every spotted scout, upon hearing the signal that they have been seen, considers it a point of honour to withdraw from the game immediately. Several judges, stationed along the route, are to ensure there are no abuses, and at the end of the game, they will assign penalty marks for disobedience on one side and false signals on the other. The patrol or scout who reaches the objective unseen in the shortest time, either by crawling or sneaking, wins.

---
