author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Capturing the Flags
body:
In this game, the troop is divided into two halves (the minimum number of players on each side is two patrols). The flags represent provisions, ammunition, etc. If 2 patrols from each side take part in the game, then the first patrol (A) forms the advance guard to defend 3 flags by day and 3 lanterns by night, while the second patrol (B) is tasked with scouting the opponents' positions and capturing the flags. The flags are placed 180 meters (lanterns 90 meters) behind the line of guard A, and 18 meters apart from each other (lanterns additionally 2 feet above the ground).

The defending guard A may position itself either together or, preferably, in a line parallel to the flags, with 2 scouts grouped together and 75 meters between each pair. Patrol B stands 50 meters behind the line of flags and sends scouts to reconnoiter the enemy’s position (C+D), who in the meantime have positioned themselves similarly. The lines of flags of both sides are at least 360 meters apart. Each side has 2 judges, one at the guard line (A, C) and the other at the patrol’s post (B, D). The judges from both sides give a trumpet signal when everything is ready to start the game; they maintain order during the game and distribute points after its completion. The setup of both sides for the game:

At the given trumpet signal, the scouts designated from patrol B (D) set out stealthily or crawling to scout the enemy patrol’s position and its guard, as the enemy line need not be parallel to their own but may be at any angle, and patrol B (D) need not stand directly behind the flags but may be positioned more or less to the side. Once they have scouted the position, the same scouts crawl around the enemy guards, trying not to be seen, and upon reaching the flags, they capture them. Each scout may take only one flag.

Any scout who approaches within 45 meters of the enemy leaves the game if spotted and notified by an agreed-upon signal, but continues playing if unseen.

A false alarm from one side may facilitate the capture of a flag from the other side. Defenders A (C) may not move from their guard position or approach the flags closer than 180 meters, but they may send a message to a neighboring guard or to patrol B (D), who may intercept an enemy creeping toward the flags, provided they have not sent all their members on reconnaissance or raiding.

After the allotted time expires, a gathering takes place at a designated spot for delivering reports to their judges. The judges record and distribute points: 5 points for a captured flag; 5 points for a detailed report on the enemy’s deployment or a sketch of their position; 2 points for each report on the movement of the enemy patrol (unit) B (D). The side with the higher total points wins.

A variation of this game may introduce the following difficulty: after scouting the enemy’s position, the scouts from patrol B return to their patrol, and other scouts, following their instructions and a detailed sketch (croquis), set out to raid or capture the flags.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: The Traitor's List
body:
The most suitable terrain for this game is a forest or fields overgrown with bushes, or possibly willow thickets; however, in their absence, hilly ground may also serve.

The troop is divided into **2** parts: for example, Italians and Turks. Each half camps on opposite sides of the forest. In the Italian camp, there is a traitor who has conspired with the Turk to place a list containing very important documents in a certain tree, which he will mark in an agreed manner. This tree should be located in the very center of the forest, equidistant from both camps.

The game begins as if camping, and the traitor leaves the camp (before the guards are posted), places the list, and returns. Meanwhile, his absence is noticed, betrayal is suspected, and upon his return, he is arrested on charges of treason. He refuses to reveal the hiding place of the list, yet is sentenced to exile and, as an outlaw, remains only a passive spectator for the rest of the game.

At a signal given by the judge’s bugle, the Italians begin searching for the list and strive to prevent the Turks from obtaining it. Upon hearing the bugle, the Turks also leave their camp, search for the tree with the agreed marks, and monitor the Italians’ movements. The traitor should be cautious when hiding the list so as not to break twigs or leave footprints, lest he make it easier for the Italians to find the list.

Each scout is armed with a tennis ball or a pinecone. If **2** enemies meet during the search for the list, they strike at each other with the balls (pinecones), and the one who is hit first must withdraw from the game under pain of dishonor. The main objectives of this game are searching for the list, ambushing, tracking, and stalking, while striking the opponent with a ball or pinecone is only a last resort for self-defense. After a predetermined time has elapsed, the judge gives the bugle signal for assembly and awards points. For hitting an opponent with a pinecone so that they withdraw from the game, **1** point is awarded. For finding the list, **4** points are awarded. The party with the most points wins.

This game can also be played in winter, though the traitor must be as cunning as a fox and, using various ruses, leave misleading tracks if possible—walking backward, kneeling, or repeating jumps with the aid of his scout staff. Snowballs serve as ammunition.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Cutting the Telegraph
body:
An invading army disrupts a foreign country’s means of communication, primarily telegraph wires, and it is the duty of national defense to safeguard their integrity.

For this game, select roads with telegraph poles in a location well-suited for stalking and crawling.

The attackers’ task is to cut **3** telegraph poles, accomplished symbolically by tying handkerchiefs around the poles, while the defenders prevent this by taking the attackers prisoner. Capturing a prisoner is done when two defenders touch—or lightly strike with a hand—an attacker. If the defenders are outnumbered, they must wait for reinforcements. The attack consists of one patrol, and the defense of two patrols. The game relies on continuous coordination among defenders, allowing them to rush to aid where the enemy advances. For each pole tied, the judge awards the attackers **2** marks, and for each prisoner captured, **1** mark. (Only defenders take prisoners.)

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Fox Hunt
body:
The chosen fox is given a head start of 20 minutes, during which time they must set off and hide. The rest of the patrol’s task is to locate their hiding place and catch them. The fox is considered caught when struck by the hand of any pursuer. The chase advances in a semicircle, with the scouts spread out. The hidden fox wins if they are not found within the allotted time or if they manage to return to the starting point untouched.

The hunt takes a different form in the case of fox hunting in the field. (It is well known that the fox is such a great pest that it is hunted all year round to exterminate it.) Two scouts set out as foxes into the field, and after 5 minutes, the rest of the patrol follows their trail as hunters. If the foxes evade capture for an hour, they return to camp victorious. Foxes must not cross human tracks, so if they encounter such, they must turn back in another direction. However, to mislead the pursuit and avoid leaving traces, they may resort to various ruses: one may carry the other on their back, one may step into the other’s footprints, both may walk along fences or walls, or, using a stick as a pole, they may leap sideways and advance in such bounds. This game works exceptionally well in snowy conditions. For the pursuing party to win, both foxes must be caught.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Scouting Patrols
body:
One patrol is sent out on reconnaissance to observe the movements of an approaching enemy. The enemy may be either another patrol or the rest of the troop.

Once the scouting patrol has advanced, the enemy remains alert, sending two scouts ahead for reconnaissance while moving forward in a close, urban formation rather than a field formation. If the enemy spots the scouts, they organize a capture and take them prisoner by striking them with the hand. However, if the enemy fails to capture them within a distance of 2 kilometers, or at least manages to take more than half of them prisoner, the scouts win, and the second patrol takes their place. By repeating this game several times, the monotony and boredom of a long excursion can be greatly relieved. The winning patrol receives 4 marks.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: The Ambush
body:
The main army advances along the highway, and to avoid danger or surprise, it sends scouts on reconnaissance along both flanks.

Two enemy patrols, following behind the army, attempt to halt its march and for this purpose try to set an ambush. One patrol circles the army so far that it moves ahead of the army’s front, then settles into hiding in a suitable place and waits until the army reaches its concealment before attacking. The second patrol waits for the signal from the first, given once it has circled the army and chosen the right place and time to strike. It then immediately attacks the army from the rear.

The army, which has allowed itself to be outflanked in this way, is taken captive and must pass under the yoke: 2 the victorious patrols, linking hands at shoulder height, form a lane, and the defeated, bowing their heads, must pass beneath 8 the gallows created by the interlocked arms of the victors.

If, however, the first patrol is spotted, a roundup is organized against it, and anyone struck by a hand is taken prisoner.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Seeking the Instructor
body:
The instructor hands sealed letters to the patrol leaders, strongly emphasizing the importance of their contents and forbidding, under loss of honor, their opening before the designated time (e.g., not until the second day in the morning at a certain hour). These letters contain a sketch of a certain part of the area and instructions according to which the patrol, together with its members, is to gather at a certain point or place where the search for the instructor’s nearby hiding spot will begin. Obviously, the boundaries of this place cannot be too narrow, or the game would end too quickly.

Each patrol should strictly follow the route marked out for it on the sketch (croquis), and although each patrol takes a different path, the length should be calculated, and the terrain difficulties taken into account, so that all patrols can arrive at the designated assembly point at precisely the same hour. A lack of punctuality among subordinates has caused the loss of many a decisive battle. (Maciejowice. Königgrätz).

The patrol that finds the instructor first wins and receives a prize or points. Each patrol searches independently and according to its own instructions. If, after half an hour from the moment all patrols have arrived, the instructor has not been found, he gives a whistle signal that the game is over.

The chosen assembly point should be a dense, undergrown forest over a large area, so that it is well-suited for hiding.

Similar orders in sealed letters teach youth to restrain their curiosity while simultaneously arousing greater engagement and interest.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: For the Treasure
body:
A game that trains the power of observation and requires considerable skill in tracking. One or 2 patrols take part in it. Of the many ways to conduct this game, I will mention only 3 methods, according to which other variations can be arranged.

I. The Ariadne’s thread consists of clues written in short sentences using an agreed cipher. The first note is placed on a designated gate, telegraph pole, a certain company’s poster, etc., and reads, for example: »Go north and pay attention to the posters under the railway bridge.« There, the second note is found: »Go south to telegraph pole No. 22.« There should not be too many of these clues, and the points should not be too easily accessible. This method can be used to compete for a prize among several patrols, which are then sent out every 15 minutes. The winner is the one who reaches the treasure in the shortest time. Alternatively, a different task can be assigned to each patrol, e.g., for patrol A, the route: abcdef, and for patrol B, the route: acbedf. In this case, the clue notes will need to have 2 halves: under A will be the task for the first patrol, and under B for the second patrol.

II. The Ariadne’s thread is represented by colored wool or flannel patches attached to gates, fences, etc., every 3 meters, leading in a certain direction. When they end, a specified number of steps and a designated direction should lead to the treasure, usually represented by some letter. To prevent this from being merely a hare-and-hounds game or cotton-gathering, several false trails should be deliberately created, diverging from the main direction for a dozen or so meters and leading astray. All patches must, of course, be collected.

III. Each participant receives a description of a different route to the hidden treasure. For example: »Go to the spreading oak in locality NN., or to the crossroads NN., then take 300 steps north, and when you align with the tower NN., go west for 50 steps. From there, follow the path to the shrine, from which 10 steps to the left lies the treasure (a letter).« At the designated points, there should be patches or notes that scouts must collect as proof they did not shorten their route. The first to reach the treasure should not reveal they have arrived but should pretend to be diligently continuing the search.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: The Torn Note
body:
Suppose there is an underground corridor in the area leading to a labyrinth of cellars and dungeons of an old castle, or a cemetery resembling catacombs or a cave monastery like the Lavra, or finally limestone caves with stalactites and stalagmites, such as those in Bielsko in the Tatras or in Krzywiec on the Dniester. From a note containing a description of the plan of this corridor, only half has been preserved. This half of the torn note should be a sufficient guide for a scout.

The game is played as follows: the path leading to some unknown hiding place is described on a note, then this note is torn in half. Handing one half of the note to any patrol, they are instructed to reach the hiding place and search it. Obviously, one must be careful not to let the name of the hiding place or the location where it is situated slip out during conversation.

Variation of the game. Both halves of the torn note are given to two patrols (naturally without the knowledge of one about the other, so they cannot complete the note) and both are ordered to reach the destination. The patrol that finds the hiding place first wins.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Worob's Testament
body:
It is an example of peasant cunning in an illiterate man who, using just a few very simple symbols, was able to map out a route so well that it indeed led to the spot where a treasure was buried.

The account of this testament from *The Prophet’s Eye* by Władysław Lubicz is summarized as follows: Worobie, a *hamał* (a lowly servant), is entrusted by Hanusz, upon the latter’s departure for Turkey, with a pouch containing a diamond for safekeeping. The *hamał* falls gravely ill and, sensing his impending death, buries the treasure in the ground. He then sketches hieroglyphs of his own invention on a wooden plank and, before his passing, hands this testament to an acquaintance to deliver to Hanusz upon his return from Turkey. The hieroglyphic signs appear in the following order: a gallows, a sickle, an axe, a sickle, a cross, the number nine, and a spade. Through these, he meant to say: "When you reach the gallows standing by the city walls, to the right you will find a stubble field; beyond the stubble field, you will come upon a forest; after passing through the forest, you will see another stubble field, and at its edge stands a cross. From there, 9 paces to the right lies your buried treasure."

To train sharp deduction, scouts should be tasked with finding a location based on a route marked by similarly clever hieroglyphs of their own design.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Photographic Reconnaissance
body:
Show the scouts a series of photographs or drawings of objects from the immediate vicinity or from a village they have passed through. They should immediately recognize these objects and describe the place where they saw them. Here is an example series of photographic objects: a wayside shrine, windows of unusual shape, a weathercock on a church, a distinctive gate, a house with a porch or balustrade, an orientation tree, a roadside statue, a reflection in water (identify the reflected object), etc. Award marks for the greatest number of recognized photographs.

A variation and complication of this exercise will be the order to sketch all those peculiarities they passed during the last excursion.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Urban Tracking Games
body:
The patrol leader designates one scout to flee and hide. The rest of the patrol gathers in the quietest part of the town—that is, where traffic and pedestrian movement are minimal. The chosen fugitive has **2** minutes to hide, slip away, and get ahead, during which the rest of the patrol does not follow him, except for two who walk unseen just behind him. After two minutes, one of the tracking pair returns to the patrol at a run to lead them to the spot where he stopped trailing, while the other continues forward and leaves behind traces in the form of confetti. Naturally, all must be well-trained in pursuit and reading signs, for the fleeing scout employs every possible means and ruse to mislead the chase.

At the start of the game, a time limit must be set by which, if the fugitive manages to evade capture, he wins.

A touch by the pursuers’ hand on the fugitive signifies that he has been caught.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: The Cigar as Traitor
body:
A habitual worshipper of tobacco, having escaped from prison, first and foremost secures tobacco and matches. The police pursuit proves fruitless. Only the smoking habit betrays him into the hands of justice.

On a dark night, scouts are informed that the fugitive has been spotted in the forest, calmly indulging in the pleasure of smoking. This news alarms the entire troop, which surrounds the forest and, straining their ears, peering with their eyes, and above all tracking by scent, attempts to approach him in utmost silence. The scout chosen to play the fugitive must ensure the cigarette does not go out and, additionally, lights a match every 3 minutes. If there is no willing volunteer to take on this role, any scout may assume it, with the modification that, as a non-smoker, he uses a whistle, blowing it every one or two minutes while simultaneously lighting a match. If the scouts are not attentive enough, they may pass the fugitive, who then slips away, and they will see his light behind their backs. An hour or two of such an exercise will teach scouts once and for all to gauge direction and distance by hearing, smell, and sight in the dark of night. No other game trains the senses of sight, smell, and hearing so perfectly as this one.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Ephialtes at Night
body:
All scouts, except for one patrol, formed the garrison in a certain town or village for defense.

On roads, passages, and in easily traversable places, guards were prudently stationed.

One of the garrison scouts, chosen by lot as the traitor, inspects the guard posts and tries to memorize the less guarded spots, then slips away unnoticed from the village to meet the enemy patrol. Naturally, the enemy’s position must be communicated to him by the judge at the moment he is selected as the traitor.

The traitor attempts to lead the enemy into the center of the town through the previously identified spots. He guides them either in pairs or in groups of three beyond the guard line, or orders them to follow him in Indian file. If a guard touches one of them, they all go into captivity.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Night Hearing Exercise
body:
This game involves two scouts and is best played on a moonless night, or during the part of the night after dusk before moonrise or after moonset. Stars are not an obstacle. One scout sits in place, while the other approaches stealthily and by crawling from a distance of 90 meters. To mislead vigilance, the approaching scout should throw small stones in the opposite direction from which they are advancing.

This exercise trains the ear exceptionally well to distinguish the rustle made by a thrown clod of earth or stone from the sound caused by crawling or footsteps.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Tracking by Scent at Night
body:
This exercise is carried out during a calm but dark night, and in a place that is as open as possible—not in a forest or thicket. Smoke can be quickly produced by burning paper or a single box of matches. Finally, with appropriate precautions, ordinary gunpowder (not smokeless) may also be used. One patrol is sent out as the enemy to set up camp in a convenient location within a designated area. This patrol behaves entirely freely, lighting a fire and preparing a meal. Meanwhile, the camp guards report disturbing signals and sounds. The patrol leader immediately orders the fire to be extinguished with water, earth, or sand—only the traitorous smoke cannot be helped. Absolute silence falls over the enemy patrol so that the rest of the scouting unit (our side) cannot rely on hearing while tracking the enemy, but only on scent.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Chase by the Trail of Light
body:
The game takes place at night and in the countryside, or alternatively outside the city. Two scouts are sent in a designated direction with shining torches. After **2** minutes, the entire patrol sets off in pursuit. The scouts with torches must uncover the light every minute to signal their location, but for the rest of the time, they cover their torches. The scouts with torches turn in different directions, which aids their escape, especially when the torches are uncovered at different times.

The pursuing scouts must stay together or communicate with each other using passwords and signals, for in the darkness, they might easily mistake a friend for an enemy.

For often, when one of the pursued is in danger, the other, having hidden their torch, blends in with the pursuit and facilitates their companion’s escape.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Judging the Distance of Lights (Will-o'-the-Wisp)
body:
This night-time game is an excellent exercise for the eyes in judging distances.

A selected Scout ventures across fields, carrying a lit but shaded lantern. At a given whistle signal (from the patrol leader or judge), the Scout uncovers the lantern light for 5 seconds. Then, the lantern is covered again, and the Scout remains still and completely quiet. The rest of the Scouts, who stayed with the patrol leader, first estimate the distance in paces and determine the direction using compass rose names. Once the patrol leader has noted their estimates in turn, the second part of the game begins: everyone rushes toward the light, which, like a will-o'-the-wisp, appeared only briefly and vanished, trying to reach the Scout standing quietly in the field with the covered lantern. The Scout hands the lantern to the first one to reach them. Upon seeing the lantern light, everyone returns to the judge, who marks points for those who correctly estimated the distance and for the one who received the lantern. The exercise is then repeated, and the Scout who received the lantern from the first "lantern-bearer" takes their turn moving away from the group and playing the role of the will-o'-the-wisp.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Night Watches
body:
Two or more scouts set out on the road, carrying lit lanterns, and take up a position no closer than one-quarter of a kilometer from the camp (or the starting point, respectively). These are called the watches and should not change their position, but may, according to preference or calculation, now cover and then uncover the light of their lantern.

After 10 minutes, a scout with a strongly shining lantern (e.g., an acetylene lamp with a reflector) sets out to find the watches. This scout is called the runner and should not cover the light of their lantern at any time during the game.

After 2 minutes, the remaining scouts set out to catch the runner and the watches.

The watches uncover their lanterns when they think the runner is near, generally to make it easier for them to find their positions; they cover the lantern lights from the pursuit, however, so as not to betray their position.

When the runner discovers a watch, the latter extinguishes their lantern and returns to camp, and when the runner has found all the watches, they too return, and the victory in this case belongs to the runner and the watches. Conversely, if the pursuit catches the runner and the watches, the pursuers win. If only the runner is caught, or a few watches, the points are divided.

No scout should be within a radius of 100 paces from the starting point (camp, scout house, etc.) during this game.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Dispute Over Morskie Oko
body:
Two patrols send one guide each to a chosen spot called the *Morskie Oko* (Sea Eye). Naturally, both take different routes. The rest of each patrol sets off after a quarter of an hour, following the tracks of their own guide. Once the two guides reach the *Morskie Oko*, they wait there for their patrols to arrive—or for the dispute to be settled. From that point on, they remain passive, assuming the role of judges.

The patrol that arrives first prepares snowballs and arranges their sticks at a distance of 6 steps around the patrol flag, which the patrol leader has planted at the disputed boundary. When the second patrol approaches, they attempt to seize the lying sticks, but the first patrol greets them with a hail of snowballs in defense of their sticks. The number of attackers steadily decreases, as anyone hit by a snowball must withdraw from the game. Both patrols throw snowballs at each other.

Each accurate throw and each captured stick counts as 1 point. If the attacking side gains more than half the points, they win the right to possess the *Morskie Oko*, while the defenders may only invoke the right of prescription once they have eliminated all their opponents to the last man.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Pioneers. In the Wilderness
body:
A scout troop sets out for an area as remote and pathless as possible, resembling in its wildness the primeval state of newly discovered parts of the world (secluded forests, wildernesses, marshes, or the Tatras and Carpathians make such an ideal terrain). Each scout carries his own food, tent, and bedding (blankets) either on his back or on his head, depending on the terrain he passes through, such as dense undergrowth or river fords. The march proceeds in Indian file. At the head of the line is the guide, who precedes the entire troop by 180 metres. The guide’s task is to find a suitable route for travel and mark it with signs that prevent wandering. On a river, the pioneer troop must build an appropriate bridge; on a lake, a raft; and on marshes, a path made of round logs or bundles of brushwood (fascines). The guide’s signs suffice by day, but for any subsequent troop to avoid losing its way at night, the pioneers must add such traces by which one can orient oneself even in the dark.

Similarly, a chosen wilderness is an excellent terrain where scouts can be taught to measure distance by means of time. For this purpose, several scouts are sent out, each in a different direction, with orders roughly as follows: »Walk 2 kilometres to the northwest. Write there a precise report of where you are, adding a sketch (croquis) if possible. Return with the report as quickly as you can.« The received report is compared with a map to verify its accuracy.

A remote and pathless area develops in a scout the ability to orient himself, teaches him to seek out and remember all the characteristic features of the area, and so on. To achieve this goal more surely, scouts are sent out in pairs (for competition) in different directions. Each pair, starting from a different »starting point,« must reach the same destination by a different route, finding that route with the help of a map and without being seen by the other. Such an exercise also trains them in concealment and tracking, etc.

In the wilderness, it is desirable for everyone to instinctively guess and assess the length of time. To teach scouts this, they are sent out in different directions, each with a piece of paper on which he must note after how many minutes he should return. The judge records precisely the time of each scout’s departure and arrival, having first bound them by their scout’s word of honour that none of them will glance at a watch.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Skirmish
body:
An emulation game between 2 patrols. Both patrols stand side by side in a single line. Patrol A on the left, Patrol B on the right. Opposite them, at an appropriate distance, an equal number of bottles or bricks are set up as there are scouts in both patrols. The bottles facing Patrol A represent the scouts from Patrol B, and the bottles facing Patrol B represent the scouts from Patrol A. Additionally, the bottles are numbered from 1—8, and the number of each bottle corresponds to a specific scout (according to patrol order). On a given signal (by the referee), everyone throws prepared stones, aiming at the bottles (bricks). Each shattered bottle (or overturned brick) signifies the elimination of the corresponding scout from the opposing side, who must immediately withdraw from the game. Throwing without a signal is not allowed, and the throwing distance and number of volleys are determined by agreement.

The patrol that first eliminates all opponents wins.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: The Bear Hunt
body:
First, 3 locations are designated as dens where the bear has its lairs. Then, one of the largest and strongest scouts is chosen to be the bear, and a small balloon made of thin rubber, tissue paper, or an inflated and sealed cushion from a shop paper bag is attached to its back. The remaining scouts (1—3 patrols), armed with clubs made of twisted or tied handkerchiefs or twisted straw, attempt to strike and burst the balloon on the bear’s back whenever the bear carelessly leaves its den. The bear has a similar club and strikes the hunters on their hats.

Anyone struck on the hat by a club is considered dead and leaves the game. The bear cannot be killed (i.e., struck on the hat with a club) until the balloon (or paper bag) has been hit.

Thus, the bear constantly tries to face the hunters rather than turning its back to them.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Single-Handed Against the Bear
body:
Our ancestors went after a bear with pitchforks and a poleaxe. They drove the pitchfork into the bear's chest when it reared up on its 2 legs right in front of them, growling and advancing, ready to grapple with the uninvited guest in its own way—crushing his ribs or shattering the opponent’s skull with a paw strike and scalping him.

They braced the other end of the embedded pitchfork against the ground, so the bear, thus propped, could not move forward. Then, gripping the axe firmly, they split the bear’s head open with it.

The scout chosen to play the bear wears a strip of paper pinned to his chest, 5 inches long, and holds a club in his hand. The hunter, also armed with a club, must use his left hand to tear the strip from the bear’s chest and strike the bear’s head with the club. He may not strike first with the club and then attempt to tear the paper.

The bear may not shield the paper with his hand; his right hand (holding the club) must be raised, and his left hand placed behind his back. The bear defends himself by aiming his club at the hunter’s head (the Native Americans likely learned scalping from bears), and a hunter hit on the head with the club is out of the game, considered killed. If struck 3 times on the arm or back (no other blows are allowed), he is out as severely wounded. The next scout in the patrol takes the place of the departing hunter. Simply tearing the paper without striking the bear’s head with the club does not end the game; the bear receives a new strip of paper and play continues. The game involves 2—8 scouts, with one bear for every 4 hunters (taking turns).

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Hunting the African Elephant
body:
The scout chosen by lot to be the elephant receives a sash loosely tied around the right leg (below the knee), so that it can be easily torn off with a tug. In the absence of a sash, a scrap of paper may substitute. Two or 3 scouts (hunters) attempt to corner or outmaneuver the elephant so that one of them can seize the right moment and movement to tear off the sash (Africans, having ambushed elephants from behind, cut the tendons in their legs, and the immobilized cripple is then easily finished off).

The elephant faces the (2—3) hunters only frontally and does not allow itself to be surprised from behind. Meanwhile, it defends itself with a stick, and whoever it strikes steps out of the game, their place taken by the next number in the patrol. The game ends with the tearing of the sash as a victory for the hunters, or the elimination of the entire patrol as a victory for the elephant.

Variation: Instead of a sash, a paper balloon is attached to the back of the elephant’s leg above the heel.

The hunters, armed with sticks, must burst the balloon by striking it with their stick.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Hunting the Indian Elephant
body:
A game similar to "Interrupted King," providing activity for several patrols or an entire troop. All participants join hands and form a circle. In the center of the circle stands a chosen or drawn-by-lot elephant (inhabitants of India lure wild elephants using tame ones into a trap surrounded by a high palisade). The elephant's task in this game is to break through the living wall by a running charge outward. After one attempt, successful or not, another player takes their place.

Scouts standing on the circle's perimeter are not allowed to lower their hands diagonally downward, much less extend them forward; rather, their arms must remain raised at a horizontal side level at all times, so the elephant does not tear their hands with its belly but only with its chest or shoulders.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: The Tiger Hunt
body:
The entire troop participates. The tiger wears a badge (a ribbon or paper band, black and yellow in color, matching its stripes) on its hat, while the rest—the hunters and elephants—have no badges.

Hunters and elephants line up in pairs (2-row). At the signal to start the game, given by the referee, the first (elephants) carry the second (hunters) on their backs, and after circling once, they encircle the tiger. Between 2 adjacent elephants, a free space must be measured (arms stretched out horizontally should touch fingertips).

The tiger wins if it manages to escape beyond the circle of besiegers. The hunters, armed with sticks, defend their position and prevent the tiger from breaking through. The tiger must use all its cunning, agility, and speed to avoid being struck by a stick and escape the circle. If struck once, it must attempt to break through elsewhere, and after being struck 3 times, it is considered dead, and the hunters claim victory. Killing or escaping the tiger ends one round of the game. In the next round, roles are reversed: the second group carries the first on their backs, and a new tiger attempts to escape.

A variation of this game involves arming the tiger with a stick as well. In this case, every strike from the tiger is lethal, and whether an elephant or a hunter is hit by the tiger’s stick, both are removed from the game along with their partner. The tiger wins if it escapes the circle or eliminates half of the opponents.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Bullfight
body:
This game is as engaging as the previous one and equally exercises mental sharpness and quick orientation. After selecting 12 partners, roles are assigned: one as the bull, one as the matador or espada, four as picadors, and six as capeadors. The playing area, or arena, is enclosed by a scouting hedge: a scrum (scouts standing in a row with arms linked under each other’s shoulders) if the game takes place during a rally of several troops; if on an outing of 2 patrols, marking the arena with small flags suffices. The course of the game, which is divided into 2 periods, is as follows. The bull’s entry onto the arena, where the picadors and capeadors already await, marks the beginning of the game. In the first part, the bull’s only distinguishing feature is 4—5 paper strips, 6 inches long, attached to its back. The picadors attempt to tear off these strips, while the bull defends itself by striking approaching players with its hand or a stick. Picadors are not allowed to tear off more than one strip at a time and must display all their agility and skill, as any picador struck by the bull is considered dead and must withdraw from the game. The capeadors assist the picadors by throwing themselves between the bull and the picadors during the chase, waving their red sashes (or handkerchiefs) in the bull’s face to force it to pursue them, thereby interrupting the chase after the picador. When all picadors are eliminated or all strips are torn off, the 2-th period, or the 2-nd half of the game, begins.

On the cleared arena, only two players now appear: the bull and the matador. The bull has its eyes blindfolded, and a sash loosely tied around its neck so that it can be easily torn off with a single tug. This is the matador’s task, who must be very agile and cautious to avoid being struck by the bull, as the bull then wins. If the matador succeeds in tearing off the sash, it signifies that the bull is slain, and the matador is the victor.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Dłoniówka (a variant of fistball)
body:
A game that develops agility and precision of movement. Players divide into 2 teams (preferably 4—5 each). A string or colored ribbon is hung in the middle between them at face height, and a small inflatable ball, smaller than a tennis ball, is used for throwing. Partners try to toss the ball over the ribbon so that it rolls along the ground or floor on the other side. The ball is struck only with the palm and thrown over the string. The hand must not be raised above the string (ribbon). Mistakes are counted as points for the opposing team.

Football and basketball played recreationally, rather than competitively as all football clubs today tend to showcase, are highly desirable camp or team activities for exercising muscle elasticity, agility, and precision of movement.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Inflated Ball Game
body:
Players divided into 2 teams (5 from each side) take their places along the two longer edges of a table at least 6 feet long.

A ping-pong ball, or else a light celluloid inflated ball, is placed in the center of the table, and each team tries to blow the ball onto the opposing team’s narrower edge of the table.

If the ball is blown off the sides, it counts as an "out" and play resumes anew from the center. This game develops lung elasticity and respiratory muscle strength, and the best player is the one who can drive the ball to the opposite edge without grimacing, despite the opponents’ blowing.

The game becomes livelier and more engaging when each team draws a goal on the table and positions its five players so that one acts as goalkeeper, 2 in attack, and 2 in defense.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: First Aid Exercises. Health Service
body:
These exercises should first be practiced within the patrol, then by larger units in camp. The method of practice is as follows: half of the patrol, or unit, takes the role of patients, while the other half acts as the rescue team providing first aid (health service). The instructor checks whether the rescue is appropriate and well-executed. Marks are awarded for faithful portrayal of the patient's role, as well as for quick and correctly performed rescue.

1. Supporting the sick while leading them. 2. Carrying the sick or unconscious individually. 3. Dragging the unconscious. 4. Carrying the wounded in pairs, without equipment. 5. Carrying the wounded on stretchers, in pairs, threes, or fours. 6. Even step and mountain step. 7. Improvised stretchers. 8. Carrying on a chair. 9. Methods of rescuing those frozen, drowned, suffocated by smoke, poisoned by gas, and hanged. 10. Four methods of artificial respiration. 11. Dressing wounds and stopping bleeding. 12. Dressings for fractures. 13. Methods of rescuing after snakebite (or rabid dog bite). 14. How to treat burns and scalds. 15. Reviving the fainted and rescuing the unconscious.

16. Types of unconsciousness. 17. Methods of rescuing the poisoned.

It is beneficial to combine rescue exercises with first aid.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: The Manor Farmyard
body:
A game as engaging as it is instructive, training scouts in imitating the voices of various domestic animals, making the evening by the campfire all the more enjoyable.

The leader or instructor first divides the participants into groups representing different domestic animals. If someone can list a sufficient number of animals, or if the game is played only within a patrol, each scout may represent a different animal.

Next, the instructor or leader begins to recount an anecdote from a visit to a friend in the countryside, and whenever a particular animal is mentioned, the scout assigned that nickname must respond with a cry imitating that animal’s voice. The composition and content of the story depend on the leader’s wit and imagination.

Here is an example of a plot, to which various variations can be added: »A small, mischievous boy, not a scout, after a severe illness, went to stay with his uncle in the countryside to regain his strength. The train took him to the destination. On the first day after the journey, the boy, tired, is quiet and well-behaved, and his uncle and aunt form a positive impression of him.

But on the second day, the boy gets up earlier than his uncle and aunt and, going out into the farmyard, peeks into the henhouses and stables one by one, and his appearance everywhere causes some misfortune. In his opinion, the flower garden is a playground for pigs, so he drives them there. Then he herds the hens and ducks into the garden. Little chicks, he believes, should learn to swim so they can accompany goslings and ducklings, so he drives them into the pond, where they all drown. He lets the horses out of the stable, chases the cows onto the highway, releases the sheep into the orchard, frees the carrier pigeons from their cage, and scatters the turkeys and geese in all directions— in short, he turns the entire farmyard upside down.« At the mention of the farmyard, all the animals respond, each with the voice of its namesake. For falsely imitating an animal or responding at the wrong time, forfeits are given, or as a penalty, one must imitate the cry of a goose or a donkey several times.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Scout Chess
body:
First, one must draw the outline or plan of the area (town) on a very large scale. It can be drawn even with chalk on the floor or table of the scout room, or even on a wall, and then fixed with fixative. On such a map, all paths and roads should be marked, and if it is a map of a rural area, additionally all field paths and gaps in fences. Scouts are represented either by chess pieces or small flags.

Having prepared these materials, various scout games can be played on this map just as well as in the field. An ordinary move is counted as 1 inches in length.

For example, consider the game *Catching in the City* or *Skrzetuski from Zbarazh*. The task of one party will be to move a piece (along paths and roads) from one edge of the map to the other without being caught by the enemy. The enemy is an entire patrol, whose pieces can only be moved half a step forward each turn, or the pursuer can be advanced each move.

To capture the fugitive, 2 scouts from the enemy patrol must cut off the fugitive’s path so that they drive them into a corner or surround them with a greater number of pieces. Obviously, both the fugitive and the capturing enemies are only allowed to move along the marked paths and roads, not cross-country.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: The Painters
body:
Scouts sit around a table with sketchbooks and pencils in hand. The most dexterous or cleverest draws a head or object with thick, unconnected strokes, arranging the lines in such an unusual sequence that for a long time it is impossible to recognize what the drawing is meant to represent. Each of those seated peers over the shoulder of their partner to the right and copies the drawing one line at a time. When the first person finishes the drawing, everyone compares their drawings with the original. Illustrations from the book *Mit Blitzlicht u. Büchse* by T. Seton are exceptionally well-suited for this game.

A more difficult variation of this game is when each person at the table draws the head of their companion.

Another variation of this game exercises wit and sharpness when each person draws a caricature of their companion.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Secretary
body:
Social games exercise memory, wit, and mental agility, and are perfectly suited to dispelling boredom and inappropriate conversations on rainy days, whether in the scout house or at a social gathering. In camp, they make the post-lunch leisure hour more enjoyable and help forget fatigue in the evening.

In *Secretary*, the patrol leader or instructor, acting as the game’s director, distributes sheets of clean white paper to the participants and instructs everyone to write one question on their sheet. The sheets are then folded in quarters and handed back to the instructor. The instructor thoroughly mixes them in a stiff hat, cap, or suitable container and passes them around the table for participants to draw. If someone draws their own sheet, they may exchange it. After all questions have been distributed, the writing of answers begins. Each person writes the most appropriate answer possible on the same sheet and returns it to the instructor. The instructor then shuffles the sheets again and reads the questions and answers aloud. After reading, the sheets are torn into pieces and discarded. For example:
**Question:** Why is Scout X lost in thought?
**Answer:** Because he is worried about the fate of the Turks.
This game has the advantage of being played without forfeits.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: The Ring
body:
This is a game, like the following ones, played for forfeits. The instructor places a ring or a small hoop on a sturdy string and ties its ends with a simple knot. The players either stand or sit in a circle, holding the string with their hands, passing the ring from one to another, or, by continuously moving their hands, pretend to pass the ring. A Scout standing in the center searches for the ring, and when they find it with someone, that person replaces them in the center and gives a forfeit. If the ring is caught between two players in the middle, the one who did not want to accept the ring goes to the center of the circle.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: The Advocate
body:
In the middle of a group seated in a circle stands the instructor, posing questions to any individual.

However, none of those questioned should answer under penalty of forfeiting a token, for to their left sits an advocate who speaks on their behalf. For example, the instructor asks A: *"Do you enjoy reading?"* B, acting as the advocate, replies: *"Indeed, a book is my bedtime cordial."* To a question directed at B: *"Are you not yawning?"* C answers: *"Oh no, for in such fine company I am not bored in the least."* If the question to C is: *"But you are B’s defender,"* and B answers *"yes,"* then B must forfeit a token. The game’s variety depends on wit, that inexhaustible wellspring of ideas.

---

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: The Neighbor
body:
The instructor or patrol leader, acting as the game director, turns to their neighbor and says: »I like my neighbor,« then adds 1) why, 2) what they feed them, 3) to which city they send them, and 4) what they give them for the journey. These four terms, however, must all begin with the same letter, starting with the letter *a*, and each subsequent player must choose the next letter of the alphabet—so the second begins with *b*, the third with *c*, the fourth with *d*, and so on. For example, the first says: »I like my neighbor because they are not apathetic, I feed them pineapples, I send them to Antwerp, and I give them a watermelon for the journey.« The second says: »I like my neighbor because they do not meddle in others' affairs, I feed them bigos, I send them to Brest, and I give them a peach for the journey.« Anyone who cannot immediately find a suitable word for the above questions or makes a mistake in the order of answers must pay a forfeit as a penalty.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Counting to Ten
body:
A game combined with a memory exercise, similar to "Neighbor." The patrol leader or troop leader arranges 10 sentences or sequences loose words so that the first row contains 3 words, each beginning with *j* (one), the second row contains 4 words, each beginning with *d* (two), the next row 5 words, each beginning with *t* (three), and so on up to 9. The game proceeds as follows: the patrol leader first recites the first row, after which everyone repeats it in turn; then the second row, and once everyone has repeated it in order, the 3-th row is given, and so on. Whoever fails to repeat a row in the correct order forfeits a token or steps out of the circle of players:

1. j. tomorrow, hag, groan. 2. d. courtier, rain, mockery, claw. 3. t. grass, rhythm, rod, wolfsbane, trumpet. 4. cz. to comb; to lurk, honor, human, ambush, crest. 5. p. carrion, to water, beauty, to knock, to spin, to bake, ravine. 6. sz. happiness, rat, wardrobe, awl, wide, rag, swindler, glass. 7. s. sickle, string, ergot, oat-grass, rock, sadness, quarrels, knot, leap. 8. o. fruit, insect, bran, perch, eye, weapon, fire, hound, garden, wasp. 9. dz. mullein, woodpecker, hollow, child, javelin, bell, jug, wilderness, wonder, spear, cannon.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Rough Sea
body:
In the middle of the room, or the troop's quarters, chairs are arranged back-to-back. There must be one fewer chair than the number of participants. One person takes the name of the sea and stands, while the rest sit and take the names of various fish.

The sea walks or runs around those seated, imitates waves, and calls out the names of fish. The named fish immediately stand and follow the sea, mimicking all its movements—such as raising arms to the side and lowering them, either simultaneously or alternately, with or without side bends, and so on. When the sea calls out, »all fish,« everyone stands and follows it. When the sea gives the command, »change of wind,« everyone, including the sea, makes an about-turn and changes the direction of the march. Finally, when the sea sits and says, »calm sea,« everyone sits down as quickly as possible. Whoever has no seat gives a forfeit and takes the role of the sea. The sea may sit whenever it wishes, even after calling out just one fish; then it takes the name of that fish, and the called fish becomes the sea.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: The Deaf-and-Dumb
body:
The patrol leader or game master divides the players into 2 halves, for example by rearranging a double line into two single lines, calling the first line the deaf and the second the dumb. Both lines sit on either side of a long table, the dumb on the right, the deaf on the left, or vice versa. The patrol leader sits at one end.

If benches and a table are lacking, the game is played standing.

The leader (patrol leader) poses a question to the right and to the left, to which the dumb respond with mime and gestures, while the deaf give the most absurd answers. For example:

1. Question: "Did you get up early?" 2. "How long have you been in town?" 3. "What is your name?" 4. Answer: "Pure wool has gone up in price." 5. "I broke my mirror in the holster." 6. "I’m not hungry, just short."

The more accurate the mimed response and the more absurd the answers of the deaf, the merrier and livelier the game becomes. To prevent players from having too much time to think or prepare their answers, the patrol leader switches the roles of both sides—that is, the deaf lose their hearing and regain their speech, while the dumb regain their hearing and lose their speech. The dumb forfeit a token for every word spoken, and the deaf for every sign of hearing.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Yes and No
body:
The patrol leader asks one of the scouts to leave the room, then chooses a word for the remaining scouts to guess—a word representing an object, place, or the name of someone present or a famous person, etc. The scout who left then returns and, to guess the word, asks questions in turn to everyone present, to which only "yes" or "no" may be answered.

For example, the word chosen to guess is: »Mickiewicz«. The following questions help in guessing:

1. Is it the name of an object? No.

2. A surname? Yes.

3. Is it someone present? No.

4. Are they living? No.

5. Are they a leader? No.

6. A painter? No.

7. A scholar? Yes and no.

8. A poet? Yes.

9. One of ours? Yes.

10. One of the three bards? Yes.

11. A Lithuanian? Yes.

12. Mickiewicz? Yes.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: The Craft (Shoemaker)
body:
The troop leader or patrol leader assigns the scouts participating in the game names of various objects related to the shoemaker's craft, such as: knife, waxed thread, leather, awl, paste, etc.

Next, the patrol leader directing the game sits in the center of a circle formed by the players and starts the game by addressing one of the players, who is called the merchant, and asks: »What do you want, neighbor?« The merchant must respond with a sentence in which the last word must necessarily be one of the previously assigned names. The player called in this way stands up and delivers another sentence, which again ends with the name of their comrade, and so on, until someone says the word »workbench.« Then, everyone rushes out of the room, and the master must manage to say a sentence with any name before the runners cross the room's threshold. The mentioned player immediately returns to their place and without hesitation names one of their comrades, that one returns and names another, and so on, so that no one crosses the threshold. Everyone sits down again, and the game continues. If, however, one of the players managed to run out of the room, the game is interrupted, the remaining players and the master give forfeits, and the one who ran out becomes the game leader.

Variation of the game: After the word *workbench*, everyone except the master runs out, but not immediately—they first run around the room (or table). When the master names one of the players, the others no longer have the right to cross the threshold, even if they are already at it, but must return and go around the room (or table) once more. Meanwhile, the called player must say another sentence ending with a comrade's name, everyone circles the room again, and so on, until everyone returns to their places. The player who managed to run out of the room shouts: »I'm home!« and the game ends with the rest giving forfeits. Here is an example of the game's course:

Master: What do you want, neighbor?

Merchant: I came to ask if my shoes are ready.

Shoes: Ask Mr. Waxed Thread.

Waxed Thread: The master will answer for me.

Master: I would have made your shoes long ago, but I lack materials.

Materials: You can buy them at the shop.

Shop: You just need to have money.

Money: But the money is in the master's pocket.

Master: I'm short on funds right now, unless the neighbor lends me some.

Merchant: I won't lend you any, as I'm dissatisfied with your work; in the last pair of shoes, I completely wore out the soles and heels.

Soles and Heels (together): Ha! Poor quality goods.

Materials: No, it's the waxed thread that doesn't hold.

Waxed Thread: It's the fault of the blunt awl.

Awl: The master bought a blunt awl.

Master: It got blunt when it fell on the workbench.

Everyone: Let's run (they run).

Master: If only they left the money.

Money (returning): To buy materials.

Materials (returning): What's the use of materials without waxed thread.

Waxed Thread (returning): What's the use of waxed thread without...

Shoes (ran out the door): I'm home.

This game can similarly be adapted to all other crafts and professions, so the shoemaker can be replaced by: gardener, locksmith, carpenter, (or even an official or writer), etc.

Of course, the game participants then bear names related to the chosen craft, and the conversation also undergoes appropriate changes. For a good adaptation of this game to other professions or crafts, [merit] marks.

author: Herman A. Mojmir
title: Redeeming Forfeits
body:
The conclusion of any forfeit game is essentially the end of the first half, while the second, often more engaging part, is the so-called redeeming of the pledged forfeits. The game leader draws any forfeit from the repository (a hat), and its owner, wishing to reclaim it, must perform a task chosen by the leader. The following forfeit tasks are particularly engaging:

1. Be paper: the player who receives this task walks around the other players and asks, 'What would you write if I were paper?' and each one states: a proverb, a sentence, a calculation, etc., which they wish to have written.

2. Be a statue: the redeeming player stands in the center in a pose given by anyone. Only modest poses of classical statues are allowed.

3. Be an oracle: the redeeming player has their head covered with a scarf, and all players, one after another or just one, touch his head with a finger and ask to have their future foretold. Pythian ambiguity is desirable.

4. Be a fortune-teller: predict and describe the future fate of the players from the lines of their hands.

5. Be a mirror: reflect the faces and movements of the players who approach him.

6. Be a singer: sing a patriotic song.

7. Be a notary: make one’s own will from one’s intellectual and ethical achievements.

8. Be a parrot: repeat words and the tone in which they were spoken.

9. Be a penitent: a Pole (a nobleman, a peasant, a boor), a German, a Muscovite, a Frenchman, etc.

Confess aloud one’s faults and errors: characteristic traits of national flaws.

10. Be a priest: tell each one a different moral (with variation as 9).

11. Be a squire knighted as a knight: each one taps him on the shoulder.

12. Be a courtier: pay each one a (different) compliment.

13. Be an egoist: kiss oneself in a mirror or kiss one’s own shadow.

14. Be a magician: perform some trick.

15. Be an orator: congratulate a name-day of one of the comrades, or: propose a toast 'Let us love one another' as an aristocratic or national-democratic credo, or: deliver a candidate’s speech to the voters as a socialist or folk credo.

16. Be a historian: list Polish kings with or without dates, or list Polish kings and famous Poles during their reigns.

17. Be a geographer: list 5 seas, 10 rivers, 10 lakes, or list 5 forests, 10 mountain peaks, 10 passes.

18. Be a zoologist: list 10 mammals, 10 birds, 10 insects, and 10 fish.

19. Be a botanist: list 10 trees, 10 flowers, 10 grasses, and 10 mushrooms.

20. Be a hunter: list 12 types of game.

21. Be a reporter: communicate some news to those present.

22. Be a pearl of humor: tell a joke.

23. Be an acrobat: sit down and stand up without using hands from the ground, or similar.

24. Be a biographer: briefly recount one’s own life story.

25. Be a critic: tell each one your opinion of their attire, or tell each one what habit they have.

26. Be a diamond: ask each one what they would do with you if you were a diamond.

27. Be a ship and ask each one what they would load you with.

28. Be a flower and ask each one what they would do with you.

29. Be a basket and ask each one what they would put into you.

30. Bow to each one differently.

31. Blow out a candle that someone swiftly passes by the redeeming player.

32. Say 3 truths and 3 falsehoods, or say 3 things relevant and 3 things irrelevant.

33. 4 corners: in 1, meow; in 2, sneeze; in 3, bark; in 4, groan; or: in 1, laugh; in 2, cry; in 3, sing; in 4, dance.

34. Like and dislike: tell each one what they like most and what they dislike.

35. Be an opinion: gather opinions about oneself from everyone in turn and read them aloud.

36. Tell one of the comrades an impertinence and a politeness, or a lie resembling the truth.

37. Serve the players ice cream or sweets.

38. Be an art connoisseur: list 10 names of painters, 10 names of sculptors, and their most famous works.

39. Be a chemist: list 10 inorganic compounds, 10 organic compounds, 20 elements with symbols, metals, carbohydrates, etc.

Similarly, literature, physics, archaeology, and other subjects can be incorporated into the game.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Searching for a Natural Object in the Field, within a Defined Area
body:
The object of the search may be a certain species: trees, shrubs, flowers, insects (on the ground or in water), fungi. These could also be anthills, tree hives, or nests. We proceed in stages: from larger to smaller objects, from easily visible to barely visible ones, from common to rare specimens.

After determining the size of the area and discussing the rules, the game begins on a signal. Participants disperse in any direction. A participant who spots the sought-after natural specimen should control their joyful impulses. Their behavior must not reveal the location of the searched object. (This is a difficult task for young people, requiring self-control. It must be emphasized during the discussion that controlling one’s impulses is essential.)

After spotting the sought specimen, the participant should calmly walk away from it, and after a moment, sit in a designated place (sitting in order of arrival) or approach the instructor standing aside, reporting to them where the object is located. The first to find the object is the winner. In the case of several patrols searching for a natural object, the patrol whose members secured the most first places wins.

For skilled participants, the number of sought species should be increased, selecting diverse types (trees, flowers, insects, mosses, etc.), while simultaneously limiting the search time.

The instructor may guide the searchers, especially in cases of difficulty finding the desired specimen, using agreed-upon signals: auditory or visual.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Finding Terrain Objects, Such As
body:
Finding terrain objects, such as bridges, culverts, signposts, roadside shrines, wayside crosses, boundary stones, certain buildings, forest boundaries and clearings, road intersections, and the like. This game must take place over larger areas. A more detailed description of the given object may be provided, or only a slight hint for recognizing it among other similar ones. It is also possible to require an exact report on the condition of the given object.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Searching for Missing Persons
body:
The leader hides one or more persons within a certain area, preferably in a forested underbrush. A story about the missing persons in the wilderness should be created. Rescue expeditions will be carried out by troops or individuals.

Note regarding games: 1, 2, and 3.

This can be an individual or group search. The group that gathers first at a given object or person (called together by the group members with agreed-upon shouts) wins. The group that arrives at the location in full strength is considered the first.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Tracking Trails
body:
In any area where the leader has identified the presence of natural tracks—such as those of a hare, wild boar, roe deer, adder, crow, or other creatures—participants proceed to search for them. The instructor roughly defines the area or trail lines for the trainees. Teams report the location or path of the tracks either orally or in writing, precisely specifying their position. It is also possible to request a sketch of the trail’s course or drawings of the tracks.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Urban Object Scouting
body:
The instructor provides a description or presents a drawing of the facade of: a) a municipal, state, or social institution, b) an old, interesting house, c) a tenement building, etc.

The area where the given object (or series of objects) is located is defined by streets. Patrols set out into the city simultaneously, organizing independent searches by dividing into small groups. The patrol that arrives in full at the designated point (thus, it must organize a communication system among its dispersed small groups) and provides precise details about the object wins: "Where it is located. House number and owner details. Shops in the building, etc." If the object holds historical or socio-political value, require: a description, its history, or knowledge of the matters and issues associated with it.

A. A variation involves locating a specific house and gathering information about it based on a natural feature present on it or a special mark placed by the instructor (e.g., a coat hung on a particular balcony or a white flag in a certain window). A secondary task may be to sketch the house’s facade.

B. Another variation involves searching for a shop based on a description of one of its details. This exercise can include an observational-memory game (shop *kima*). In this case, one of the instructors must be near the shop to supervise the time spent observing the display and prevent note-taking during observation. After leaving, the patrol reconstructs, without time constraints, the items displayed in the shop window and their arrangement. Simultaneously, they provide a report on the shop, emphasizing matters related to domestic industry and trade.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: On the March
body:
The instructor announces that the following should be observed: a) points and objects along the road, b) everything that happens on the road or beside it. From time to time, they ask questions such as: How many women passed by? How were they dressed? What were they carrying on the cart? How many cows were grazing? What make was the car? What was its number? How many carriages did the train have? What was the crossing keeper doing at the crossing? How many trees were there by the water? What species were they? What sign regulating traffic (on the road or track) did we pass?

This is an easier observation exercise, consisting of directing the youth's attention. The above questions should be asked immediately after the given phenomenon has passed. Before answering, do not allow looking back (honesty in the game). After answering, allow comparing observations with reality. Determine who observed best. A more challenging version of the game will be surprising the youth with a question without previously drawing attention to the object of observation.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: On the Path Traveled
body:
The instructor announces: "Observe everything (in the first exercises—on short segments of the path itself, later—on longer stretches and the adjacent terrain). We will see who remembers the most facts." They themselves strive to memorize details, such as: a more precise description of a horse’s coat, the species of a tree, shrub, or flower, damage to the road, the type of small bridge, how many cows were passing. After covering the designated segment, everyone sits down and recounts what they saw. The best observers should be recognized, while also pointing out that even they missed many things. This remark will encourage broader and deeper observation in the future. Competitions can be held in groups. We make this exercise more challenging by requiring increasingly detailed observations. It is possible to introduce recording the noticed phenomena.

In the case of a patrol game—patrols submit a brief yet precise written report, prepared collectively.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: From the Hill
body:
We stop the class on a hill that offers a wide and varied view. The teacher asks: Where is our village visible? Where is the church tower? What church is that? Where is the town hall? Where are your own homes? Where does the road lead? Who sees sheep, cows, a woman digging potatoes, and so on.

Older youth should also determine: a) the position of a given object in relation to the cardinal directions, b) the distance of a given object from the observation point.

It is also possible to request a drawing—a sketch made using agreed-upon symbols.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Unannounced Observation
body:
After leaving the city, the instructor orders the participants to describe on sheets of paper, for example: a section of the path traveled, a street, an orchard observed during the march, a bridge, etc.

Evaluation takes place openly with the children's participation. A point is awarded for each correctly noticed detail. The highest number of points determines the winner. The game leader should discreetly note the details of the given object.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Nature Kim's Game
body:
A. The instructor lays out on a cloak a series of species of leaves, flowers, fungi, or places in a box captured insects, lizards, frogs, etc. The children form a circle and observe the specimens for a set period, striving to memorize as many specimens and their details as possible. On the leader’s signal, the youth scatter in all directions up to 40 metres, sit down, and independently attempt to note in their notebooks the maximum number of observed species, naming them correctly. After some time—on a new signal—the youth regroup. The instructor collects the sheets and, together with the youth, evaluates the results. For each missing, unrecorded, or incorrectly named specimen, a negative point is given. The minimum number of negative points indicates the winner. It is advisable to establish several winners. Avoid naming the poorest performers if possible.

The game can be made more challenging by: a) reducing the observation time, b) reducing the recording time, c) increasing the number of specimens, d) diversifying their species, e) adapting them to the background on which they lie, f) reducing their size.

Emphasis should be placed on independence in the game and recording. If "cheating" is noticed, the individual in question should be excluded from the game.

B. A more advanced form of this game will involve bringing the observed species from the terrain (plants or insects must be found in the immediate vicinity). The end time for searching should be announced with a whistle or trumpet.

C. The Nature Kim's Game can be varied by crawling, requiring silent approach to the laid-out specimens, similar to a hunter stalking game. Here, groups (troops or patrols) can compete in turn, collaboratively preparing a report on the observed specimens.

D. A further challenge will be sentries, whom we position in easier-to-approach terrain at the corners of a square 20 by 20 or 10 by 10 paces. In the centre of this square, we place a series of natural specimens or other objects. The sentries have their eyes blindfolded and attempt to detect the direction of the stalkers by sound. The instructor observes those approaching and excludes from the game anyone who stalks poorly, as well as those correctly identified by the sentries. The winner is the one who, undetected by the sentries, reports the greatest number of correctly observed objects. This is already a listening game, a stalking game, and simultaneously an observational-memory game.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Field Observer
body:
A. Position the players at a distance of 5 to 10 steps from one another and designate a section of terrain or a single, more complex field object for observation. Allow them time (2 to 10 minutes, depending on the terrain and the age of the players) for observation. After the allotted observation time, the observers execute an about-face, run, or perform several somersaults or other playful movements, then finally sit down and commit the observed terrain to paper in the form of:

- a) a description (for the youngest),
- b) a freehand drawing or topographic symbols (end of primary school and beginning of secondary school),
- c) a sketch and typographic symbols (older grammar school classes).

Looking back is not permitted. The above observations are best made on a hill, then descending to a lower position to transfer them to paper—this removes the temptation to turn around. The time allowed for committing the observed terrain to paper should be limited. After everyone has completed the task, evaluation follows.

B. Another variation involves observing: a section of a vegetable garden, orchard, field, or horse paddock; a herd of cows; or a farmyard. After a brief observation period, move away from the object and instruct the children to note on paper: which vegetable species were in the garden, which fruit trees were in the orchard, what colors and sizes of horses or cows were seen in the herd, or what was observed in the farmyard or field? These observations should be used to discuss natural phenomena or the life and work of people.

title: Who Stands Where
body:
Observing the order in which children are arranged: in a line, row, or other formations. After some time, interspersed with active play or marching, the children recreate the previous order.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Finding the Whistler:
body:
A. seated in.), B. moving.),

On small, open terrain, all listeners blindfold themselves. On larger terrain or at night, the game proceeds without blindfolds. The winner is the one who first discovers or catches the whistler.

C. 3 groups, each with whistles of different pitches, hide or flee from three groups, each of which pursues only one unit assigned a specific pitch. The fleeing groups must have a predetermined escape time and a location where they will hide after the final whistle. The pursuers should locate the correct group. After being found, the individual groups switch roles. Each whistler should initially be assigned a different direction of escape to avoid confusion and to not hinder the pursuit.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: To the Rescue
body:
The instructor, having dispersed individual groups across the terrain within hearing distance of a gunshot, conceals himself at a location equidistant from all groups and fires a shot (using a pistol or a starter pistol). Upon this signal, the groups rush to the rescue in the direction of the fired shot. The group that reaches the instructor’s hiding place first wins.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Security Outpost
body:
We are an outpost. In the forward area, we have 2, 3, or 4 sentries deployed in concealed terrain unknown to the outpost members. At an agreed-upon time, the sentries fire (blank cartridges for younger scouts; rifles with blanks may be used for older ones). Upon this signal, we dispatch patrols from the outpost in the direction of the shots, each in a different direction, to investigate the position of the given sentry and bring back a report.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Eavesdropping on Means of Transportation
body:
The youth are positioned at a certain distance (500—1500 m) from: a railway line (to know when a train passes), a highway, or a road, in such a way that they cannot see the given routes or are unaware of their existence.

In the first case, the goal is to: hear the sound of moving means of transportation, walking or talking people as early as possible by placing an ear to the ground; to distinguish individual means of transportation by their sound. In the second case, additionally, to deduce the type of road, its distance, and its course.

Often in the field, we will have the opportunity to spot an aircraft based on its noise. It is necessary not only to seize the chance to detect it but also to teach the youth to hide from it, utilizing the given terrain. The best cover will be trees, bushes, houses, fences; in their absence, one should adapt to the background, the terrain's features, or remain motionless.

The above exercises should be practiced at different times of the day and night and under various weather conditions, highlighting the influence of these factors when assessing distance.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Eavesdropping on Conversations
body:
The group is divided into two lines, which are positioned—lying down—opposite each other at a distance of 8 to 20 steps. One line (the youth lie at intervals of 2 to 8 steps from each other) orally passes a random sentence from one end to the other, ensuring it is accurately repeated at the opposite end of the line. The second line, lying opposite at the same intervals, attempts to hear and reconstruct this conversation. Then, the tasks are reversed.

---

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Approaching Sentinels:
body:
A. with blindfolded eyes ("blind" sentinel), B. with eyes open (in dense undergrowth terrain).

Approaching is performed: by stepping or crawling, individually or en masse, by day or by night.

It is also possible to approach a group of sentinels or slip between two sentinels standing at a distance of 20 — 30 meters.

In the case of "blind" sentinels (with blindfolded eyes), their accurate indication of the direction in which the approaching person is located eliminates the latter from the game as captured. In the case of a normal sentinel, calling out the name and indicating the spot where the one sneaking up is located means the capture of the person sneaking up.
