author: Jan Jasiński
title: Approaching the Camp (Creating a Tale Against the Backdrop of Polish-Tatar Wars)
body:
We post sentinels from half of the participants around a small flag representing the central point of the camp. Sentinels may not stand closer than 100 paces from the flag, and from each other at distances ranging from 20 to 30 (depending on terrain cover). The more open the terrain, the greater the distances between sentinels must be. Sentinels should be positioned in such a way as to allow the possibility of sneaking into the camp (for greater youth satisfaction). Sentinels must not change their positions; they must conceal themselves well and see everything. A spotted enemy is considered killed. Those sneaking in approach the camp from various directions. Assign specific sectors to individual groups. In this way, after the game ends (set a time limit and give a signal to finish—preferably one warning signal, and after 10 minutes, a second one to close the game), we can verify whether a given sentinel truly saw a particular infiltrator. A point is scored for their side by: a) every infiltrator who sneaks in unseen, b) every infiltrator who spots a hidden sentinel, c) every sentinel who notices and recognizes an infiltrator. Infiltrators may be detected by several sentinels or may themselves be seen by several sentinels.

These approaches must take place in silence. There should be no pursuit, shouting, or other noises. In the event of mutual sighting, the infiltrator is free to change their position (without changing their sector), and the sentinel may change their hiding spot. Such encounters are not scored.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Defense of the Telegraph Line
body:
The exercise area should be a road, preferably winding, passing through a forest of varying age and undergrowth.

One group defends it by posting sentries (two boys each) along the road every 100—300 meters. The sentries take their positions not on the road but in the forest, at a distance of 50 meters from the road. On the road itself, 2 or 3 patrols (three boys each) move about.

The other group attempts to: track down and bypass the posted sentries and patrols, and reach the road to destroy the telegraph line. Destruction is achieved if: ropes are tied to telegraph poles (in several places); or a trench of specified dimensions is dug anywhere along the road; or a thread suspended just above the ground between the poles is cut.

The defenders of the telegraph line may pursue the approaching group. Touching an approaching scout with a hand results in their capture (the captured one submits to the captor’s commands). The approaching group may defend themselves only by fleeing.

The exercise area should be bounded by natural lines (preferably water lines or open terrain lines), beyond which the approaching group must not go. The length of the guarded road should be at least 1 kilometers. The distance between individual sentries will depend on the terrain cover.

Conducting these exercises in the evening or at night (during camps or colonies) will present a significant challenge and add great variety.

This type of exercise is also possible in an urban setting.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Infiltration P
body:
Scouts (P.O.W.):

The game’s terrain is a town square, accessible via several streets and featuring passage gates or any other crossings, such as: empty lots, gardens, etc. One group, acting as secret Russian or German agents, occupies all known crossings, hiding in: gates, shops, or private houses while observing the streets. There should not be too many agents. Certain gaps in coverage must be planned, especially where traffic is light or streets are narrow. Scouts are unaware of these gaps in agent coverage.

P.O.W. members from various parts of the city aim to reach the town square, where a rally point is designated. They may choose secret routes through: gardens, fences, passage houses, etc.; they may: use vehicles, disguise themselves with the help of others, etc.

An undetected "scout" arriving at the square before the game ends, as well as a secret agent who spots and identifies a "scout," earns points.

The party with the most points wins.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Sneaking with Disguises
body:
A variation that facilitates sneaking while making capture more difficult is the ability of "Peowiaks" to disguise themselves. This type of game, full of excitement and requiring ingenuity, is easier to conduct within youth organizations, though a teacher can also organize it during afternoon games. This game type can also be applied at a colony or camp once warmer relations with the local population have been established, from whom youth can easily borrow the necessary clothing. The goal of sneaking could be: a town square or camp—a clearing in the forest. Ensure that the youth return the clothing to its owners immediately.

For example, here are some of the more interesting forms of disguise observed, both in the city and the countryside: beggar, lady, village woman, herdsman with cattle, coachman or passenger, hiding in a cart with straw, laborer with a handcart, disguising oneself as an instructor-judge, chimney sweep, gossiping women, arrival by boat of people dressed in rural attire (camp by a lake), Jew, blind man with a dog, and so on.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Tracking
body:
One group is instructed to leave their homes or the school building and reach a designated location by taking indirect routes (they know they will be tracked). Each participant in this group is followed by a member of the opposing group (disguises may also be used for this game), who waits near the first group’s starting point. The tracked individual tries to walk (running is not allowed) in such a way as to lose the tracker and reach the meeting place. Members of the tracking group, unaware of the location, can only find it if they do not lose sight of the person they are following. Limit the duration of the game. Members of the tracked group must arrive at a specified time—those who are late are eliminated from the game. Trackers brought by late-tracked individuals have fulfilled their task. The first group wins if the majority of its members reach the meeting place without being "accompanied," while the second group wins if the majority can locate the meeting place by successfully tracking members of the first group.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: The Struggle of Two Parties
body:
Participants are divided into two parties, whose members do not know each other’s affiliation and recognize one another only by means of an agreed sign, such as grasping the bottom button of a jacket or taking a handkerchief from a pocket, while uttering a certain word. The response is given through another agreed secret sign (as a last resort, a regular password and verbal countersign may be used).

The division into opposing parties is carried out secretly by the instructor, who hands out slips of paper to individual participants, designating their party (e.g., Julius’s Party) and its agreed signs.

Both parties exchange a letter. They must pass it to their own people, scattered in a forest within a defined area (both parties operate in the same area). The game consists of: cleverly obtaining the opposing party’s sign, exercising mutual caution toward encountered individuals who know nothing of each other but wish to identify a fellow member.

If an opponent is discovered, they are "killed" by tearing off the ribbon each participant wears on their arm. The "killed" player remains at the meeting spot and may no longer take part in the game. Key tactics include: surprising from concealment or eavesdropping on two others. These methods determine the recognition and observation of the opposing party’s signs or passwords. The game ends upon a specified signal.

The party wins which: captures the enemy’s letter, kills more opponents, or delivers its own letter to a greater number of its members (each member who possessed the party’s letter marks it with their own sign). For killing one of their own members, two negative points are awarded (it may happen that someone attempts to communicate with any encountered sign of the opposing party, but instead encounters a member of their own party, who—seeing and recognizing the opponents’ sign—kills the first by tearing off their ribbon).

title: Messenger
body:

The patrol sends messengers to the main force with messages and the task of slipping through the enemy group. The main force may be represented by an instructor or a specific point in the terrain. The messengers must get past the marching group’s security or bypass it.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: The Ambush
body:
One unit advances and prepares an ambush in a chosen terrain along a designated section of the road. It selects for the ambush: ditches covered with bushes, groves, forest undergrowth, villages, etc., dispersing its forces over a certain area. This unit may have the following tasks: b) capturing the rear guard while allowing the vanguard and main force to pass.

The second unit, marching along the same road with security measures, attempts to detect the ambush and protects itself from surprise.

The ambush party wins if, undetected, it attacks the center of the enemy’s main force or takes the rear guard prisoner; it loses if discovered and possibly attacked from the rear first.

In the event of capturing the rear guard, the ambushing unit may outflank the enemy group advancing ahead of it and attack again—this time, the main force.

97.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Tracking the Trail of a Dispatched Group
body:
An escaping group may split into smaller units, rejoin, or use evasive maneuvers such as: walking backward, crossing streams, or marching along their beds (not over a large area, but in a way that allows trackers to find the trail leading out of the stream with relative ease).

The fugitives may perform various actions: lighting a fire, burying something, or leaving behind notes.

Notes may be: incomplete, with torn or scorched sections, copied onto blotting paper, torn and scattered, encrypted, written in Morse code, or with invisible ink (easily done using milk or lemon juice).

The above exercises work exceptionally well on a path shortly after rain or in winter on snow (also off the path). Such games also yield good results on less-frequented seaside beaches. In winter, we can apply a variation of the previous game in the form of:

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Escape of the Insurgent
body:
An insurgent from the year 63, exiled to Siberia, escapes from their place of confinement. A dispatched pursuit follows the insurgent's tracks, striving to capture them as swiftly as possible. The pursuit sets out 10—15 minutes after the insurgent's escape. There may be several insurgents. If the insurgents are captured within the designated time (e.g., one hour), they lose. In moments of danger, they may conceal themselves by firing snowballs at their pursuers. A struck member of the pursuit group is considered killed. To eliminate an insurgent, they must be hit three times.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Tracking Trails
body:
On a known and announced route for all units or groups, we mark the path ourselves or send one of the participants to do the marking. Every sign and its surroundings or location must be noted by the messenger on a piece of paper. The route may extend over a distance of half — 1 half kilometers (initially, the path should be straight, later changing directions).

The instructor or their deputy sends out individual units or small groups of participants in succession, at intervals of 5 — 10 minutes. Each unit (group) notes the observed signs with a brief description of the surroundings, taking into account: the type of terrain, the quality of the path or terrain object, and the sign's position relative to other objects in the terrain or cardinal directions. When the path changes direction, the direction should be marked according to the cardinal points. Comparing the notes provides insight not only into the ability to find signs but, more importantly, into the knowledge of the terrain itself. In assessing priority, the description of the terrain is decisive, as finding the sign will usually be accomplished by all participants.

Tracking games conducted on a route can be organized in two ways: on a single route or multiple routes. In the case of a single route, we achieve absolute fairness in evaluation due to the uniformity of the route and signs, as well as the same length of the route. The disadvantage of a single route is the significant time lost in sending all patrols (there are often 4—6 of them) through the route in succession, at intervals of 10—15 minutes. This system will be used: when there are 2 or 3 patrols, in the case of absolute competitions between all patrols (treated as a test of observation skills), or when more time is available.

However, where time is limited, where a low-stakes competition suffices, and where there are more patrols, we will use 2—4 routes simultaneously, striving to ensure: that their length is as equal as possible and that the number of signs placed is the same. We can set up a maximum of as many routes as there are patrols (if the terrain and starting point allow), selecting two more responsible participants from each patrol to send out to lay and mark the signs. They must be given consistent, clear, and comprehensive instructions. The patrols follow the route laid out by members of other patrols.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: On Friends' Signs
body:
Following a simulated accident (e.g., a broken arm requiring bandaging) during an outing, two friends are left with the injured person. Several such groups of three can be organized, traveling along one or more routes at intervals of 5 minutes. An instructor or a more skilled participant, who simulates the main group, heads toward a certain destination, leaving signs in the form of arrows for the delayed group of friends. Occasionally, signs such as "wrong path," "we split up," or "letter" force them to: take out a map, orient themselves, or use specific terrain points, adding variety and difficulty to the game. The groups of three, unaware of the destination and route, must find the signs of the main group and, in doing so, involuntarily learn the terrain and notice its details. The winners are those who arrive at the destination in the shortest time from the moment of departure (someone must record this time) and demonstrate knowledge of the terrain they have traversed.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: In Pursuit of the Fox
body:
This game is particularly suited for winter play on skis. The fleeing fox (which may also be a group of skiers) scatters colored paper markers (from notebook covers) at intervals, choosing a varied route adapted to the participants' skiing skills and stamina. For youth well-practiced in skiing, difficult terrain may be selected.

Effort should be made to ensure the route forms a closed loop (to save time and energy). The hounds (individuals or packs), given the initial trail, set off at intervals and attempt to catch up with the fox or reach it at its den.

We may also release all packs simultaneously after 10 — 15 minutes from the fox's escape. The pack that first reaches the fox in its den (the hiding place after 1½ hours of skiing) in full wins. In the case of a group of fleeing foxes, they may split up, forcing the pursuing packs of hounds to divide as well.

If the terrain is unused and covered in fresh snow, we may forgo scattering paper markers. Tracking will then proceed by following the natural ski trail.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Arctic Expedition
body:
Two boys set out into snow-covered terrain, pulling sleds loaded with food, cooking utensils, and the like. After an interval of 15—30 minutes, the rest of the expedition follows, attempting to reach the campsite by tracking the sled marks left behind. The game will be more challenging during a light snowfall.

Along the way, the messengers with the sleds perform various tasks and encounter adventures, such as lighting a fire, cooking, eating (leaving behind bone remnants), hunting (traces of feathers and blood), repairing the sleds (wood scraps), or having their sleds overturn, and so on.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Reaching the Pole
body:
Emissaries from two rival nations competing to discover the pole advance from two directions toward a specific target in the terrain (the pole). They depart simultaneously from points equidistant from the pole. They may travel on skis or, as in the previous case, pull sleds. Following the emissaries, the rest of the expedition sets out along their tracks, striving to reach the goal as swiftly as possible. They depart **10** minutes after their forerunners have left. En route, at one-quarter of the distance to the pole, an unfortunate accident befalls both leading patrols, forcing them to halt. The groups following the front patrols carry aid to them (specify rescue tasks) and only then proceed to the final conquest of the pole, transporting the injured. The group that arrives first at the pole in its entirety claims the pole for its nation.

The above games may also be adapted for those who cannot ski. In summer, they can be conducted in any urban or rural terrain with an altered storyline. By requiring a description of the terrain traversed, the purely physical aspect of the game is expanded to a more purposeful one.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: The Manhunt
body:
The terrain (covering an area of 2—3 kilometers) is wooded, varied, and enclosed on all sides by roads. Fresh snowfall. One patrol represents a Bolshevik sabotage band cut off from the border and moving within this area enclosed by roads. They do not emerge onto the roads, fearing contact with people and outposts. Four other patrols represent Border Protection Corps (K.O.P.) units, acting in coordination but operating separately and examining the terrain from different directions. The sabotage band enters the manhunt area at a location unknown to the K.O.P. units. The first task of the K.O.P. is to find the initial trail of the Bolsheviks and then skillfully organize the manhunt. The band misleads, maneuvers, erases its tracks, and may split up. It can also ambush smaller K.O.P. groups, firing snowballs at them. A hit by a snowball disables a unit on both sides. The footprints of the sabotage band may be distinctive. These tracks should be examined and memorized by the K.O.P. groups upon first encountering them.

The game should be time-limited. For example, within 1 and a half hours, the band must be surrounded and eliminated. Otherwise, the surviving members of the sabotage band go free. If a "policeman" or border guard touches a band member with their hand, the latter is taken prisoner.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: By Different Paths to One Goal
body:
The game is conducted over a larger area (from 5 kilometers). From our base, via 3 routes (we strive to ensure the lengths of the routes are roughly equal), we send out to village N a number of guides who mark the path with colored wool or cotton thread. After 5—10 minutes from the departure of the guides, we simultaneously release three groups. They follow different paths according to the respective markers, striving to reach the unknown goal as quickly as possible.

Paths may cross, but in such cases, each guide must mark the route with a distinct color of thread, known to the group following them. The wool should be placed: on terrain features, at road intersections or bends, on bushes or trees, at the boundary between two differently sown fields, or on varying types of terrain. The tracking groups should, using the appropriate topographic symbol or the name of the identified plant species, note the location where the wool was found.

The instructor, familiar with all routes, may move between them. They should monitor the groups' activities and guide them toward accurate and proper execution of the game. It is advisable to have a bicycle for these control duties.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: On the Trail
body:
From a military depot (in the town), a granary (in the countryside), or a camp storehouse, food (flour, beans, etc.) was stolen during the night. It was carried away by cart or on the backs of thieves in sacks. Fortunately, without the thief’s knowledge, one of the sacks was torn, so the escape route is visible thanks to traces of flour or beans spilling out from time to time through the hole in the sack.

Variations in this game may and should include actions of the thief deduced from the traces, for example: a) leaning the sack (in reality, sprinkling flour) against a tree, fence, or trunk, b) the thief stumbling with the sack, c) leaving the path into the bushes—startled by someone, they hid.

A group or groups of young people follow the thief’s trail, interpret their actions, and finally catch them at their destination. Require an oral description of the route taken.

The messenger or instructor preparing the traces will have the opportunity to demonstrate creativity in arranging traces that reflect the thief’s various actions. Certain terrain features will assist them.

Flour should be carried in a linen sack. Beans can be placed in pockets.

A positive factor in such a game will be a convincing staging of the theft, so that the young people believe it really happened. Here is an example.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Locating the Removed Goods
body:
One time at camp during the night, with the 2 older boys, we transported more valuable food to the village, to the village head, using a borrowed wagon. We marked the transport route with scattered flour. The camp leader knew nothing of this matter, so in the morning, he raised a great alarm that the storeroom had been robbed and that wagon tracks were visible. Summoned, I put on a very tragic expression, ordered a gathering, and organized a pursuit by patrols along the wagon tracks, which soon merged with others on the road. There was great difficulty in choosing the correct direction at the point where the roads branched. However, the situation became clear when one of the patrols noticed traces of flour on a small bridge (a jolt when entering it and likely a torn sack). The patrols were already on a certain trail, with flour marking the thief’s path at every turn. Before reaching the village, I instructed the best patrol in tracking to determine, without drawing the villagers' attention to their true activity, whether our food had accidentally ended up in one of the houses, and to report the result without entering it. After discovering the village head’s house, I explained to the boys that this was only a staged exercise. The disappointment was great. Many wise and combative suggestions on how to surprise the thief and what to do with him remained unrealized. Nevertheless, the tracking succeeded thanks to a certain purposefulness.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: On the Trails of Game
body:
Individual groups or units act as hunters tracking game (bear, wolf, etc.). The game flees, leaving a distinct trail in the form of, for example:

- a) a boot studded with a specific number of nails,¹)
- b) galoshes or slippers with new rubber soles,
- c) a boot with an iron shape attached, resembling the track of a bear, wolf, or triangle,
- d) a widened ski pole disc if the exercise is conducted on skis,
- e) a staff with a particularly wrapped or reinforced tip,
- f) a board with nails hammered in as a rake.

There may be a herd of game with identical or different tracks. Each group of hunters tracks one "animal" until capturing it along the way, if they set off immediately after the trail, or until finding the "game" in its lair if they begin tracking after some time.

Tracking pursuit games can always be concluded with target throws,

¹) Once, in the Vilnius region, while leading an independently operating patrol from an instructor’s course on an outing, I came across the tracks of another patrol, which had boots studded with nails. Thanks to the rain that had fallen in the morning, I was able to apply natural tracking over the course of half a day’s march, following the opponent’s route, interpreting their actions from the tracks, and approaching them at certain easier points for visual observation. It was one of the finest tracking games for me and my patrol. Such opportunities should be created.

(using grenade-throwing preparation), employing pine cones, stones, or snowballs for this purpose. Upon catching up with the tracked "game," each member of the patrol has the right to three throws. The target may be a cardboard figure of the given animal in reduced size or a spot marked on the ground or a tree. The accurate throws of the patrol are divided by the number of members in the patrol, yielding an average result.

Alongside throws, we should also use shooting: a) with a slingshot, b) with a sports catapult, c) with a crossbow, d) with a military air rifle, e) with a small-caliber firearm.

This may involve shooting at targets. However, it is better to shoot at figures set up in natural conditions, in more challenging lighting situations.

It should be remembered that shooting is a great pleasure for youth and is also a significant need from the perspective of our goals.

For youth in the heroic and transitional age, crafting military equipment and using it in terrain-based combat for supremacy is such an emotional and beneficial experience that neglecting this fact would be a culpable oversight on the part of the educator. The sooner we move on to shooting with air rifles and firearms, the better. Let us not hesitate to use shooting frequently, not only in tracking but also in other terrain-based scouting activities.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Finding a Man Who Has Lost His Memory
body:
Patrols track a fleeing man who has forgotten who he is. He drops various personal items. The tracking patrols must find these items and, based on them, determine: the personality, profession, and name of the man who has lost his memory.

In all tracking games conducted along routes, a sketch along the path may be used as a form of report on the actions taken. In its legend, we will require explanations regarding all anthropogeographical phenomena, i.e., human works related to agricultural culture, the quality of communication routes, nature, etc.

Another group in tracking consists of so-called "trail stories." Games of this type are organized when there is a larger space untouched by human feet, such as: a seaside, lake, or river beach, or snow. In such virgin terrain, we improvise stories using natural traces, which individual groups read in sequence.

During this type of game, it is important to ensure that those interpreting the traces do not walk on the prepared trails but beside them. Below are examples of such "trail stories."

author: Jan Jasiński
title: History in the Snow
body:
a) Tracks of 3 people skiing (if the track is narrow — a good skier, wide — a poor one); b) various forms of movement: incorrect stride (pole marks not roughly at the midpoint of the skis), long step (good use of the pole), running (long distances between pole marks); c) overlapping tracks; d) divergence with position changes (determining from the tracks, in comparison with the first ones, where the left-flank, center, and right-flank skiers went); e) the fall of one of the skiers; f) others arriving to assist him; g) transporting the skier who suffered an accident, etc. The desire to read history based on tracks compels reasoning, requires clear judgment, and a certain sharpness of thought. A well-prepared exercise is an interesting challenge. The patrol that reads the history with the greatest probability wins. Points are awarded separately for each action marked in the snow.

This type of tracking requires the instructor to have a little initiative and creativity, as well as time to prepare the route. To prepare it calmly, the practicing groups should be sent into a more distant area beforehand with the task of conducting another game.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: A True Story
body:
It may sometimes happen that a "story" in snow or sand is natural; one should then make use of it.

I had the opportunity to exploit the following event. I was leading a scout camp in the Rudawska Forest. One day, a calf was purchased, quartered, and placed in cauldrons, which were then set in water at the lake's edge (as a cooler). Having the habit of rising early before the participants, I noticed that one of the cauldrons was overturned. Upon closer inspection, I found animal tracks on the lakeside beach, indicating that it had dragged a quarter of the calf and other parts from the cauldron and carried them into nearby bushes. There were many signs of the animal stopping and consuming the meat.

I ordered tracking before washing and breakfast. The story was more or less accurately read by everyone in the troop. With great interest, they deduced and finally concluded, after a joint discussion, that it was a wolf and that they should lie in wait for it the following night. This led to a new and interesting exercise, which I utilized. After a few days, disappointment followed, as a large dog, managing the storeroom, was caught instead.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: During the March
body:
During a march: on a highway, road, or street, we instruct the youth to estimate distances in paces from their current position to various objects: trees, telegraph poles, road intersections, houses, forest edges, and so on. When determining distances along the road itself, a helpful reference will be the roughly constant distance between telegraph poles or planted trees. Estimating distances to the side of the road will be more challenging.

title: From a Certain Point
body:

It is possible to point out the inaccuracy of estimation and varying visibility in relation to the postures of the observed person (a soldier in war): lying down, crawling, kneeling, standing, running directly toward us, or parallel to us. Conduct this exercise practically in the form of the following game.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Observing the Enemy
body:
One group observes another, which attempts to approach the observers as closely as possible: crawling, concealing itself behind natural cover, running, etc. (choose appropriately varied terrain). The leader stays with the observation group, which shares its observations and estimates the distance of the enemy's position, e.g.: N or A lies at a distance of Y paces. To the running M, we have Z paces. An observed enemy whose distance is accurately estimated is considered eliminated. The number of undetected enemies determines victory. Limit the duration of the exercise.

In the above games, attention should be paid to the factors affecting distance estimation: a) the individual's adaptation to the background (visibility and assessment differ against the sky, forest, ground, or a building), b) the influence of lighting and weather conditions (assessment differs when facing the sun versus having the sun behind; distance is judged differently in humid air, dry and hot air, or during rain; differently at dusk and in broad daylight).

This also provides an opportunity to discuss camouflage—blending into the terrain (both for ground observation and from aircraft). However, it must be emphasized that, in addition to camouflage, the full ability to observe and estimate distances for effective enemy fire must be maintained. Note the differences in distance estimation when lying down, kneeling, and standing.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Measuring Distances
body:
Each time, verify the given estimates by measuring with steps. Steps are always counted on one leg, for example, the right leg. Multiply the resulting number of steps by two. Teach the youth to quickly convert steps into meters—we achieve relative accuracy by establishing a step of 75 centimetres = 3/4 m (usually a normal male step). For instance, if the measured number of steps is 84, simply divide it by 4 and multiply by 3 to obtain the number of metres. In this case, the distance is $$ rac{84 \cdot 3}{4} = 63$$.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Observing the Concealed
body:
Place one of the groups, preferably a patrol, in varied terrain (undulating with cover). Conceal them using available terrain features at various distances (from 200—1200 meters) from the observers (minor movements of the concealed in their positions may be allowed). Call other groups in turn to the observation point. Participants observe the opponent within a defined sector of the terrain and assess the distance for effective shooting (sector boundaries are marked using terrain landmarks). Observation time is limited. The group that locates the greatest number of concealed individuals and best assesses the distance to them wins.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Determining Position Using Fingers
body:
During the exercise, pay attention to determining the position of an object or person in the field using the width of the fingers of the hand. The instructor may ask, for example: “Look for a solitary tree that is located at a width of 4 fingers from the bend in the road,” or: “Find the enemy observer lying at a width of 2 fingers to the left of the hilltop,” etc. When using this method of determining position, extend the straightened arm with the thumb raised upward in front of your own eyes. The width of the thumb serves as our positional measure.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Measuring Width
body:
This may be the width of a river, pond, lake, marsh, ravine, sown field, etc.

Fig. 3.

Emphasize the practicality of this measurement in cases such as building a bridge across a river or ravine, determining the time needed to swim across a river or lake, etc.

We choose an arbitrary point A in the form of a bush or stone on the opposite bank and point B on our own bank, where we plant a stick or position one of the boys (Fig. 3). Next, we draw a perpendicular to the line thus obtained in space on our bank, at an arbitrary point (C) where we position a second boy. We extend the line BC and, depending on the terrain, measure from point C the full length of segment BC or a part of it (1/2, 1/3, 1/4). At the point D thus obtained, we position another boy and at this same point, we mark a line perpendicular to line BD, running along the bank. We move along this perpendicular with our eyes fixed on point C until the latter covers point A on the opposite bank. We then obtain point E, and having measured line DE, we can, based on the proportionality of triangles ABC and CDE and the known lengths of segments BC, DC, and DE, find the width AB using the formula $$
\frac{AB}{DE} = \frac{BC}{CD}
$$, from which $$
AB = \frac{DE \times BC}{CD}
$$.

Practically, for the youngest, it is sufficient to state without proof that if segment CD was equal to CB, then segment DE will also be equal to AB. In the case where CD is a part (1/4, 1/3, 1/2) of segment CB, then segment DE will be that many times smaller than AB. It is therefore enough to multiply the number of steps of segment DE by 4, 3, or 2 to find the inaccessible width, i.e., AB.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Laying Out a Line
body:
This skill is necessary when constructing a bivouac or camp and in sketching. At the point from which we wish to lay out a line, we place a staff or a person, standing ourselves facing the given direction. A second person positions themselves or a staff at any point along the correct direction. We align them precisely on the intended direction using hand signals. The direction of adjustment is indicated with the hand: left hand—adjustment is also to the left, right hand—to the right. We will use this method for: laying out straight lines between two points, marking points on a given line, indicating a certain direction in the terrain, and during cross-country marches (we then select a series of terrain features along the line of march).

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Establishing a Right Angle in the Field (Fig.
body:
4).

Fig. 4.

On line AB, from point B, we wish to lay out a line at a right angle. To do this, using a string or cord tied to a peg, we mark two equal segments from point B along the straight line AB, obtaining two points: a and b (we drive pegs into these). From these points, with a radius greater than Bb, we draw two arcs in the direction of C—their intersection will be point C on the perpendicular we wished to lay out. We connect B with C and extend this line. The extension is done in the same way as when laying out a straight line.

A second method is even simpler. We know that the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the legs. Based on this principle, it suffices to measure 3 metres from point B, thus obtaining point b. From this point, we draw an arc with a radius of 5 metres in the direction of the presumed perpendicular, and from point B, in the same direction, an arc with a radius of 4 metres. The intersection of these arcs will give us point C, through which the desired perpendicular will pass. The principle: 4² plus 3² equals 5².

If we possess a Bézard compass, establishing a right angle in the field will be quicker and easier.

4 Measuring height, e.g., of a tree, chimney (Fig. 5), house, or hill. a) According to the ratio of shadow and actual height of the object, based on the formula:

Fig. 5.

$$\frac{\text{shadow of the rod (a)}}{\text{shadow of the tree (b)}} = \frac{\text{height of the rod (c)}}{\text{height of the tree (x)}}$$

We can measure the shadow of the tree and the shadow of the rod, as well as the height of the rod. Knowing these three dimensions, we can find the fourth, sought-after one, based on the transformed formula: $$x = \frac{b \cdot c}{a}$$.

This formula can be applied at any time of a sunny day or a moonlit night.

b) In case the sun is not visible, we can measure height based on the principle of similar triangles (Fig. 6).

Fig. 6.

To measure height, in this case of a chimney, one participant must lie down and look along the end of a rod (preferably 1 or 2 metres in length), positioned between themselves and the base of the chimney. They adjust the rod with the help of another participant so that their eyes, the end of the rod, and the top of the chimney lie on a single line. Then, based on the similarity of triangles ABC and EDC, we can find the desired height (point C is the position of the lying pupil’s eyes) thanks to the proportionality of the sides $$\frac{BC}{DC} = \frac{AB}{ED}$$, from which $$AB = \frac{BC \times ED}{DC}$$.

Practically, we must determine how many times segment DC is smaller than segment BC, and then, having multiplied the height of the rod by this ratio, we obtain the sought height of the object.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Calculating the Speed of a Water Current
body:
Having measured a length of 1 or 2 metres along the riverbank, we throw a stick, bark, or grass into the main current (upstream of the starting point of the measured length). We note the moment the object passes the starting point on the second hand of a watch. Then, having overtaken the floating object, we record the time at the end of the measured distance. If we have a stopwatch, the entire procedure is simplified.

Suppose that over a distance of 2 metres, the time taken for the object to float was 30 seconds; then, by dividing the number of metres by the number of seconds, we obtain the speed in metres per second. In this case, 1/15 m/s, or 4 m/min.

Apply this exercise as a competition between canoeing groups to calculate the speed of movement with the current without using paddles. At a lower level, use this method to determine the speed of the local river’s current and compare it with the speed of mountain streams.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Measuring Water Depth
body:
To measure the depth of water in streams, brooks, and small ponds, a straight stick of length 2 metres will suffice. We immerse it at the desired spot until the bottom is felt. The mark left by the water on the stick will allow us to measure the depth.

When measuring depths greater than 2 metres, a string weighted with, for example, a stone must be used. On this string, we mark measurements in metres with knots (a knot every 50 centimetres). The weighted and marked string is immersed until the moment we feel and see that it is no longer taut (it does not hang vertically). It is then sufficient to read the measurement on the string to obtain the exact depth of the water.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Determining Wind Direction
body:
This is necessary for: setting up a kitchen, pitching a bivouac or camp; in water journeys, and often also for orientation.

We determine the wind direction by tossing dry grass or paper upward. Their descent, deviating from the vertical, will indicate the wind direction for us. To ensure accuracy, the obtained data should be verified several times.

When setting up a camp for a longer period in open spaces, the prevailing wind directions in Poland should be taken into account, i.e., NW, W, and SW.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Determining the Exact North–South Direction Using Natural Phenomena
body:
By day: a) the sun, b) the sun and a watch, c) a cut tree stump (rings thicker on the south side), d) moss on solitary trees not standing near water (moss on the north side), e) the tree crown (greater branch development on the south side).

¹) Before the instructor proceeds with terrain games and exercises, they should familiarize themselves with the basic knowledge in this field, contained in the following books:

Niezbrzycki J., *Terrain Science*.

Gąsiewicz S., *Terrain Orientation Handbook for Non-Commissioned Officers*.

*School of the Young Soldier*.

Gawkowski S., *Field Sketches of a Scout*.

At night: a) the North Star and the Great Bear, b) the Milky Way, c) the constellation Orion (in winter), d) the moon.

Game no. 1 and 2 is conducted as follows: Participants equip themselves with straight branches about a dozen centimetres long and sharpen one end. On the instructor’s signal, they lay them on the ground using the requested method mentioned above, pointing the sharp end toward the north or another direction specified by the instructor. After placing the sticks, the boys step aside. The instructor then checks the direction with a compass and determines who marked the direction most accurately.

This exercise should be repeated frequently in various circumstances and times of day, in the most diverse terrain, and under different weather conditions. However, it should always be required that each participant be able to transfer this direction into the terrain, defining it using terrain landmarks, e.g.: “North lies in the direction of the white house’s chimney” or “Marching east, I must head toward the left poplar,” etc.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Determining the Exact North–South Direction Using Instruments:
body:
a) compass, b) Bézard prismatic compass, c) map.

When determining North, one must remember to account for declination. It is essential to become accustomed to the concept that the magnetic needle indicates only magnetic north. The sought-after geographic north can be found only after accounting for the angle of declination for the given locality, and only then will the North–South line drawn on the base of the compass or prismatic compass indicate true north.

In terrain-based games for youth above the age of 15, directions should be determined precisely using a compass, Bézard prismatic compass, or map. Youth should become familiar with these instruments, and therefore, several compasses or maps of the given area should always be available during exercises. (Compasses and maps may be acquired by the youth themselves. The geography teacher usually has a prismatic compass. Efforts should be made to acquire larger quantities of these instruments.)

One should make use of the prismatic compass. It is necessary to overcome the general passivity stemming solely from ignorance of the directional and operational value of the compass in the field. Those who have not verified that, with the help of a prismatic compass, one can reach a designated point in the field with great accuracy will always overlook the compass when training others. I have repeatedly observed on scout instructor courses that participants only become convinced of the usefulness of the prismatic compass after traversing several kilometers off-trail in completely unfamiliar terrain without a map.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Cross-Country March by One's Own Shadow
body:
A sunny day. Patrols are released from a certain point into varied and wooded terrain, with the task of reaching a bridge located by the road leading from locality A to locality B. The instructor provides the angle of the marching scout's shadow relative to the direction of the march (determined by the instructor using a compass and map). When the youth know how to determine the direction of the march based on the map, one member of the group then determines the shadow angle.

During the march, patrols ensure that the angle between the direction and their own shadow remains constant. They assist themselves in determining the direction of the march using terrain landmarks.

The patrol that reaches the indicated road closest to the given bridge wins.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Cross-Country March by Cardinal Directions and Terrain Points
body:
We are an exploratory expedition in the Gobi Desert (sandy terrain), or a reconnaissance expedition in the Amazon forests (forested terrain), or a military unit in the field (normal terrain). We have sent several reconnaissance patrols into the field. From one of them, we receive a radio message: "S. O. S.!... We are to the north-west of the last position..." (or camp). The message is interrupted at this point, evidently they could not transmit more details.

To the rescue, we send search groups one after another. They determine the correct direction using: a compass, a sighting compass, or a map¹). They memorize a series of auxiliary points in the terrain along the given direction, as well as the last one on the horizon, and march according to them, searching for the missing.

In terrain with limited visibility (the exercise will be more difficult), the search patrols must determine the direction with a compass or sighting compass several times. If the starting position is located higher, thus

¹) Use the same type of instrument or a combination of them (sighting compass and map) for everyone.

offering an extensive view, then it is sufficient to orient the compass once.

If older troops participate in the game, the instructor leaves a note with the message at the starting point, then goes as the missing person to a certain position in the given direction (should be hidden), from where they observe the approaching troops.

When leading beginner troops, it is necessary to stay at the starting point to correct their direction-finding errors. In such a case, the missing patrol can be simulated by a clever individual or group, settling at the designated point in hiding.

The troop that finds the missing or has the smallest deviation from them wins.

Troops may set out simultaneously or one after another every few minutes.

With simultaneous departure, there may be a concern that weaker groups might rely too much on those better at orientation and not perform the exercise independently. This method can therefore be applied only to better-trained units or groups.

Directional games can be conducted on water if the exercising youth can swim and row, and most importantly, if they are accustomed to the fact that bravado is not allowed on water. Our numerous lakes and ponds can be a beautiful terrain for these exercises. One boat or kayak is sufficient. If there is more equipment, even better. With beginners in swimming and rowing, the instructor should go out on the water with them. Experienced individuals can be sent under the command of a responsible troop leader.

When we have only one boat, we send crews (do not overload the boat) one after another, waiting for the return of the previous group (the instructor can thus be with each group and better observe the participants' behavior). We will finish the game faster if we have two or more boats.

With a larger number of kayaks or boats, we can launch the entire flotilla simultaneously.

We can give various forms to directional games on water.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Retrieval of a Drowned Person
body:
We lower to the bottom of a lake, pond, or river—a sack with a stone or a specially made human figure (the best and cheapest way is to make a covering from old sacks, stuff it with hay, and weigh it down with stones in the legs and head).

The depth at which the dummy is submerged will depend on the swimming and diving proficiency of the participants. It may reach even 3 meters.

From any starting point, we release groups either sequentially or simultaneously, who receive the following messages: "In lake M, 20 meters east of the bridge near forester’s lodge D, a person has drowned. Rescue them!" Or: "In the lake, at a directional angle of 140°, a person is drowning. The distance from the shore is 10 meters. Hurry!" For better staging, it is good to place a cap at the approximate location of the drowning. The task of the rescuing group is not only to reach the specified location but also to retrieve the dummy to the shore. In connection with this game, we will practically demonstrate artificial respiration to the participants.

N o t e : In these games, the distance to be run should be short (at most 200 meters for youth over 18 years of age). The run should be interspersed with marching so that after a short rest, diving and probing can be allowed. During such a search, a lifeguard boat or kayak should be present at the site.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Whale Hunt, Which Will Be Either a Large Beam or a Car Tire
body:
In games of types 7, 8, and 9, besides locating the whereabouts (of people) of the game using a map or directional angle, the goal will be to tow the sought-after object to a designated point on the shore, determined based on the map. An element of competition between two settlements for the caught whale or seal can also be introduced. By assigning different towing destinations to the settlements and releasing them simultaneously after 2—4, we encourage speed of action and skillful towing. It is assumed that the catch can be snatched from one another. Combat is limited by the rule that only one crew member may grab the catch with their hands, while others row. Fighting with oars or engaging in brawls should not be allowed. The group that tows the most seals or other game to their harbor wins.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Defense of Ports
body:
Two warring maritime states organize the defense of their main port. These ports lie on bays of a lake, situated on opposite shores. Both maritime states protect their port by laying mines. The mines are tin cans filled with preserves, anchored with wire and a stone so that they float on the surface. To avoid misunderstandings, they should bear special markings. Their quantity is predetermined. Taking a fixed point on land as the starting base, the position of the mines is determined by a directional angle and distance in meters. Each maritime state possesses a mine-laying vessel (a kayak), which is hidden somewhere along the shore in reeds or thickets.

Both warring groups also possess a flotilla composed of any number of: kayaks, boats, sailboats, etc. These are stationed in their own ports.

At a specified hour, the fleet commanders receive from their spies (by opening sealed envelopes) information about the location of the mine-laying vessel. This information may also be transmitted via: semaphore signaling, received by telephone or telegraph, encrypted, etc. The position of the mine-layer is determined based on map 1: 100000 or plan 1: 25000, or from a sketch enclosed in the envelope.

The fleets set out from their ports with the aim of destroying the mine-layer. On the mine-layer (kayak), they obtain reports about the positions (determined by directional angles) of the mines in the enemy port’s bay. Based on the found reports, they locate the fixed point on land that serves as the base for the directional angles. The fleet commander organizes the destruction of the mines through their flotilla, assigning each kayak one or two (depending on the number of mines and kayaks) directions in which the mines are located. The state that: 1) brings back all the mines or the greater part of them, 2) arrives with its entire flotilla more quickly at the designated location, wins (captures the port). This location should be equidistant from both ports.

Directional games can also be applied on snow and skis, for example:

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Fox Hunt
body:
The instructor has discovered a fox's den.

He indicates the direction or the bearing angle in which the den is located. Additionally, a distinctive landmark along that line must be provided, near which the den should be sought.

We can diversify this game in the following way: We prepare a life-sized fox, cut out of cardboard, and place it near the given point. Participants should find it and, upon finding it, "kill" it. "Shooting" conditions: distance of 25 meters, 3 throws per participant. Shooting is done with: snowballs, stones, slingshots, bows, or small-caliber firearms.

The evaluation of shooting accuracy and the time taken to discover the fox determine the victory of an individual or group.

In all direction-based terrain games, the direction can be specified in two ways: 1) using cardinal directions, 2) using a bearing angle.

The first method is used at the lower level of instruction, the second at the higher level.

Before proceeding to games that involve using a bearing angle, this skill must be practiced. This ability is essential in all more difficult situations, such as: marching through large forests, in covered and obstructed terrain, and in war in devastated areas. It is also necessary for all shortcuts that facilitate and speed up our march.

There will be three needs for determining a bearing angle: a) having a designated direction in the form of a point in the terrain, find the bearing angle for it, b) having a given bearing angle, designate the direction in the terrain to reach a certain point, c) locate a target on the map and reach it by following the found bearing angle.

A typical exercise for marching according to a bearing angle will be case c. We will use it as often as possible in the form of the games mentioned above, as well as in the military-type games presented below, in which we give specific tasks for reconnaissance patrols or military units. In principle, all directional marches should be carried out using the Bézard compass as absolutely reliable. A regular compass does not perform its task well—it discourages directional marches due to its imprecision.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Village Reconnaissance
body:
We are a military patrol tasked with investigating the position of village A, located on the opposite edge of the forest. To achieve this, we must determine the directional angle using a Bézard compass based on the map and use it to reach the given village. Individual groups—patrols—are dispatched every 5 minutes. After all patrols have been sent out, the instructor travels by the nearest route (a bicycle is useful) to village A, where they receive the arriving patrols. The patrol that reaches the destination in the shortest time (patrols may calculate the march time based on the map—this will help with orientation) and with the smallest deviation from the march direction wins. Each group should have a compass. The march should be conducted without a map.

More challenging objectives in such a march may include smaller points such as: road intersections or bends, a forester’s lodge, a hill, etc.

To save time during the exercise, we may shorten the directional march route. It is sufficient for the marching group to reach a line (a road, forest clearing, etc.) that intersects the march direction. The exercise may end at such a line. Patrols mark their arrival point and step aside to avoid interfering with others' independence. The instructor assesses which point was most consistent with the designated directional angle. However, such forms should be avoided as they are artificial and weaken the value of the game. It is better to bring the march objectives closer by taking a cross-country route.

Initially, the march through the forest will be short, around 1—2 kilometers, while in later exercises for more experienced groups, it may extend up to 10 kilometers. Such exercises can be excellently conducted on larger, branching lakes where the destinations are not visible.

More difficult exercises will involve games over a larger area, such as individual cross-country marches in which youth will use a compass and map to determine direction.

Another type will include exercises and games based on sketches or maps.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Return by the Same Route
body:
The instructor leads the group (preferably in a forest) along paths, constantly changing direction. After covering at least 1—2 kilometers, participants are instructed to return individually to the starting point.

In the early versions of this game, the return by the same route should be announced in advance so that participants can prepare by observing and orienting themselves in the terrain. They should even be randomly asked to determine each change of direction using a compass.

Later, once they are more practiced, the return should not be announced but instead used to surprise the participants. To verify whether individual participants truly returned by the same route, they should be instructed to write their names on cards left by the instructor at several key points along the way. Alternatively, one participant can be stationed as a control judge at the most critical point, or the instructor can take this position themselves. The return march may initially be done with a map, but later without one.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Skill of Reporting the Path Traveled
body:
The participants are divided into two equal even parties. In each party, pairs of friends are formed. The friends are then separated, creating two groups within each party. Next, the instructor takes one group from each party and leads them along winding paths to a certain destination, where they hide as many colored cards as there are boys with them at that moment. After hiding the cards, the witnesses return as quickly as possible to the starting point, where they inform their friends about the location of the hidden cards and the shortest way to reach them. The informed friends then set off along the indicated path to the hiding place of the cards. The party that retrieves the greater number of hidden cards in the shorter time wins. Each informed friend brings back one card. The same game can be conducted between friendly patrols. In case of a larger number of youths, several hiding points for the cards should be created.

---

author: Jan Jasiński
title: March According to a Blind Sketch Received by Individual Groups (Game Applicable in a City)
body:
On the blind sketch, names and situational points are not marked. It contains only: direction, length (to scale), types of roads, and their intersections. Such a sketch can be presented in two ways (see fig. 7a and 7b).

Fig. 7 a.

Upon receiving the sketch, groups proceed to the final point indicated on it.

At this point, we may leave a letter with instructions: a) to return by the same or the shortest route, b) to perform a certain task there, e.g., collecting a number of plant specimens, doing a good deed, conducting an inquiry, etc.

Efforts should be made to ensure the terrain is unfamiliar. Sketches should be collected after reaching the indicated destination.

Fig. 7 b.

Returning by the shortest route will be the most challenging, and therefore, in the initial exercises, this type of return should be announced so that the boys strive to better recognize the terrain based on the sketch. The game without prior announcement will be used for older youth. We will make the exercise more difficult by increasing the length of the march and by marching based on a briefly viewed blind sketch. In the latter case, after completing the route, one may require the drawing of the path taken.

Games of types 14, 15, and 16 should be woven into a story (youth of 13—16 years). However, the plot should be modernized or linked to Polish history and values.

---

author: Jan Jasiński
title: March According to the Map
body:
a) individually, b) in groups.

In this game, if we have a sufficient number of maps, we primarily use individual competition or small teams. This creates good conditions for independent work with the map by all participants. However, most often we will have a limited number of maps and thus be forced to operate in larger groups. In this case, we must personally ensure that during the march, each participant takes turns holding the map, reads it, is able to orient themselves at any moment, and finds their own position.

We conduct the game as follows. The groups locate their own position on the map. Next, we designate the march's destination. Initially, this may be an object dominant in the terrain (a village, forest, elevation point, road intersection), later—something more difficult to find (a small bridge, a small glade, a hillock, a pond, a forester’s lodge), and finally—only a location designated between specific points on the route, in a field, or in the forest.

The groups set off for the given point in turn, at intervals of 5—10 minutes, or head toward it via different routes, either designated by the instructor or chosen independently.

The group that reaches the designated point in the shortest time wins.

For younger and beginner participants, the route will need to be discussed in detail, and the map read together (participants will do this in turn).

For older participants, it is sufficient to designate only the point and leave them complete freedom in choosing the route. The leader of each group should only ensure that everyone collaborates in selecting the route and in orientation during the march.

Base such exercises on war stories or military tasks.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Map and March Inspection
body:
A march guide is chosen, who receives from the leader a secret instruction on where to lead the entire unit according to the map. (The route should be varied and conducted along secondary roads.) The remaining participants receive maps (aim to assign a map to each unit). They do not know the destination of the entire unit. Their task is to indicate at any moment, upon the leader’s request, the unit’s position on the map and to report changes that have occurred in the terrain (point out discrepancies between the terrain and the map’s situational and vertical depiction). The leader scores and evaluates the orientation results based on the answers received from individual march participants. The march guide should be rotated.

For rest during the exercises, we may introduce a seated game, such as:

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Terrain Recognition Game¹)
body:
This game reinforces the memorization of topographic symbols and provides practice in drawing them.

The instructor presents an imaginary sketch or one taken from a map, drawn within a grid of marked squares (square size: 3 × 3 cm). The number of squares may vary: from 4 × 4 (in the initial training period) to 10 × 10 (at a higher level of training).

Two examples of such sketches are provided.

Fig. 8.

In Fig. 8, we have a smaller sketch with few details and uncomplicated road directions. This will be used in the initial training period. Fig. 9 depicts varied terrain with many details and complex terrain line directions. It also contains certain

¹) Idea proposed by the author in the year 1924 in the monthly magazine *Czuj Duch*.

deficiencies that the youth should detect. (Find them.) This will be a sketch for older youth in the final training period.

Students draw a similar grid in their notebooks, matching the instructor’s sketch (it is possible to announce a reduction scale, such as a twofold or threefold reduction). Depending on the age and skill level of the youth, the instructor initially allows direct copying of the sketch with the goal: “who copies the symbols better.” At a higher level, the game will involve time-limited observation and memory-based copying of the sketch. The youth are allowed to look at the sketch for a set amount of time (5—10 minutes). Once the time is up, they attempt to recreate the observed sketch in their grids. Accuracy in the placement of symbols within the given squares and correct drawing of the symbols is required.

Negative points are assigned for each missing symbol, each incorrect direction or misplacement of a symbol, and each incorrectly drawn symbol. The lowest sum of negative points determines the winner.

Additionally, we will teach drawing and reading symbols as well as terrain relief using the so-called

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Topographic Dictation
body:
We can dictate a specific route by providing details of the terrain and the direction of communication lines. The youth then draws this route using appropriate topographic symbols at a predetermined scale and in accordance with the given cardinal directions. Once the youth has mastered drawing the symbols, we can apply this skill in exercises and games conducted while marching.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: On the March Along the Road
body:
Along a road varied with different terrain features, we send out individuals or groups. They record using topographic symbols:

Fig. 9.

A) terrain objects, B) type of terrain, C) terrain relief, D) the road itself at a certain scale, and finally, it is possible to produce

E) a proper sketch along the road.

With the youngest and least experienced, we begin with notes or a topographic drawing of individual objects (chapel, house, small bridge, brickworks), without marking their locations on the road or in the terrain.

We will pay attention to the fact of noting all terrain objects and their accurate depiction.

From the more experienced, we will require the indication of the type of terrain (forest, meadow, field, swamp, garden) and marking its extent, along with the ability to record the terrain's shape.

With the skilled, we will produce a correct sketch along the road, complete with an attached legend.

Everywhere, we will demand a neat and precise written report (see the chapter "Patrolling and Reconnaissance").

The team that notes and draws all road details most accurately and correctly wins.

Sketching, as a result of the ability to draw topographic symbols and the capacity to orient oneself in the terrain, should be applied as early and as frequently as possible in field training.

Making sketches is one of the direct goals of terrain studies. It can and should be the result of any observation, tracking, reconnaissance, scouting, patrolling, and—the final conclusion of every report in higher-level games.

The matter of sketching is somewhat neglected in the fieldwork of organizations and schools. This neglect, resulting from the lack of knowledge of sketching among youth work leaders, should be corrected. I am convinced that through the application of terrain games and exercises provided in the terrain studies section, this neglect will disappear¹).

A terrain sketch is an essential skill for every commander in wartime. Terrain sketches form the basis of attack and defense. Thanks to them, important decisions of higher commands are made. They are the most accurate and durable transmission of acquired information about the terrain and the enemy, additionally not requiring personal contact between the sketch creator and the person using it.

Topographic and perspective sketches are also an excellent way to preserve interesting terrain phenomena during summer hikes. They are: valuable, cherished, and pleasant records of excursion and tourist impressions, comparable to diaries, chronicles, and photographs.

The ability to sketch can be woven into almost every terrain game. The most common types of sketches incorporated into games will be: intersection sketches, route sketches, map sketches, and perspective sketches of smaller terrain sections.

To execute sketches, the following tools are necessary: a) a notebook without lines, with a hard cover, b) a ruler with millimeter divisions, c) a Bézard compass or a higher-quality compass, d) a pencil 3, an eraser, 3 pins.

These should become indispensable items of personal equipment, on par with a map.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Cross-Country March Using Topographic Signs
body:
Units or groups receive sheets marked with topographic signs in sequence.

Example (fig. 10):

¹) The booklet *Field Sketches for Scouts* by S. Gawkowski will facilitate learning sketching.

Fig. 10.

Starting point — Małka mill, then — bridge over the stream, roadside cross. From there, go northeast to a solitary wild pear tree and finally to the forester’s lodge. From the forester’s lodge south to the edge of the small woods, where the assembly point is marked with a small cross.

Possible approaches for patrols: a) send them out one after another along the same route; b) guide them to the same assembly point using different terrain signs; c) arrange routes so that all patrols return to the starting point (the instructor may prepare another game in the meantime).

Before departure, everyone copies the given signs (we score their execution).

At a more advanced level of this game, we may require the completion of a sketch of a section or the entire route traveled.

In all cases of our presence in the field with youth over the age of 15, we will continuously practice orientation using a map at any moment, whether on the march or during rest: a) by lines, b) by 2 points, c) by compass or sighting compass.

This will be conducted in the form of competitions between units as well as between groups. Orientation should be part of directional march games.

Orientation and map reading alone are not sufficient. A common flaw is the youth’s tendency to look only "as far as their own nose." A boy may point to the bridge he is standing on or the road he must turn onto on the map. However, he cannot name the village lying a few kilometers off the road. It is difficult for him to locate a distant, visible grove on the map. We must teach youth to observe the surrounding terrain broadly. This will be achieved by: a) constantly drawing attention to distant terrain features, b) requiring them to indicate these on the map, c) searching for distant topographic elements seen on the map in the terrain.

Exercises related to terrain formation should not be forgotten. Youth should be able to read terrain relief well.

For this purpose, triangulation and intermediate points should be frequently used. They should be compelled to march via the highest points, and more importantly, to choose hidden routes leading through valleys, depressions, saddles, etc., along the lowest lines of the terrain.

This skill will be acquired if we frequently practice reading relief through contour lines, requiring: a) determining the height of one’s own position, b) calculating the ascent or descent of the road between two points, c) finding places hidden from observation and potential fire.

Elements of these exercises should be included in the above-mentioned games as a special task or applied in games of another type.

To conclude this section, I present a larger terrain game as an example.

---

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Establishing a Defensive Line
body:
We are a military company tasked with occupying the line between the villages of Kicin and Wierzonka and organizing a defense there. (Fig. 11).

For this purpose, 1 platoon (which may be a single unit or several participants) will take position at the northern road junction in the village of Kicin, 1 squad of 2 platoon—on hill 102, the remainder of 2 at the road junction in the village of Wierzonka, while 3, held in reserve, will reach the village of Wierzenica with the task of establishing communication with the preceding platoons. All squads will submit reports on occupying their positions to the company commander, who will be located in front of the defensive line at the northern edge of the village of Kliny.

The starting point for these exercises will be the manor of Nowy Dwór.

Before departure, each group locates its position on the map. The instructor assesses the speed and accuracy of the orientation performed. Next, the groups

Fig. 11.

determine the time within which they are to occupy the designated positions. The instructor verifies the completion of this task as far as possible. He may send participants from opposing groups (individual exercise) with synchronized watches to control the individual positions. The boys assigned for control may have a further task—returning to their own units occupying the designated points. It is also possible to set a time for messengers to meet each other along with terrain sketches, giving them in turn new instructions to reach other units with certain orders.

This type of game can be expanded over a larger area into a series of orientation and directional exercises. The aim is to achieve as much movement in the terrain as possible, carried out based on the map by individual units as well as groups.

Among orientation games is the so-called "treasure hunt," which is elaborated in the next section.

---

author: Jan Jasiński
title: The Treasure of the Iroquois
body:
We are trappers who, after the last battle with the Indians, found birch bark on the slain old chieftain, bearing the following pictographic inscription:

Fig. 12.

The question arises as to what it means. All participants ponder this pictorial riddle. Eventually, it is concluded that the inscription conveys the following thought: "Follow the current of the stream 'Swift' to the weir (waterfall) located at the narrowing of the stream. There grows a broadleaf tree—an oak (as indicated by the drawn leaf). The aforementioned elements should be unknown to the general public but must be found in the immediate surroundings.

The next conclusion is that the oak likely contains further details.

The instructor personally takes the youngest to the oak, while the older boys are sent in groups with the instruction to preserve any further traces found in their original state.

The dispatched groups reach the oak and find an upward-pointing arrow carved into the tree bark, and in a small hollow on one of the large branches—a roll of birch bark with the following drawing:

Fig. 13.

We read it as: "Look to the east (it should be assumed from the place where the bark was found), and you will see a hill, forested on one side." The cross above the summit indicates that further information must be sought there.

Indeed, at the summit, we find a cross made of stones partially buried in the ground. What does it mean? Consider it. Everyone will conclude that this is where we must search.

It is likely that one of the participants will suggest lifting the central stone (let it be the larger one). If no such proposal is made, it should be suggested. We carefully lift the stone, beneath which we find a tin can (a box from paste, canned goods, etc.), and inside it, another piece of birch bark with a drawing:

Fig. 14.

The sight of this drawing suggests that somewhere in the terrain, there are three spruces of different sizes standing together. We find them and head toward the largest one, as indicated by the cross on the drawing. At the largest spruce, we find a stump with an Indian sign: 20 →, meaning: "search for a message 20 paces in the given direction." We find the message (also on birch bark) in another stump. This message again contains a drawing:

Fig. 15.

We read: "Dig to the west of the stump, and you will find lumps of gold." (Place some object in this spot.)

Depending on the available time, we may create more or fewer such intermediate stations, and according to the age and skill of the boys, we can make the pictorial rebuses more difficult.

---

author: Jan Jasiński
title: The Bandits' Treasure
body:
We are bandits. From our leader, we have received the order to retrieve a treasure hidden by his predecessors, about which he has the following information: a) Follow the ravine (gorge) located north of village A. Soon, you will see a huge rock. b) Stand on it so that you have the peak M in front of you, and then your right hand, stretched out to the side, will indicate the further direction. c) Walk in that direction for 20 meters to a hornbeam growing on the slope (all other trees around are beeches, so knowledge of trees determines further orientation). d) Stand on the slope above the hornbeam so that your gaze, directed over the first branch of the hornbeam and simultaneously to the right of the main trunk, falls on a cottage facing you sideways. On the extension (look through the chimney of that cottage), you will see a group of 5 spruces. e) Beneath the largest one, you will find the treasure.

This may be, as in the given case, information provided in full, or individual pieces of information may be placed in lists hidden at specific locations. These lists must be found by the searching groups (the leader’s envoys).
