author: Jan Jasiński
title: Hidden Rifles of the P.O.W. Scouts
body:
We are P.O.W. scouts. The location of our arms cache is changed after every exercise for security reasons. Therefore, before a new exercise, each unit member receives preliminary information about the cache’s location. Caution dictates that the search be conducted by individual scouts.

In this case, members of the P.O.W. received the following message from their commander: a) Go to the intersection of the roads leading from A to B and from C to D, and look for a letter there. b) Letter number 1 contains the message: "Head northwest to the edge of the small forest, to a heavily overgrown pine with twisted branches. Look for a letter." c) Letter number 2 reads: "Follow the edge of the small forest southwest. Beyond the wooden bridge by the third black alder, search for a letter."

Along the way, there may be another type of bridge, such as a concrete one, or a different species of alder, such as a white alder. These facts will then pose a challenge, as the youth—even those familiar with tree species—will search literally for the "third" alder, will see a bridge in general without distinguishing its construction, and will not immediately notice the adjectives "wooden" or "black." Through such "traps," we compel the youth to pay sharper attention while reading and to draw conclusions.

d) Letter number 3: Climb the alder, stand on the first branch, determine the north direction, and you will see two elevations. Go to the second one in order. In the pile of stones, the final message.

e) Letter number 4: Head southwest. A thicket of blackthorn bushes. You will receive a rifle.

At the final point, one of the game participants may be stationed, directing arrivals to a nearby assembly point, set apart from the march route.

Letters should be placed so that they are partially visible but at the same time difficult to notice, for example: under bark, in a crevice, in the ground near a tree, on a branch mimicking a leaf, under a stone, written on a stone, etc. They may be written in Morse code or encrypted (in this case, they should be written in cipher).

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Who First?
body:
Divide the youth into two groups. Each group sets out from a different starting point, receiving a route sketch (as in fig. 16).

The group's task is to reach the designated destination according to the provided sketch. This is essentially an off-road march. The marked terrain points are not visible from previous points and are located at great distances (up to 1 kilometers) from one another.

The march is conducted based on given directional angles, marked for a specific point.

One group starts from point A, the other from point B, moving along the same route toward each other to reach the opposite group's starting point. The group that reaches the final point of its route in the shortest time wins.

Fig. 16.

Note: a) Different directional angles are calculated for each group, depending on the direction of the march; b) directional angles are determined at the center of a given terrain feature (road intersection, small bridge); c) a compass should be used.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Directional Marches in the City
body:
A. Moving based on directional angles and the number of given steps, or precise meter measurements using a tape (game in a small area). The goal of this game may be searching for: a) a water hydrant in the city, b) a bird’s nest or an animal’s burrow in the park, etc.

B. Moving through city streets based on directional angles and a designated sequence of subsequent street corners, serving as new positions needed to determine the next directional angle.

C. Instead of a sketch for the entire route, we may designate only the directional angle to the next point. There, one must find a note containing the next directional angle. Then, reach the next point again, and so on.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: To the Rescue
body:
A person has been kidnapped for ransom. The pursuit sent out finds a note on the road with the words: "To village N — — signature."

The pursuit will consist of patrols, setting out in succession from a certain point. They locate, according to the map 1: 100.000, designated rest or overnight stops, about which the captured person informs by leaving messages in the form of letters.

In village N, further information must be obtained with the help of a discovered sign, letter, or by conducting an interview with people who indicate the bandits' further route.

Subsequent messages may be as follows: a) a small forest east of point 103, b) a mill on the river M, c) lake P, the mouth of stream K, etc.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: On Reconnaissance
body:
Each patrol is a team tasked with reaching a certain point. The patrol marches according to a map, having specific intermediate points along its route.

Patrols depart every few minutes. The patrol that accomplishes the task the fastest (running is not allowed) will perform best.

Initially, the task should be made easier by selecting a point that is simple to reach, such as a village or a road junction. The march will always take place along main roads.

For experienced groups, a more intricate route (even cross-country) should be used, with details that are harder to determine from the map, such as forest clearings, hills not marked with elevation points, small bridges, and the like.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Gathering Intelligence
body:
The instructor leaves notes at various points in the terrain (road intersections, forest edges, solitary trees, hills, ditch crossings, fences near houses, bridges, river bends, etc.).

These locations are provided to the patrols, which find the designated positions using a map and locate the left notes, copying their contents. The original notes left by the instructor must not be taken. The notes may contain instructive information: about the terrain, nature, the life of villagers, their customs, etc. They may also include—as a further challenge—orders related to reconnaissance. They may be encrypted or written in Morse code.

The patrol that finds all or the most pieces of intelligence, and whose members know the contents of the left notes, wins. Verify their knowledge through questions.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Messenger Service
body:
All participants in the game serve as messengers (a tale of the scouting messenger service during the struggle for independence, and the importance of such a messenger during war). They receive a verbal command from the commander (instructor) as follows: "Company N will occupy hill 104 at 20 o’clock."

¹) A messenger is an envoy sent to other units or unknown individuals.

²) A liaison is an envoy from their unit to higher formations or leading groups, from which they bring back orders.

Messengers, standing at attention, repeat the received order, then at a signal, they run (part of the way they sprint, part they march, part they crawl—depending on the terrain cover) a distance of 100—200 meters to a point specified by the instructor (the location of Company N’s commander). Upon reaching the designated spot, they return, line up at a distance of 15 paces from one another, and repeat or write down the content of the received order. If writing on slips of paper, they do so at the last moment. The best messengers are those who have not forgotten the command.

A. We can make the game more challenging by adding a report received from Company N’s commander (the instructor moves to the designated spot and provides new content, e.g.: "An enemy force the size of a company is outflanking us from the east").

B. It is also possible to use the delivery of written orders to a person who must be located at a specific point on the terrain. Messengers must find this point and locate the individual.

C. We create from 2 to 5 chains (relays) of messengers. We position them along a road or, preferably, directly in a field or forest.

The task of each chain will be to verbally transmit any order, with content common to all.

Messenger chains can be spaced even over a distance of 1 kilometers, depending on the number of participants. For ease, they can be arranged in an arc. Then, the instructor, without moving from their position, can easily become the recipient of the transmitted order. Message transmission can also be done by running. However, the run must not exceed the established norms: for those under 12 years of age—40 meters, under 16—60 meters, under 18—100 meters. Longer and more sustained runs may be used for youth over 17 years of age.

The aim of this game is not speed but, above all, the accuracy of the verbal order’s transmission.

In the case of written message delivery, the time of arrival determines the outcome (limit the running distance to the capabilities of the participants’ age).

D. We can effectively practice the liaison chain during a march on a road. We distribute pairs along our marching route, walking side by side on both sides of the road at intervals of 20—60 meters. This distance will depend on the time of day, terrain cover, and road bends.

Each liaison sees their predecessor, and in more difficult spots, such as road forks, they indicate the correct direction to the next. One side of the liaisons (e.g., the left) is the line transmitting orders forward, while the other (the right) is the line along which reports are sent backward.

Orders and factual reports, such as those about one’s own position, the terrain, and events occurring on it, should be fairly frequent.

The above exercises can also be conducted in winter, on skis.

If bicycles are available, they can be used as a variable means of locomotion for one liaison chain or as a fast-moving tool for individual messengers. In this case, all liaisons should be able to ride a bicycle. On water, we can use kayaks or boats as means of communication, or even employ swimming.

---

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Visual and Auditory Signals During March
body:
Alongside the use of messengers, young people should be familiarized with the simplest visual and auditory signals listed below, which are used by the military.

| Command | Whistle Signal | Sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Attention" | 1 short whistle | Arm raised vertically upward and held in that position. |
| "March" | 2 long whistles | Quick bending of the raised arm, fist at shoulder height. |
| "Double time, march" |  | Repeated quick execution of the "March" sign. |
| "Direction" |  | Turn in the given direction and point with the hand. |
| "Halt" |  | Slow lowering of the arm sideways downward, previously raised upward. |
| "Take cover" |  | Arm extended to the side, palm facing downward or the action of taking cover. |
| "Assembly" | 1 long whistle | Extending arms horizontally to the sides, then crossing them on the chest. |
| "Skirmish line" |  | Swinging arms to the sides from the "arms in front of chest" position. |
| "Enemy" |  | Raising a cap held in the hand or on a stick upward. |

These signals will be practiced during protected march and approach march as commands from the leaders of individual teams.

During a protected march, the leader should be positioned with the scouts or the point.

Methodical training of visual and auditory signaling in the field.

In scouting groups or others that include Morse or Semaphore signaling in their training, we can conduct a series of games that will accelerate learning and make the results more fruitful. Interest and necessity will be the incentive for faster, practical mastery of the alphabet. However, even in groups that do not study signaling, the following games can be an excellent way to diversify activities and bring participants closer to this knowledge. As a rule, we do not consider the fact that young people may not know the Morse or Semaphore alphabet. Precisely, signaling games in the field are a method that teaches practical use of the agreed-upon alphabet.

In the initial learning phase, each participant should have the individual alphabets noted in a notebook or on a sheet (prepare machine-printed copies of the Morse alphabet) in a clear form so that at any moment one can recall certain signs. It will not harm anyone if individual trainees glance at the sheet. They will more easily memorize the signs. However, in the later stages of training, the use of an alphabet notebook should not be allowed.

Training should begin with the direct method—demanding that young people repeat the actions performed by the instructor.

# Morse Alphabet According to Exercise Groups

| I gr. | II gr. | III gr. |
| --- | --- | --- |
| e . i . . s . . . u . . . . 5 . . . . . | † — m — — o — — — ch — — — — O (zero) — — — — — | a . . — u . . — v . . . — 4 . . . . — |
| IV gr. | V gr. | VI gr. |
| u — . d — . . b — . . . 6 — . . . . | g — — . w . — — p . — — . x — . . — | c — . — . r . — . l . — . . f . . — . |
| VII gr. | VIII gr. | IX gr. |
| y — . — — k — . — 2 . . — — 3 . . . — — | 1 . — — — — j . — — — 9 — — — — . | ż — — . . 7 — — . . . . 8 — — — . |

Fig. 17.

The instructor begins by first showing the I group of the Morse alphabet (see fig. 17) or the I circle of the Semaphore alphabet (see fig. 17a). Then, they demand the immediate execution of the above signs by all trainees. It is good to arrange them in two rows facing each other (not only do they perform the signs, but they also see them in the correct arrangement). Practice the letters slowly at first. Then proceed to increasingly faster arrangements, eventually performing them at varying speeds and in different orders (randomly). Once the directions become mechanized, though not necessarily in perfect form for everyone, we can move on to the next II group or II circle, repeating the entire system, and so on. Meanwhile, we can apply the following games to individual groups or circles: 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9 listed below.

Once the arrangement of individual letters is understood with mechanized movement, point out the letters that are the reverse of each other in their position. Practice the aforementioned games again on these. For a break between the above games, practice:

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Signal Kim's Game
body:
These games will allow youth to relax after active signaling games, while also demanding: observation skills, attention, and memory.

A signaling dictation can be conducted in two ways: a) the instructor dictates — the youth write using the appropriate alphabet, b) the instructor sends commands in the alphabet for execution — the youth carry them out quickly.

Both dictation and commands should be linked to observations made in the field, connected to facts that exist in the given terrain. Commands should have a purpose: improving skills, abilities, etc.

For the signal kim's game, signs of the alphabet are needed: written and the given signaling alphabet, made with ink on stiff paper, each sign separately.

The kim's game can be conducted in various ways: a) We show part of the signs of a given alphabet (10—20), instructing them to be memorized and faithfully reproduced. b) We present part of the written signs in a certain order. The players must reproduce them in the given order using the signaling alphabet signs. c) We reverse exercise b).

# SEMAPHORE ALPHABET ACCORDING TO PRACTICE CIRCLES

FIRST CIRCLE

SECOND CIRCLE

THIRD CIRCLE

FOURTH CIRCLE

FIFTH CIRCLE

SIXTH CIRCLE

SEVENTH CIRCLE

Dark flag, motionless

Light flag, changing its position

Fig. 17a.

d) We create words and sentences from the signs, instructing their reproduction.

A variation of the ordinary signal kim's game will be the grid signal kim's game (see the analogous terrain recognition kim's game on page 146). The variety of its execution is analogous to the ordinary kim's game.

In groups that have mastered signaling, the use of the Morse or Semaphore alphabet should not be ceremonial. This skill should be applied at every step, not only in specially conducted games. A good opportunity for practicing signaling will be a secured march. Signaling between individual members of the marching column or reconnaissance patrol will diversify this march, increasing the youth's interest. However, it is necessary to ensure that such communication is natural, related to the group's tasks, connected to the terrain, and forces the youth to focus their attention on the surroundings. The purposefulness of signaling will increase if an enemy unit is operating in the terrain. The purposefulness and frequency of using signaling will depend on the ingenuity of the field game leader.

---

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Setting Up Signals
body:
Several groups participate in the game simultaneously. In each group, there are several participants wearing headgear (representing dashes) and several without (representing dots). Initially, the instructor calls out letters, later words, and finally sentences, while the youth arrange themselves in lines or rows, forming the pattern of dashes and dots corresponding to the called words. Accuracy and speed of arrangement are scored. Leaders familiar with the alphabet are appointed to organize and manage the lines.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Signal Ball
body:
Place a punchball in a small pit. Everyone sits around it. Each participant represents one letter of the alphabet or a name: an animal, geographical term, etc. The instructor or one of the designated boys signals from a distance greater than 100 meters a letter, e.g., "g," or a name. The boy assigned to the letter "g" or the given name then runs to the ball and tries to tag the others, who scatter. The same game can be played using auditory signals with a whistle (short whistle — dot, long whistle — dash).

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Collective Decoding of a Dispatch
body:
The patrols form rows (other formations are also permissible) with their backs to the signaling instructor, who stands at a distance of at least 150 meters from the rows. He holds signal flags and a whistle. At the first whistle blast, the last boys at the end of each row turn to face him.

The instructor transmits a letter or word to them using the flags. At the second whistle signal, they turn back to their previous position, and the next boys from the end of the row turn to face the instructor, who then transmits another, subsequent letter or word to them. This continues until all members of the row have received individual letters or words. Once the dispatch has been transmitted in this manner, the rows scatter in different directions upon an agreed signal. There, they assemble the individual letters (words) and deliver the completed dispatch in writing to the instructor. The evaluation will depend on: the accuracy of the decoded dispatch and the speed of its delivery.

---

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Elimination
body:
We arrange the youth in a relaxed double rank or quadruple rank (intervals and distances of 2 metres). The covering pairs (or fours) are assigned the name of a single letter or any short word. The instructor, standing in front of the column at a distance of 150 paces, calls out individual letters (or words) in varying order. Upon hearing their assigned letter (or word), the corresponding pairs or fours begin a run. They always start the run to the left and from the front of the rank, circle around the last person, sprint along the rear of their rank until they reach the right-flank member, then pass them and return from the front to their original positions. The winner of this run and the second-place finisher (in the case of a quadruple rank) proceed to further rounds. The rest sit down and form passive positions in the ranks. From the winners, we form new pairs or fours under a different name. In this way, we create more and more 'dead points,' and fewer participants take part in the run (though all continue to listen). Eventually, one winner remains—the one demonstrating the best knowledge of the alphabet, quick orientation, and speed. A consolation competition may also be introduced for those eliminated in the first half of the game.

---

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Signal Relay Race
body:
Several rows are formed. On the instructor’s signal given by a whistle, the first in each row, holding flags (which can be a stick with a handkerchief tied to it), run to the instructor positioned at least 100 meters in front of the rows. The instructor quietly gives them a letter. Upon hearing it, the runners take their positions opposite their groups, level with the instructor, and signal the letter to their group. After signaling, they leave the flags in place and move away in the opposite direction from their row. As soon as the row understands the given letter, the next participant runs to the instructor, who provides another letter to signal to their row. The row that decodes the message accurately and delivers it the fastest wins (the row leader records and assembles the given letters). We may give each runner entire words or even sentences.

After mastering letters, we can provide runners with words and then short sentences. The words and sentences should be nonsensical and unrelated. This arrangement of messages prevents guessing and forces maximum attention on the signaled signs.

When conducting signaling exercises and games, the instructor must remember two fundamental principles: a) Signaling should take place at distances that prevent vocal communication.

b) The distance for signaling in initial games should not be less than 100 meters.

We must always remember that signaling exercises and games should take place in natural conditions, meaning in larger spaces and over greater distances.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Deciphering Secret Telegrams
body:
The instructor obtains rolls of old, unused telegraph tapes from post offices or railway offices. By selecting certain words, they assemble a series of telegrams with mysterious and intriguing content. These telegrams are left along the route of their unit's march (they should be in an envelope—addressed to someone), creating a natural need to read them. Knowledge of the alphabet proves indispensable here. Such an adventure can be woven into a series of games of other types.

When the youth are well acquainted with the Morse alphabet and can use it in the field, this skill can be utilized for larger signaling games, as listed below.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Individual Competition in Receiving a Telegram
body:
To test the signaling skills of individual participants, we use the following game. We arrange all participants loosely, spread out in width and depth, while we ourselves, from a point visible to everyone and at least 200 meters away from the nearest boy, transmit a telegram composed of several or a dozen or so unrelated words with no thematic connection.

The speed of transmission will depend on the training level of the youth. The telegram may be sent by the best signaler. To evaluate groups (patrols) consisting of a larger number of participants, we can form trios (in the case of three groups) at one location, composed of individuals from different groups. By summing the number of words correctly received by all members of a group and dividing by the number of group members, we obtain the score for the best patrol.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Who Faster?
body:
There are two enemy groups in the field, separated by a distance of 500 to 2000 meters. Their advance guards are to occupy a certain point, preferably a hill located equidistant from both main force positions. (Fig. 18). Along their march route, the advance guards leave behind one signaling station (x 2) in communication with the station (x 1) at the main unit.

Fig. 18.

The advance guards reach the hill, where a skirmish ensues. Simultaneously, they dispatch messengers to their signaling stations (x 2) with a written message of the following content: “The enemy, in the strength of one company, is marching on hill 99. Assistance as quickly as possible is necessary.” This dispatch is then relayed to the main force using flags or signaling boards. The victorious group is the one whose main forces, thanks to the received dispatch, occupy hill 99 more quickly.

Note: The game’s premise should not be known to the boys; only the order for the main forces to halt at the designated locations should be issued, simultaneously instructing the advance guard to reach the marked hill and leave a signaling station en route at a location where communication with the main force is possible.

Several intermediate stations may be established between the hill and the main force position.

Signaling Station. During training, it should consist of two individuals: a scribe and a signaler. Later, a third person—the commander—is added. The station’s operations will be based on selecting an appropriate background for the signaling boards and occupying a position where the neighboring station is clearly visible. However, in special cases, it must be remembered that the station should not be spotted by the enemy.

The signaler receives individual signs and dictates them to the scribe: initially as separate marks (dot, dash, etc.), later as letters. The scribe repeats the given sign (letter) and records it. When transmitting, the scribe dictates the sign (letter) from the written dispatch, while the signaler repeats and signals it. These roles should be frequently rotated.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Chain Race of Signal Stations
body:
We set up on level or undulating terrain two or more chains of signal stations (each patrol provides one chain). A chain may consist of two or more stations.

The first stations receive a written dispatch from the game leader through their messengers, then transmit the dispatch to the next stations using signaling.

The chain that fastest delivers the dispatch to its final station in unchanged form wins.

Stations in the chain are placed in the terrain so that each subsequent station sees only the previous station.

A complication in this game will be requiring a reply to the sent dispatch. For this purpose, the dispatch should be composed to compel an answer. A variation of the game may involve interrupting the signal chain by introducing a messenger: on foot, by bicycle, by kayak, etc.

---

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Observing Enemy Signaling
body:
In undulating and varied terrain, we establish one or more signaling stations operating in a certain direction, concealed from other sides.

Patrols dispatched from a certain point are to detect enemy stations, observe them, and report back the content of the message, specifying the station's position. The signaling station operates for a set time from 15 to 30 minutes (depending on the size of the exercise area), transmitting the message at 2—3-minute intervals. The content of the message is always the same.

The patrol that brings back the correct content of the signaled message the fastest wins.

The game leader may also serve as the signaling station.

Patrols noticed by the station fail their task—however, they should still read the transmitted message.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Elephant Hunters
body:
Terrain covered with thickets and bushes, with varied topography, featuring a height in the center dominating the area, bounded by natural lines (a river, forest edge, road). The size of the terrain ranges from 2—3 kilometers to ².

One of the patrols is a herd of elephants hiding in the jungle (they must not cross the defined boundaries). The other patrols (3—4 in number) form elephant-hunting parties. They establish a signaling station on the hill, which overlooks the elephants' movements and directs the hunting parties accordingly via short dispatches. Each hunting party should be marked with a letter, which is placed at the beginning of a dispatch. This indicates that the dispatch concerns that particular party. The objective of the game is to surround the elephant herd with the hunting parties within a set time, for example, 1½ hours. If this does not occur, the elephants win.

The "wise elephants" may also read the dispatches and use them to mislead the hunters. The signaling station may be operated by the instructor, who should, in any case, remain near the station to regulate the game's progress. The initial positioning of the hunting parties and the elephant herd can be determined using a map or signaling dispatches.

We must not forget auditory signaling. It has fully permeated everyday life today and will dominate future warfare. Every well-organized unit beginning training in auditory signaling should procure an old buzzer telephone or construct a telegraph key independently. In the worst case, a system of tapping on resonant objects or using a whistle can be employed. Familiarity with the Morse alphabet, on which auditory training will be based, will facilitate conducting these games.

In the Morse method, we phonetically distinguish two sounds: a) short — *tit* (dot) — lasts half a second. b) long — *taa* (dash) — lasts 1 raised to the power of 1/2 seconds.

Pauses between individual sounds should not exceed half a second; between letters, 1¹/₂ seconds; between words, 2¹/₂ seconds (6 *tit* sounds).

In gradual training, we can apply the entire system of preliminary games designed for visual signaling, slightly modifying them. A whistle or a strong buzzer will be used to produce sounds. Additionally, the following games will be conducted:

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Tit, Taa
body:
Form parallel lines with 4 participants each, spaced across any terrain at a distance of 50 meters apart. Individual participants should be positioned within up to 10 meters of each other, so they can pass a message sequentially using spoken sounds (tit-tit-taa, etc.) without excessive strain. The instructor delivers a message, in the form of words or a single sentence, to the first boys in each line. The last boys return the message to the instructor, who by then has appeared at the ends of the telegraph lines. It is permissible to note down the received message at each station. However, ensure the message is not passed on paper. Do not allow direct contact between two nearest neighbors or verbal communication. Announce this rule and unconditionally remove from the game any neighbors who do not comply. In cases of blatant violation, disqualify the entire line. The same game can be conducted using whistle signaling (each player must have a whistle). In this case, increase the distance between boys to 100 meters.

---

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Broken Bridge — Stop the Train
body:
A double-track railway line, winding in sections, running through undulating terrain. We deploy two competing teams along the track, on both sides of it, in the ditches (do not position on the track). The distance between individual relay stations may reach up to one kilometer.

We may set up any number of stations. However, do not exceed 5 kilometers in length due to the time lost in deployment. To minimize time loss, individual stations should be positioned directly from the starting point. This will provide an opportunity to achieve a more challenging point on the map, as we may designate a culvert or a location 100 meters from a crossing, etc., as the station. Near crossings, the relay station should always be positioned so that the crossing is behind it, ensuring that traffic at the crossing does not hinder message reception. We will also introduce a punctuality exercise by designating a specific time for occupying the station. The message (content as in the title) may be transmitted via: a) foot messengers, b) whistle signaling, c) optical signaling.

Before starting the game, verify that all stations have taken their positions. The last stations send an agreed readiness signal. Once it is relayed through intermediate stations to the first stations, only then do the first stations begin simultaneous transmission of the message. Each station must have its own call signal, known to neighboring stations. The instructor, equipped with a bicycle, may check reception at individual stations while also receiving the message from the final ones.

Signaling games are excellent for night exercises in the form of light signaling. It is worthwhile to adapt one of the above games to conduct it at night using battery-powered flashlights.

Below is an example of a typical nighttime light signaling game combined with orientation exercises.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Occupying Positions
body:
Flat terrain, varied with roads, woodlands, and buildings, from which a dominant point is visible: a church tower, the roof of a tall building, a hill. Before the game, the instructor places lists at certain points in the area, informing about the nocturnal life of insects or animals, or lists requiring answers to certain natural history questions—related to the night. The assembly of individual patrols is carried out using an alarm network, designating a common meeting place for all patrols. Only there, at the hour specified on the envelope, is the following order opened:

"Find the light signaling station located in the N.W. direction.

Each patrol will receive individual orders from the station, designating its appropriate positions. March in a secure formation.

After occupying the designated position, find and copy the hidden lists there. The station will begin transmitting new orders at the hour 22.30 and the next at the hour 23.15. Execute them strictly. Patrols read and note all dispatches but carry out only the dispatch intended for them.

A dispatch for a given patrol begins with the name of the patrol's emblem.

The patrol that flawlessly reads all transmitted dispatches, executes the orders issued for it within the prescribed time, finds all the lists, and is not late to the final assembly point wins.

Be Prepared!

Maned Horse, Troop Leader.

Janowa Dolina, the 20 of July, at 19 o'clock."

The Troop Leader transmits dispatches personally or with the help of assistants, having prepared the entire route of the patrols and the content of the dispatches. Dispatches should be as short as possible but clear. They are transmitted only once, and therefore this game can only be conducted with patrols for whom light signaling is not a novelty. This game should be conducted in terrain familiar to the youth. There should be twice as many points with lists as there are patrols. Patrols should not meet at the points where lists are hidden. Before the game, it should be checked whether the signaling station will be visible from each point. The time for transmitting the next dispatch must be calculated according to the path of the patrol that receives instructions last, plus 15 minutes reserve for unforeseen circumstances. The last dispatch provides a common meeting place for all. There, the Troop Leader receives reports and evaluates the results of the games. This game can be expanded and made more difficult by crossing the patrol routes and introducing competition between patrols, according to the principle: "See and hear without being seen or heard."

---

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Collecting Papers
body:
In the woods lying outside the city, a common and uncivilized phenomenon is the littering of papers. Pointing out that this should not be done will be good and beneficial for the future.

We recommend collecting papers abandoned in the forest. Children gather them in groups at one location. For hygienic reasons, they should not be allowed to collect them by hand. For this purpose, we instruct each child to cut a stick and sharpen its end—picking up papers is only permitted with the stick. The group that collects the most papers within a set time wins.

An extension of this activity could be burying the collected papers or burning them.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Collecting the Wounded from the Battlefield
body:
On a certain defined area, the wounded are placed in various locations, more or less concealed. In each location, there are as many wounded as there are groups participating in the exercise. Each wounded individual is assigned to a specific group and carries a card or any distinctive mark. From the dressing station, medical patrols set out with the task of finding their assigned wounded and bringing them back to the dressing station. Patrols consist of four young people. Patrols may use stretchers made by themselves. In competing groups, there may be several patrols.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: To the Rescue of the Airman
body:
There are two enemy groups separated by concealed terrain. At a certain moment, they receive news that two aircraft have crashed in their forward area. The task of each group will be to reach the crash site, provide first aid to the airmen (bandaging the head, broken arms, and legs), and transport them to the starting positions. Caution must be maintained, as the enemy may be present in the forward area. The group that finds the airmen first wins. The injured airmen may be specially designated boys. It is permissible to recapture the airman. The recapture can be carried out by a numerically stronger unit (the group may split into smaller units for faster discovery). The airman’s location can be determined using a directional angle.

A series of exercises in which youth must demonstrate knowledge of first aid (¹) can be conducted as a competition between patrols. For these games, an appropriate amount of dressing materials, disinfectants, etc., must be mobilized. After distributing the materials, patrols begin performing the designated actions at the instructor’s signal. Efforts should be made to ensure that

1) In learning first aid, use the following books: Dr. Dudziński J. *A Scout Brings Help to His Neighbor*. Dr. Hilarowicz H. *First Aid in Emergencies*. Szyryński W. *The Scout Ambulance*.

all patrol members have some task. In evaluation, the quality and precision of the work performed, followed by the speed of execution, should be taken into account.

From time to time, staging should be employed—that is, creating situations in which first aid becomes a natural life necessity or closely resembles one.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Leg Fracture
body:
We organize a free-form game involving running. A boy (or girl) who is in on the scenario falls, writhing in pain. After a brief examination, the instructor determines that a bone in the lower leg has been fractured. Consequently, he issues a series of orders related to first aid for this unfortunate accident. He assigns specific tasks to the more responsible boys: a) preparing splints, a stretcher, cotton wool, and bandages, b) removing the shoe and sock from the injured leg.

He designates boys to assist in applying the dressing. He sends one (who is in on the scenario) to fetch a cart from the nearest village, etc. A general sense of tension and interest arises. After the dressing is applied, this interest should be utilized. Explaining the necessity of skilled rescue using this example, he organizes exercises—a patrol game. Each patrol designates a boy with a "broken leg," then repeats the rescue method demonstrated by the troop leader. This is done once without competition, and then repeated as an emulation, noting each element of first aid performed. After the explanation, the staged accident is revealed.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Disaster
body:
Arrange, with the help of an acquaintance familiar to you but unknown to the boys, an accident along the route of your march in the form of: a) a passerby who has fainted; b) an unconscious cyclist who has crashed into a tree (a broken bicycle handlebar also requires repair); c) a drowning person; d) a drowned person pulled from the water, surrounded by a helpless group of rural youth, etc.

Note: In all such exercises, pay attention to: organization, division of labor — utilizing many boys for assistance, the calmness of the rescuers, speed, and purposefulness of action.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Excellence in Concealment
body:
One group conceals itself along a road over a certain distance, utilizing terrain depressions and cover.

The second group, moving in patrol formation, observes the sides of the road. It calls out anyone spotted who is poorly concealed.

The roles are then switched. The group with the greater number of well-concealed participants wins.

Note that the concealment location must also ensure the possibility of observation.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Ambush
body:
One party, sent ahead, conceals itself at a location designated by the leader or chosen by themselves (limit the route by designating a point before which the ambush should be set).

The second party, ensuring its security, marches along the road. (It sends a security patrol as the advance guard and a group to the rear as the rear guard).

The group on the march wins if it discovers the ambush through its scouts. Otherwise, victory goes to the ambushing group. The ambush attack should be directed at the main forces or the rear guard.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: The Best Report
body:
One patrol occupies a certain area: in front of a village, on a hill, etc.

Other patrols are on reconnaissance. We send them out every 5 minutes in the direction of the enemy's defensive line. Their task is to scout the enemy's force deployment and report on it.

The enemy deploys their group in any manner, without changing its position during observation by individual patrols. Their task is also to observe the patrols and report on their behavior.

The patrol that delivers the best, most precise written observations, while simultaneously being seen the least by the enemy line, wins.

---

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Enemy Patrols in the Field
body:
Divide the youth into two groups—patrols. Each group marches along a designated route in a secure formation. The routes are arranged so that they have common points of contact. The route may be a circular path along which the two groups move toward each other. The opponents are aware of the possibility of encountering one another and thus maintain great caution.

The patrol that prevails is the one that:

- a) first spots the enemy through its scouts,
- b) having spotted the enemy, is able to organize an ambush,
- c) bypasses the enemy while still observing and noting their formation and the arrangement of individuals within it,
- d) having bypassed the enemy, follows them undetected,
- e) having allowed the enemy’s vanguard to pass, attacks their main unit or rear guard.

The game leader should be positioned at a possible point of contact between the two groups. They will resolve any disputes.

If simultaneous sighting occurs (as in point a), the opponents then separate until they lose sight of each other, after which the game continues.

In the scenario described in point c, mutual visibility may occur at various points; in such cases, the patrol that delivers the better report and observes more of the enemy prevails.

---

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Approaching the Enemy
body:
One group serves as the outpost, positioned at the edge of a forest, village, etc. The foreground in front of the outpost should be varied. The outpost deploys two to three sentries (a sentry consists of 2 persons) as its security.

The second group, knowing approximately the location of the outpost, attempts to surprise it. For this purpose, it sends scouts to reconnoiter the positions of the sentries, trying to bypass them or capture them by silent calling. Approaching and calling the sentries from a distance of 10—20 paces, depending on the terrain, is considered their capture. The attacking group wins if it bypasses the sentries or captures them and attacks the outpost. The outpost, warned by the sentries, wins. It may execute a counterattack.

A more advanced form of patrolling will be terrain reconnaissance, always based on marching in patrol formation and reporting along with a topographic or perspective sketch (¹). These will be games for youth above the age of 15. In case of inability to sketch, we will limit ourselves to a written report only.

Reconnaissance games will involve examining and describing various terrain features within the scope of: communication (railway lines, roads), waters and crossings (rivers, bridges, fords), soils and vegetation (marshes and forests), and other terrain features (villages, brickworks).

They will include an element of competition in good and accurate sketching as well as discussing the given object. We will simultaneously pay attention to

¹) The school drawing program should take into greater account the principles of terrain perspective.

the correctness of the report and the speed of reconnaissance execution.

The description of a given terrain or object will include its positive and negative features in relation to a certain tactical task.

The description should be brief and clear, presenting the most important details of the given object.

Initially, we will provide reconnaissance patrols with points to which they must respond. Later, we will require that the game participants know them by heart.

These questions will vary for individual terrain features, namely:

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Bridge Reconnaissance by Enemy Patrols
body:
The youth are divided into two patrols or more. They are tasked with conducting reconnaissance of a bridge over a river situated in a forested area. These patrols are mutual enemies. Objective: each patrol must perform reconnaissance without being seen by the opposing patrol. To achieve this, patrols must survey the surrounding terrain before reaching the target and ensure they are not observed by other patrols.

Patrols are dispatched simultaneously from different points on the terrain, varying in distance from the reconnaissance target, or from a single point at intervals of 5—10 minutes.

The instructor should reach the reconnaissance target before the patrols arrive, conceal themselves nearby, and observe.

In their reports, patrols should include not only the bridge reconnaissance but also the time at which they spotted other patrols and details of their activities.

In all types of reconnaissance games, patrols must be informed of the time and place of assembly.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Run 1
body:

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Projectile Combat:
body:
a) pine cones (lying on the ground, dried, and thus light), b) snowballs.

In these combats, conducted between two parties, the fighters are separated by a neutral zone, the width of which will be adjusted to the average throwing strength of the given group. This way, we avoid the unpleasant consequences of stronger and accurate throws. A participant in the game, hit anywhere, is eliminated as killed. Aiming at the head is not allowed. The party that, within a specified time, has killed more opponents or pushed the opposing party back from the neutral line wins. A rule may be introduced that a person hit in the head does not count as killed, but the one who hit them is eliminated instead.

The game can be varied by organizing the defense of a fortress (a hill, embankment, fortress made of packed snow or sand, a building).

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Capture of the Flags
body:
We choose a forested area with clear side boundaries (forest edge, water, road). At a distance of 300—500 paces, flags are placed in two locations known to all participants. Two teams compete to capture these flags. Each team divides into defense and attack (scouts). The defense positions sentries every 30—100 paces (depending on cover) across the entire width of the chosen area. The line of these posts is at least 50 paces away from their own flags. The attack (scouts) is scattered across the entire terrain in front of their own defense line. Scouts have the following tasks: sneaking through the sentry line, capturing the flag (there may be several flags in each team), and bringing it to a specific designated place. Along the way, they must evade scouts from the opposing team, who have the same tasks regarding the enemy’s flags.

The game relies on mutual surprise. Touching an opponent with a hand is equivalent to taking them prisoner. Only sentries have the right to take prisoners. Attackers fight quietly, avoid opponents (both scouts from the attack and sentries from the defense), try to sneak unnoticed through the sentry line, and flee if detected. Cooperation among attackers is desirable, for example, one distracts a sentry by fleeing, while another takes advantage of the situation to slip behind the sentry toward the flags. A scout returning with a captured flag can be caught, in which case the flag must be returned to its original place.

Scouts do not capture opponents; they only try to remember them.

A scout or a member of the defense spotted by an opposing scout receives a negative point.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Spy Crossing the Border
body:
The game takes place over a larger area, preferably along a road running through wooded or hilly terrain. The Border Protection Corps has outposts positioned every half a kilometer, set up at road intersections, in buildings, or on elevations. Between and ahead of the outposts, patrols (each consisting of between **2** and **3** riflemen) move about in numbers unknown to the spies.

Spy groups (unfamiliar with the terrain) start from a point **1—3** kilometers away from the outpost line. They have maps scaled **1** : **100.000** with the outpost positions marked on them (reported by their intelligence) and are also aware of the existence of patrols.

Spy groups consist of **5** to **8** individuals. There may be several such groups. Each spy group selects, based on the map, locations between outposts suitable for sneaking through and advances cautiously, covered by scouts. To hinder their activities, we tie the hands of two spies together with a rope (they carry more weapons—less freedom of movement).

A location in the terrain is also designated where spy units gather after crossing and where everyone assembles after the game ends.

The spy groups that win are those that do not encounter "patrols" or manage to hide from or escape them.

Border Protection Corps patrols win if they capture more than **50** percent of the spies. A spy, once caught (touched by hand), can no longer escape and must submit to the orders of the Border Protection Corps riflemen, who must, however, escort them to their outpost. An alerted outpost may send additional patrols or redeploy patrols operating in the area to threatened locations. Spies may disguise themselves.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Enemy Patrols
body:
Enemy patrols operate within an area of 5—10 kilometers by ². They march along roads or terrain lines designated for them based on map 1: 100.000. The assigned march routes may align or oppose each other in direction along certain road segments and frequently intersect. This interconnection of routes can occur at various points and across different lines among all patrols (if there are few) or a subset of them (if there are more than 5). We will complicate this exercise by expanding the operational area, primarily by assigning patrols special tasks within military reconnaissance or regional-natural-economic reconnaissance.

Each patrol must strive to complete its assigned tasks in such a way as to avoid being seen by others while simultaneously observing and monitoring the activities of enemy patrols.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: On the Paths of Your Patrol
body:
We create a route (there may be several) forming a closed loop. From one point, two units set out in opposite directions. The marching time varies depending on the time available. In the first stage, which constitutes 1/3 of the time allocated for the game, each unit should cover half of the designated route and meet at a specified location. The longer such a route, the better for the exercise itself. For example, I provide such a route for a half-day excursion (6 hours).

During the first 2½ hours of marching, the units perform: a sketch of their route, reconnaissance of a chosen or designated object, a perspective sketch from any point, and place a series of letters, the locations of which are marked on the sketch. The route sketch is made by individual members of the given unit on designated sections. These sections combine to form a whole. In this way, every patrol member is compelled to sketch directly.

After a certain time and at a certain place, the units moving toward each other meet. This meeting may serve as an opportunity for a new game if we assume that the unit which first notices and observes the opponents' actions wins, based on the principles: to see and hear without being seen or heard. After the meeting, there is a rest period, completion of sketches, and exchange of the route sketches made, on which are marked: the location of hidden letters, the reconnaissance object, and the position for the perspective sketch. The middle part lasts 1 hour.

After the rest, based on the exchanged sketches, the units continue their journey, finding the left letters, conducting reconnaissance of the same object, and drawing a perspective sketch from the same point.

Finally, the units reach the starting point from which they marched. There, their work is compared and evaluated.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Raid on a Bivouac
body:
One patrol is assigned a specific point on the map (a hill in varied terrain, a clearing in the forest, etc.), where it is to establish a bivouac and secure it with outposts and sentries or just sentries. This patrol sets out 10 minutes earlier than the remaining, larger part of the game participants. The rest are divided into 3 or 4 patrols. These patrols receive orders to attack the established bivouac. They are given the bivouac’s location on the map and assigned a direction (according to the cardinal points) from which each patrol is to strike the bivouac. Additionally, the exact time for the attack to begin is set (synchronize watches before dispersing).

Each patrol selects its route using the map, carefully examines the terrain nearest the bivouac, and devises a plan for the closest approach, conducted in complete concealment. En route, patrols advance in patrol formation.

The patrols encircling the bivouac will have a more challenging task, as they must hurry to take up attack positions. Other groups will need to delay their march. If the attacking patrols manage to occupy their attack positions unnoticed and execute a simultaneous joint assault, victory is theirs. However, if the bivouac patrol, thanks to its sentries or dispatched scouts, knows the positions of the opponents and preempts their attack by directing its own assault against any of the attacking units, it is considered that the bivouac patrol has repelled the enemy.

A variation of this game may be assigned to the bivouac patrol:

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Slipping Away from an Area Threatened by Encircling Advancing Patrols
body:
We then mark the time within which the bivouac can be struck.

This may occur either at the moment the enemy is discovered or, regardless of that, at the arrival of a specified time. The bivouacking group wins if they slip away unnoticed from the encircling attackers. They are allowed to flee but must retreat the moment they see the enemy before them. The task of the attacking patrols will be to prevent anyone from the bivouac from escaping. Successively driving them back toward the bivouac and ultimately blocking their escape routes will be considered a victory.

The bivouac site is marked by lighting a campfire.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Breaking Through a Route Blocked by the Enemy
body:
**Assumption.** The White party has dispatched a reconnaissance platoon marching from locality C (position of the White main forces) to B.

The enemy is reported along the line A—B.

**Execution.** The platoon marches in a secured formation and surveys the terrain not only ahead but also observes its rear. Meanwhile, the Reds, in company strength (also in a secured formation), emerge from locality A onto the road leading to B and cut off the White platoon from their main forces in C.

After some time, the White platoon’s rear guard spots the Reds and, from an elevated point in the terrain, assesses the enemy’s superior strength.

The White platoon commander, upon seeing this situation, acts as follows: a) Dispatches messengers to locality C with reports about the enemy cutting them off. These messengers face the difficult task of crossing terrain occupied by the enemy’s march. They carry two messages: one factual regarding the platoon’s intentions, the other deceptive. The first is to be destroyed if the messenger is captured by the enemy, while the second should be found by them.

b) Prepares an ambush at a suitable point further along the route. The first ambush, consisting of a 5-th or 6-th part of the platoon, is ordered to let the enemy’s main forces pass before striking their rear units. If combat ensues, they are to withdraw into the woods. The remaining detachment prepares the main ambush half a kilometer further, striking the main forces of the enemy company after some time.

**Possible outcomes may vary:** a) The platoon’s plan succeeds. The first ambush, undetected, strikes the rear; combat ensues, drawing part of the enemy company’s main forces. The ambush then withdraws to the side, pulling a significant portion of the pursuing forces with them. The weakened company is then attacked by the platoon’s main ambush. b) The platoon’s plan partially succeeds. The first ambush, spotted by the enemy’s advance guard, is attacked and forced to withdraw to the side. After a brief halt and sending reinforcements for pursuit, the company continues marching and falls into the second ambush. c) The platoon’s plan fails. The first ambush is neutralized or pushed aside, failing to create confusion or divert part of the Red company. The second ambush is also discovered and repelled toward B.

In the first two cases, the White platoon prevails; in the third, the Red company wins.

Other possible outcomes include: a) A strike by the main forces from C against the company, thanks to messages delivered by the messengers. b) The Red company earlier detects the White platoon, flanks it with a detachment to outmaneuver and strike from two sides. c) The Red company, having identified the enemy ahead and behind, attacks the White platoon.

The course and resolution may vary, but they will always rely on patrolling, maintaining communication, map-based orientation, and the tactical acumen of the leaders of individual groups. The exercise may be left to unfold naturally (at a higher level) or dictated in specific resolutions, at least for one group (at a lower level). These are not difficult exercises, as they might seem. They require only greater experience from the leaders of individual detachments. Such exercises can easily be conducted by teachers or instructors who are reserve officers.

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Hunting-Style Shooting
body:
Ordinary shooting, now accessible to all youth, can be transformed into a game incorporating elements of hunting.

The cheapest and easiest way to conduct it is with an air rifle (¹). However, small-caliber shooting is best.

¹) Borrow from a military training officer; 1000 rounds cost 5 złoty.

For the terrain of our hunt, choose the edge of a river terrace, a hillside, or a cliff, varied with vegetation.

Prepare at home 3 to 5 animal shapes of natural size and color, made from cardboard or paper and glued onto boards cut to the shape of the given animal (youth will have no difficulty making these models). These can be images of: a crow, fox, rabbit, marten, or sparrow. Place them in their appropriate terrain: on a branch, behind a bush, in the grass, on a tree trunk, behind leaves; at varying distances from the shooting position, from which all the game is visible (not necessarily completely). The shooting distance is 25—50 meters.

To add variety and difficulty to the game, movable targets can also be used, sliding before the shooter’s eyes or disappearing momentarily (room for creativity).

The shooter, positioned at the stand, must spot the game and shoot it. One shot per animal is sufficient. Shooting time is limited. Scoring is as follows: for spotting the game — 1 point, for killing it — 2 points, for wounding — 1 point (hitting a leg, ear, beak, or the edge of the animal shape). This shooting is exceptionally interesting, as it incorporates hunting elements, providing much excitement and satisfaction to participants. Moreover, it teaches terrain recognition (the more covered the terrain, the more shadows and light, and the greater the distance from the stand, the harder the exercise), sharpens observation skills, and quickens decision-making (limited shooting time). Youth experience the same sensations as a hunter at the stand.

This type of shooting can be used as an activity—an obstacle in a scout run or as the conclusion of a regular march (from 2—10 kilometers).

author: Jan Jasiński
title: Intelligence on the Enemy
body:
Within a designated area of 2—3 kilometers by ², in undulating terrain with heavy cover, Group A is tasked with performing the following activities: a) measuring the width of river N near forester’s lodge G, b) measuring the height of the chimney at distillery S, c) conducting reconnaissance of the sources of stream W and producing a sketch of it over a length of \(1 / 2\) kilometers, d) measuring the depth of the river and the speed of its current near the bridge (road from M to T) and at the bend (both inner and outer banks) below village B, e) producing a sketch of the grove located east of mill F using the method of offsets.

Group A is aware that it is operating in enemy territory. It must therefore maintain security during movement and while performing its tasks. It locates the designated points using a map.

A second group, Group B, receives intelligence about the presence of an enemy unit within the area marked on the map. The tasks of Group B will be:

1) locating Group A, 2) observing and reporting on their activities (Group B is not informed of the specific tasks assigned to Group A), 3) replicating the observed activities.

The principle "See without being seen" applies in this exercise.

If Group A detects Group B tracking it, it should attempt to evade and mislead the enemy. To this end, it may split up or take cover in any available hiding places, with the condition that it must complete the assigned tasks within the specified time (2—3 hours) and that the entire group must remain together during all activities.

To locate Group A, Group B must initially deploy a series of patrols into the designated area. Upon spotting Group A, it endeavors to follow discreetly, observe their actions, and subsequently replicate them. To carry out these observed tasks, Group B leaves a small patrol at the location, maintaining contact through a system of messengers, while the main force covertly follows Group A.

After the allotted time has elapsed, both groups assemble at the designated meeting point, where they organize their work and submit their reports to the exercise leader.

Group B wins if it successfully observes and accurately replicates more than 50 percent of Group A’s activities.

The activities performed by both groups should be compared, and the observations of Group A (performing the assigned tasks) regarding Group B (the tracking group) should be taken into account.

Each task completed by Group B should be downgraded in the overall assessment if the trackers (Group B) were well observed by those being tracked (Group A).

author: Jan Jasiński
title: A Several-Day War
body:
An agreed-upon game between two neighboring camps or colonies at least 5 — 10 km apart (the greater the distance between neighbors, the more interesting and instructive the game will be).

The camp commanders establish the timeframe of the war, e.g., from 18 on 20 July to 4 on 23 July. This timeframe constitutes a state of war. Each camp is obliged to maintain: guards, lookouts, and outposts (certain hours of the day may be excluded from the state of war to allow for normal camp activities—however, the night must never be excluded). Each camp may harass the enemy with its scouts, patrols, and a general attack.

The purpose of this continuous war is: to keep both camps in organized readiness; to demonstrate the tactical abilities of individual leaders; to train in night approaches, stealth, and patrolling; to test the psychological endurance and courage of individuals and the entire camp community.

Games of this type have a long tradition in many old scout troops (¹). These traditions date back to pre-independence times and are linked to the earnest, uncompromising preparation of youth for the struggle for freedom.

It is worthwhile to return to these old models of chivalrous combat, one of the most beautiful and valuable. It is worthwhile to revive such field games, so universal in training and testing the combat value of leaders and their troops. It is worthwhile to introduce these old field maneuvers into the work of our camps, leaving unforgettable, strong memories and indelible experiences in young hearts.

Below are the exemplary rules governing this game:

A) Valor lies on the side where there is more: calm, action in complete silence, unnoticed approach to the enemy, unexpected surprise, good humor (not malice) in playing tricks on the enemy. B) Under no circumstances should brawls be allowed. Only wrestling, without harm to clothes or bodies, may occur sporadically during the approach and neutralization of a guard (lookout).

¹) Based on wars of this type: 9:8 Warsaw Troop (Pomerania, 1921) and 14:17 Poznań Troop (Zakopane, 1923).

C) Both sides should be guided by the following principles: a) to see and hear as much as possible about the enemy camp’s actions and life; b) to carry out as many effective, harassing, and provocative actions against the enemy as possible; c) to prevent the enemy from gaining insight into the camp’s work and life, as well as any secret actions within one’s own camp.

D) Harassing and provocative actions against the enemy include the following activities: a) seeing and hearing as much as possible about the enemy camp’s actions and life; b) drawing pictures or writing on camp objects; c) hanging unnecessary and humorous items at various points in the camp; d) taking objects belonging to the camp or individuals, always leaving one’s own calling card to avoid misunderstandings; e) moving certain camp objects; f) toppling tents by loosening ropes or pulling them from pegs (cutting tent ropes is forbidden).

All the above and other actions are only successful if the enemy does not know when they were carried out or by whom. Any open attacks with superior forces are contrary to the spirit of this game.

Excluded from this game are the removal of the national flag from the mast and the taking of the troop’s banner.

Only a struggle for a signaling pennant, bearing special markings and placed in an agreed-upon location, may be introduced.

To carry out the above actions and gain an advantage in them, camp commanders must organize the security of their camp and frequently reconnoiter the enemy camp using scout patrols.

Security must cover not only the camp itself but also the approaches to it—through outposts, lookouts, and patrols sent further into the field.

Frequent encounters between enemy patrols will occur. In such cases, they should disperse. The goal will always be good observation of the enemy’s actions and concealment of one’s own activities.

The main time for action will be at night, following prior reconnaissance of the terrain during the day. During the night, the known rules of action apply, as stated on page 287, with silence and surprise being paramount.

The basis of all nighttime action will be diverting attention from certain points and directing the enemy’s actions into a prepared ambush.

Throughout this war, communication must not be forgotten: foot messengers, optical signals, and reports.

Success will depend on its good organization.

After the designated war period expires, a summary of actions and observations is made, and trophies are tallied at a joint staff meeting. After settling these matters, each leader discusses the entire operation within their group.

It is important to remember, both during the game and after its conclusion, to extend the morning sleep of the boys and allow them freedom to sleep during the day.

---

title: Kim's Game
body:
Kim's Game is widely known (see Kipling's *Kim*). Its variations primarily involve increasing the difficulty to different degrees. One can either increase the number of objects to be memorized, progressively shorten the observation time, or select objects that differ little from one another (e.g., various types of nails, pins, and "thumbtacks").

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Kim's Picture Game
body:
A sheet of paper divided into 12—16 rectangles. In most of the squares, one must exert effort to win—indeed, even beyond gathering, practice is necessary—until, at the end of such a cycle, a great test arrives: either a rank trial (or part of it), a major competition between patrols, or simply a contest in a given subject within the patrol.

For example: a cycle of signaling games. Increasingly difficult. More and more must be known. More and more practice is required. More and more training. Finally, at the conclusion, a great obstacle course, exercises, or an alarm—where victory depends on mastery of signaling. As a result—granting of skills for rank advancement. Or: a cycle of observation games. Ever more challenging ways to hide sought-after objects. Ever more unexpected tasks to observe. It is no longer enough just to notice—one must also remember what was seen. And not only that—but also pay attention to several things at once. Further—it is not enough just to observe, but one must also act appropriately. Be able to decide quickly. Increasingly difficult. More and more comprehensive exercises. The boys are thrilled by the escalating difficulty. They practice at school, at home, on the street. Until finally—a great observation contest.

The principle is thus: arrange games in cycles of increasing difficulty and comprehensiveness, concluding each cycle with a concrete result—a rank trial, a contest in a given subject. Record the successive results of all games for each boy in the patrol leader’s notebook on a specially ruled page—announce these results.

Drawings from various areas of life or geometric figures, etc., are placed in the squares. The sheet is shown to the patrol for observation for a time dependent on the boys’ skill and age, then they are instructed to redraw it. For remembering the drawing or figure and placing it in the correct square—2 points are awarded during evaluation; for remembering the image but placing it in the wrong square—1 point. Points are summed—whoever has the most wins. Examples of what can be placed in the squares: pictures from a scouting hike—task: redraw them, place them in the correct squares, and number them to indicate the order in which they should be arranged; various geometric figures—each in a different color; finally, Kim’s picture game can be used for rank advancement training by placing Indian signs or Morse alphabet letters, or conventional signs, etc., in the squares.

Instead of the above sheet, one can prepare 3—4 strips of paper, each containing 4—5 geometric figures in different colors, which repeat on the strips but in a different order. Each strip is shown for half a minute, but never all at once.

Another variation: show a chessboard with checkers or (for added difficulty) chess pieces set up. After observation—redraw it.

Whether to inform the patrol in advance that they must observe in order to redraw later can be decided: after showing something, e.g., a chessboard supposedly for another purpose, declare: now redraw it!

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Whose Hands
body:
Everyone shows their right hands to the observer. Then, from under a blanket lying on the table, they extend their hands, intertwined in such a way that it is difficult to recognize to whom they belong based on their direction. The observer must identify this by the shape and color of the hands. The game can be played in teams.

Variations: identify shoes previously observed, displayed through a door crack, or tracks left in the mud after observing the shoes beforehand.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Describing a Postcard
body:
The patrol leader distributes postcards to the boys for 2 minutes (as identical as possible). After 2 minutes, he collects them, and then the boys must describe on sheets of paper (or draw) what the postcard contained. Points are awarded based on the number of errors.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Trick Questions
body:
The patrol leader shows the boys a picture depicting some complicated scene. After hiding it, he asks several questions. Some of them concern objects actually shown in the picture. But others concern things that were not in the picture at all. For example: what color was the little dog running after the girl? Meanwhile, there was no little dog in the drawing at all! Points are of two kinds: for answers to relevant questions and for whether someone was tricked by a question about things that did not exist in the picture.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Memory Games
body:
A deck of cards, preferably made by the boys themselves, is scattered randomly on the table, face down (left side up). Each boy takes turns lifting **2** cards. The goal is to draw a pair of cards with the same number of pips (e.g., a pair of eights, a pair of threes, etc.). Initially, of course, the cards are picked at random, but later, one remembers where previous players placed them. The cards are dealt, and pairs are matched. If, when lifting the cards, no pair with the same number of pips is found, they are placed back in the same spot, face down. If a pair is found, it is set aside, and the player may draw again. The one who collects the most pairs wins. The troop can be divided into **2** teams—

boys take turns drawing from both teams alternately. The team with the most pairs in total wins.

title: Finding the Object
body:
A widely known scouting game involving the search for a hidden object. The rule is that no one should reveal they have found the object or guide others to it. Points are awarded for the order in which the object is found and for self-control—proper conduct during the search. Nothing should be touched while searching.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Detecting Disorder
body:
The patrol is brought into a room where some disorder has been created: spilled ink, a crooked picture, a poorly closed window, and the like. The changes made are announced without specifying their nature; anyone who notices all of them sits down, writes them on a slip of paper, and hands it to the patrol leader. No one may reveal that they have noticed something, as this would disrupt the game for others.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Near — Far
body:
A long-known game. The patrol walks along a street or road and must observe the greatest number of details previously indicated by the patrol leader. Each member, upon spotting a given object, reports it to the patrol leader in a whisper. These details may be more or less distant, for example: a man with a load, an antenna across the street, a cigarette box on the sidewalk, a coal cart, and a puddle on the roadway.

title: Changes in Clothing
body:
A widely known game; we show the patrol someone twice, making certain changes to their clothing the second time. Each participant lists the changes they notice. The one who identifies the most wins. It can be played in teams, in which case members of each team are allowed to confer.

**Stricter Rule.** A boy may only state as many changes as were actually made, regardless of whether he is correct or not. For example, if 5 changes were made, and a boy—who is told at the start how many changes were made—lists 5 changes, with three of them correct, he may not continue, even if he truly noticed 2 additional changes. The game teaches the reliability of observation.

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: The Warriors
body:
The patrol sends one boy out of the room, announcing that upon his return, he will have to guess what is going on. When he comes back—everyone precisely imitates his movements and words. He must then deduce that by this imitation, they are trying to distract his attention from the fact that everyone, without exception, has, for example, their jackets unbuttoned or a piece of paper pinned to their lapel, and so on—and that "this is precisely what it is all about."

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Straight Ahead — Crosswise
body:
The patrol sits in a circle. Several among them are initiated into the secret of the game. The patrol leader hands 2 pencils to the neighbor on the right, saying: "straight ahead"—or "crosswise"—depending on whether, while sitting, they have their legs crossed one over the other ("crosswise") or placed side by side ("straight ahead"). However, they pretend as if it depends on the special arrangement of the pencils when handing them over. The neighbor must pass the pencils to their own neighbor in turn, saying "straight ahead" or "crosswise." They will, of course, make mistakes, observing others, especially the initiated, until finally, everyone figures out what determines the use of one of the two terms. The patrol leader should specify each time whether the correct phrase was used when passing the pencils. Scoring is based on the patrol leader's observations.

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Ducat I
body:
Two teams sit on opposite sides of a table covered with a blanket. One team has a large coin, which they discreetly pass under the table to one of their members, while the others pretend to be the one holding it. On the signal “hop,” the entire team places their hands on the table in front of them, palms down—beneath one of these hands lies the “ducat.” The opponents observe whose hand the coin flashed under or clinked against the table—and each in turn points out which hands should be lifted from the table (each may order the lifting of 2 opponents’ hands), striving to ensure that the last hand remaining on the table is the one under which the ducat lies. If they succeed—they win the ducat and 1 point, and now they place their hands down; if not—the opponents gain 1 point. The game is played, for example, to 15 points.

**Games that exercise keen observation, quick orientation, rapid response to stimuli, the ability to reason and strategize; focusing attention on several objects simultaneously.**

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Storm at Sea
body:
Everyone is seated, with one person left without a place. That person walks around and tells a story, during which, whenever they say "storm at sea," everyone must jump up and switch places, while the storyteller also tries to find a seat. Anyone who fails to react to the words "storm at sea" loses a point. The person left without a place becomes the next "storyteller."
