author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: The Ring
body:
A well-known game. The patrol stands in a circle, facing inward, holding a ring threaded on a string in their hands. They move their hands so that the ring circulates from hand to hand—unseen. A boy standing in the center tries to catch the ring in the hand of one of the players. If he succeeds, he takes that player’s place, and the caught player goes to the center.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: The Electric Handkerchief
body:
The patrol sits in a circle, facing inward. The boy in the center tries to catch the handkerchief, which circulates in such a way that the boys take it from the knees of a nearer or farther neighbor and place it on their own. The handkerchief may only be caught when someone is holding it in their hand. The caught boy goes to the center, and the catcher takes his place.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Knocking Bum
body:
Boys take turns quickly striking the edge of a table with their fists. The goal is to avoid accelerating the strike—that is, each boy should strike only after his predecessor has knocked. Whoever rushes is out of the game. The last one remaining becomes the "Bum King."

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Hens — Roosters (with Variation)
body:
Two teams stand in lines, facing each other, parallel to the longer walls of the hall or field. One team is the "hens," the other the "roosters." The patrol leader, standing to the side, imitates clucking: "cluck, cluck, coo, coo, cluck"—and ends it with a call: "hens!" or "roosters!" The team called by the patrol leader runs as fast as they can toward the wall. Anyone from that team who is caught by the opposing team before reaching it loses a point for their team. Anyone who, instead of running, charges at the opponent, assuming at first that their team is supposed to chase, also loses a point, of course.

Variation: (Gilcraft 4/60). The patrol leader sometimes also calls: "chicks!"—and then everyone must remain completely still. Anyone who runs loses a point.

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: To the Water
body:
(Gilcraft 8/19). The patrol forms a circle around the patrol leader, outside a line drawn on the floor with chalk. On the command: “to the water!” they jump inside the circle. On the call: “to land!” they jump out. If the command “to the water” is given when everyone is already “in the water,” no one moves—and the reverse. Two mistakes eliminate a player from the game. The last one remaining wins.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Drop — Hold!
body:
All boys hold (each with one hand) a scarf stretched between them. The patrol leader runs a finger along it and stops it at one of the hands, saying: “drop!” or “hold!”—which must be done in the opposite way. Whoever fails to react correctly leaves the game or loses a point. Instead of holding one scarf together, each boy may hold an object individually, in which case the patrol leader points with a finger.

---

title: By Order of the Comrade
body:
(Gilcraft 12/20). At the beginning of the gathering, the boys are informed that orders preceded by the words: "by order of the comrade" (or others as given by the patrol leader) should not be carried out. Whoever makes a mistake and executes the order loses a point. The game continues until 3 points (or otherwise—as agreed).

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Nose, Floor, Lamp
body:
The patrol forms a semicircle in front of the patrol leader. The leader says: “nose,” “floor,” “lamp,” and points with a finger at these objects, but when saying “nose,” for example, points at the lamp, and so on. The boys must, while continuously watching the leader, indicate the correct objects that are being named. Whoever makes a mistake loses a point or is eliminated from the game.

title: Do This — Do That!
body:

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Lost Memory
body:
The patrol leader announces that a man who has lost his memory has been found—and displays the contents of his pockets. **2** teams (or more) race to determine, based on these items, who the man was and provide as much information about him as possible.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Espionage Exercise
body:
In the park, each boy chooses a person to sit beside and observes them discreetly. The most sensibly constructed account of who the observed person might be, their profession, where they came from, why they are sitting there, and so on, wins a reward. Attention must be paid to the boys' proper conduct toward those being observed.

title: Count, Poet
body:
Players take turns. Specifically, after briefly considering their choice, each must recite from memory a poem while simultaneously performing simple arithmetic operations on numbers written by themselves or provided on a slip of paper by someone else. The speed of performing the calculations and harmonizing the recitation with the counting determine the number of points each player earns.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: The Thief in the Room
body:
Before the game, the patrol leader discreetly selects someone clever to be the "thief." The thief must snatch a cap hanging in the room and reach the door with it without being caught. Simultaneously, a "search for an object" takes place. The boys must both search for the object and observe each other to identify the "thief." Points must be allocated for both activities. Whoever catches the thief receives, for example, 5 points, while finding the sought-after object earns 5 points. If the thief "steals" the cap, they also receive 5 points. The boys enjoy this game very much.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Boom
body:
The patrol forms a circle, and each member in turn says the next number in sequence (e.g., A says “one,” B says “two,” C says “three,” and so on). Instead of numbers that begin or end with 7 or are divisible by 7, one must say “boom.” Whoever fails to notice and says, for example, 17 (instead of saying “boom”) is out of the game. The last one remaining wins. Instead of seven, one may choose, for instance, three, and then “boom” is said for numbers beginning or ending with 3 or divisible by 3.

---

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Bum — Bam
body:
(Gilcraft, 26/24). A game similar to "bum"—but more complicated: "bum" is said to replace numbers beginning with, ending with, or divisible by 7, while "bam" replaces those for 5. For example, 17 — bum, 15 — bam, 57 — bam - bum, 75 — bum - bam, 35 — bum - bam - bam, and so on.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Whispered Commands (with Variations)
body:
The patrol stands in a line. The patrol leader, from a distance of several steps, gives commands such that their execution by those who hear them is invisible and inaudible to others. For example: close one eye, smile, and so on. Whoever hears—executes and earns a point in this game. The game is played, for example, to **10** points.

*Variation:* Whoever hears—steps back one pace; if they hear the next command—they step back again. Who will hear from the farthest point?

*Variation:* The same with eyes covered, so as not to read lips visually.

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Long-Distance Telephone
body:
2 teams—these are 2 rows, with a distance of 6 paces between them, and the same distance between the boys in each row. The patrol leader whispers a word to the first boy in the first row. He turns around, stands at attention, and whispers (from a distance of 6 paces) the word to the next boy in his row, who, upon hearing it, passes it further. However, the boys in the second row eavesdrop—and when one of them hears it (without moving from his place), he passes the word further in his own row. The row that first transmits the word to the end wins a point. The game is played to 10 points. The patrol leader alternates giving words to both rows.

---

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Finding the Watch Under the Caps
body:
On the table lie 6—8 caps. Under one of them, a watch is "ticking." Each participant listens in turn and must eventually say under which one. This can be combined with an observation game by asking the participant to describe the cap under which, in their opinion, the watch is hidden.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Finding the Watch in the Room (with Variation)
body:
A watch is hidden in the room so that it is not visible but can be heard—quite distinctly. In complete silence, the patrol searches; whoever finds it must not reveal this but instead pretends to keep searching—only later reporting to the judge. Points are awarded for the order of discovery and for maintaining silence and self-control upon finding it.

*Variation:* The hidden watch is placed by oneself in a trouser leg, under a cap, or the like. The boys search in turn; the one who finds it in the shortest time wins.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Stealing an Object
body:
In one corner of the room, a boy is seated with his eyes blindfolded, and next to him, within a radius of 1—2 metres, a series of objects is placed. At the opposite end of the room, a patrol is assembled. Boys are indicated one by one, who attempt to sneak as quietly as possible toward the guard and steal one object. If, during the approach, the guard points a finger in the direction of the approaching boy, that boy is out of the game. The boys take turns stealing objects. Points are calculated based on the skill of the approach and the successful acquisition of an object (suitable for team play).

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Blind Camp
body:
This is a strange camp. A flag planted in the center is guarded by blind sentries (with their eyes blindfolded) seated on the ground in a circle with a radius of approximately 6 — 10 paces (depending on the terrain), spaced 4 — 5 paces apart. Meanwhile, the rest of the patrol attempts to sneak into the center unheard from outside the camp. If a sentry hears one of the infiltrators, they point in their direction, and the patrol leader, who acts as the referee, gestures for them to retreat and try their luck from another side. Whoever crosses the sentry line undetected captures the camp by seizing the flag. Then, a change occurs: the attackers "go blind" and become the sentries, while the rest attempt to capture the camp. Points for the teams are awarded based on the amount of time lost during the "siege." Scouts rely on their honor not to seek victory through unchivalrous means (peeking from under the blindfold).

---

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Burglars
body:
A game similar to "Blind Camp"—played indoors. The task is also to sneak into the center of the guard circle, but while carrying a gym bench or another large object in one's hands—which makes maintaining balance and silence more difficult.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Words (with Variations)
body:
The patrol leader reads aloud a list of 15 unrelated words three times. The boys must write down these words from memory in the same order. For remembering a word in the correct order—2 points, in the wrong order—1 point.

*Variation:* The words are related to one another.

*Variation:* Instead of words—7 two- or three-digit numbers. Naturally, in all variations, we begin with the easier exercise before moving on to the more difficult one.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Submarine Boats
body:
Boys from one team, with their eyes blindfolded, form a cordon across the room, standing with legs apart so that their neighbors' feet touch. They must not bend their knees, but they may move their arms. The others try to slip through the cordon—preferably under the legs of the cordon—without being touched by a hand.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Wall of the Blind
body:
The troop is divided into two parts. One group has their eyes blindfolded and the boys are positioned 1—2 paces apart from each other (arm's span). The other group must sneak through the wall of outstretched arms. The boys forming the "wall" may wave their arms. Anyone touched is out of the game. After finishing, the roles are switched—the ones who were sneaking now form the wall, and so on. We calculate which side has more successful sneakers.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Passing Through the Room
body:
The door of the room is opened, and the patrol is led out of the room, leaving one boy who sits with his back to the door. The boys sneak into the room one by one and sit against the opposite wall. When the boy sitting with his back turned hears a rustle, he points his finger, and the one pointed at moves to sit on the opposite side. After the game is finished, we determine who sneaked in and who did not.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Where Are You, Little Jacob?
body:
Little Jacob and his pursuer are "blind"—they have their eyes blindfolded. Little Jacob must answer "here" to every question from the pursuer. In this way, he is eventually caught. The patrol stands around them, protecting them from collisions.

*Variation:* The pursuer is the one of the two who finds a belt placed somewhere on the ground by touch. When he catches Little Jacob, he strikes him with the belt. Little Jacob whistles from time to time.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Chase the Whistle
body:
At dusk, in a dense thicket... Two boys with whistles hide somewhere deep inside. One of them whistles. The patrol rushes in pursuit in that direction. Suddenly, they hear a whistle from another side. So they turn toward it (not knowing that there are two being sought), thinking that the same one has slipped through—and let him escape; in this way, the two hidden boys lure their comrades this way and that, until the trick is revealed and both fall into the hands of their avengers. The game can also take place on a playing field or in a hall, but with the boys' eyes blindfolded.

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Kim's Game of Strikes (with Variations)
body:
The patrol leader strikes successively a cupboard, wall, windowpane, table, and floor—the patrol listens and watches. Then the patrol turns away—and the patrol leader strikes the same objects again—but in a different order; the boys take turns stating (without looking) which objects the patrol leader strikes.

*Variations:* instead of strikes—tones of varying pitch on a piano, trumpet, etc., or various sounds: clinking scissors, bouncing a ping-pong ball, and the like.

title: Recognize by Voice
body:

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Kim’s Watch Game
body:
Each boy in turn listens to the “ticking” of 4—5 watches, which the patrol leader holds to his ear, allowing him to examine them. Then the boy turns away, and the patrol leader presents the same watches to his ear from behind, but in a different order. Finally, he must determine the order in which the watches were presented.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Seeking by Sounds
body:

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Prisoner's Dispatch
body:

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Marek Went
body:
(Gilcraft, 23/23). Someone begins the game by saying: "Marek went to the fair and bought himself an axle"—then turns to the next player, who repeats this and adds one more item besides the axle. Each subsequent player repeats the previous player's sentence and adds one more item of their own. Whoever does not make a single mistake—and remains the last—wins, earning the maximum points. The others, in reverse order of elimination, receive correspondingly fewer points.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Who Said It?
body:
(Gilcraft, 49/30). The patrol leader notes approximately 15 of the most interesting sentences or remarks made by different boys during the gathering. At the end of the meeting, he reads them aloud. The one who most accurately identifies the authors of these sayings wins.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Kim's Game of Touch
body:
The patrol forms a circle, facing outward. We hand (from a prepared set of approximately 15 objects) the first scout in the circle an object, such as a nib, to their hands, which they hold behind their back. They feel the object with their fingers and pass it to their neighbor, then receive a second object, and so on. When the objects have gone around the entire circle and reach the last scout, they return them in order to the patrol leader. Then, "disperse," and for 3 minutes, everyone writes down the objects in the order they were passed by the patrol leader. Afterward, 2 points are awarded for each object recorded in the correct order, and 1 point for remembering it but in the wrong order.

Variation: The objects are small cardboard rectangles with grooves embossed in the shape of figures, letters, and the like.

Variation: A letter or several words are composed from such cardboard pieces with embossed letters.

Variation: Each scout receives one of the above cardboard pieces—in 2 teams, where the embossed letters form a word. On "disperse," the teams gather and assemble the word from the letters they received. The team that shouts out the word first earns a point. The game is played, for example, to 10 points.

Variation: The objects circulating in the circle are small bags containing salt, sugar, coffee, rice, tea, and the like—or pieces of satin, linen, raw silk, cotton, wool, and the like.

---

title: Identifying Coins
body:
Identifying coins given for examination in a bag is easier when the coins are different, much harder when they are similar—for example, 50-grosz coins and one-złoty coins, 10-złoty and 5-złoty coins.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Message on a String
body:
This is a challenging game! Tedious to prepare. We tie knots on a string: 2 close together signifies a dash, one knot alone signifies a dot, and in this way, we create a secret signaling message using Morse code. A splendid game, demanding great dedication from the patrol leader.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Identify by Clothing (with Variations)
body:
The boy who is to identify others first examines with his fingers the roughness, thickness, finishing method, and the like of the edges of all the scouts' jackets. Then his eyes are blindfolded, and each scout approaches him in turn, while he identifies them by their clothing.

*Variations:* identify by hands, hair, face, and so on.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Leashed Serpent
body:
One boy starts the game. He holds onto a door handle with one hand while trying to touch one of the other boys teasing him around him with the other. When he catches someone, he takes him by the hand, and together they form a serpent, catching further victims—and thus "growing" longer. The last one caught wins.

body:
(Gilcraft, 93/39). In the center of the room stands a table, with the "stag" and the "wolf" positioned on opposite sides. During the chase, both must continuously touch the table with any part of their body. If the stag avoids capture for 3 minutes, it wins.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Feather Blowing
body:
A feather—down—is tossed above a line drawn with chalk across the room. Two teams attempt to fan it with their caps onto the opponent's territory so that it lands on the ground there. Usually, boys cannot resist blowing on it, but the rule should be to fan it with caps. Boys enjoy this game for its cheerfulness and amusing tricks.

title: Snake Fight
body:
Two teams form snakes, made up of boys standing one behind the other and holding onto each other's belts. Each snake aims—using the hands of the first boy—to grab the tail of the other snake while also protecting its own tail from the other's attacks.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Ball to the Cap
body:
(Gilcraft). The boys' caps lie close together in the center of a circle with a radius of about 10 feet. The patrol stands on the circumference of the circle. One boy throws a tennis ball, aiming at one of the caps, but not his own. If he misses, a marker is placed in his cap; if he misses 3 times, he yields his place to another. The owner of the cap into which the ball falls runs to grab the ball and shouts: "Stop!" The rest scatter but halt upon hearing the word. The player with the ball may not step outside the circle and attempts to hit one of the boys. If he misses, a marker is placed in his cap; the one he hits will be the next to throw the ball at the caps. The patrol with the fewest markers in their caps wins.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Weaving Race
body:
(Gilcraft 4/56). Two or three teams in a circle, facing inward, spaced one meter apart, arranged so that every third person belongs to the same team. On the call “hop,” the first from each team runs to the right, weaving like a shuttle between those standing alternately to the left and right; upon reaching their place, they slap the hand of person number 2 of their team, and numbers 2 start. The team wins in which the last one slapped returns to their place first.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Tumbler
body:
(Gilcraft 31/25). About 12 boys sit on the ground in a circle, touching shoulders, legs stretched toward the center where one remains. Holding himself stiffly, he falls onto the outstretched hands of one of the seated boys; that boy pushes him so he tilts onto someone else, and so on. Whoever lets the Tumbler fall, fails to hold him, takes his place in the center.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Bullfights
body:
(Gilcraft 26/50). Players: 1 bull, 1 matador, 4 toreadors, 6 people with sashes. Phase I: The bull enters the arena with 5 strips of paper (8 cm in length) hanging from its back. The toreadors try to tear them off. Anyone touched once by the bull "dies." The people with "capes" try to distract the bull from the toreadors, who may run outside the arena no more than 3 times. Only one strip of paper can be torn off each time. Phase II: When all the strips have been torn off or the toreadors have been eliminated, the bull is "blinded" by tying a sash below its waist like a tail, and the matador tries to tear it off while avoiding being "touched."

title: Rat
body:
The patrol leader stands in the center of a circle of boys, holding a string with a sandbag attached to the other end. He swings it in a low circular motion just above the ground, so the boys must jump to avoid the string touching their legs. Whoever jumps at the wrong time or too low, so that the string touches their leg, steps out of the circle.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Precious Stick
body:
(Gilcraft 21/49). The patrol sits in a circle on the floor, each with a drawn number.

In the center, the patrol leader holds a stick upright with a finger—at some point, they call out a number and remove their finger. The called scout must catch the stick before it falls. Instead of numbers, bird or animal names can be drawn; in this case, besides catching the stick, the scout must also make the cry of the given bird or animal. Whoever fails loses a point; whoever loses 3 points is eliminated from the game, and the last remaining wins.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Cossack and Tatar
body:
A common active game. In the center of the room lies an object. Along two walls are the 2 playing teams: Cossacks and Tatars. The game begins: on either side of the object stand a Cossack and a Tatar. The Cossack performs various movements and contortions, which the Tatar must mirror as precisely as possible. At an inconvenient moment for the Tatar, the Cossack grabs the object and flees to his team. If he reaches them untouched by the Tatar, he takes him captive. Now, the "skirmishes" resume in the center of the room, but the imitator is the Cossack, while the Tatar grabs the object. The team that fully captures the opposing side wins.

title: Apple Thief
body:
(Gilcraft 18/48). The patrol stands in a circle, with an apple lying in the center. One of the boys leaves the room—he will be the thief; another is designated as the gardener in the thief’s absence. The thief returns to the room and must seize the apple, escape from the circle by the same path he entered, and avoid being touched by the gardener—without knowing who the gardener is.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: One-Two-Three
body:
Who hasn’t played this? At the finish line stands one boy—covering his eyes with his hand while he counts: one—two—three; during this time, the troop, initially lined up in a row at a distance of about 25 steps from him, approaches. When the boy says “three,” he uncovers his eyes, everyone freezes in place, and whoever is caught still moving, even the slightest bit, must return to the “start.” The first one to approach the “wizard” in this way and touch him becomes the wizard himself.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Obstacles in the Fog
body:
(Gilcraft 17/62). Chairs arranged in a room serve as obstacles for ships navigating through fog—boys with their eyes blindfolded, starting from one end of the room toward a designated finish line, divided into 2 teams. Whoever touches an obstacle must circle it three times. The team whose ships reach the port first wins. Care must be taken to ensure that overly bright light does not provide a clue about the direction of the port.

title: Yes — No!

One boy leaves the room, and the rest choose a single word that he must guess upon returning by asking about its characteristics. However, only the words "yes" or "no" may be used in response to his questions.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: What Is It?
body:
(Gilcraft 27/24). Each player is allowed to voice their guess once. The patrol leader describes an object using ten descriptors, each subsequent one narrower than the previous (e.g., if describing a duck—the first descriptor: "bird," the last: "says quack-quack"). Whoever guesses correctly writes down on their sheet at which descriptor they guessed and scores accordingly. For example, if guessed at the fourth descriptor, they award themselves 6 points. Naturally, at the end, everyone states their guess for verification. The game is played, for instance, to 60 points.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Mama — Papa
body:
One boy leaves the room, and the rest choose two words that have some logical connection, one masculine and the other feminine (e.g., collar and neck). To the guesser, everyone says a pair of sentences in which the masculine noun is replaced with "papa" and the feminine noun with "mama." For example, in our case: *mama* is washed, *papa* is laundered; *papa* can be stiff, then it has little horns in front, and so on. The guesser must deduce these words.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: My Mimi
body:
Two boys agree between themselves—they choose a word called a homonym, that is, one with a double meaning, for example: *zamek* (castle/lock), or *lód* (ice/deck), and then carry on a conversation in front of the troop, replacing that word with the phrase “my Mimi,” each of them speaking about a different meaning of the word. Their task is to steer the conversation so that, on the one hand, it is witty, and on the other, the definitions of the word gradually become more precise, making it easier to guess. The troop tries to guess, and the first one to correctly say the word wins.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Proverbs
body:
As before—but instead of a word, a proverb is chosen. The guesser asks questions, which must be answered logically, and the answer must include that word of the proverb which was assigned to the respondent during the division of the proverb’s words among the players. By considering the answers, the guesser must deduce what the proverb is.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Intelligence Game
body:
On a sheet of paper, each person writes a short word chosen by everyone—vertically down the left side and vertically up the right side. For example, with the word *dog*, the letter "d" on the left corresponds to "g" on the right, and so on. Then, each person constructs words beginning with the left-side letters and ending with the corresponding right-side letters. In our example, the 1-th word might be *cigarette*, and so forth. When everyone has written their words, each takes turns defining the first word so that everyone else can guess it. The first to guess correctly earns a point. After everyone has defined the first word in turn, they proceed to define the second, and so on. The person with the most points wins.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: What Is the Ship Loaded With?
body:
The patrol sits in a circle. One letter is chosen, for example, A. Someone starts the game by tossing a handkerchief to another Scout and asking: "What is the ship loaded with?" The recipient answers with a word beginning with the chosen letter, for instance, in our example: watermelons. The game can be made more difficult by not selecting a letter beforehand, instead allowing the person tossing the handkerchief to specify the letter with which the answer must begin.

Another variation of this game is that when tossing the handkerchief, no letter is specified, but the first syllable of the answer is called out, which the partner must complete. For example, A, tossing the handkerchief to B, calls out: "What is the ship loaded with?" "On...", and B finishes the answer by saying "On-ions." Whoever fails to answer loses a point or gives a forfeit.

Yet another variation of the game involves players composing rhymes in the above manner to the word spoken by the first player.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Alphabet Game
body:
The patrol sits in a circle. Someone tosses a handkerchief to another Scout and calls out, for example, A. That Scout must immediately answer 3 questions: What is your name? Where are you from? What is your profession?—and the answers must start with A, for example, Adam from Afghanistan, artist. Whoever fails to answer loses a point.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Ship C
body:
(Gilcraft 18/21). Players sit in a circle. The patrol leader names a letter, for example, C, and asks the nearest Scout: "Name of the ship?" The Scout gives a reasonable name starting with "C" and asks the next: "Captain’s name?" Further questions, asked in turn by the next boys: "To which port is it sailing?", "What is it loaded with?", and so on. The letter may be changed over time. Whoever makes a mistake is eliminated—or loses a point.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Great People
body:
We choose a letter. Then, each participant tries to compile as many names as possible of people known from literature, or generally those who have contributed to culture—or to the fight for Poland’s independence—or to scouting—or the names of athletes, and so on. Next, each person in turn reads out the names they have listed, while the others cross out those that appear on their own lists as well. The person who ends up with the most uncrossed names wins.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Syllable Chain
body:
(Gilcraft, 88/38). The patrol forms a circle. The first person utters a two-syllable word and addresses another, who must then say a two-syllable word whose first syllable matches the last syllable of the previous word. For example: First: Mar-ia, Second: Ia-nek, Third: Nek-tar, Fourth: Tar-cza, and so on. Whoever cannot think of a word loses a point, but only if their predecessor can form the required word from the syllable they provided.

title: Five-Minute Word Game
body:
Choose a word. From the letters of this word, form as many new words as possible—nouns in the nominative case. For example, from the word "kraska," we can form: kara, rak, krasa, rasa, and so on. The one who has the most words after 5 minutes wins.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Black Magic (with Variations)
body:
Someone with an initiated ally poses as a magician: they leave the room, the others choose a certain word, and upon returning, the magician guesses it. If the troop is naive, they may allow the initiated ally to leave, fetch the magician into the room, and whisper the word to them along the way. Alternatively, the entire troop may conspire to convince one person that such guessing is possible, making everyone allies of the magician to deceive the one being tricked.

Another *variation*—without secretly prompting the magician with the word, the ally loudly recites a series of words whose first letters form the chosen word, or among which the word itself is always spoken after a word denoting, for example, a four-legged animal—many combinations are possible here. A good game for a troop’s tea gathering—it forces an effort of deduction to uncover the trick.

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Court I
body:
Two escorts lead the wrongdoer before the judge, who sits on a chair placed on a table. A blanket hangs down from the table, behind which one boy is hidden; the wrongdoer stands on a rug—the blanket, one edge of which is under the table, behind the hanging blanket. The court scene takes place, and when the judge loudly proclaims the verdict: “perish!”, the boy hidden under the table pulls the “rug”, causing the “condemned” to fall flat; the escorts then catch the falling person, who must be very careful—and carry him away.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Marmot Club
body:
We are to admit a novice into the Marmot Club. The club's "President" delivers a lofty speech about the club's moral duties. Finally, they drape a cloak over the novice's shoulders, lead them among the club members, and declare that they will be accepted once they seize a whistle from someone—one which the members will blow and pass from hand to hand (the whistle, however, hangs at the back, by the collar of the novice's cloak). Then, whoever is behind the novice blows the dangling whistle, and when the novice turns toward it, the person pretends to pass the whistle to another, while someone else behind them blows it again—this continues as the game goes on.

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Secretary
body:
Each participant receives a piece of paper and writes a masculine personal noun on it. They then fold the top of the paper to conceal what they have written and pass it to their neighbor, while receiving another piece of paper from their other neighbor, on which that person has already written (as they did) a masculine name. On the received papers, everyone now writes feminine personal nouns. In this way, each person answers the following sequence of questions: masculine name, feminine name, where they were, what they were doing, what came of it, what people said about it? Each answer is written on a separate piece of paper, meaning each piece of paper contains the successive answers of 6 players. The papers are then read aloud, resulting in much laughter. It is necessary to appeal to the boys' sense of honor and decency so that they do not abuse their discretion and write anything indecent.

title: Testament

The game is played like "Secretary," but the successive questions are as follows: who? to whom? what did they bequeath in the testament? for what reason? was the recipient pleased?

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: The Poet
body:
Each participant receives a small piece of paper. At the top, they write one line of verse (1 line)—as if the beginning of some work. The paper is passed to a neighbor, and each person receives a paper from another neighbor. On the received papers, everyone adds a second line—rhyming with the previous one—folds the paper so that both lines are hidden, then writes the next line, no longer rhyming, as if continuing the work—and passes the paper on. In this way, a "poem" written by everyone emerges on each paper, with each 2 lines by a different author. When read aloud—much laughter ensues!

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: What-If
body:
The patrol sits in 2 rows facing each other. Each person in the 1 row whispers a sentence to their neighbor, beginning with the words: "What would happen if...". In this way, everyone in the row receives a question from their neighbor (each one different), starting with the above words. In the second row, in the same manner, each person receives a whispered sentence from their neighbor as an answer: "Then this and that would happen" (e.g., "Then it would be the end of the world"). After this preparation, the patrol leader points to the first pair—and from it, one person sitting in the first row speaks their question aloud (e.g., "What would happen if the light went out now")—the second person, sitting in the second row, speaks the sentence received from their neighbor (e.g., as above: "Then it would be the end of the world"). From the combination of these questions and answers, funny combinations arise.

---

The patrol stands in a circle. One of the boys approaches each in turn and imitates a cat’s meow three times in front of them. The one thus "challenged" must keep a straight face and say: "Why do you meow, little, white kitten?" If they laugh at this, they switch places with the "kitten."

title: Buffalo Stable
body:
(Gilcraft 9/61). Four teams in the four corners of the hall. Two of them—opposite each other diagonally—attempt to convey a question and a sensible answer to one another, but not through gestures or signaling. At the same time, they strive to raise an enormous uproar to hinder the communication of the other two opposing teams. The first pair to successfully communicate wins.

title: Persian Eye
body:
Girls sit in a circle, boys—each stands behind his lady, with only one of them having an empty chair in front of him—and he "winks an eye" at one of the seated girls, who quickly moves to sit by him if she is not stopped by her suitor. If the suitor is distracted and fails to stop the girl, then, as the abandoned one, he himself "shoots an eye" at another.

The one questioned is not allowed to answer—this is done for him by his neighbor on the left, meaning each boy answers the questions asked of his neighbor on the right. sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Mast Competition
body:
The patrol shall construct from wood and canvas models of masts with movable flags. The best-made masts win, and the single finest one will serve for the following ceremony: at the beginning of each patrol gathering, the flag is hoisted solemnly, and at the end, it is lowered. The competition may be varied by including a contest for the most beautiful flag for the "international scout republic" or for the troop's own banner.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Blind Maps
body:
In the Książnica - Atlas (Warsaw, Nowy Świat 59), "blind maps" of Poland (without inscriptions) are available for purchase. Various types of games involve drawing on the map cities, rivers, mountains, industrial centers, and the like. These maps are very inexpensive. The one who makes the fewest mistakes wins. The game can be varied: Where would I place the Scout Troop Leaders' School, and why here? How could railway lines in Poland be laid out in a wiser way than they are now?

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Quartets
body:
We make a set of cards from bristol board—and proceed to prepare a game, for example, a geographical one. At the top of 4 of them, we write: "coal," and below, 4 towns where the largest mines are located. Then, on each of these four cards, we underline a different town, meaning each of the 4 towns is underlined on a different card. We do the same, for example, with cotton, oil, and so on. We shuffle the cards and deal them among the participants. Each player aims to collect four cards related to, for example, coal—and set them aside as a "trick"—earning them 1 point. Someone begins the game. They might have, for example, 3 cotton cards—and lack one on which Bielsko is underlined. They then turn to someone they believe has that card, demanding it be given to them. If they are correct—they receive the card, handing over one of their own cards in return, and continue their turn; if not—the turn passes to the person they asked. Instead of a geographical game, one can prepare, for older participants, a literary game, for example: at the top of each set of 4 cards, we write the name of an author—below, 4 of their works; on each of the 4 cards, a different one of these works is underlined. There are many variations of this game.

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: The Wanderer's Journal
body:
“Vigilant Spirit” No. 10 from the year 1932 presents the following game: An excerpt from a supposed journal of two Scouts wandering through a certain region of Poland is read aloud. This could be a car or airplane trip across all of Poland or a walk through a city. The journal omits (as if “faded away”) the names of towns, rivers, and the like that the wanderers reach, but these can be deduced from the included descriptions and historical references. Additionally, in the form of conversations between the friends, there are questions concerning Poland’s territory, population, and other statistical data. Whoever, within a specified period of time (even outside the gathering), answers all the questions and identifies the names of all the places—wins.

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Examples
body:
The following game, when applied judiciously, may be used: we read aloud a story written by ourselves about the conduct of a boy or a group of boys, containing examples of the application or violation of various points of the Scout Law. Whoever correctly identifies which points of the Law these examples pertain to wins. The judicious application consists in avoiding the creation of rigid mental templates in the boys regarding the Scout Law: for instance, Point III of the Law—picking up a bag on the street, Point V—giving up a seat on the tram, and so on—boys may believe that such courtesies compensate for deeper shortcomings in scouting life.

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Torn Letter
body:
The Patrol Leader prepares as many identical cards containing the text of the Scout Law as there are boys in the patrol, or half that number. Then, he tears these letters into pieces—all in exactly the same way—and distributes them to the boys or pairs (each receives only fragments of his own letter). The boy or pair who reconstructs the entire letter first wins. Variation: the text of the Scout Law is written in an order different from the established one.

Variation: instead of the Scout Law, the content of the letter can be anything else, such as a sketch of the district, a plan of the room, a map of Poland, etc.

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Kim's Game of the Law
body:
On a sheet of paper divided into 12 squares, we draw—similarly to the game described above under the title "Examples"—scenes from the lives of scouts, which the boys must identify by the points of the Scout Law when copying the square, writing them into the corresponding squares on the card.

Another variation: the squares contain the texts of the points of the Law—in the appropriate squares, when copying, the numbers of the points of the Law must be written.

I do not think it necessary to add that the inculcation of the scouting ideology in boys cannot end with the memorization of the Scout Law; however, since we teach the boys the Law by heart, it is better to do so in an engaging way rather than a dull, school-like manner.

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Scout Cross
body:
The boys make a cross out of cardboard, in which the wreath, circle, and fleur-de-lis can be changed (attached) — and are kept in reserve — in silver and gold colors. The patrol leader displays this cross in various versions (different parts are attached to it), after which the patrol must write down which ranks of crosses they saw (for the Tenderfoot rank, this skill is not required in full).

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Who is Under Whom?
body:
On figures of scouts cut out from paper by the boys, the patrol leader draws colored pencil function cords. Each one in turn arranges these figures according to hierarchy: "who is under whom," meaning "according to the importance of functions." It will be much more fun when the patrol leader colors a certain number of "function cords" at home—then the boys will draw lots among themselves to see who receives which cord—and they will line up according to seniority. This can be combined with a "moral": he who works and is energetic "advances" and becomes the Chief Scout by the end of the gathering.

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Changes in the Uniform
body:
We present a boy in the regulation uniform. The patrol observes him. Then we take him out of the room and make changes to his uniform: we pin the cross in the wrong place, position the service-year leaves or troop numerals incorrectly. We then present our "model" a second time for a 1-minute observation, after which each scout must list the noticed changes on a sheet of paper.

It is even better to reverse the order, so that the correct way of wearing the uniform, rather than its faults, remains in memory. However, this is not essential.

A variation described in the book titled *Exercises and Games* from the *Skrzydeł* library involves immediately showing a scout in an improper uniform—without prior observation—and having the boys identify the uniform’s faults.

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Alarm on the Map
body:
The first part of the game involves the boys tracing a map of the district of the city where they live. After checking and correcting the maps, and calculating the points, the second part of the game follows: marking with crosses where the members of the patrol live. Once this part is completed—the finale: "what should the patrol's alarm plan look like on this district map" or: "what does an already prepared alarm plan look like on this map?" It is hardly necessary to add that it would be nonsense to play the above game without conducting a few real alarms.

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: The Scatterbrained Secretary
body:
The patrol leader reads out the addresses (surnames and positions only) of 4 letters in which a scatterbrained secretary has mixed up the positions and surnames of the following individuals: the troop leader, the Scout Region Commander, the Chief Scout, and the Chairman of the Z.H.P. The boys must sort this out: properly address these letters. For example, the letters read: Asst. Patrol Leader Michał Grażyński; Asst. Chief Scout — Janek Czupiralski. They must correctly match these surnames and positions.

---

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Invalid Patrol
body:
Half of the patrol suddenly becomes "wounded"—this is one team. The other team bandages their comrades. Then, the roles are switched. The team that completes the task faster and with better results wins.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Ships
body:
Groups of 4 to 6 scouts—"sinking." The patrol leader calls out, for example, "square knot," and begins counting consecutively, for instance, up to 10. If the ship captains manage to tie a square knot from the ropes they have within the counting time, they save their sailors. If not, one of them sinks. Then the patrol leader calls out: "fisherman's knot," and the same process repeats.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: The Sea
body:
The captains are already on shore, and the sailors are drowning; to rescue a sailor, one must tie a knot—throw a rope to the drowning person, then untie the knot. The captain who manages to rescue all of his sailors in this way first wins. It can be required that both the captain and the drowning person tie the knots. The thrown rope may be too short, so it must be spliced. The captains are constantly different boys—(“there are frequent mutinies”).

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: The Hike
body:
"On the Trail," from the year 1932, presents the following game: the patrol leader reads a story they have composed, for example, about a Scout’s hike during which he needed to use a rope several times. As the patrol leader recounts these incidents, the patrol ties the appropriate knots. Whoever ties all the knots correctly wins.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Bridge
body:
The patrol is divided into 2 teams: these are the brigades of workers building 2 bridges for a competition. Each brigade receives 10 strings, each approximately 30 to 50 centimetres long. The riverbanks are represented by 2 benches turned upside down. Building the bridge involves stretching a string (tied from short segments) between the two benches, securing it to the bench legs, arranging ropes by which one can "slide" from the high pillar to the ground, along with a safety loop. The team that: a) completes the bridge first, b) uses the most varied knots, and c) ties them without error, as well as d) engages all workers in the task—wins (fourfold scoring).

---

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Marching with a Compass
body:
The “Expedition” sets out—“for real”—onto the playing field, or “pretend” with a pencil on paper, and receives “via radio” the order to head in various directions of the world. Whoever correctly plots the directions or marches on the field earns positive points. The same applies in the field and in the forest.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Rejecting Letters
body:
The patrol forms a circle. The patrol leader stands in the center, points to one of the boys, and signals a letter to him. The boy must respond by signaling the next letter in the alphabet. Whoever makes a mistake loses a point. The more points someone loses, the more often they should be prompted to encourage thinking.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Changing Places
body:
The patrol forms a circle, with each scout assigned 2 letters—one scout has no place and stands in the center. The patrol leader signals 2 letters, and immediately the scouts designated by those letters exchange places, while the one in the center tries to take one of their spots. If successful, they receive that scout’s letters, and the "homeless" one moves to the center.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: What Is the Ship Loaded With? II
body:
Two teams sit facing each other. Someone from the first team tosses a handkerchief at one of the scouts from the second team and signals a letter, then asks: "What is the ship loaded with?" The boy who receives the handkerchief must immediately answer with a word beginning with the signaled letter; otherwise, his team loses a point. The team that first earns 8—10—15 points, or drives the opposing team to the appropriate number of minuses (depending on the scoring system), wins.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Dots — Dashes
body:
Two teams in ranks. Each boy holds his cap in hand. The patrol leader calls out, for example, "b". Each team strives to be the first to arrange itself so that the boy with the cap on his head (representing a dash) and three with bare heads (dots) form the letter "b" according to the Morse alphabet. The first team to do so earns a point, and the game continues until 10—15 points are reached.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Pair Race
body:
Two teams sit on the ground in rows parallel to each other. The first in each row receives one letter, the second another, and so on. The patrol leader, positioned at a certain distance in front of the heads of both rows, signals one of these letters. The pair designated by it jumps up, runs to the patrol leader, touches his hand, and rushes back to their place. The first of the two earns a point for their team. The game is played to 10–15 points. The game can be varied by increasing the requirements during the race, for example: the racers must hop on one leg or jump over a bench, or run with an egg on a spoon, or draw their letter in Morse code with chalk on the floor around the patrol leader (if the patrol leader signaled with semaphore flags), and so on. From time to time, the patrol leader claps. This means that everyone now has the next letter in the alphabet, i.e., whoever had "a" now has "b," whoever had "p" now has "r," and so on.

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Signalers' Club
body:
Each person is assigned 2 letters. In the center of the field lies a ball, with the patrol gathered around it. The patrol leader signals a letter (using flags or a whistle)—everyone except the one designated by that letter scatters, while the latter grabs the ball and throws it at the others. If they hit someone, they earn a point, and the person who was hit now calls out the next letter.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Kim's Signaling Game
body:
On a card divided into 12—16 rectangles, letters in Morse code or semaphore, as well as in the regular alphabet, are drawn in some of the squares. The patrol observes the card for 1—1⅓ of a minute, after which it must reproduce it from memory, replacing signaling letters with regular ones and vice versa. For each correctly written letter in the proper rectangle—2 points; for incorrect placement—1 point.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Constructing Words
body:
Two teams stand in rows, parallel to each other, with their backs to the patrol leader, who devises a word composed of as many letters as there are scouts in each row. On his clap, the two nearest scouts (the first in each row) turn toward him, and he signals the first letter of his word to them. They then silently move to the start of their row (farther from the patrol leader). Another clap follows—the next scouts turn around—receive the next letter, and move to the front. Once everyone has received one letter, meaning the entire word has been signaled one letter at a time to each scout, the teams gather and race to shout out the word the patrol leader signaled. The team that does so first earns a point. The game continues until 10—15 points are reached.

Complications: The word has 2 times more letters than there are boys in the team—and the queue rotates 2 times, with each scout receiving two letters, one per rotation. Alternatively, instead of signaling a single letter to each scout, the patrol leader gives them the entire word—everyone then receives a full sentence, which they must reconstruct.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Signaling Task
body:
The patrol leader presents the patrol with a topographic sketch of the area drawn by himself; on it, he has marked two points on hills with crosses, between which rises a higher elevation—these points must be connected by means of signaling, having at their disposal one additional relay station. The sketch must be drawn in such a way that the placement of this intermediate station is such that it is visible from both points and yet presents some difficulty in finding the appropriate location. The task can be made more challenging by ordering that all or some of these points be invisible from the enemy position marked on the sketch. The game consists of two parts: the first is copying the sketch (from memory—or according to a visible model), the second—the actual task. Scoring is also double.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Prisoner's Tap Code
body:
The prisoner taps his message through the wall: two quick taps in succession—a dash; one tap—a dot; a longer pause—the end of a letter; an even longer pause—the end of a word. Who can decipher it best?

This game belongs to the group of competitive games that a patrol leader must constantly organize during gatherings. Tapped messages; secret messages—for example, by blinking eyes or one eye, or by subtle movements of the lips, fingers, shoes, etc.; light signals from a window to the street or somewhere in a park or outside the city; sudden contests in deciphering flag messages, and so on, should constantly diversify gatherings and separate lectures on the "theory" of signaling—on finding a position, dividing functions at a signaling station, relay stations, agreed-upon signs and abbreviations, other alphabets, signaling devices and apparatuses, the history of signaling, and the like. It is highly desirable to organize an excursion to a post office or telegraph school, try using a Morse apparatus, build primitive devices, and so on. However, everything, including the games described above, is only preparation; the proper field for signaling practice is the excursion terrain, vast, hilly fields. It should be organized there as often as possible.

---

title: Dispatch Race
body:
A dispatch race among relay stations set up over a space of several kilometers.

Approaching the camp according to dispatches sent from a hill or the top of a tree, either by whistle or flashlight. The principle of capturing opponents must be numerical superiority in a given location, so that simultaneous command of all is genuinely necessary. In individual approaches, general leadership is not required, as the ingenuity of individuals suffices.

title: Chase of the Fugitives
body:
The chase of fugitives (usually two) within an area enclosed by boundaries, entirely visible from a single point where a signaling station is located, directing the pursuit. A fugitive can only be captured when surrounded by a significant numerical advantage over the opposing party.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: The Siege of Czorsztyn
body:
The starosta, besieged in Czorsztyn Castle, wishes to send a message through the chain of Kostka Napierski’s highlanders surrounding him to the royal troops concealed in the forests behind, in such a way that the highlanders do not intercept the dispatch. Conversely, the royal troops attempt to signal something to the starosta without being seen by Kostka’s men.

In the above manner, by complicating various games with one another, it is necessary to ensure that the skill of signaling remains continually useful during the outings of patrols and the troop. The content of the dispatches that the boys are instructed to signal must also suggest to them the circumstances in which this skill may be of use—such as fires, rescuing flood victims, assisting in the pursuit of a bandit, and the like.

body:
The patrol is shown a collection of several medicine bottles, powders, and other pharmaceutical materials for two minutes. After covering them, each member must list these items, noting at least one use for each medicine. Scoring: for remembering the items and for correctly identifying their uses.

title: Stretcher Race
body:
The patrol divides into several teams of 2 boys each. Beforehand, as many scouts as there are teams step aside and fall down as wounded. author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Disaster
body:
In a disaster, several people have sustained identical injuries. A competition between teams for the best and most efficient rescue.

Such competitions—whether in the form where several teams simultaneously rescue their wounded or where they take turns attending to the same individual—should be organized an infinite number of times during first-aid training. Only practical application can benefit scouts. During the competition, no one should be allowed to say, "Now I would do this or that"; everything must be carried out practically.

title: Injured in the Mountains
body:
Teams consist of 3 boys. One of them is injured, lying on an inaccessible rock in the mountains. He signals a message designated by the patrol leader with his hands, receives a response from the team, and then, after overcoming certain obstacles such as: jumping over a table, walking in balance along a rope stretched across the floor, and the like, reaches the injured person. After performing the appropriate rescue (all as a race), he carries him back on a stretcher. Scoring is triple or quadruple (signaling, obstacles, rescue, speed).

sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Radio Orders (with Variations)
body:
Boys "march" with pencils on paper or "in reality" on the field and receive short orders "via radio" sounding, for example: 5 N, 7 SW, 15 SWW, and so on, which means: 5 kilometers (centimeters on paper, steps on the field) in the north-northwest direction; 7 kilometers in the west-southwest direction, and so on. In the field, this can be combined with signaling: these orders are signaled.

Variation: boys, walking in this way on the field, draw the same on paper.

Variation: boys, having already written such a "dictation," must each define the directions with symbols and then walk accordingly on the field. A storyline is added to this.

Variation: 2 teams receive different orders of the same type, involving counter-dances of units across a certain area—who will encircle whom, block their path, and so on.

Each boy undertakes a journey around the room, stairs, and nooks of the school, continuously making a directional sketch.

title: Drawing Plans
body:
After drawing the plan of a room, a contest is announced for imaginatively sketching a plan—

a design for the most exemplary scout room or Scout House. Who is the most inventive as an architect and the most skillful in sketching?

title: Mountains of Wisdom
body:
The patrol leader arranges stacks of books on a table to form what resembles mountains—larger books at the bottom, with progressively smaller ones toward the top. The boys then create a contour-line sketch of this "terrain"—the upper edges of books of medium thickness represent the shape of a contour line, while the next book on top represents the next contour line. Thus, these "valleys" and "mountains" are marked as on a map—using contour lines.

title: Signaling on a Sketch (with Variation)
body:
The patrol leader presents a sketch of a certain terrain to be copied, on which crosses mark 2 locations that must be connected by signaling stations. However, a mountain (indicated by contour lines) rises between them, blocking the view—there is generally only one spot on its slope from which both points are visible. Find this spot and place a relay signaling station there.

*Variation:* There are multiple such spots, but only one meets the condition that it is not visible from the point where an enemy observer is located.

On a sheet divided into 12 to 16 rectangles, various conventional symbols are written in these squares. It is shown to the boys for 1 to 1 and a half minutes.

During observation, the boys must copy the sheet, placing descriptions in the appropriate squares instead of the conventional symbols—explaining what they represent.

author: Juliusz Dąbrowski
sourceTitle: Gry i zabawy w izbie harcerskiej
title: Terrain Lottery for Scouts
body:
Each boy has on cardboard, divided into 12 rectangles, a drawn sketch of fairly simple terrain, such that each rectangle contains a different conventional symbol or several. Someone "holding the bank" has in a bag a corresponding number of squares for each sketch—a number of small rectangles identical in drawing to the squares on the sketches. Taking such a rectangle in hand, they show it to everyone, after which the one who has such a square on their sketch must state what the visible conventional symbol means, then receives that rectangle. The first to cover their entire sketch with these rectangles wins (a standard game of "lottery").

author: Mieczysław Schreiber i Eugeniusz Piasecki
publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Expedition to the Pole
body:
Each patrol purchases or makes its own sled. Two people take turns pulling it by a rope. It is advantageous (if possible) to train dogs for this purpose and harness them. Two scouts advance the troop by 2—3 kim., cutting across the field, while the rest follow with the sleds and must find the way according to their tracks. They are permitted to aid their orientation with signs left by the vanguard in the snow or made visible to them in any way. All other signs encountered along the way must be examined and their value assessed, having noted them beforehand. On the sleds are provisions, blankets, cooking utensils, firewood, and the like. During rest, snow huts are built, as small and narrow as possible, taking into account the length of the sticks intended to serve as roof bindings. The roof itself is made of brushwood, thoroughly covered with snow.

---

title: Snow Fortress
body:
One patrol builds a fortress out of snow, according to their own design. They equip it with loopholes to have a view of the entire surroundings. Once everything is ready, the enemy patrol launches an attack on it, using snowballs. Every scout hit by a snowball is considered 'killed.' The number of attackers should be at least twice as large as the defenders of the fortress.

author: Mieczysław Schreiber i Eugeniusz Piasecki
publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: The Escape of a Siberian Exile
body:
One of the scouts slips away as a fugitive from a labor camp and flees through the snow in any direction toward some hiding place. There, he conceals himself from the guards, who have just discovered his disappearance. The patrol allows him at least **20** minutes to escape before beginning the pursuit, following his tracks. As they approach the hiding place, the fugitive starts pelting them with snowballs. Anyone hit by the fugitive steps aside as if killed. The fugitive must be hit three times to be considered captured.

author: Mieczysław Schreiber i Eugeniusz Piasecki
publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: The Cossack and the Tatar
body:
Individually, in pairs, or in entire patrols, scouts set out to meet "enemies" distant by some 3 kilometers. To prevent them from straying off course, they may be positioned on a main road or given a direction in open terrain according to some distant visible landmark toward which they must head. Such a landmark could be a steep hill, a tall tree, or a church tower lying in the enemy's rear. The patrol that first spots the opponent is considered the winner. The patrol leader then raises the flag high and gives a whistle signal to notify the entire patrol of the discovery. It is not necessary for patrols to march in a tight group; however, since the patrol whose leader first raises the flag wins, scouts should remain in constant contact through agreed-upon signals, calls, and messengers. All ruses are permitted, such as climbing trees, hiding in wagons, and the like—only disguising oneself is forbidden. Such a game can also be organized at night.

---

author: Mieczysław Schreiber i Eugeniusz Piasecki
publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: The Messenger
body:
A scout is sent to find a designated location, such as a post office in a nearby village or a little-frequented district of a large city. Upon arrival, he mails a registered postcard containing details of the post office building's appearance, addressed to the scoutmaster. After completing this task, he attempts to return to his starting point. However, all routes leading back are already occupied by scouts whom the [patrol leaders] position to cut off the messenger's return. Individual sentries must not approach closer than 200 meters to the post office building. The fugitive, meanwhile, is entitled to use any ruse, even disguises, to slip through the sentry line.

---

author: Mieczysław Schreiber i Eugeniusz Piasecki
publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Kim's Game
body:
The patrol leader places **20** or **30** small objects on a tray, table, or floor (for example, **3** different types of buttons, pencils, corks, scraps of cloth, nuts, pebbles, penknives, pieces of string, pictures—whatever is at hand) and covers them with a cloth or coat. They list these items and prepare a chart with the scouts' names to record their answers about each object. Then, they uncover the items for one minute so the scouts can see everything before covering them again. Finally, the patrol leader takes each scout aside individually and has them whisper into their ear what they remembered from the objects they saw; the patrol leader then records this under the scout's name on the chart. The scout who remembers the most items wins.

---

title: Guide
body:
The Scoutmaster marches with the patrol (in dispersed formation) to a foreign town or more challenging terrain, also unknown, using a cycling map (i.e., 1:750.000). He explains where they aim to reach, after which each Scout takes turns as the patrol guide (for 7 minutes if by bicycle, for 15 minutes if on foot). The guide must find the way using only the map; for skillful map reading, marks are awarded.

author: Mieczysław Schreiber i Eugeniusz Piasecki
publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Where is North?
body:
The Scoutmaster positions the scouts at a distance of 30 paces from one another. Each then places their staff on the ground in the position they believe to be exactly north-south, without using any instrument, and steps back three paces from the staff. The Scoutmaster compares the placement of the staffs with a compass; the scout who is closest to the truth wins. This game should be practiced on sunny days, cloudy days, and at night.

author: Mieczysław Schreiber i Eugeniusz Piasecki
publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Sentry Approach
body:
At night, a scout is positioned as a sentry, and others are instructed to approach him. If the sentry detects their approach, he signals with a whistle, at which point those approaching throw themselves to the ground and remain still, waiting quietly without moving. The patrol leader determines the distance at which the sentry allowed himself to be approached and questions him about where he heard the rustling and expected the enemy; if he identifies the direction correctly, he wins. The game can also be arranged in such a way that those approaching, having stealthily closed to within 15 steps of the sentry, leave behind an object as proof of their presence in that spot and retreat a few steps as they came. Only then do they raise the alarm, forcing the sentry to signal with a whistle and prompting the patrol leader to appear, who records the outcome of the game. Practice the same exercise during the day, blindfolding the sentries.

publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Marmots
body:
At dawn, three scouts called "marmots" are sent out into the mountains to hide. After breakfast, the scout troop, acting as "highlanders," sets off to detect the marmots by a certain hour, for example, 4 in the afternoon. The highlanders win if they spot the marmots, even with the aid of binoculars, by accurately identifying the person and their hiding place (the "burrow"). Certain boundaries are set, beyond which both the marmot and the highlander are considered out of the game.

author: Mieczysław Schreiber i Eugeniusz Piasecki
publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Whale Hunting
body:
At a distance of 1 half a kilometer from each other, two scout troops establish two landing points and wait for the signal. Someone not participating in the game then launches a log of soft wood into the water midway between the two landing points, representing a whale, and gives the signal to begin the hunt. At this signal, the scouts set out in their boats from opposite landing points, and whoever reaches the whale first strikes it with a harpoon and pulls it to their port. However, the second boat does the same and tries to drag the catch to its own side. Victory depends on discipline and good rowing. Sometimes, it may even be possible to pull not only the whale but also the entire opposing boat, which has become attached to the log with its harpoon, to one's own port. Each boat is led by a troop leader (Captain), one scout serves as the harpooner (the harpoon resembles a spear with a barb like a fishing hook so that once embedded, it cannot be pulled out; the other end is tied to a thick rope), while the others row.

author: Mieczysław Schreiber i Eugeniusz Piasecki
publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: His Majesty's Royal Courier
body:
The Scoutmaster (acting as the king) gives one of the scouts, as the courier, a letter with the order to infiltrate besieged Zbaraż—which may be any town, village, or house—and return with proof of delivery. The courier must wear a colored ribbon, **60** cm long, pinned to the arm. The courier sets out from a distance of at least **6** km from "Zbaraż." Scouts playing the roles of besieging Tatar and Cossack forces, in order to track the courier down, may choose any positions, but no closer than **300** m from Zbaraż (it is best to mark clear, easily visible boundaries). A Cossack or Tatar encountered by the judge within these boundaries is disqualified from the game. The courier may use any ruses except disguising as a woman; however, the courier must always wear the aforementioned colored ribbon on the arm. The courier is only considered captured when the enemy removes the ribbon. The game may last up to **10** hours. Within this time, the courier must deliver the royal letter to the Zbaraż commander and return to the king with proof of delivery. Each besieger earns **3** points if they capture the courier, but loses the same number if they fail.

title: Caravan
body:
Scouts form a Central African caravan; each carries spare clothing and provisions in a small bundle on their head. They march in a line, preceded by a "guide" at a distance of 200 meters, and follow scouting signs left by the guide. They build bridges across rivers, rafts for crossing ponds, lay fascines on marshy ground, and the like; they also leave signs for other caravans.

publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Scout Race
body:
The Scoutmaster places three scouts or three groups of scouts, each differing in clothing details and objects held in hand, at distances of 300—1000 metres from the starting point. If there are other people in this area, these groups are given a distinguishing posture (e.g., kneeling on one knee) to set them apart from passers-by. The Scoutmaster then designates three points along a circular route measuring approximately 400 metres, which the competitors must traverse. When they reach the point 1, the judge stationed there tells them in which direction the group they must report on is located. Upon spotting this group, each competitor writes a report including: 1) the number of people in the group, 2) clothing and other identifying marks, 3) position relative to a nearby landmark, and 4) the distance of the group from their station. They then run to the second and third points, repeating the same task, and so on, finally returning to the starting point to report to the Scoutmaster. For each correct and precise description of a group, 5 marks are awarded, thus 15 marks for the entire race. From this total, 1 mark is deducted for every 10 minutes of delay compared to the first returning competitor; marks or half-marks are also deducted for errors and omissions in the report.

author: Mieczysław Schreiber i Eugeniusz Piasecki
publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Seek the Thimble
body:
The Scoutmaster sends the patrol out of the room. Then he takes a thimble, ring, coin, piece of paper, or any small object and places it so that it is perfectly visible, yet in a spot where it will be easily overlooked. He calls the patrol back and instructs them to search. When one of the Scouts spots the place, he must not let it show; instead, he moves to another side and sits quietly. After some time, the Scoutmaster asks him to point out the sought-after object.

author: Mieczysław Schreiber i Eugeniusz Piasecki
publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Shop Windows
body:
The Scoutmaster leads the patrol down a street past six shops and allows them to look at each display for half a minute. Then, having moved them a certain distance away, he gives each a pencil and paper and instructs them to write down from memory what they saw, for example, in the third and fifth shops. The Scout who correctly lists the most items wins. This game can also be usefully played by dividing the patrol into 4 pairs, with each pair having one Scout compete against the other. The four losers then split into two pairs again, and the two who lose this time play once more, until the Scout weakest in observation is identified. (This method, contrary to sporting practice, provides the most exercise to those who need it most.)

title: What Does the Room Contain?
body:
The Scoutmaster sends scouts one by one into a room for half a minute; each, upon exiting, must list the furniture and other objects they noticed. The winner is the one who observed the most. The simplest way to record the items will be to prepare in advance a list of objects on a table divided into columns, labeled with the scouts' names (as in Kim's Game).
