author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Matching Colors
body:
Prepare a series of strips (pieces of cotton, paper strips) in various shades of a single color, for example, red, ranging from a light pink shade to a dark claret. Color samples should be available in two identical sets for each participant in the game.

Game: a) Hand one of the color strips to a participant and instruct them to find the matching color among the mixed samples of the second set.

b) Mix all the strips and instruct participants to arrange them in order according to the degree of brightness.

c) Matching as in a), but from memory, without looking at the original sample.

d) Answer questions: Which of these colors is brick-red, orange, ash-gray, sky-blue? — What is the name of this (shown) color?

NOTE. The exercise can be graded as follows: 1) increasing the number of shades; 2) shortening the time the shades are shown in method c; 3) showing and instructing to match several shades instead of one; 4) providing not shades of one color but mixing different colors and instructing to find the shown colors (shades) among them.

When conducting these exercises, they can be varied by organizing competitions: a) who can select 5, 10, etc., colors shown by 2, 1 within half a minute; b) who can find the most colors within a given time (6, 3, 2 minutes).

---

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Luring with Feints (Cossacks and Tatars)
body:
The patrol divides into two parties: Cossacks and Tatars, who stand facing each other at a distance of 20—30 steps. Between the parties, slightly closer to the Tatars, a handkerchief is placed on the ground. A Tatar approaches the handkerchief by one step and makes various movements, which the Cossack must imitate. At an opportune moment, the Tatar snatches the handkerchief and flees to his own side, while the Cossack gives chase. If he succeeds, he takes the Tatar captive; if not, he himself is taken prisoner. The party that has the most captives after the allotted time wins.

---

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Hop-and-Catch Granny
body:
Everyone hops on one leg, while the hop-and-catch granny tries with nimble leaps to catch and tag one of the fleeing players, who then becomes the hop-and-catch granny.

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Relay Race
body:
In addition to the methods provided in Prof. Piasecki’s manual, the relay race can be conducted as follows: a) patrols line up in rows a few paces apart, with the scoutmaster standing several dozen paces away from them. The first in each row runs toward the scoutmaster upon a given signal, strikes his hand (with a handkerchief, etc.), returns, hands the handkerchief to the last in their row, and takes their place at the end. In this manner, all members of the patrols run in turn—the patrol wins whose last scout strikes the scoutmaster first. b) Relay race without competition: Scouts position themselves at intervals of several or several dozen paces, depending on their training, and are tasked with carrying an object (or an order) given by the scoutmaster to the other end of the chain in the shortest time possible (similar to the method described in Dr. Piasecki’s manual, p. 65—except without competition between patrols; even a single patrol may conduct such a race).

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: The Bird-Catcher
body:
Number of players: 4—20. One is chosen as the buyer and another as the bird-catcher; the rest each receive from the bird-catcher the name of a bird, though the buyer must not be present for this. The birds line up in a row. The buyer approaches to select a bird, and the bird-catcher orders the birds to sing. After some time, the buyer says, for example: I wish for a sparrow. The bird-catcher calls: Fly, little sparrow, fly!—whereupon the one who is the sparrow runs away, and the buyer chases them. If during the chase the sparrow is in danger, the bird-catcher releases all the birds, who then try to hinder the chase. When the sparrow returns to the bird-catcher, the others also return. If the buyer catches the sparrow, the sparrow becomes the buyer, the buyer becomes a bird, and everyone receives the names of other birds. (Instead of birds, other animals may be imitated.)

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Bullfight
body:
Among the 12 players, one is the bull, one the matador (or espada), four are picadors, and six are capeadors. The playing area (arena) is enclosed by a "hedge" (skrum) formed by spectators linking arms. If there are too few spectators, the arena is marked with small flags. The game is divided into 2 periods. The bull’s entry into the arena, where the picadors and capeadors already await, begins the game. The bull’s mark consists of 5—6 strips of paper, each about 15 cm long, attached to its back. The picadors attempt to tear off these strips, while the bull defends itself by striking approaching players with its hand or a bat. Only one strip may be torn off at a time, and any picador struck by the bull is out of the game. The capeadors assist the picadors by intervening when the bull chases a picador—waving a sash or handkerchief in the bull’s face to divert its pursuit toward themselves, thus halting its chase of the picador. The capeadors cannot be eliminated.

When all picadors are out or all strips are torn off, the second half of the game begins. The arena is cleared, leaving only two players: the bull and the matador. The bull has its eyes blindfolded and a loosely tied sash around its neck, which can be torn off with a single tug. This is the matador’s task; they must be very agile and cautious to avoid being struck by the bull, as this would mean the bull wins. If the matador succeeds in tearing off the sash, it signifies the bull has been slain, and the matador is the victor.

---

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: The Deer Hunt
body:
In the afternoon period, a game such as "the deer hunt" was organized, in which one of the players, the "deer," left the camp equipped with 12 soft balls. Twenty minutes later, four "hunters" set out after him, following his tracks, each with one ball. After covering a kilometer or two, the deer would typically hide, attempting to lure the hunters into an ambush, since any hunter hit by the deer with a ball was considered "gored to death by antlers." If, however, three balls struck the deer, he was deemed killed.

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Approaching the Blindfolded
body:
Divide the patrol into pairs. The chosen scout sits on the ground with eyes blindfolded. The terrain selected for this game must be covered with dry twigs, leaves, gravel, and small stones. The second scout, approaching cautiously from a distance of 20 metres, must cover this distance in 1½ minutes and touch the seated scout before being heard. Then, they switch roles: the one who approached becomes the blindfolded scout and vice versa. Before the game, remind participants of the 1. point of the Scout Law regarding honesty.

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Sneaking Past (Wall of the Blind)
body:
The patrol divides into two halves. One half, with eyes blindfolded, is arranged in a line with spacing slightly greater than both arms outstretched. The other half of the scouts must sneak through this living wall from a certain distance. Both groups are allowed to make any movements, but those standing as the "wall" may not move from their spot (they may sit, kneel, or wave their arms), while those approaching may not retreat.

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Expedition for Plants
body:
An expedition for plants sharpens visual acuity, trains in identifying plants, and enriches memory—or reinforces the store of botanical names.

Scouts may be instructed individually or in pairs, by bicycle or on foot, to go in any direction they choose and bring back specified (rarer in the given area) plant species. For example, 10 tree branches, or 10 field flowers, or 10 poisonous plants. When selecting plants, one should use a handbook describing the geographical distribution of plants in our country.

The patrol leader or judge will award points for the fastest return with the requested plant.

To start, begin with a few, two, or even one plant.

---

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Collecting Cotton
body:
Prepare pieces of cotton or yarn, each 1 foot (30 cm) in length. The type may be the cheapest available, as long as the color is not bright (khaki is best). Using these pieces, mark a path as the instructor, through pastures, forests, rocky areas, or generally less frequented places. Avoid cultivated fields unless they are your own property or you have permission from the owners. Do not simply throw the cotton on the ground; instead, attach it to trees, fences, bushes, or low-hanging branches, spaced 20 paces apart. Then, send out 1 or 2 patrols to collect all the pieces and reach the end of the marked path as quickly as possible.

When a scout participating in the game spots a piece of yarn, they must announce it by calling their patrol so that both patrols can more easily orient themselves in the search. Apart from the case of finding a trail, no other shouts are allowed.

Each patrol collects the found yarn into the hands of their patrol leader. The patrol whose leader has the greater number of cotton pieces at the end of the game wins. This game gives the instructor an opportunity to identify the most skilled trackers. If the trails are skillfully laid out, the winning patrol’s scouts deserve an additional mark for their cleverness. This method of tracking has the advantage over tracker’s irons in that it teaches scouts to pay close attention not only to the ground but to all directions.

The same exercise can also be conducted with a single patrol, in which case the goal is simply to see which scout collects the most pieces of cotton. Instead of cotton, long strips of paper or so-called wood wool may be used—though these are inferior as they are too visible and litter the area more if the scouts do not collect them carefully.

Tracker’s irons are used to leave traces that distinguish them from the tracks of ordinary passersby.

---

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Campfire Race
body:
When setting up camp, especially after prolonged strenuous games, it is possible to keep the weary engaged through the excitement of competition. It suffices to promise a certain number of marks to the entire patrol that, in the shortest time, gathers kindling, arranges it, and lights a campfire, using the fewest matches for this purpose.

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Near — Far
body:
The patrol leader leads their unit in patrol formation through the town or surrounding area. Having prepared beforehand lists of objects for the scouts to observe, they distribute these lists at the moment of departure and instruct the scouts to mark with strokes each time someone spots an item on the list. The patrol leader compiles the list of objects to train scouts in observing both near and far distances simultaneously, and to break the habit—common among those trained in tracking—of focusing only on the ground beneath their feet. Example list of objects: broken window, damaged chimney top, matchstick, button, dog tracks, bird tracks, tower, landmark tree, statue, number of birds in flight, types of birds, lame horse, horse tracks, the horse’s gait, and the like. The scout with the most observations—marked by strokes—wins.

For variety, this exercise can be modified so that scouts are only required to observe and remember their observations, while the patrol leader notes them down. Later, through cleverly posed questions, the leader determines which scout in the patrol has the keenest sense of observation.

Initially, observations are made over a distance of 2 kilometers, later gradually extending to longer excursions. Example questions: What sound reached your ears as we left the town? From which direction was the wind blowing? How was the smoke rising? How many carriages were coming toward us? How many were behind us? What was the inscription on the statue? How many geese were swimming? How many roosters were crowing? From which direction were the crows flying?

---

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Tracking by Scraps (Hare)
body:
A scout chosen by lot, equipped with a good quantity of some grains or paper scraps (the latter being worse as they litter the area), goes along any path, marking the trail every several dozen steps by dropping scraps or grains. They may create false trails, i.e., deviate from the correct path, leave a mark, and return to the original direction. The rest of the patrol sets off after 10 minutes and tracks them by following the trail. The end of the exercise is marked by the place the tracked scout is to reach, which the rest should not know, or by the hour the exercise concludes.

---

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Tracking Footprints
body:
Have one patrol sit so that the soles of their boots are clearly visible. The second patrol is given 3 minutes to observe. Then, the scouts of the first patrol are allowed to leave, except for one who is instructed to take several steps on soft ground, prepared specifically for this purpose. Afterward, the scouts of the 2 patrol are called back and, based on their observation of the boots, are asked to guess whose footprint it is. Naturally, the second patrol does not know which scouts were told to leave and who was asked to stay to make the footprint. A good exercise in winter. It can also be practiced with a single patrol divided into 2 parts.

---

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Approaching the Guard
body:
The instructor sends the scouts in different directions to places half a kilometer away from him. Then he waves a flag to signal the start of the game. At that moment, everyone drops to the ground and, hiding behind bushes or ground irregularities, sometimes moving stealthily, other times crawling, they approach him closer and closer. When the instructor gives a second signal with the flag, everyone stands up, approaches him, and delivers a report. In the meantime—that is, between the first and second flag signals—the instructor performs brief movements, such as sitting down, kneeling, looking through binoculars, removing his hat, waving his hat, wiping sweat from his forehead, sneezing, walking in circles, counting on his fingers, shading his eyes with his hand, clapping his hands, and the like. The scouts must observe, remember, and later recount all these movements to him upon their return.

Additionally, the instructor carefully scans all directions, and whenever he spots one of the scouts, he marks 2 minus points against them. During the report, the scout who correctly lists all the judge’s movements in order and observed from the closest distance receives 3 points.

To save time, the scouts can be given cards on which they write down the observed movements under their names.

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Stalking Game
body:
The instructor plays the role of the game, while the scouts move away from him by 100 steps, drop to the ground (preferably on undulating terrain or sparsely overgrown with bushes), and by crawling, attempt to get as close to him as possible without being seen by the instructor. If he spots any scout, he orders that scout to stand up and cease playing. After some time, he gives a signal with a bugle or a password, everyone stands up, and the one who crawled closest unnoticed wins and receives marks.

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: The Urban Roundup
body:
A Scout known for cunning, agility, and ruses is chosen as the fugitive (smuggler). The starting point for the fugitive must be a location 2 kilometers away from the camp (or meeting room). If possible, the starting point should be one from which the greatest number of routes lead to the camp. The game is to last one hour, assuming this time is sufficient for the fugitive to return to the camp.

The fugitive sets off from the "start" precisely at the designated time, which is also known to the opponents. It is better if a judge is assigned to ensure the punctuality of the start.

The rest of the Scouts hide along all the routes, straining their eyes to recognize the fugitive, who approaches the camp in any disguise. The rule must be observed that no ambush may be set within a radius of 300 paces from the start or finish. The fugitive, however, is not allowed to disguise themselves in women’s clothing or use a carriage, tram, or cart. They are also forbidden from entering a shop to hide if enemies have already approached nearby. Whoever recognizes the fugitive calmly approaches them, greets them with the agreed-upon password, and accompanies them to the camp or meeting room. Any scuffling or fleeing is strictly prohibited. After one hour, everyone returns to the camp, and the winner receives marks.

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Drawing a Track
body:
After leading your patrol outside the town and showing them a certain track, offer a reward for the best and most accurate drawing of the imprint (track) of the left and right foot. Scouts are allowed to follow the track for a short distance until they reach ground where the tracks are most clearly imprinted. A variation of this game will be drawing hoof prints of a horse, including measurements of the stride length, and based on these, identifying the horse's gait—whether it walked, trotted, or galloped.

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Snow Fortress
body:
This game involves two groups (two patrols). One group builds a snow fortress according to their own ideas, if possible with loopholes—either round (a rondel), four-sided (a bastion), or zigzag-shaped—a bastion. Once the fortress is completed, the group that built it becomes the garrison of the stronghold and prepares for defense, gathering a full supply of snowballs as ammunition.

The second group acts as the enemy, launching an attack on the fortress and aiming snowballs at its defenders. The defenders likewise try to hit the attackers with snowballs. Any scout struck by a snowball is considered "killed" and withdraws from the game. The number of attackers should generally be twice that of the defenders. After a quarter of an hour of attack, the game ends, and victory is awarded to the side that, after counting the casualties on both sides, has a greater number of survivors than the opposing side.

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Two Couriers with Dispatches
body:
A game in which 2 patrols, or 2 units, compete for superiority. The patrols stand at a distance of 4 kilometers from each other. The instructor (the troop leader acting as referee) is positioned at an equal distance (2 km) from the patrols, in a town at the junction of two streets, or on an outing in the middle of a forest. At the appointed time, couriers from opposite sides set off simultaneously and punctually. The task of the remaining scouts in each patrol is to skillfully place obstacles in the way of the opposing courier so that he cannot deliver the letter. To this end, they lie in wait for him in an ambush along the route he is most likely to take to his destination. However, they must leave 200 meters from the start and 200 meters before the finish line free. A captured courier may be held, and his letter taken from him, but it is not permitted to struggle with him, much less strike him. Simply touching the courier during pursuit by opponents already signifies that he has been captured.

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Fox Hunt
body:
The chosen fox is given a head start of 20 minutes, during which time they must set off and hide. The task of the rest of the patrol is to locate the hiding place and catch the fox. The fox is considered caught when struck by the hand of any pursuer. The pursuit advances in a semicircle, with the scouts spread out. The hidden fox wins if they are not found within the allotted time or if they manage to return to the starting point untouched. The winter version of the fox hunt differs. (It is known that the fox is a great pest, and hunting it takes place all year round to exterminate it.) Two scouts set out into the field as foxes, and after 5 minutes, the rest of the patrol follows their trail as hunters. If the foxes avoid capture for an hour, they return to camp victorious. Foxes must not cross human tracks, and upon encountering them, they must turn in another direction. However, to mislead the pursuit and avoid leaving tracks, they may employ various tricks: one may step into the other’s footprints, both may walk along fences or walls, or using a stick as a pole, they may leap sideways and advance in such bounds. This game is particularly successful in snowy conditions. For the pursuing party to win, both foxes must be caught.

---

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: The Spider and the Fly
body:
A piece of field, forest, or part of a town measuring 1—3 square kilometers is chosen as the spiderweb. Its boundaries are described, and the game's end time is marked. Several players are the flies, who go out and seek a comfortable hiding place. The other half sets out a quarter of an hour later to search for the flies. Each group is accompanied by an impartial referee. If the spider does not detect the fly within the designated time (e.g., one hour, two), the fly wins. The fly records the names of the players from the spider group, while the spider does the same with the flies, additionally noting the hiding place. Each such report counts as a mark. Both sides should have colored badges for easy distinction.

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Cossack Maneuver in the Steppe
body:
This game is an excellent school for stalking and has the added advantage of requiring no equipment. It can be played by 2 groups, 2 pairs, or two individual players. The terrain can be city streets—just as suitable as undulating plains overgrown with bushes, roads with ditches and avenues, ravines, or forest paths. The principle of the game is to spot the opponent while remaining unseen yourself.

Both sides set out (at the same time, as enforced by the referees) from two opposing points, for example, 2 kilometers apart, and move toward each other, utilizing terrain unevenness, trees, and bushes to conceal themselves. In this way, they advance stealthily by crawling or moving furtively, striving not to expose themselves while straining their eyes to spot the opponent. They may also employ ruses, such as climbing trees, sneaking in a cart, and the like, but disguises are not allowed.

Opponents are taken prisoner according to the general rules stated above.

The side that is stronger (has lost fewer people) after a set period of time wins.

---

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Urban Reconnaissance
body:
The patrol leader designates one scout to flee and hide. The rest of the patrol gathers in the quietest part of the town, that is, where vehicular and pedestrian traffic is minimal.

The chosen fugitive has **4 minutes** to hide, slip away, and gain a lead, during which the rest of the patrol does not track him—except for two scouts who follow invisibly just behind him. After two minutes, one of the tracking pair returns to the patrol at a run to lead them to the spot where he stopped trailing, while the other continues forward, leaving behind clues such as scraps of paper.

Naturally, all must be well-trained in pursuit and reading tracks, for a cleverly escaping scout employs every possible means and ruse to mislead the pursuit. At the start of the game, a deadline must be set by which the fugitive must evade capture to win. A touch by the hand of a pursuer signifies that the fugitive has been caught.

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: Expedition to the Pole
body:
Each patrol participating in this expedition, having equipped themselves with sledges, loads them with provisions, sled bags, shovels, and the like. The sledges are pulled in turns by all the scouts in pairs. Ahead, **2** scouts march some **2** kilometres before the convoy and mark the route, either by the tracks of their boots or by various signs.

The rest follow behind, read the signs, and upon arriving at the destination, build huts from snow using the shovels. During this, staffs serve as supports, and brushwood is used to reinforce the walls and roof.

**NOTE.** Depending on the weather, organise an outing into the field, where the "expedition to the pole" or, alternatively, a "snow fort" and the like may take place, or else limit the exercise to the city.

author: Stanisław Sedlaczek
title: The Escape of the Siberian Deportee
body:
A Scout playing the role of an escaping Siberian deportee runs in any direction across snow, where tracks are clearly visible, until he finds a suitable hiding place in which to conceal himself. The rest of the patrol sets out 20 minutes later, following his tracks to reach his hiding place. When they come within a snowball’s throw, the hidden deportee aims snowballs at them, and each hit player steps out of the game. The pursuers also try to hit the deportee with snowballs. The deportee is allowed to take refuge in a tree, but must be hit three times before being considered "killed." In summer, the game changes in that the deportee attaches tracking irons and fills his pockets with corn or peas, so that on rocky or muddy terrain, where tracks disappear, he can mark his path by dropping a grain or pea at each step. Snowballs are replaced either with pinecones or tennis balls (see "deer hunting" in the *Introduction*).

title: FINDING THE OBJECT
body:
The group goes out to the adjacent room. The patrol leader places a small object (a lead soldier) in a visible spot. The Cubs return and begin searching. The first one to find it hides the object in the next game.

Several nails or nibs can be hidden. The Cub who finds the greatest number within the set time wins and starts the game anew by redistributing the nails in the group's absence.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: MATCHING HALVES OF CARDS
body:
We cut a dozen or so postcards in half in various directions. Some of them are distributed to the group, while the remaining halves (a few more than those distributed) are laid out in an adjacent room or at the end of the hall. The cubs must not look at their halves before the agreed signal. Only upon the command do they search for the missing halves and line up, returning to the starting point in the order of their arrival, thus securing successive places in this race.

To make it easier to separate the cards for the next game, we mark one set of halves with a cross and the other with a circle.

title: MATCHSTICK PUZZLES
body:
A group sits in a circle. Each Cub has a box of matches.

The Sixer gives commands: "Arrange the name of a river using 15 matches," "Arrange a little house," and the like.

In evaluation: who is faster? whose is prettier? the whole group takes part.

More difficult puzzles: 1) arrange 5 little squares from 9 matches, 2) from 15 matches arrange 5 equal adjoining squares and remove 3 matches so that only 3 squares remain.

title: MATCHING COLORS
body:
A small group stands in a line. Each girl receives a ribbon several centimeters long. The ribbons should be of different colors, and they may even be in different shades.

At the opposite end of the room, the patrol leader lays out ribbons of the same colors on a table; she may also add more colors.

Whoever matches the correct color (on a given signal) lines up in the order of their return to the assembly point.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: ARRANGING LEAVES
body:
Cub Scouts scatter through the forest in search of 5 different yellowed leaves.

At the whistle, they return and arrange their leaves by colour—from the lightest to the darkest.

The group in which more Cub Scouts have arranged the leaves correctly wins.

Variation for younger ones: From the collected leaves, arrange a carpet for the ‘Queen of Autumn.’

The group that arranges the most beautiful carpet wins.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: MOSAIC
body:
There are two types of mosaic: geometric and folk. The geometric type consists of a set of the most commonly encountered shapes: circle, square, triangle, and rectangle; the folk type is made up of forms predominant in folk art: little heart, peacock’s eye, star, sprig, flower, and the like.

A mosaic can be prepared at gatherings by gluing colored glossy paper on both sides of cardboard and cutting out the desired elements. Thanks to the variety of colors and shapes, mosaic is loved by children; it can also be used in activities to train the cubs’ observation skills, aesthetic sense, and develop creativity.

The following activities and games can be used in packs:

1. Place a box with mosaic pieces in the middle of the pack sitting on the floor. Each cub chooses any shapes and arranges a pattern of their own design. Then everyone looks and decides whose pattern they like the most. — The sixer observes how each one copes, how they work, takes part in the evaluation, draws attention to color harmony, indicates which elements should be turned for better color combination, which should be moved or discarded.

2. Divide the pack into two or three groups. Several cubs then work together to arrange one pattern. This involves cooperation and group competition. Evaluation — as above.

3. The sixer instructs one of the more skilled cubs to arrange a not-too-complicated star or "paper-cut" design, which the pack observes for three minutes and then replicates using similar templates.

The pattern is revealed, and together they check how many made mistakes.

4. Mosaic can be used at a pack gathering by conducting the following game:

In front of the packs standing in rows lie identical sets of mosaic pieces. The first ones run up and start arranging a pattern, then the next ones run up, and so on. Only two elements may be placed at a time. The pack that arranges the prettiest pattern wins.

title: CINDERELLA
body:
Each of the girls sitting around the table receives a box containing a certain number of mixed small objects, such as nails, buttons, and coins. Those who most skillfully arrange the objects on the table by type win.

This game can also be used as a touch exercise by blindfolding the cubs.

title: CHARADE
body:
One of the girls leaves, and the remaining ones choose a word, for example, *excursion*. They divide into groups according to the division of the word into syllables, and upon the return of the absent one, at a given signal, they simultaneously pronounce the previously chosen syllable. The task is to recognize the syllables and guess the word.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: FOLLOWING THE WHISTLE'S CALL
body:
The game can take place in a forest, on built-up terrain, in a large hall, and the like. Two groups take part. Two cubs, each from a different group, hide 100 paces from the gathering spot. One cub has a siren, the other—a whistle.

Orally or by means of a note, the leader gives each group the task of finding their cub, indicating which whistle each of the girls has. Following the sound of the whistle, the group tries to locate the cub as quickly as possible.

The side that first brings the found cub to the leader wins.

title: COMMANDS «BY GESTURES»
body:
The patrol leaders step out and confer. They are to issue a command, each to their own group. The command cannot be spoken; it must be shown by gestures. The content and form of the command are the same for all groups. The patrol leaders return and demonstrate to their groups what they are to do.

The group that first correctly guesses and properly executes the command wins.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: MOVEMENT TELEGRAM
body:
Groups stand in rows, facing away from the troop leader. At the troop leader’s signal, the first in each group turns around. The troop leader performs several movements, for example: kneels down, listens intently, places a hand to the forehead, waves above the head. Then, the first ones turn back and repeat the movements they saw, the second ones repeat them to the third, and so on. Silence must be maintained during the game. The last ones step forward in front of the group line and repeat the movements. The group that repeats the movements most accurately wins.

title: DISTRIBUTING ITEMS
body:
Groups stand in rows. The first members collect some small item from each Cub. These items are placed three paces in front of the group, then the collectors run three times around their group and afterwards distribute the items. Whoever receives their own item raises a hand. The group wins in which the most items reach their rightful owners.

title: HOLD — RELEASE
body:
A game for a group or two. The Brownies stand in a circle. They hold the edges of an apron or dress with their fingers. The patrol leader, standing in the circle, turns to one of the girls and calls: "hold." She should release, and only hold again when the patrol leader says "release." Whoever makes a mistake leaves the game. The "unerring" Brownie wins.

title: CHANGING THE BALL'S DIRECTION
body:
Cubs form a circle, throwing the ball to each other or passing it in turn. On the patrol leader's whistle, the ball must change direction. The girl who makes a mistake and does not change the ball's direction leaves the game. The "unerring" one wins.

title: IT'S BURNING, IT'S FALLING
body:
Two groups sit facing each other in rows, cross-legged. The first group jumps up at the leader’s call of "it's burning," and the second does the same when they hear "it's falling."

We begin the game. If any of the girls makes a mistake—that is, stands up when she should have stayed seated or delays standing when the whole group is already up—

she is out of the game. The group that has the "unerring" Scout left wins.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: POTATO GATHERING
body:
Groups stand in rows. Circles (bowls) are drawn 10 paces in front of each group. Between the group and the bowl lie as many potatoes as there are children in each group. The first cubs receive a spoon. At the signal given by the troop leader, they place their left hand behind their back and, with their right hand, scoop one potato onto the spoon and carry it to the bowl, then pass the spoon to the next cubs.

The group that gathers its potatoes first wins.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: With a Little Bag
body:
The cub groups stand in rows. The first cubs receive little bags. On the signal, they place the bag on their leg and carefully, so the bag does not fall, walk forward to the designated spot and return to their groups. They remove the bag and pass it to the next child, then go to the end of the line. The group that finishes the race first and drops the bag the fewest times wins.

Complication: The cubs receive a small ball and a little bag; they place the ball on the back of their hand and the bag on their leg.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: With Little Balls
body:
Groups stand in rows. The first cubs receive little balls, which they place on the back of their hand. At the leader's signal, they move forward so carefully that the ball does not fall, reach the wall or a marked line, and return the same way to their group, after which they pass the ball to the next child, who, without waiting for the other groups, does the same as the previous one. The group wins where the ball falls the least number of times or not at all, and which returns to the starting point the fastest.

Cubs bring shoe polish and brushes to the gathering. At the patrol leader’s command, they begin cleaning. The three who shine their shoes most beautifully win.

title: LITTLE STEWARD
body:
A pack game. Cubs stand in small groups. At a signal, children from each group run out in turn and carry out commands, for example: cover the table with a napkin, pour tea, wash a glass, saucer, teaspoon, place the glass on a tray, and so on. For faster and more efficient execution, the cub earns a point for their group. The highest number of points wins.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: DRESSING DOLLS
body:
Groups stand in rows. In front of each group sits a doll (a Cub in full uniform). At the signal, the first from each group runs out and removes the beret from the doll, then returns to the end of the row. The next ones run out and remove the bows (sashes, shoes, socks, etc.). Each girl knows in advance what she has to do.

Once the doll is undressed, the same Cubs dress it again. The group that undresses and dresses the doll the fastest wins.

title: THREADING THE NEEDLE
body:
Groups stand in rows. At a certain distance, a bench is placed, and on it, for each group, a needle and thread. At a signal given by the leader, the first in line run up, thread the needle, and return to the end of the row; the next run out and do the same. The group that finishes the race first wins.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: LITTLE SEAMSTRESS
body:
Cubs stand in small groups. On the table, we prepare appropriate tasks. We distribute slips of paper with instructions to the cubs, with the first group having the same exercises, the second group likewise, and so on. At the signal, everyone reads their assigned tasks and hurries to complete them. The group that performs the tasks most neatly wins.

Examples of instructions: Sew on a button. Repair a hanger. Mark your letters, darn a sock, make a patch, and so on. — A similar exercise can be conducted as a test of skills for the Little Seamstress proficiency badge.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: POTATO PEELERS
body:
I. Cubs stand in groups in rows. In front of each group, at a certain distance, lie potatoes and knives. At the signal, the first ones run out, peel one potato, and return to their place; the next ones run out. The group that finishes first and peels the potatoes best wins.

II. Group race. All Cubs peel potatoes simultaneously. The group that peels the most and best within the set time wins.

The above races are suitable for conducting on an outing or at a gathering "with cooking," when the peeled potatoes can be boiled.

title: ORDERS

At the whistle, they immediately stop, standing back to back. This game and several that follow develop discipline and self-control.

title: THE LEADER COMMANDS

The troop leader gives commands: Jump, sit, tie a knot, fall in, and the like. If the words "The leader commands" precede the order, the command must be carried out. If these words are not spoken, the group stands still.

One of the cubs is a dragon that bursts from its cave and captures any cub who moves.

This game should be played briefly and quickly. After three commands, the prisoners may be freed.

Each Cub prepares a parcel to be sent by post, writes the address, and hands it to the leader (post office). Parcels are thrown into a corner onto a pile. When all are ready, they are sent by tossing from one Cub to another and so on around the room. The farther the parcels travel, the better. Those parcels that withstand the test are delivered; others are lost.

title: SIGNALING
body:
One sixer stands opposite the others, and on the command given by the team leader, each Cub shows one letter of the alphabet—using semaphore or the deaf-and-dumb alphabet—so that the letters form a word. Two or three remaining groups read the word in silence. The group that reads it first writes the word on a piece of paper and delivers it to the game leader—wins.

title: COMPASS
body:
Each Cub draws a slip of paper with the name of one cardinal direction. The leader draws a large circle—a compass—and calls out any cardinal direction. The Cubs must stand in the correct place before the leader counts to ten. Anyone who makes a mistake loses a point.

A more challenging version involves the Cubs positioning themselves relative to the leader’s place in the circle, with the leader then serving as “north.”

title: POINTS OF THE COMPASS — BLINDFOLDED
body:
The entire group has their eyes blindfolded and stands in the middle of the room. The troop leader stands to the north and says: "I am in the north." She then changes direction and, after stopping, asks: "Where am I now?" The Cub who gives the answer first earns a point.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: THE ORIGIN OF THE ROE DEER
body:
A group game for Brownies. The "Roe Deer" stands in the center, with the other girls positioned at a certain distance around her. A Brownie designated by the patrol leader approaches the Roe Deer as quietly as possible. If the Roe Deer hears a rustle and correctly points in the direction with her hand, the approaching girl retreats to her previous spot, and another girl approaches at the patrol leader’s signal. The winner is the one who approaches unheard and touches the Roe Deer’s shoulder.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: ORIGIN OF THE GUARD
body:
This game is best played on an outing in the bushes. The Cubs form a circle, and the guard stands in the center. Then the girls scatter within a radius of 50 or more paces. At the agreed signal, they approach, hiding behind the bushes.

The guard, looking around, points with their hand at the spotted Cubs. Those pointed out sit down in the exact spot where the guard saw them. The one who approaches the guard unnoticed or to the closest distance wins.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: SENTRIES
body:
A group game. One player stands on sentry duty, while the others are at the opposite end of the playing field or hall. As soon as the game begins, the sentry stands with their back turned to those approaching. All try to approach as close as possible without being noticed. The moment the sentry turns around, the group must stand still. Whoever moves must return to the starting point and approach from the goal line again. The Cub who touches the sentry with their hand before being noticed by them wins.

title: The Enchanted Princess
body:
One group forms a circle. The Cubs stand at a certain distance from each other and cover their eyes.

In the center of the circle stands the enchanted princess.

The other group tries to enter the circle, reach the princess, and touch her to «disenchant» her. Whoever manages to do this without a sound wins.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: CAPTURING THE FORTRESS
body:
Cubs draw a large ring. One group stands on the "wall" as guards. The other group approaches the guards, and each attacker performs certain movements. The guards must imitate them but are only allowed to move along the wall. The goal is to distract the guards and sneak into the fortress. If, after a set time—for example, 5 minutes—the majority have managed to break into the fortress, the besieging group wins.

title: NAVAL PORT
body:
A narrow passage, such as a door, or two trees at a green assembly point, serve as the entrance to the port. Two girls with blindfolds act as cruisers and stand on either side of the entrance. Other cubs, as enemy ships, try in turn to slip through so quietly that the guarding ships do not stop them.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: BORDER GUARD
body:
The Guard stands in a line facing away from the smugglers. The smugglers crawl from a considerable distance, and when they are near the border, their leader gives the command: **Take cover!** A moment later, he shouts: **Fire!** The smugglers clap their hands. The Guard turns around and chases the smugglers. Those caught are out of the game. The game can be played 3 times, and the number of those caught is counted.

The roles are then swapped in the groups, and after the third game, the number of captured smugglers is compared.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: HIDING GAME «IN THE LOCKED-UP»
body:
This game is organized in a forest or a place where there are many hiding spots.

From the group, one girl is chosen to be the one who "hides" by an agreed-upon tree and counts aloud to one hundred. Meanwhile, the rest must conceal themselves. Then, the first girl sets off to search. If she spots any of the others, she runs back to the tree, knocks, and counts aloud: "One, two, three, Hannah locked-up," and then goes searching again.

In the Cubs' troop. 19.

When the girls notice from their hiding spots that the seeker has moved away from the goal, they rush to the tree and knock (each for herself). The one who is first to be "locked-up" becomes the hider in the next game.

However, if the last player reaches the goal and knocks, she can rescue all those previously locked-up, and then the first one must hide again in the next game.

title: SENTRIES
body:
Cubs sit back-to-back in two rows at a distance of 10 to 15 metres. One cub from each party attempts to crawl across the opponents' line without being heard and carry over the assigned object.

Sentries catch the sneaking cubs as soon as they hear a rustle. A cub who succeeds in crawling across earns a point for their pack.

title: RESCUING THE PRISONER
body:
The troop detains one Cub from each pack as a prisoner at its outpost. The packs have their hideouts at an equal distance from its camp. Each six attempts to sneak up to the camp and free the prisoner. Cubs who are spotted and called out must retreat to their hideouts. The pack that first frees its comrade wins.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: HIDING GAME WITH CHASE
body:
The Cubs form a circle in a designated spot on the glade. The patrol leader gives a signal and closes her eyes. Everyone scatters and hides as far away as possible.

After a certain amount of time has passed, the patrol leader gives a prearranged signal to indicate she is starting the search. When she finds two girls, all three set off to search for the remaining ones. Each searches on her own or all three together—this depends on the agreement.

A girl spotted in her hiding place tries to return to the circle; if the searcher catches her on the way, she gets a mark. The game continues until everyone has been spotted. In the next game, the patrol leader hides and records marks for those caught. Whoever was caught three times, having received three marks, hides in the new game.

title: SECRET LETTER
body:
In the hollow of one of the trees, we hide a letter for each little group, written in their secret alphabet. The Cubs are told the location of the tree, and the groups must find the letters intended for them and carry out the instructions contained within.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: HIDDEN ORDERS
body:
One of the girls runs in a certain direction, leaving agreed-upon signs behind her. When she finds a suitable place to hide, she leaves a note with the following content: "Find as much food suitable for birds as possible."

At a previously designated time, a group sets out following the signs. When they find and read the note, all the young scouts scatter to search for various seeds, fruits, and the like. The scout who brings the most wins.

The content of the note can be changed to vary the game, for example: "Climb a tree," "Who will be the first to reach the old oak standing alone in the glade?"

The scout who wins leaves the signs for the next game.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: TREASURE HUNT
body:
A group takes part in this game.

The patrol leader says: «40 paces to the south lies a stone. Look for the letter hidden beneath it.»

Under the stone is a note: «Search beneath the hazel bush growing beside the thickest tree you can see from here.» Beneath the hazel bush is an order to seek a hollow tree to the east. The next note points to a path leading to the hiding place where the treasure is concealed. The young scouts begin the search in pairs; they should use a compass.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: FOLLOWING THE SIGNS
body:
Two small groups set out into the terrain for 10 minutes and hide some objects. Then they meet at the assembly point and set off to search for the object hidden by the other group, tracking by the signs left behind (a piece of string or similar). The first group to return with the found object wins.

The number of signs, the distance between signs, and the terrain should be as uniform as possible and determined in advance.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: KNOW THE LEAF
body:
Two small groups stand in a limited space, facing each other. Each group has its own judge. The judges pin a silhouette of a leaf cut from colored paper onto the backs of the participants. At the whistle, the groups move toward each other, trying to see and recognize the sign on the backs of the opposing group without revealing their own.

Whoever identifies the leaf communicates it in a whisper to their judge, who records a point for the group. After 3 or 5 minutes, the points are tallied to determine which group has won.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: FAIRIES AND WITCHES
body:
The troop divides into two equal parties: "fairies" and "witches".

The fairies must carry orders hidden in their clothing to the fairy queen’s palace.

At a certain moment, the witches emerge from ambush and attempt to capture the fairies and find the orders.

A witch may search while counting to 100; if she does not find the orders in that time, the fairy runs away counting to 10, after which the witch has the right to chase her again.

The side that has more orders wins.

title: TREK THROUGH THE THICKETS
body:
Each Cub receives two armbands made of coloured yarn.

At a given signal, two packs approach each other through the forest undergrowth. The aim is to encounter a Cub from the opposing party and snatch their yarn. A Cub who loses one armband is wounded; if they lose both, they are killed.

The pack with the most “living” and unharmed Cubs at the end of the game wins.

title: CAPTURE OF THE TREASURE
body:
Near the marked tree, a treasure is hidden. Two groups from two opposite ends set out to capture the treasure.

Upon meeting, the opponent is "killed" by removing their beret (scalping). The group that discovers the treasure and brings it to the troop leader wins.

title: SECRET ORDER
body:
From among the group, 3 to 5 young scouts are chosen in such a way that the others do not know about it, and they are tasked with finding the secret order. Whoever already has the order in hand passes it to the next initiate, and thus the order must pass through the hands of all the initiates in turn. The last one hides it.

The entire group tries to uncover the initiates and take the order being passed.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: SQUIRRELS
body:
Each group chooses a hiding place at an equal distance from the pile of nuts (cones). Each Cub ties a sash behind their belt as a tail.

At a given signal, the groups run to fetch nuts (each Cub may carry only one nut) and return to their hiding places, trying to snatch the tail from a squirrel in another six.

A squirrel without a tail is wounded, unless the group redeems it for 4 nuts from the six to which the Cub who captured the tail belongs.

The six with the most nuts wins.

A captured tail counts as four nuts.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: CAPTURING THE ARSENAL
body:
The game takes place in the field. Cubs divide into two parties: the reds and the yellows. Each party has an equal, specified amount of ammunition, e.g., 12 cones each, arranged in a row at a distance of 1 step from 1 another.

Half of the cubs from each party surround the arsenal and defend it. The other half sets out to capture the enemy’s ammunition.

Whoever manages to seize ammunition (one cone) can no longer be pursued.

If an attacker is touched by a defender, they are wounded and must go to the enemy camp as a prisoner, but they can be rescued by a cub from their own party who leads them by the hand back to their own camp.

When rescuing a wounded cub, ammunition must not be taken.

After a predetermined time has elapsed, the amount of captured loot is calculated.

---

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: THE INVISIBILITY CAP
body:
This game can be conducted on school grounds, especially if several floors are available. It will also work well in other terrain.

The troop divides into two equal parties.

The first party’s task is to carry letters to a designated place and hand them over to a specified person. They defend themselves against encountered enemies by stopping and putting on the cap, which makes the Cub invisible and forces the enemy to retreat and hide while the Cub in the cap slowly counts to 10.

In the cap, one must not move forward.

The second group hinders the delivery of the letters, trying to touch as many Cubs from the first group as possible (it is not allowed to touch those standing in the cap, but one must retreat at least 10 steps from them). Those touched retreat to the starting point and try their luck again, or leave the game, depending on the agreement. For moving while wearing the cap on one’s head, one is removed from the game.

The first group wins if they deliver more than half of the letters. In difficult terrain, victory is counted for delivering even a single letter.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: INDIAN RAID
body:
The entire group, except for one six-person patrol, forms the four walls of a room, leaving space for a door. This house stands in the American forests. The Indians are to raid tonight. Three white settlers enter the room, lie down to sleep, removing their belts, footwear, and the like. They carefully fold their clothes and blindfold themselves, for it is night.

The remaining white settlers from the designated group stand outside on both sides of the door.

One of them whistles. The "sleepers" dress with their eyes still blindfolded, find their way to the door, and escape before the walls slowly count to forty.

The white settlers waiting outside grab each other’s hands, remove their blindfolds, and flee together.

The walls turn into Indians, chase the fleeing settlers, who are safe once they cross the marked boundary (e.g., a grove).

Each group takes turns playing the role of the "white settlers."

title: WATER WARDEN
body:
A rectangle drawn in chalk represents a pond. In the middle stands the water warden. The children stir the water (by running and touching the ground with their hand), and the warden tries to catch them. When the tired warden sits down, running through is not allowed. A caught child becomes the water warden.

title: WOLF IN THE FOREST
body:
Mark the boundary of the forest (polygon, circle) where the wolf—one of the children—resides. Cones lie in the forest. Cubs enter the forest to collect cones but, upon spotting the wolf, flee. The wolf tries to catch them but must not step outside the circle. Children keep running in and out, attempting to gather as many cones as possible. A caught child stops participating in the game. The cub who collects the most cones wins; in the next game, they become the wolf.

title: BLIND GRANDMA WITH RANSOM
body:
One of the girls is the "blind grandma." She has her eyes covered and holds a small bag containing various types of fabrics. A girl caught by the "blind grandma" must ransom herself by selecting, through touch, the named type from the bag. If she fails to recognize it within the set time or guesses incorrectly, she becomes the blind grandma.

Other types of ransom may be used, such as: the caught girl draws the requested object from the bag, for example, a hazelnut, a rubber band, and the like.

title: DOGS AND RABBITS
body:
Cubs divide into threes and form small circles, holding hands. The «Dog» chases the «Rabbit», which, while fleeing, runs into one of the circles, touching any of the cubs. That cub in turn flees, and the rabbit takes their place.

The dog must chase the new rabbit, which again defends itself by darting into another circle, and so on.

When the rabbit is caught, the roles are switched.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: OVER OBSTACLES
body:
Cub groups stand in rows. A few paces in front of each group, a rope is secured; further on stands a long bench, and still further, in a marked circle, lies a scarf. At the leader’s signal, the first cubs run, crawl under the rope, run further, jump over the bench, then toss the scarf over themselves and return to their place; the next ones do the same. The group that finishes first wins. On hikes, natural obstacles can be used, such as: a fence, a ditch, a stream.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: TARGET THROW
body:
We set up targets with a diameter of 10 centimetres against the wall. There should be as many targets as there are small groups.

The small groups line up in rows; the game leader directs the aiming exercises with small balls. The patrol leaders by their groups count the accurate throws, the greater number of which decides the win.

Aiming can be done in various stances, for example: 1) Lying prone, throwing over the head with the left hand or the right. 2) Cross-legged sitting, throwing with both hands. 3) Kneeling sitting, throws as in point 1 or 2.

We make the game more difficult by increasing the distance between those aiming and the targets.

title: BALL TAG
body:
Every Cub stands in any place on the field. One tries to hit the others with the ball. Whoever is touched must pick up the ball and try to hit others with it.

Each child tries to avoid being hit by jumping, bending down, or moving to the side.

The one aiming is not allowed to run with the ball. Breaking the rules results in exclusion from the game.

title: HUNTER AND GAME
body:
One of the children is the hunter. They put on a sash and receive a ball. As soon as the game begins, the hunter tries to hit one of the game with the ball. The child who is hit puts on the sash and becomes the hunter. The hunter is not allowed to run with the ball; instead, they position themselves so it is easy for them to tag the game, and they are allowed to pass the ball. The last one remaining of the game wins.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: PYRAMIDS
body:
In the center of a circle formed by a group of children, three small pyramids are set up, each made of four small balls, arranged so that three balls lie on the floor and the fourth rests on top of the first three.

The children try to knock down the pyramids by aiming a large ball, while one of the cubs stands in the center and tries to defend them.

If one or two pyramids have been knocked over, the child standing in the center attempts to rebuild them after first rolling the ball along the ground as far away as possible.

The game ends when all the pyramids have been knocked down.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: BOMBARDMENT
body:
Two groups take part, or a single group is divided into two parties. Two goals are marked with lines, behind which the two parties stand facing each other. A line is drawn to mark the center of the field separating the groups. A large ball is placed on this line. Each child receives a small ball. At an agreed signal, the game begins. All aim with their small balls. The objective is to move the large ball into the opponent's goal. Before the game starts, two ball collectors should be appointed—one stands on the field closer to Party A and, during the game, returns to Party B any small balls that stop there. The other, conversely, stands on the field closer to Party B and returns balls to Party A. These two girls must be impartial. They run in such a way as not to interfere with the aiming.

author: praca zbiorowa pod redakcją Jadwigi Zwolakowskiej
title: RACE THROUGH THREE CIRCLES
body:
On the playing field, two parallel lines are marked at a distance of 20 paces. Between the lines, 3 circles (three paces in diameter) are marked—two closer to one of the lines, one in the middle between the lines. At the center of each line, a place is designated for the leader. The group divides into two teams: the reds and the whites. Each team selects a leader from among themselves. Lots decide which team begins the game. The teams stand opposite each other behind the lines, while the leaders take their designated places.

The leader of the red team, throwing the ball as far as possible in a straight direction toward the opponents, gives the signal for their "run."

The red team runs through the three circles in sequence and returns to their place. If any member of the white team catches the ball, they throw it back to their leader, who

is not allowed to leave the designated spot. The leader tries to hit one of the running scouts with the ball. If they hit, the white team scores one point, and the teams switch places; if they miss, the teams remain in place, and the red team scores one point.

If anyone catches a so-called "candle" (a high throw) with their hands, they become the leader in the next throw.

body:
A game widely popular in Poland; suitable for children's gardens and elementary schools. An even number of children form a circle, holding hands; one (without a pair) stands in the center of the circle. After these words, the one in the center chooses a pair for themselves, which all participants immediately imitate. Whoever is left without a pair goes to the center, and the game begins anew.

body:
A rural girls' game from Mazovia and Greater Poland, suitable for secondary girls' schools. The girls form a circle, holding hands; one stands in the center of the circle. All move in a circle. Then the one in the center places a handkerchief in front of one of her companions; both kneel on it and kiss (in the air!). Finally, they switch places, and the game continues.

title: Konopki (Hemp Stalks)
body:
A game for urban and rural children in Lesser Poland and Mazovia, also known among Kashubians under the name "żórawi" (cranes). Suitable for kindergartens and lower grades of primary schools. After these words, children circling in a ring choose one participant, then continue circling and singing, and so on, until all join the ring. Then they begin singing the same song with the change that instead of the words "small" and "little," they insert "big" and "much," and instead of "come to us," they sing: "go away from us." After each verse, they remove one child from the ring until it shrinks back to its original size. In Sierpc County (Mazovia), the game starts with two people joining their right (or left) hands and spinning around an axis passing through their joined hands. New participants place their right (left) hand on the joined hands of their predecessors, forming a spinning star with an increasing (and later decreasing) number of rays (like the figure called a "cross" in the mazurka).

title: The Maple Tree Game
body:
A game for urban and rural children, widespread in Poland (known here and there as "The Bridge"); suitable for elementary schools. Two children stand apart as the "maple tree people" and secretly agree among themselves, before the rest of the participants, which one will be the "angel" and which the "devil." They then stand next to each other and join hands via a ribbon or handkerchief, forming a gate in this way. The end of the ribbon, hidden in the devil’s hand, is tied in a knot. The remaining participants line up opposite the gate and ask a series of questions, to which the maple tree people respond. After these words, the children pass under the gate in a line, holding hands. The maple tree people let everyone through except the last one, whom they cut off from the rest with the ribbon, asking: "Whom do you side with—Kasia or Marysia?" or: "The apple or the pear?" The child chooses and accordingly stands on the side of the angel or the devil. Then the song, approaching, and cutting off one child at a time continue until only two remain (who become the maple tree people in the next game). Then the secret is revealed. The devil chases away his group with lashes from the knotted ribbon, while the angel rejoices and dances with theirs.

body:
A rural children's game from Greater Poland, suitable for secondary school girls. The girls form a double line, holding hands in pairs. The last pair (6 in the illustration), having circled the double line from the side, passes under the * arms of the first pair, waving their arms above their heads. They then circle the double line again from the other side and pass from behind under the arms of each pair in turn, finally positioning themselves in front of the first pair. The same is repeated by each subsequent pair in order (thus 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 in the illustration).

title: Zelman
body:
A game widespread among rural children and youth in various regions of Poland; suitable for secondary school girls. The girls join hands and stand in two rows facing each other. These rows sing alternately, with the singing row moving forward while the other retreats. One row (A) represents Zelman’s procession, and the other (B) represents the procession of a maiden of marriageable age. After each verse, Zelman’s procession approaches the raised hands of the opposing row, which allows all the girls to pass except the last one, whom it incorporates into its own ranks. The game ends when Zelman’s procession is reduced to two people. The number of verses may be adjusted according to the number of participants, adding details of the trousseau (dress, handkerchief, shoes, etc.) or various types of bread (peasant, princely, royal, etc.).

title: Little Garden Path
body:
A rural children's game from the Łomża region, suitable for elementary and secondary girls' schools. The children join hands and form a semicircle (solid line in the illustration). Then, one of the end players begins a procession along a serpentine path (dotted line in the illustration), leading the others, while the opposite end remains in place. After circling the semicircle from behind, the children pass under an arch formed by the hands of the other end player and her neighbor, then return to their original formation. Next, the other end begins the same procession, and so on.

title: Threading the Needle
body:
A rural children's game from the Kraków region, similar in application to the previous one. Children hold hands and stand side by side, forming an arch. The last two children from one end of the arch raise their hands, creating a gate; they ask a companion from the other end of the arch: — Do you have the keys? — I do. — Will you give them to the throne? — I will. — Let the gate pass through my barn! — After this dialogue, the children, still holding hands, run under the leadership of the first child under the gate, and when all have passed through, they stand again in a semicircle, and the game repeats as above, until all subsequent pairs form gates with their hands and let the next children pass through. In this way, the children eventually form a woven chain, standing in two rows opposite each other; each, with arms crossed in front, holds two others standing directly and slightly diagonally opposite.

body:
A game widespread among urban and rural children, known by various names (Father Migeljusz, Hyacinth, Gerginje, etc.), suitable for children's gardens and elementary schools. The children form a circle, holding hands; inside the circle stands one of the players (Father Virgil). All move around in a circle. After these words, the one in the center performs a movement (bends over, jumps 1, etc.), and all the children imitate it. Whoever is late or imitates awkwardly swaps places with Father Virgil.

title: Trades (Musician)
body:
A game from the rural children of the Ropczyce and Rzeszów districts (Lesser Poland), suitable for children's gardens and elementary schools. The children gather around a companion chosen as the "judge." The judge assigns each of them a trade, then begins to mimic movements typical of, for example, a blacksmith while standing opposite the shoemaker. This serves as a signal for each to engage in their own trade. If, for instance, the shoemaker makes a mistake and repeats the blacksmith's movements, they forfeit a token. The game lasts as long as the previous one. Under the name "Musician," Gołębiowski describes a similar game in which the judge is replaced by a conductor, and each player standing on the circle's perimeter is assigned an instrument to play instead of a trade. Otherwise, the rules remain the same.

title: The Princess
body:
A rural girls' game from certain regions of Lesser Poland, suitable for primary schools and the lowest grades of secondary schools. The girls form a circle, moving in time to the singing. In the center of the circle stands the princess, who after each verse of the song gives her courtiers a command—either verbal, whistled, or silent (depending on the troop's training). Whoever executes the command incorrectly or is late switches places with the princess. A command issued in error is invalid.

title: The Widow on the Marriage Market
body:
A game from certain rural areas of Lesser Poland, suitable for girls' secondary schools. The girls form a circle, moving while singing; in the center stands the widow, and on the circumference are her daughters. They sing similarly: *d e a f*, *l a m e*, adding appropriate movements each time; then *y o u n g*. At this, the widow, who was limping during the previous verses, begins to hop. Finally, she leaps out of the circle over the arms of her daughters; the one whose right hand the widow jumps over takes her place in the center.

title: The Quail
body:
A game widespread throughout Poland, most commonly as a component of wedding ceremonies, existing in many variations. Suitable, in simpler forms, for primary schools and the lowest grades of secondary schools, and in more challenging variants—for grades three to five of girls' secondary schools. It is most often danced with a mazurka step.

**a)** The most widespread way of dancing *The Quail* involves all participants, except two, forming two lines facing each other while holding hands. These lines make small forward and backward movements, while one of the separated dancers (the "hunter") chases the other (the "quail") between and behind the lines. When the hunter catches the quail, the next pair takes their turn, and so on until the end. The chorus of both lines sings along during the dance.

**b)** In Łuków County (Mazovia), each pair dances along both lines (which move closer together) before the chase, so that the hunter runs on one side of the lines and the quail on the other, both holding their joined hands above the heads of those standing in the lines. During the chase, the lines hinder the hunter and help the quail, who claps her hands while fleeing. When the hunter catches his prey, the roles reverse: the quail becomes the hunter and vice versa.

**c)** In Sierpc County (Mazovia), the dance is performed differently: During the first verse of the song, **all** participants form two lines that move toward and away from each other. In the second verse, each dancer pairs with their vis-à-vis, and they dance pair by pair. In the third verse, the movement returns to that of the first, and so on until the end. Here, *The Quail* ceases to be a game and becomes a playful dance figure or amusement.

---

title: The Mushroom
body:
A game described by Ł. Gołębiowski in the year 1831, suitable for secondary school girls. An even number of girls form a circle, holding hands, and spin with a dance step. In the center stands one (odd) girl, whose task is to devise a dance figure. When everyone is occupied with performing the figure, the girl in the center chooses a partner for herself, and others follow suit; whoever is left without a pair goes to the center (cf. 1, "The Little Bird").

title: The Shepherd
body:
A peasant wedding game from the Kutno district (Mazovia), suitable for upper primary school classes and girls' secondary schools. Couples dance in a circle, one behind the other, while in the center stands an (odd-numbered) "shepherd," holding a stick with which they occasionally strike the floor 3 times. At this signal, the dancers release hands and seek new partners; the shepherd does the same. Whoever remains without a partner becomes the shepherd in the next round.

title: The Rose
body:
A rural girls' game, suitable for secondary girls' schools, known in two distinct forms.

(a) In Mazovia, the girls form a circle, holding hands, while one remains inside the circle. The Rose chooses one of the dancers on the circle's edge and bows to her. The circle continues turning as they sing the verse: *The Rose kisses (in the air) the same girl she bowed to*; the circle turns further as they sing: *The Rose dances with the companion she kissed*. Then they switch places, and the game continues. A Krakowiak step is used.

(b) In the Kraków region, the game begins as in (a). After singing the first verse, however, the Rose selects a companion to join her inside the circle. Then the first verse is sung again, and the second girl selects a third, and so on, so that a second circle forms inside the first. When the inner circle has as many girls as the original one, it moves outside (under the arms of the girls in the first circle), creating two circles side by side. In the second (new) circle, the girls sing: *The girls called in this way enter the center of the new circle in turn.*

title: The Abbess
body:
A game from the rural girls of certain regions of Lesser Poland, suitable for secondary girls' schools. At the start of the game, two circles are formed: one large circle with the "abbess" in the center and her daughters on the perimeter, moving slowly (by walking), and a smaller one with 2—3 "bridesmaids," spinning with a dance step. Here, the bridesmaids detach one of the abbess's daughters and join her to their little circle. Then the process repeats from the beginning and continues until the abbess is left alone.

title: Matchmakers
body:
A rural youth game, once widespread in many regions of Poland, now preserved almost solely in song form; suitable for secondary school girls. The girls form two lines facing each other, holding hands. One line—the matchmakers—advances and retreats with a **dancing step** (mazurka). The other line represents the maiden of marriageable age and her family; they step backward with a **walking step** as the matchmakers approach and, conversely, move forward as the matchmakers retreat. During the final verse, both lines join into a circle and dance. Then the roles switch: the former matchmakers become the maiden’s entourage and vice versa.

title: The Dyna
body:
A peasant wedding dance from the Kutno district (Mazovia), suitable for girls' secondary schools. Dancers form pairs in two rows facing each other, holding hands. The rows move together and then retreat. When they meet, they bow. Finally, as they sing: "And four dynas came together," each dancer makes several turns, first taking hands (tour de mains) with her vis-à-vis, then with her partner. Afterward, they retreat back into their rows. The step is a mazurka step.

body:
A rural girls' game from Sierpc County (Mazovia), known elsewhere only as a song or nursery rhyme; suitable for lower primary school classes (and with certain simplifications, also for kindergartens). The children form a spinning star (like the "cross" in the mazurka; see 6. *Konopki*, a variant from the same Sierpc County). At the appropriate lyrics of the song, they let go of hands and mimic the hen or the activities of her chicks with movements. The step is a mazurka step.

title: Cornflower
body:
A rural girls' game from the Sierpc district (Mazovia), suitable for secondary school girls. The girls divide into pairs (designating one as the "dancer" and the other as the "dancing partner"). These pairs form two lines facing each other, holding hands. Singing the first verse (and the following refrain: one, two, three), both lines glide forward with a mazurka step until they are half a step apart. During the second verse, they retreat to their original positions. On the third verse, they advance toward each other again, and on the fourth, they perform a hołubiec dance with the dancing partner from the opposite pair. On the fifth verse (i.e., the repetition of the fourth), the dancers return to their original positions with their partners exchanged. The game then repeats from the beginning until each dancer returns with their original dancing partner.

title: Little Hares
body:
A game popular throughout Poland, suitable for children's gardens and elementary schools. Location: a field, here and there overgrown with bushes, or a forest. The game leader ("hunter" or "master") by lot (see the relevant chapter in the General Part) successively separates half of the players as "little hares"; the rest are "dogs." Then he sends the hares off and ensures that the dogs do not see where the hares hide (most often by covering their heads with a jacket or sheet). Finally, he gives the signal to the dogs, which run out to search. After some time, he calls the dogs back, who come one by one with or without prey. Then the following conversation takes place between the leader and the dog: Where have you been? — Beyond the mountains. — What did you see? — A hare with claws. — Did you catch it? I caught it. — Well done! (or: — I didn’t catch it — Then you’re a fool!) Afterward, the caught hares become dogs, and the game continues.

title: Beaver
body:
A rural children's game from certain areas of Lesser Poland, suitable for elementary schools and children's gardens. Very similar to the previous one. The children choose one among themselves to be the beaver, another to be the Hunter, and the rest become hounds. The Hunter designates a place for the hounds to stay until the beaver hides. Then they search for the hidden beaver and catch it. The hound that first spots the beaver becomes the beaver in the next game.

title: Hiding
body:
A game popular among urban and rural children in Poland (known here and there as "Hide-and-Seek" or "Tag-and-Hide"); suitable for children's gardens and lower grades of elementary schools. It is a simpler variant of "Hare and Hounds," usually played indoors. Half of the players, chosen (by drawing lots), go to hide; the other half, at the signal "go!", rushes in from the neighboring room and searches. In Mazovia, it is also played so that one child searches while the "rest hide." The seeker, upon finding someone, must hurry to the finish line where a stick is placed, tap it three times, and call out the name of the discovered player, who, however, may outrun them and seize the stick. In the first case, roles are switched; in the second, they are not.
