title: Bandits and Haiduks
body:
A favorite game among boys, especially those in urban areas, suitable for higher grades of primary schools and lower grades of secondary schools. A well-defined section of a forest serves as the playing field; a particular corner of the forest is designated as the "castle," where haiduks bring captured bandits. Participants, numbering **12—50**, divide into two camps: the haiduks led by the elder and the bandits led by the hetman. The haiduks wear a visible badge (e.g., a scarf on the shoulder). At the start of the game, the haiduks do not leave the castle for a prearranged time agreed upon by the elder and the hetman (no more than **10** minutes), giving the bandits an opportunity to hide. After this time elapses, the elder sends the haiduks out in several detachments in different directions. A bandit struck three times in succession by a hand is taken prisoner and must go to the castle, where they remain under guard. A prisoner can only be freed by a free bandit who sneaks into the castle undetected and strikes them three times; this succeeds best when several bandits storm in simultaneously to liberate their comrades. The game lasts for a prearranged amount of time (e.g., one hour). Halfway through, the roles of the two camps are switched. The camp that has taken more prisoners wins.

title: Sieve
body:
A game for rural children in the Kraków region, suitable for elementary schools. Around the circumference of a circle, the positions of all players are marked (spaced several paces apart) with pegs, small stones, or (indoors) with chalk. Then, they leave their places and run around the circle several times. At a given signal, each must stand by their own peg (stone, mark). Whoever makes a mistake or is late forfeits a token. In some villages, this game is called "Cranes."

title: Four Corners
body:
A popular game in Poland, suitable for children's gardens and elementary schools. Five participants; four stand in the corners of a room (or on a playing field, with stakes, flags, or similar arranged in a square), while the fifth stands in the center, calling: *Four corners, and the fifth in the middle!* — At this signal, everyone changes places, and the one in the center tries to take one of the spots. Whoever is left without a place goes to the center.

title: The Circle Game
body:
A game described by Gołębiowski, similar to the following ones, suitable for primary schools and the lowest grades of secondary schools. Draw one fewer small circle on the perimeter of a large circle (on the playground with a furrow, indoors with chalk) than the number of players. Players stand in the small circles, with one player inside the large circle. At their call: "To the circles!", the players change places; whoever is left without a circle goes to the center.

title: The Merry Gardener
body:
This game differs from the previous ones in that the participants stationed in their places take the names of various flowers. The gardener calls out: — Oh! They ask him: — What’s the matter? — My heart aches. — For what? — For the rose (tulip, etc.). Then the rose hurries to the gardener’s place. If someone calls out: — My heart aches for the merry gardener — everyone changes places.

Players standing around the circle at marked spots adopt the names of various people and objects found in an inn (innkeeper, innkeeper’s wife, bread, water, milk, meat, hay, oats, etc.). A "traveler" arrives and calls out these names in turn, at which the named players stand up and switch places. At the call "the inn is on fire," everyone switches places.

title: The Starosta's Lady
body:
The central player (the Starosta's Lady) calls out, in turn, the players seated around the circle, assigning them courtly roles (such as marshal, equerry, chamberlain, lady-in-waiting, maidservant, etc.), saying: — The Starosta's Lady is setting out on a journey and is taking, for example, the marshal with her. Each of those named follows the Starosta's Lady. Once everyone is moving, the Starosta's Lady suddenly calls out: — The Starosta's Lady has arrived — and takes one of the marked places. Then, everyone does the same; whoever is left without a place becomes the Starosta's Lady.

title: Pairs
body:
Players form a double line (pair behind pair). In front of the pairs stands an unpaired player. The last pair splits up and runs along the sides of the double line to rejoin in front of the lone player. The lone player tries to outrun one of them and take their place in a pair. If successful, the slower runner stands alone at the front.

title: Gander
body:
A game for rural children from the Sieradz region, suitable for children's gardens and elementary schools. The children stand in a line as "ganders"; one of them walks around the line, asking:— Ganders, why aren’t you eating? — Because we’re afraid. — Of what? — The wolf. — Where is he? — Beyond the mountains. — What’s he doing? — Plucking a goose. — Which one? — The saddled one. After these words, the children scatter, and the one who does not return to their place in the line must walk around, asking the questions.

title: Circle
body:
A game of rural children in the Kraków region, also known in the Ropczyce district (Lesser Poland) as *"Buhaj"* and in Greater Poland as *"Zajączek"*. Suitable for elementary schools. The children form a circle, holding hands. In the center of the circle is a player who runs in all directions, trying to break the circle by striking it with their torso where the hands are held more weakly. If they succeed, they switch places with the one who let them through on their right side.

title: The Ram
body:
A game once widespread in Poland, now almost entirely forgotten. Suitable for children's gardens and folk schools. The children form a semicircle, holding hands. In the center stands one participant as the "ram." The semicircle rotates in time with a song composed of the children's questions and the ram's answers. After each verse, the ram attempts to break the semicircle by striking it with its torso (as in the previous game). If successful, the ram flees while the others chase it. Whoever catches the ram becomes the ram in the next game.

title: Interrupted Army
body:
A game for urban and rural boys, widespread in Poland; suitable for primary schools and lower grades of boys' secondary schools. (Other names: *Parciane*, or *Cut Army*, *Interrupted King*, etc.). The boys divide into two camps, equal in number and strength, each composed of "knights" led by a "king." Both armies stand opposite each other at a distance of 2 0 to 3 0 steps, each forming a line while holding hands firmly. Each king alternately sends one of his knights, who charges and attempts to break the opponents' grip with a torso strike. If successful, the entire section of the chain to the right of the breaker joins the victors' line as captives. If unsuccessful, the attacker himself becomes a captive. If a king is left alone, he is entitled to three attempts to break through. The game ends when one of the kings is captured.

title: Blind Man's Buff
body:
A game widespread throughout Poland (other names: Blind Granny, Blind Man’s Bluff, Kutyubabka); suitable for children’s gardens and elementary schools. The “Granny” has her eyes blindfolded, after which she is asked a series of questions:
— Where are you from, Granny?
— From Pacanów.
— What’s the news there?
— Heavenly words.
— Is the bread big there?
— As big as your head.
— Will you eat mushrooms?
— I will.
— What do you prefer: clapping, thumping, or tiptoeing?
— (If the Granny chooses clapping, the children, running away from her, clap their hands; for thumping—they lightly tap her on the back; tiptoeing means running quietly on tiptoes). The Granny sets off in pursuit; whoever she catches becomes the next Granny.

title: The Corncrake
body:
This game, also described by Gołębiowski, is suitable for primary schools and the lowest grades of secondary schools. The children form a circle, into the center of which two players enter with their eyes blindfolded. One of them—the corncrake—strikes two small sticks together, producing a sound like the call of this bird, thus making his presence known. The other—the hunter—tries to strike the corncrake.

title: Goslings
body:
A rural children's game from the Kalisz region and Lesser Poland, suitable for children's gardens, primary schools, and the lowest grades of secondary schools.

(a) The children choose from among themselves a "mother" (or "grandmother"), who stands in the "nest" (a circle several paces in diameter, drawn on the ground), and a "wolf" (or several wolves). The rest are "goslings." A conversation takes place between the mother and the goslings:
— Go to the field, goslings!
— We're afraid!
— Of what?
— The wolf!
— And where is he?
— Behind the fence!
— What is he doing?
— Tearing cats.
— How many has he torn?
— Three *kopy*.
— What does he drink?
— Swill.
— What does he eat?
— Dry cheese.
— What does he cover himself with?
— A wolf's tail.
— Chase him, wolf! (or: — Goslings, to the field!)
The goslings run out of the nest (where the wolf is not allowed to catch them); the wolf catches them one by one until all are caught. Then the game ends, and in the next round, the last caught gosling becomes the wolf.

(b) In other areas, the goslings start the game behind the nest, and the mother calls them to her, while the wolf blocks their way and catches them. Here, the beginning and end of the conversation are:
— Goslings, come home!

title: The Hawk and the Doves
body:
A game for urban and rural children, quite widespread in Lesser Poland; suitable for children's gardens, elementary schools, and the lowest grades of secondary schools. The children choose a hawk (by a method such as counting out, e.g., I. 5, General Part); the rest of the players take on the role of doves. On the playing field (or indoors), they mark a "dovecote" (or "nest"), most often in the shape of a circle several paces in diameter. The hawk lies in wait for the doves and catches them, but only outside the dovecote, where they can always take refuge from pursuit or for a rest. Doves that are caught leave the game or (in other regions) turn into hawks. In the next game, the dove caught last becomes the hawk.

title: Round-Up
body:
A game for urban and rural children, quite common in Lesser Poland; in Mazovia known as "Tag". Application as 54. Very similar to the previous one. Played with a "nest" or without. One player chases, the others flee. When they catch someone (i.e., tap them on the back with a hand), they immediately flee themselves, and the caught player chases. Additionally, there are two variants: "round-up with retaliation," where it is allowed to immediately return the tap, and "round-up without retaliation," where this is not permitted.

body:
A game for rural children in Łańcut County (Lesser Poland); application as above. The player chosen as the "dunker" sits in a ditch (or in a designated area on the field marked as the "pond") and pretends to be asleep. The children approach and provoke him. Whoever he catches becomes the dunker. (Older children may also play this game in the water during bathing, under appropriate supervision).

title: The Strzygoń
body:
A rural children's game from the Kraków region: application as in the previous one. A player chosen as the "strzygoń" lies on the ground, pretending to be asleep. The others circle around him, calling out:
— The first hour, the strzygoń sleeps,
The second hour, the strzygoń sleeps, and so on, up to the eleventh, at which they call:
— Strzygoń, wake up, give us dumplings!
— The strzygoń jumps up in pursuit, while all the others flee. Whoever he catches becomes the strzygoń.

publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: The King
body:
A game for urban and rural children from certain regions of Lesser Poland, Mazovia, and Podlasie, suitable for elementary schools. The "King," chosen by drawing lots, stands aside. The rest of the players secretly agree before the king on what actions they will mimic in front of him, then approach and say:
— Good day, King!
— The King replies: Good day!
— Where have you been?
— (e.g.) In the garden.
— And what were you doing?
(Here, the children mimic the previously agreed-upon action, such as digging, weeding, chopping wood, swimming, or the like. The King names the action; if he guesses correctly, everyone runs away, pursued by the King. The one caught becomes the King in the next game. If the King does not guess, the game repeats with the same roles.

title: The Little Cook
body:
A rural girls' game from the Kraków region, suitable for children's gardens and elementary schools (for girls). The girls form a circle, holding hands0. In the center is the "lady," searching for her cook. The lady strikes up a conversation: — Have you not seen my little cook? (The one who feels guilty responds): — What has she done to you, ma'am? — She burned the peas, drank the milk, and fled up the chimney! At this, the "little cook" runs away, and the "lady" chases her; when caught, they switch places.

title: Cat and Mouse
body:
A game widespread throughout Poland, suitable for children's gardens, primary schools, and the lowest grades of secondary schools.

(a) The most common form of the game involves children, except for two, forming a circle while holding hands. Inside the circle is the "mouse" (which has complete freedom of movement, as the players let it through), and outside is the "cat," which they do not allow inside. When the cat catches the mouse, another pair is chosen.

(b) In Sierpc County (Mazovia), players line up in two rows facing each other; the chase takes place between and beyond them.

(c) In Kutno County (Mazovia), players also stand in two rows, but these rows are very close to each other, and each player holds both hands of their vis-à-vis. This creates a "hole" through which only the mouse is allowed.

publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Third Man
body:
A game described by Gołębiowski; suitable for primary schools and lower secondary schools. The number of players must be even, 10—20. All stand in 2 circles, one inside the other, with an equal number of participants, so that each player in the outer circle stands behind one in the inner circle. They then step backward so that gaps of several paces form between each pair. Finally (by drawing lots), one pair is selected, from which the front player flees while the rear player pursues. The fleeing player tries to stand in front of any pair, causing the player at the back of that pair to become the "third man," exposed to a tap (with the hand on the back) from the pursuer if they do not quickly notice and flee before the next or another pair. If the third man is tapped while still at the back or before standing in front of a pair, they switch roles with their pursuer. However, they may not return the tap immediately but only after running in front of at least one pair. The fleeing player may not deceive by standing in front of a pair and then fleeing again. They are also not allowed to run more than half the circle during their escape. On the other hand, they may occasionally (for greater surprise) jump in front of the same pair behind which they stood, making it very difficult for the new third man to avoid being tapped.

title: Fox
body:
A popular game in Poland (in some places called "Pebbles"¹), suitable for primary schools and lower secondary school classes.

 a) The most common variant of this game is described by Gołębiowski: "Everyone stands in a circle, but each keeps their hands behind their backs; one walks with the pebble until they skillfully pass it to someone. That person hits a neighbor and chases them, having the right to hit until, after running around the circle, they return to the place they started from, then passes the pebble to whomever they choose, and so the game continues."

 b) In the Sieradz region, they play as above, but the players stand not in a circle but in a line.

 c) In the Sierpc and Kutno districts (Mazovia), the "fox" does not pass the pebble but tosses it behind one of the players. If that player notices, they grab the pebble and "drive the fox to its den," that is, chase and hit the fox with the pebble until the fox, after running around, takes the place of the chaser, who then circles as the fox. If the player misses the toss, the fox drives them out with the pebble, hands it over to them, and they switch places¹. Everywhere, the fox has the right to hit a player who looks back (in variant c: who looks back in vain when the pebble was not tossed to them). While the fox is circling, the children shout: *A fox walks by the road, Has no hands, nor feet, Praise God, three weeks, We haven’t seen the fox* or *Whoever the pebble touches, Will never expect it.*

 ¹) In the Kraków region, this variant is sometimes played under the name "Little Sieve," and in the Kutno region under the name "Shepherd."

---

body:
A game described by Gołębiowski, with an application similar to 66. "Persons standing in a circle hold a tied ribbon with both hands; one person inside the circle walks around until they give someone a slap on the hand, while the others quickly withdraw their hands. Whoever fails to withdraw in time takes the place of the one who slapped."

title: The Snake
body:
A rural children's game from Ropczyce County (Lesser Poland); application as in 66. The children form a line, with each, except the first, gripping the shoulders or hips of the one in front. (This formation is called a 'key'.) Through various twists of this key, the first player attempts to catch the last. When this happens, others are chosen for these positions. In the Łomża region, a similar game is called 'Ducem.' The leader, holding a switch, taps the children who fall during sudden movements.

title: The Wolf and the Goslings
body:
A game for rural and urban children, widespread in Poland; suitable for children’s gardens, elementary schools, and the lowest grades of secondary schools. (Alternative names: Goslings, Gosling, Wild Geese, Little Wolf, The Gander and the Fox, The Raven). Children form a wedge (see 56) under the leadership of the "gander" (or "mother"). To the side, the "wolf" pretends to dig a little hole in the ground. A conversation unfolds between the wolf and the gander: — What is this little hole for? — For a little fire. — And this little fire? — For heating water. — And this water? — For washing little plates. — And these little plates? — For cutting up goslings. — And where are they? — Behind your belt. — Here, the wolf lunges at the wedge of geese and tries to snatch the last one, while the gander defends it with sudden turns of the wedge. The game continues until the wolf catches all the goslings. In the next round, the gander becomes the wolf and vice versa. In some regions, the game concludes with the following scene: The captured goslings pretend the wolf has lamed them, that is, they hop on one leg around the field. The "mother" scolds the wolf: — Why, wolf, did you spoil the geese, lame the flock? — (The wolf replies) — Why did you eat a barn of oats, a barn of millet, and drink a pond of water? — I will repay you for the damage; you geese, mend yourselves. — Then the wolf taps the goslings on the legs with a switch, "so they will not limp."

title: The Linen
body:
A game from the rural children of certain regions of Mazovia and Lesser Poland; suitable for kindergarten gardens and elementary schools. The children choose (by drawing lots) a "housewife," a "washerwoman," a "dog," a "hen," and a "thief." The rest become the "linen": a row of children, holding hands, stands in a semicircle. The housewife "rolls up" the linen (the chain of children coils up, as in the well-known parlor game of "bouquet") and goes to sleep (moves aside and pretends to sleep). Then the thief comes, tears off an "ell of linen" (one child) and runs away with them to a hiding place. The hen crows, the dog barks; the housewife comes and "measures" the linen (counts the children). She asks the hen: — Where is the ell of linen? — The washerwoman washed it, didn’t finish, and threw it into the well. — The same question is asked of the washerwoman—she replies: — I washed it but didn’t finish, threw it into the well, and placed a stone on it. — Then the housewife rolls up the linen again and goes to sleep, and the theft repeats anew, and so on. During the last theft, the washerwoman says: — I don’t know. — Then the dog picks up the thief’s trail; the children flee from the hiding place, and the housewife chases them and brings them back home.

title: Birds (Colors)
body:
A game quite common in Lesser Poland; application as above.

**a)** All children except two stand in a line (in some regions, in a circle). In front of the line stand the "birdkeeper" and the "merchant." The birdkeeper (whispering) assigns the children names of various birds. The merchant arrives and demands a particular bird. The named bird jumps up and flees, while the merchant chases it. If the bird, having run around the line of children, takes refuge in its place, it remains in the line (having received a new name from the birdkeeper). If the merchant catches it along the way, he leads it aside. The game continues until the merchant has caught all the birds.

**b)** In other regions, three players stand outside the line: the birds are alternately demanded by the "angel" and the "devil." (The angel says: — Ding, ding! — Who’s there? — An angel from heaven. — What do you want? — A bird. — Which one? — A golden oriole (magpie, etc.). The conversation with the devil is similar, only the introduction differs: — Clop, clop-clop! — Who’s there? — A black boot.

**c)** In some regions, an ending is added to either version of the game, involving a battle between two camps: **a)** the children not called remain with the birdkeeper, the rest with the merchant;

**b)** the camp of the angel and the devil. In the Buczacz region (Lesser Poland), this battle consists of drawing a boundary between the two camps, and the children, having joined hands, try to pull their opponents across this boundary. The camp that pulls even one opponent across wins.

**d)** Under the name "Colors," a nearly universal variation of this game is played, in which different colors take the place of birds.

title: Fabjan
body:
A game for rural youth in the Rzeszów and Ropczyce districts (Lesser Poland), suitable for boys in the lowest grades of secondary schools. The boys choose (by drawing lots, see the General Part) an "elder" and a "Fabjan." The rest stand in a row, and the elder assigns them the names of various animals. Then the call goes out: — Come, Fabjan! — I have nothing to ride on. — What animal do you sit on? — A horse (an ox, etc.). The named "animal" runs away. Fabjan chases it and, upon catching it, sits astride its shoulders and rides back before the elder, who asks: — What have you brought? — Needles. — And in those needles? — Gold. — Throw him into the mud. — The "horse" shakes off its rider (who dismounts), and the rider becomes Fabjan; the former Fabjan is then whispered the name of an animal by the elder and sent to the spot vacated by the horse—and the game continues. If Fabjan fails to catch the pursued "animal," he returns to his place, and Fabjan remains in his role.

title: The Village Mayor and the Partridges
body:
A game from the rural children of Lesser Poland, suitable for kindergarten gardens and elementary schools. The children sit in a row (indoors—astride a low bench; outdoors—on the grass, with the "mayor" at the back, another child between his knees, a third between that child’s knees, and so on). One participant walks along the row, asking: — Is the mayor far? — At the end. When they reach the mayor: — Is that you, Mr. Mayor? — Yes. — Lend me your spade. — Partridges are sitting on it. — May I shoo them away? — You may. At this, the mayor jumps up, and so do the other children. The mayor runs away, while the others chase him. Whoever catches the mayor becomes the mayor in the next game, while the former mayor becomes a "partridge" and sits in front of the new mayor.

title: Crane
body:
Or would you like me to tell you how... you played Crane. Łukasz Górnicki. A game of village boys in the Kraków region, suitable for elementary schools and the lowest grades of secondary schools. The children choose from among themselves a "crane," who, with a stick in hand, guards a pile of caps (balls, or similar objects). The rest of the players form a circle and move around the crane. At these words, the children run into the center, and each tries to take as many caps as possible and escape from the crane’s blows. If the crane strikes someone, that person must return their loot. The game ends when no caps remain, and in the next round, the one who collected the most becomes the crane.

title: Black Folk
body:
A game for rural children in Greater Poland and Mazovia (other names: Black Peasant, Black Man); suitable for primary schools and the lowest grades of secondary schools. Number of players: 10—50. On a rectangular field measuring 40 steps in length and 20 steps in width, two goals are marked with lines, each 3—4 steps away from the shorter sides. Behind one goal stands a player chosen as the "black folk," while all the others stand behind the opposite goal. At the signal given by the black folk—"Are you afraid of the black folk?"—the children respond: "No!" and run toward the opposite goal (turning back is not allowed); the black folk does the same, trying to catch as many children as possible along the way. Those caught assist the black folk. The game continues with constant changes of goals until all children are captured. The last one caught becomes the black folk in the next game.

title: At the Border
body:
A game for rural and urban youth in the Poznań region (sometimes called "The Black Man"); suitable for lower secondary school classes. The number of players and field dimensions are as previously described. However, no goals are marked near the shorter sides of the field; instead, at its center, two transverse lines mark a "border strip" with a width of 4 steps, divided lengthwise by a line into two halves. Within this entire border strip, the "king," chosen from among the players (by drawing lots), moves freely. The remaining participants divide into two camps ("whites" and "reds," "Mazurs" and "Kuyavians," etc.); each, led by a "prince," occupies one half of the field beyond the border strip before the game begins. At a signal given by the king, the princes send one of their subjects through the right half of the border strip to the opposite side. Once all, including the prince, have run across, the return run begins, always through the same half of the border strip and also at the king's signal. During these runs, the king, turning left and right, attempts to catch one of the runners within the border strip (by striking them with a ball or a hand on the back). The caught player becomes the king, while the former king takes their place in one of the camps; subsequent kings return to their own camp if caught. The camp that supplies fewer kings within a set time (e.g., half an hour) wins.

title: Village Mayor
body:
A game of rural boys from Podhale, suitable for elementary schools (as an introduction to the game of 'Poprz'). The playing field is as in 'Poprz'. Participants (5—20) do not divide into teams but all run back and forth across the boundary line, where the 'village mayor' catches them. A caught player switches places with the village mayor.

publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Fox and Hounds
body:
A game played by village boys in Stanisławów County (Lesser Poland); application as in the previous. A group of 10—50 children select a "fox" (by counting-out: *How many buttons, Red little buttons, And over the sea, Fox, go to your den!*); the rest are the "hounds." The playing field is arranged as in "Black Man." One of the goals is the fox’s "den," while the hounds stand behind the other. At a distance from the hounds’ goal—agreed upon by the fox but always closer to that goal than the center of the field—a light object (a cap, sash, 1, etc.) is placed on a small flag (1, etc.). The fox runs out of the den, snatches the object, and flees back, pursued by one or several hounds (who may only leave their goal once the fox has touched the prize). A hound who catches the fox before the den (by slapping his back) swaps places with the fox. Additionally, a fox who is caught, as well as a hound who fails to catch the fox, must forfeit a token (hence the game’s name), and the game ends with their redemption (see General Section).

author: Eugeniusz Piasecki
sourceTitle: Zabawy i gry ruchowe dzieci i młodzieży
publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Plinje
body:
A common game in former Polish schools (also known by names such as *Obóz*, *Gonitwa o więźnie*, *Captivus*), still played today by rural youth in some regions of Lesser Poland (northern *Król* or *Król klaskany*); suitable for secondary schools. Based primarily on Gołębiowski’s description, the following reconstruction of this beautiful yet unjustly forgotten game can be made: The playing field is a rectangle 40 metres long and 30 metres wide. Parallel to its shorter sides and 3 metres toward the centre of the field, both goals are marked. The area between the goals and the side boundaries of the field constitutes the *szranki* (lists). Within these lists, at the midpoint of the side boundaries of the field, two semicircles with a radius of 3 metres are drawn—these are the *więzienia* (prisons) designated for captives. The number of players in competitions is 22; in practice games, it may vary from 12 to 30. They divide into two camps, white and red, each under the command of a king, and gather behind their respective goal. Before the game begins, the kings cast lots; the one upon whom the lot falls has the right, at their discretion, either to choose the goal or to make the first move, leaving the other privilege to the opponent. After choosing the goal, the whites plant a white flag at the right end of their goal, while the reds plant a red one. Competitions last an hour; practice games often shorter (from 20 minutes). The king of the camp making the first move begins the game by sending one or two of their subjects toward the opponents’ goal to challenge them. These stand with one hand extended forward, palm upward, so that the challenger may touch it. The one whose hand the challenger touches pursues the challenger, who flees toward their own side. If the challenged player strikes the challenger’s back with their palm before the latter reaches their goal, they take them captive and lead them to the prison located directly opposite their own flag. This, however, rarely succeeds, as the pursued player’s comrades rush to their aid, threatening the pursuer with capture. The pursuer must then often swiftly turn back toward their own goal and rely on similar assistance. The following rules apply: 1. Only the one who ran out from behind their goal *after* the opponent has the right to take a captive. 2. Upon taking a captive, the *ustęp gry* (game segment) ends, and all return behind their goals (the captive goes to prison). Simultaneously with striking the captive, one must loudly call: *stój!* (halt!). Only one captive may be taken in a single game segment. Thus, only the first strike is valid; all subsequent ones are void. If both camps take captives simultaneously, neither goes to prison, and both return behind their goals. If the same camp takes two captives simultaneously, they have the right to choose one. A captive also includes: a) a player who runs beyond the side boundaries or behind the opponents’ goal; if several players do this, the first one is taken captive; b) one who strikes an opponent they had no right to take captive (see rule 1). Each subsequent game segment begins—that is, the camp that won the previous segment (took or freed captives) issues the challenge. During each game segment, captives may be freed from prison by striking them with the palm and simultaneously shouting: *wolny!* (free!). If the king does this, a single strike frees all. Freeing a captive ends the game segment, just as taking one does. Taking a captive simultaneously with freeing an opponent’s captive cancels both actions. Both the liberator and the freed may be taken captive before returning behind their goal. 8. During each game segment, one may also attempt to seize the opponents’ flag. If successful in carrying it behind one’s own goal, this also ends the game segment, and the flag is planted at the midpoint of the side boundary. From there, any freed captive may carry it back to their side. 9. The camp that, after the allotted time, holds more captives wins, with the flag counting as two captives and the king as three. 10. In competitions, a referee is appointed to settle all disputes definitively. The referee has the right to exclude a player for persistent rule violations or dangerous play (e.g., deliberately leaning or falling in front of a running opponent to knock them down). Plinje provides an opportunity to develop a certain *tactics*, especially among older youth, which can only be acquired through experience. The king should be a master of game tactics. They assess the physical and mental qualities of their subjects and assign roles accordingly, determining who is best suited for challenging, aiding, freeing captives, seizing the flag, and so on. Royal foresight should also not fail in defensive tasks. Never, even for a moment, should the flag or captives be left without entrusting them to players specifically suited for their protection. An equally important task of the king is to discern the right moment for each undertaking. This applies above all to freeing captives and seizing the flag, which must be done when the opponents least expect it or when their attention is diverted elsewhere. Subjects must obey the king unconditionally, for otherwise, even the best-laid game plan is ruined. With beginners, the king must eradicate the habit of thoughtlessly running out before the goal. Nothing is more harmful than this, for such a player, wandering aimlessly in the lists, under rule 1 has no right to strike anyone, while conversely, anyone who has just run out from behind their goal may take them captive. After completing any action, the player must immediately hasten back behind their goal and await an opportunity for further action. For younger pupils, certain simplifications and facilitations are usefully introduced at first. Besides a smaller playing field, this includes removing aid, freeing captives, and seizing the flag, so that only the chase between the challenger and the challenged remains. The lack of aid is compensated by the rule that a challenger who fails to catch an opponent before their goal goes into captivity themselves. Such a game may be called: *Plinje bez odsieczy* (Plinje without aid), or simply: *Plinki*.

title: The Hunt
body:
This game, briefly mentioned by Gołębiowski, in more recent times, following the English model, is called the game of "Hares and Hounds" or cross-country running. It is suitable only for adolescent boys, and participants should be examined by a doctor beforehand, as it is very exhausting and dangerous for the weaker and less agile. Two teams of 5 participants take part in the game. Each team selects one "hare." The hares set off (from a rural or suburban cottage, convenient for changing, bathing, and having a meal) cross-country through fields and forests, not avoiding obstacles such as hills, ditches, fences, and the like. They mark their trail quite densely with a "scent," which consists of scraps of paper thrown from a pouch attached to their belts. From time to time, one of them deviates to lay a false trail over a short distance (in places where the deception can only be discovered at the end of the trail). They run along a curved line that returns to the starting point, covering 5—8 kilometers. A quarter of an hour after the "hares," both teams of "hounds" set off. They must follow the trail the entire time. The hounds arriving at the finish line are assigned numbers corresponding to the order in which they arrived. The team with the smaller sum of these numbers wins: for example, if the players of the white team arrived as 1, 3, 4, 8 (sum = 16), and those of the red team as 2, 5, 6, 7 (sum = 20), the white team wins.

title: Relay Run (Wici)
body:
This game imitates the method favored by our forefathers of sending messages via relay horses. Suitable for secondary schools.

**a)** Its proper, original form requires a large space and takes place on a (little-traveled and not dusty) highway. If two teams of 10 participants each are to compete over a distance of one kilometer, we position the white camp on the left side and the red camp on the right side of the highway. The first runners from each camp stand at the starting point, while the others are spaced at intervals of 100 meters—with the last runners positioned 100 meters from the finish line. Both first runners receive a "wici" (a message in a cardboard tube, a ribbon, or a small flag) and set off simultaneously to pass it to the second runners, who then pass it to the third, and so on. The team whose wici reaches the finish line first wins.

**b)** On a school field, the game is conducted as follows: The "white" and "red" teams take positions next to each other along the longer sides of the field (in the diagram, for example, whites on the left, reds on the right). Players from each team line up in pairs facing each other at designated spots—1 from 3 at 3—5 meters, and 1 from 2 at 30—50 meters. At the given signal, the first runners (white and red) set off simultaneously, handing the small flag or ribbon to the second runners—white to the first white runner, red to the first red runner. The second runners immediately run to the third, the third to the fourth, and so on. The team that first succeeds in carrying its marker to the finish line wins; the finish line is located opposite the last runner (in the diagram, opposite the eighth runner).

title: Frogs and the Stork
body:
A game described by Gołębiowski—also played by children in the Przemyśl region (Little Poland); suitable for children's gardens and elementary schools. »The players divide into two sides, one of storks, the other of frogs, each taking their name; a finish line is marked on each side. The frogs almost reach the storks' finish line, with two of the bravest frogs stepping slightly forward. A conversation begins between them, mimicking the frogs' calls: — Hi, hy, kruin, krum! — Hi, hy, krum, krum! — Little wife! What? — Do you have a husband? — I do not. — Where did you put him? — The Lord took him. — What Lord? — Lord Stork. — At these words, the lurking storks cry: Radi, radi! and rush at the poor frogs, but they may only chase them on one leg. The game continues until the storks catch all the frogs, or the frogs catch the storks, for if a stork crosses the finish line, it becomes the frogs' property."

title: Hopscotch Variants
body:
A game especially widespread among urban children, existing in numerous variations; suitable for primary schools and the lowest grades of secondary schools.

**a) Simple Hopscotch.** Each child (there may be two or more) takes turns standing at the base of the figure, drawn with a stick on the ground or with chalk on the floor (the length of each square’s side = one step), and, without bending over, tosses a small pebble into the “hopscotch” square 1. Then, they hop into that square on one foot, pick up the pebble, and hop out the same way. If the pebble does not land in the square 1, the foot touches a line, or the player stands on both feet, the attempt is counted as failed, and next time, the player must repeat the square 1 (instead of 2). When everyone has tried the square 1, the first player tosses the pebble into square 2, then likewise into 3... 8. The rule applies that for each square, one must hop from the base of the figure through all previous squares in order and return in the same reverse sequence. The child who, in a given round, first reaches square 8 wins. Often, however, further trials are added: 1) traverse all squares with the pebble balanced on the toes of the foot without letting it fall, 2) traverse the squares with eyes closed, 3) hop through all squares on both feet.

**b) Hopscotch with “Heaven,” “Hell,” and “Sea.”** Similar to a), but players hop partly on both feet (straddle) and partly on one foot. Specifically, to enter square 2, the left foot lands in 1 and the right foot in 2. When exiting, the player makes a half-turn backward in a hop, then a forward hop on both feet. Likewise, to enter square 4, the left foot is placed in the third square, 7, while the right foot lands in 6. After square 8 comes “Hell” (one-foot hop), then “Heaven” (both feet), and finally “Sea” (one foot).

**c) “Jewish” Hopscotch.** Like a), but the hops are more difficult due to a different arrangement of squares, often forcing players to leap over intermediate squares. (The name may derive from this intricate ordering of the squares.)

**d) Clock (Warsaw), or Snail (Lviv).** Players take turns standing at the entrance of the spiral figure drawn on the ground and hop on one foot through all the compartments to the center, then return the same way. Whoever completes this entire journey correctly (i.e., on one foot and without stepping on a line) earns the right to write their initial on one of the compartments. This is their “home,” where in subsequent rounds they may rest on both feet, while others must hop over it. The game ends when there are so many homes that hopping becomes impossible. The winner is the one with the most homes.

title: Little Hare
body:
A game described by Gołębiowski; suitable for elementary girls' schools. On the floor or ground, a circle is drawn and a cross is inscribed within it. Then, one of the girls jumps into the circle and, spinning continuously in time with a song, hops alternately on her right and left foot, always into a different segment of the circle. If she makes a mistake in the rhythm, stands on both feet, or finally jumps onto a line or outside the circle, she yields her place to the next player. The winner is the one who, without error, jumps through the greatest number of verses.

publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: The Leap
body:
A boys' game found in various regions of Poland, suitable for upper primary school classes and lower secondary school boys.

**a) With Support.** The boys line up in a row, spaced several paces apart; all except the last bend forward and stand in a lunge, resting their hands on the knee of the leg extended forward. The last boy then takes a running start and leaps astride, with hand support, over his predecessor, followed by all the others in turn. Having done this, he himself takes up the same position at the front of the line. Meanwhile, his former predecessor (now last in the row) begins the same action, and so on. The line thus advances slowly forward. Instead of a row, the boys may also form a circle.

**b) Without Support.** More skilled boys leap without hand support over their companions, who are bent forward to a greater or lesser degree and turned sideways to the jumper. The formation is similar to the previous one, only with greater spacing.

title: Football in a Circle
body:
A game suitable for higher grades of primary schools and the lowest grades of secondary schools. Equipment: a spherical leather-covered ball, with a diameter of 20 cm. Children stand in a circle, each 2—4 steps apart from one another. In the center stands a player who tries to kick the ball out of the circle, while the others attempt to prevent this by kicking as well. The player who allows the ball to pass on their right side goes to the center. (From time to time, it is good to practice the left foot by having the player who allows the ball to pass on the left side go to the center instead.) Otherwise, players are not allowed to run into the center, and may only run sideways to defend the empty space on their right (or left) side. The ball may only be touched with hands if it leaves the circle.1

1) From the quoted fragment, it can be inferred that football was not unknown to our sixteenth-century ancestors. Later, however, the tradition faded, so that in this area today we must rely on foreign models.

title: Football with a Tower
body:
Application as in the previous. To the equipment is added a "tower" (3 poles of height one and a half to 2 metres, tied near the upper ends with a cord and set freely on the ground in the shape of a pyramid), standing in the centre of the circle. The outer players strive to knock down the tower by kicking the ball towards it, while the central player defends the tower by shielding it with their body and kicking the ball away or deflecting it with their torso. (Regarding the use of hands, the rule is as in the previous.). When the ball goes out of the circle, the player over whose head or to whose right it passed brings it back, places it in their position, and kicks it towards the tower. When the tower falls, the one who knocked it down takes the place of the guardian.

author: Eugeniusz Piasecki

publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Football with a Goal
body:
A game suitable for male secondary schools. On a field measuring at least 30 metres in length and width, a goal is set up in the centre, consisting of two poles driven into the ground 7 metres apart, connected at the top at a height of 2 1/* metres by a wooden crossbar (or a strap). Each team occupies a part of the field bounded by a line passing through both poles. On either side of the goal, teams are positioned, each consisting of 4—6 boys. In the first row of each team, 3—5 players stand at a distance of one and a half metres from the goal, spaced 6—10 metres apart (the "attack"); an equal distance behind them stands a player designated to pass the ball to the first row when it has gone too far back (the "reserve"). The game begins with a team chosen by lot, where one of its players places the ball directly in front of the goal at a distance of 11 metres and (with a running start) kicks it into the goal. If he scores, he goes to defend the goal (the "goalkeeper"), and his team earns a mark; if not, the opposing team attempts to score, and so on, until someone succeeds. Once a goalkeeper is in place, scoring becomes more difficult; however, there is no restriction on the distance from which the goal may be taken. The team on whose side the ball lands gains possession; the "attack" players pass it to one another with lateral movements, confusing the goalkeeper. Then, one of them, spotting an opportune moment, kicks ("shoots") at the goal. The order of the game is overseen by a "referee," who belongs to neither team. He ensures that only the goalkeeper may use his hands to stop, catch, or deflect the ball (and even he is allowed to take only 2 steps with the ball in hand) and that the goalkeeper does not deflect the ball if it passes by the goal onto the opponents' field. For breaking these rules, the referee awards the ball to the opposing team. Finally, he does not award a mark or a change of goalkeeper if, in his opinion, the goalkeeper deliberately defended poorly against a shot from his own team. The team that has earned the most marks after a given time (e.g., one hour) wins.

title: English Football
body:
This game has gained enormous popularity in our country since the early years of the current century. Today, it is the most beloved game among male youth, to the detriment of other games of no lesser value. It is suitable for strong and healthy students of higher grades in secondary schools. R u l e s (1) 1. The game involves 11 players on each side. The field dimensions should be as follows: length 90—120 metres, width 45—90 metres. The entire field must be bounded by lines. The shorter boundaries are called the goal lines, and the longer ones the touch lines. The goal and touch lines must form right angles. At these corners, flags with poles no shorter than one and a half metres should be planted. A halfway line, the 'centre line,' is drawn across the middle of the field. The centre of the field must be clearly marked, and from it, a circle with a radius of 9 metres is drawn. (Lines should not be sunken but lie flush with the field. The flagpole must not be pointed at the top.) The goal consists of two posts driven vertically into the goal line, equidistant from the corners of the field and 7,30 metres apart; a crossbar is placed on them at a height of 2,40 metres from the ground. The width of the posts and crossbar must not exceed 12 cm.

i) Established by the International Football Association. The statements in parentheses are official rulings of the same Association on disputed matters. At a distance of 51/a metres from the goalposts, a line 5/* metres long should be drawn parallel to the touch lines; the ends of these lines are connected by a line parallel to the goal lines; the area between these lines is called the 'goal area.' Similarly, lines 161/a metres long are drawn at a distance of 16/a metres from the goalposts, and their ends are also connected by a line. These mark the 'penalty area.' At a distance of 11 metres from the goal, a spot is clearly marked on the field from which the penalty kick is taken. The ball should have a circumference of 67—70 cm. The outer cover of the ball must be leather, and the use of any material that could be dangerous to players is prohibited in its manufacture. The length of the field should be 100—110 metres, and the width 65—75 metres. The ball should weigh 400—450 grams. 2. The game lasts 90 minutes unless otherwise agreed by both sides. The toss decides either the choice of goal or the right to start the game. The game begins with a kick from the centre spot towards the opponents' goal. (A kick from the spot is when the ball is kicked while it lies motionless on the ground. The ball is in play from the moment it has made a complete revolution or has travelled a distance equal to its circumference.) During the kick-off, opponents must not approach the ball closer than 9 metres, nor may any of them cross the centre line towards the opponents' goal line. 3. After 45 minutes of play, a break is called, lasting 5 minutes unless the referee decides otherwise; after the break, the teams change ends, and the kick-off is taken, according to rule 2, by the side opposite to that which started the game initially. After each goal is scored (when the ball has entered the goal), the game is restarted by the side that conceded the goal. (If the game is tied after 45 minutes, it is considered a draw; in cases where a result is necessary, the game is extended by 2 periods of 15 minutes each with ends changed at half-time. If still tied, the game continues until the first goal is scored. Before the first 15 minutes, a new toss is held.) 4. Except in cases specifically mentioned in the rules, a goal is considered scored when the ball has passed between the posts and under the crossbar, provided that the attacking players have not thrown, flicked, or carried the ball with their hands. If the crossbar falls for any reason during play, the referee may award a goal if, in his opinion, the ball would have passed under the crossbar had it been in place. (The ball passes through the goal only if it is entirely beyond the line.) The ball remains in play if it rebounds back onto the field from the goalposts, crossbar, or flagpole. The ball remains in play if it touches the referee or assistant referee while they are on the field. The ball is out of play when it crosses the goal line or touch line entirely. (The ball must be entirely beyond the line to be out of play.) 5. If the ball crosses the touch line, a player from the opposing side to the one that last touched the ball throws it back into play from the point where it crossed the line. The player throwing the ball must stand on the line, touching it with both feet, facing the field, and must throw the ball with both hands from behind the head in any direction. The ball is in play as soon as it is thrown. A goal cannot be scored directly from such a throw, and the thrower may not touch the ball again until it has been touched by another player. 6. When any player kicks the ball, any player from the same team who is nearer to the opponents' goal line than the kicker (or thrower) is offside until the ball is touched by another player; such a player may not touch the ball, interfere with opponents, or take part in the game in any way; however, a player cannot be offside: 1) on their own half of the field, 2) if there are at least three opponents between them and the goal line, 3) if the last player to touch the ball was an opponent, 4) at a goal kick, 5) at a corner kick,

6) at a throw-in from the touch line. (The key to understanding this rule is to realise that a player is offside not at the moment they kick the ball, but when a teammate kicks it; if an opponent touches the ball, the player cannot be offside under any circumstances: 1) if there are three opponents in front of them and 2) if they receive the ball from in front; in other words, a player can never be offside if they are behind the ball.) 7. If the ball crosses the goal line having been last touched by an attacking player, it is put back into play by a free kick taken by one of the defending team; for this purpose, the ball is placed on the ground in that half of the goal area which is nearer to the point where the ball went out. If, however, the ball was last touched by a defender, one of the attacking players kicks it from any point within one metre of the nearest corner of the field. In both cases, opponents must not approach the ball closer than 5 and a half metres until the kick has been taken. (At a corner kick, the corner flag must not be removed.) 8. The goalkeeper may use their hands on their own half of the field but must not carry the ball. (Carrying is defined as taking more than two steps with the ball in hand or bouncing it in the air.) The goalkeeper must not be charged except when holding the ball, obstructing an opponent, or when outside the goal area. (If the change of goalkeeper is not notified to the referee beforehand, and the new goalkeeper touches the ball with their hands within the penalty area, a penalty kick is awarded.) 9. Charging is permitted but must not be violent or dangerous; players must not kick, trip, or jump at an opponent. (In general, any violent play or attempt to bring down an opponent by tripping, leaning in front of or behind them, etc., is prohibited.) A player (except the goalkeeper) must not deliberately handle the ball. It is not permitted to charge an opponent from behind unless they are deliberately obstructing, facing their own goal. (In this rule, the 'hand' includes any part of the arm that is away from the body at the moment of touching the ball or opponent. If a player faces their own goal knowing they are being challenged, this is considered deliberate obstruction.) 10. If a free kick is awarded, the opposing player taking the kick must not be closer than 5 and a half metres to the ball. The ball is in play when it has made a complete revolution, i.e., it must roll or travel a distance equal to its circumference. The kicker may not touch the ball again until it has been touched by another player. A goal kick, corner kick, and penalty kick are considered free kicks and are subject to this rule. (No free kick may be taken before the referee's whistle. A player may be closer than 5 and a half metres to the ball if they are on their own goal line.) 11. A goal may be scored from a free kick awarded for an infringement of rule 9, but by no other type of free kick. 12. Footwear must not have any protruding metal parts; the heads of nails in the sole must be flush with it; metal or gutta-percha plates on boots and shin guards are prohibited; leather studs on the soles must not be higher than 1 cm; round studs must be at least 1 cm in diameter and must not be pointed or conical; strips must not be narrower than 1 cm and must cover the entire width of the sole. Any player whose footwear does not comply with this rule must leave the game. The referee may, if necessary, inspect players' boots before the game or during the interval. 13. At every match, there must be a referee responsible for enforcing the rules and deciding all disputed points; their decisions on matters of fact are final. The referee keeps time and prepares a report on the game. In the event of any player's misconduct, the referee warns them; in the case of a repeat offence or any other misconduct, and in the case of violent conduct even without warning, the referee has the right to send the offender off the field, about which they must inform the Association. The referee may extend the game if they deem it necessary, terminate it due to darkness, spectator interference, or whenever they consider it necessary; but in all cases where the game is interrupted, they must inform the Association, which decides the matter finally. The referee may award a free kick in all cases where the conduct of players seems dangerous or likely to become dangerous, but not sufficiently irregular to warrant more severe measures. The referee's authority extends to the entire time the game is temporarily suspended and the ball is out of play. (Persistent infringement of the rules is considered misconduct. In the event of a player being sent off, a free kick may also be awarded.) The referee's duties and powers extend to the interval and even after the game has ended. The referee submits a report to the Association within three days of the game. A player who leaves the field without sufficient cause and without the referee's permission commits an offence.) 14. At every match, there must be assistant referees; their duty is to decide when the ball is out of play, which team is entitled to a throw-in from the touch line, a goal kick, or a corner kick; the assistant referees assist the referee in enforcing the rules, but their opinion requires the referee's confirmation. In the event of unnecessary interference or misconduct by an assistant referee, the referee has the right to remove them from the field and appoint a substitute; the referee must report this to the Association. 15. In the event of an alleged infringement of the rules, the ball remains in play until the referee has given a decision. 16. If the game is interrupted for any reason while the ball is within the boundaries of the field, the referee must drop the ball at the place where the game was interrupted, and it is in play as soon as it touches the ground. If, in any case, the ball goes out of play untouched by any player, the referee again drops the ball. Players must not touch the ball until it has touched the ground. 17. In the event of an infringement of rules 6, 8, 10, or 15, the referee awards a free kick to the opponents of the offending team at the place of the infringement. In the event of a deliberate infringement of rules 5, 6, 8, 10, or 16, or after a player has been sent off under rule 13, the referee awards a free kick to the opponents; if, however, rule 9 is deliberately infringed by defenders within the penalty area, the referee awards a penalty kick to the opponents, which is taken from the designated spot and under the following conditions: all players, except the kicker and the opposing goalkeeper, must be outside the penalty area; the goalkeeper must stand on the goal line. The ball must be kicked forward. The ball is in play as soon as the kick is taken, and a goal may be scored directly from such a kick, but the kicker may not touch the ball again until it has been touched by another player. If necessary, the duration of the game may be extended to take the penalty kick. If the ball is not kicked forward or if the kicker touches the ball again, a free kick is awarded to the defenders. The referee should not apply rule 17 in cases where it would benefit the offending team. If, during a penalty kick, the ball enters the goal, the kick is not considered invalid due to any infringement by the defenders.

Technical Instructions for Correct Kicking
The beginner will learn the rules of kicking in preparatory games 87—90. The only way of kicking that every novice knows is the toe kick. However, this method plays a minor role in football; it can send the ball far, but due to the small striking surface, it is very difficult to give it the desired direction. To increase its accuracy, players' boots have transversely cut toes. Nevertheless, in games 87 and 88, only the centre forward will use it to send the ball far, and in games 90 and 91, the goalkeeper and defenders will use it for the same purpose. The foot should strike slightly below the centre of the ball, and the axis of the foot should be aligned with the direction in which we want the ball to travel. Far greater use is made of striking with larger surfaces of the foot. The outer side of the foot is most often used when we want to pass the ball to a teammate to the side. However, it is also often used to score a goal in this way. An easier, more reliable, and stronger method is kicking with the inner side of the foot. However, to deceive the opponent, good control of the outer side is very valuable. It is also essential to acquire skill in striking with the instep. Most often, the foot is strongly extended in this case. We do this when we want to kick the ball strongly straight ahead in a strictly defined direction; thus, most shots on goal look like this. But passing the ball to a teammate to the side over a greater distance is also usually done with the instep, not to mention passing forward. If the ball is approaching a player in flight above the knees, and they want to pass it behind to one of their teammates, they often use a kick with a bent foot: the ball flies over the player's head to the back. If we want to pass a rolling or low-flying ball to the back, we use the heel for this. This also includes passing the ball from the ground to the hands of one's own goalkeeper (often used at a goal kick). In this case, the player lightly 'lifts' the ball by sliding the tip of the foot under it, avoiding any striking: this is not a kick but rather a throw with the foot. In all these kicking methods, two details must be carefully observed: Firstly, it is essential to train both the right and left foot equally, for one can never predict which of them the ball will present itself in a favourable position for kicking. Secondly, one must be able to kick the ball not only from the ground when it is stationary, as stopping it wastes too much valuable time and gives an advantage to the opponent. One must be able to give the ball the desired direction immediately, regardless of whether it is rolling towards us slowly or quickly, flying in the air, or bouncing. Attention should be paid to this even in the earliest preparatory games (87 and 88). Sometimes, however, it is worth stopping the ball: for example, if the opponent is far away, or if we want to lure them towards us and then pass the ball in an unexpected direction. When the ball is coming low, we face the direction of its travel and stand on tiptoes in a crouch so that the ball can only rebound a short distance in front of us. A higher-flying ball is 'killed' (i.e., brought down to the ground) by a light tap with the sole from above, or by a nudge with the knee, thigh, or body directed diagonally downward. In all body rebounds, the beginner should get used to keeping their arms close to the body, as even touching the ball with them does not infringe rule 9. All players (except the goalkeeper) must remember that a ball flying at a certain height can only be effectively rebounded with the head. These rebounds also have enormous application. Sometimes (especially at a corner kick or a high pass from the wing), goals are scored with them; very often, the ball is passed to teammates to the side, forward, or back, etc. The rebound should be made with the surface of the head facing the direction in which the ball is to fly—and add to it the appropriate movement of the neck, and if greater force is needed, jump in the direction of the intended flight of the ball. Dribbling, or 'the wheelbarrow,' is overused by beginner players (see further tactical instructions). But even an experienced player resorts to it sometimes (e.g., a winger when their wing is not threatened, etc.). Then, while running, they push rather than kick the ball alternately with the right and left foot so that it never moves away from their feet. However, as soon as they see themselves threatened, they should immediately stop dribbling and pass the ball to an unthreatened teammate. Stopping an opponent is one of the more difficult tasks for a player, given the strong temptation to infringe the rules. If an opponent is preparing to kick, we can relatively easily knock them over or unbalance them with a light body check and 'take' the ball (i.e., kick it towards our own team). For when they are standing on one leg, their balance is worse than that of the attacker standing on both. If an opponent is dribbling the ball, we can stop it with our foot. Even if the dribbler falls as a result, there is no infringement of the rules, as we aimed at the ball, not the player. In both cases, the player's fall is usually light and without any consequences. However, one must avoid not only tripping but also leaning in front of or (when retreating) behind the player, kicking them, hitting them with the knee, or stopping them with the hand; finally, any charging from behind, unless the player is deliberately obstructing us while facing their own goal. For any such infringements, an alert and conscientious referee will penalise severely—often even by sending the player off without warning. The technique of the goalkeeper's play will be discussed in the next chapter.

Tactical Instructions
The tactics prevailing in this game have undergone fundamental and very characteristic changes over time. Initially, individual play predominated. A skilful player would take possession of the ball, dribble it near the opponents' goal, and, to the applause of the crowds, often score a goal themselves, having successfully evaded the defenders. However, as soon as clubs appeared that abandoned this tactic in favour of collective play, where the ball is passed from player to player and all cooperate for a common goal, individual play began to suffer defeat after defeat and quickly disappeared. At the same time, however, the value of the game itself as an educational tool increased enormously. In addition to the division of labour provided for in the rules themselves, which designate a goalkeeper and grant them the privilege of using their hands, experience has taught that it is beneficial to divide the rest of the team into three lines. The first consists of five attacking players (namely: the centre forward, right and left wings, and two inside forwards between them). The second consists of three midfield players (centre half, right half, and left half); the third consists of two full-backs, right and left. The full-backs, together with the goalkeeper, form the defence; the midfield, as its name suggests, assists either the attack or the defence as needed. Assigning players to these categories according to their abilities is an important task for the team captain ('mother'). However, it would be a mistake to establish this division too rigidly. On the contrary, changes from time to time are necessary, both for the all-round development of the players and for practical purposes, and often during the game, a player who has been injured must be replaced by someone who usually plays in a different position. The attack should consist of light, agile, bold, and decisive players. All of them must master the art of quickly and accurately passing the ball to the side; all, and especially the wings, should be able to dribble when necessary. Finally, for all, and particularly the three central players, the ability to shoot accurately at goal from any position in which the ball may present itself at an opportune moment is an essential condition. For example, if the white team starts the game (as in the illustration on page 151), the centre forward moves the ball diagonally forward a little more than the distance prescribed by the rules (equal to its circumference); one of the inside forwards runs up and passes the ball to the winger, who, being least threatened by opponents, dribbles it straight ahead. The other attacking players run, maintaining their original distances from each other but always slightly behind the winger leading the ball (to avoid being offside in case of a pass from the wing near the goal). At a distance from which an effective shot can already be considered (or earlier if threatened with losing the ball), they pass to the centre, and then the three central players, still running forward, pass the ball to each other until one of them spots a moment when part of the goal is unguarded and kicks the ball into it. (Beginners are prone to the fatal mistake of shooting into the goalkeeper's hands instead of into a corner they cannot reach.) If the goalkeeper deflects the ball a short distance, shots must be repeated until successful. If, however, the red defence manages to pass the ball to their attack, the white attack retreats beyond the centre line, but only far enough to more easily regain the ball (passed by their midfield or full-backs) and renew the attack. However, attacking players should never interfere with the defence. Throughout the game, the attack runs spread across the width of the field, and each strictly adheres to their position so that their teammates, without looking, know where to pass the ball. Only near the opponents' goal does the attacking line somewhat converge. The midfield consists of experienced players, familiar with both attacking methods (passing to the side and forward, long-range shots at goal) and defence (stopping and taking the ball, etc.), but above all, the most enduring runners. This trio is in constant motion throughout the game, assisting either the attack or the defence. The midfield must always be near the ball. When the attacking line is leading the attack, the midfield's task is to run behind the attack at a distance of several metres and pass the ball back to them immediately if the opponent knocks it away. Near the goal, the midfield must also often shoot, especially when the attacking players are offside. When the opponents are attacking, the first line of defence is again the midfield. If they do not manage to knock the ball away immediately, the midfield players do not give up and constantly harass the attackers, in later stages of defence coordinating their efforts purposefully with the play of both full-backs. They always remember to kick the ball taken from the opponent as quickly as possible to their own attack and enable a new attack for their team. The midfield moves across the field, maintaining the players' positions relative to each other as in the illustration (page 151). When attacking opponents pass the ball to the side, the midfield, together with the full-backs, can interfere with each of them in passing and receiving the ball. When an opponent is dribbling the ball, it is best to take it from them in pairs, with one player charging the dribbler and the other dealing with the ball. Midfield players usually take throw-ins from the touch line and free kicks when the referee awards them far from the goal. The full-backs consist of strong players capable of effectively stopping an attacker and rebounding the ball from any position to a significant distance (if possible, to their own attacking line). However, they should also be skilled in accurate passing (to the other full-back or a midfield player), which sometimes serves their team better than a showy 'high kick,' which takes a lot of time and is less accurate. The full-backs must work well together, with the goalkeeper and the midfield, so that together they form a truly cohesive defence. One of the full-backs should never move too far from the goal and, if necessary (when the goalkeeper runs forward), even temporarily stand in it. However, the other can beneficially stay further away, especially knowing how to move forward when this can put the opposing attackers offside. Neither full-back should, under any circumstances, cling to the goal and obstruct the goalkeeper's view of the ball. The goalkeeper occupies the most difficult position in the entire team. They should be tall to be able to rebound high shots; extremely agile and nimble to never lose a fraction of a second in which they can still run to a threatened corner of the goal; moreover, brave and resilient, as well as strong, to endure rough charges from opponents. They must also be able to accurately judge the direction and speed of the projectile. The goalkeeper should use their privilege of using their hands whenever time permits and only kick or stop the ball with their feet as a last resort. If time allows, the ball should be caught rather than rebounded. The best way to save the goal for a longer time is to toss the caught ball and kick it in flight towards the wings. If the attackers interfere, the ball is thrown with the hands. A high shot that cannot be caught can sometimes still be rebounded with the fist (or more reliably with both fists). If a shot goes just under the crossbar, the goal can be saved by lightly tapping the ball upwards: the ball flies over the crossbar, and the referee awards a corner kick, which, however, is not always dangerous for the goal. A low shot into the corner of the goal can be repelled by a lightning-fast dive to the ground. The goalkeeper carefully observes the movements of the forwards and tries to anticipate the direction of the shot in advance. Only exceptionally and briefly may the goalkeeper leave the immediate vicinity of the goal. Their usual place is at 1= 1 ½/9 metres in front of the goal. If they move further forward, they can be bypassed by an attacker with the ball. Standing in the goal itself exposes it to being scored upon if, for example, while catching or rebounding, they pull their hands too far back, so that the ball is momentarily beyond the goal line. The goalkeeper has more opportunities to rest than the full-backs. Therefore, they should take the goal kick, either directly from the ground or (after being 'lifted' from the ground by a full-back) from the hands. The captain ('mother') is an experienced player who knows how to command the respect of others. They lead the entire team, assign positions to players, direct their preparation for matches, and ensure that they work well together. They also devise certain tricks and surprises for opponents and generally the tactical details most suited to the relative strengths of both teams. It is most beneficial for the team if the captain is in the second line of players (midfield); then they have the best view of the game, both during attack and defence. The captain carefully ensures that players do not sacrifice the good of their team for personal momentary pleasure. They reprimand unnecessary possession of the ball and dribbling it for too long; they reprimand showing off to the public with spectacular 'high kicks' and powerful shots when an unobtrusive short pass would often bring greater benefit. The referee also has a very difficult and responsible position. If possible, they should not belong to any of the playing teams and, in any case, must remember well that from the moment they assume the duties of referee, they stand above their personal feelings of friendship or dislike. Moreover, they should be chosen from among people who not only know the rules of the game perfectly but also all the details of their practical application, and even, which is particularly important, the more commonly used ways of circumventing or subtly infringing the rules. Keen eyesight, presence of mind, decisiveness, calmness, and tact—these are further qualities needed by a referee. The referee should run almost as much as a player. Their duty is to always be as close as possible to the ball to be able to judge the game themselves, not relying on the opinion of the assistant referees, let alone the players or spectators. When the ball approaches the penalty area, they must pay close attention to possible offside situations for the attackers. When shots on goal begin, their accurate assessment requires taking a position next to the goal. Showing even the slightest hesitation, the referee diminishes their authority. Their decisions must be quick, clear, and decisive. All unnecessary conversations and disputes with players, and especially with the public, are excluded. Only the referee's whistle can stop the game, and only with it can the ball be put back into play. The task of the two assistant referees is much simpler. Running (alongside the ball) on the touch lines, they signal (by raising the flag) to the referee when the ball goes out of play. In addition, the referee may ask for their opinion if they did not see some detail of the game. The assistant referees are most often provided one by each team. It is, of course, better if they are also taken from outside the competing sides.
