title: Parsley (Lady Rose)
body:
A game for urban and rural children, widespread in Poland under various names (Lady Rose, Turnip, Beetroot, Carrot); suitable for children's gardens and primary schools.

**a) Cracovian version:** "The oldest girl — Lady Rose" — sits on the ground with legs stretched out. Between her knees sits another child, and so on, and they encircle each other with their arms, each taking the name of a vegetable. To the side, a boy — the "messenger" (sometimes accompanied by his "master," "parson" 1.1, etc.) — approaches the one sitting at the front, knocks on their head three times, and asks: — Where is Lady Rose? — There, further behind me. — He then asks the next one, and so on, until he reaches her; then he asks: — Are you Lady Rose? — I am; what do you need? — I was sent by my master for celery (carrot, etc.). If such a vegetable is among those sitting, Lady Rose points to it, and the messenger drags it out from among its companions (despite resistance) and sets it aside, announcing to the "master" that he has received the requested plant. If it is not there, but the messenger insists it should be, Lady Rose says: — Dig up the old man from the end, Don’t spoil my young horse. — The messenger then goes to the one sitting at the front and, pretending to dig with a stick beside them: — Dig, dig! Is the peasant here? = I can’t dig him out, I must take off my cap! — Then he throws his cap, grabs the child by the legs, strikes one leg against the other (as if cleaning roots of soil), shakes them all over, and drags them despite their resistance and that of the entire chain. When he tears them away, he throws them aside and reports to the master. If the chain breaks in another place, the messenger jumps there and tears away some child, while the others gather "into a heap" and "back" to bind the chain. This continues until Lady Rose is reached. Then the game ends.

**b) Kuyavian version:** The setup is as in a), except the children sitting before Lady Rose are not "vegetables" but "geese." The messenger walks around and knocks: — Knock small, knock big, Where does Lady Rose live? — Here nearby. — Finally, he receives the answer: — I am. — Then he announces: — Madam, there are geese in the garden, at your expense! — Then drive them out on one (two... five) leg(s) (on five means on all fours and head). — Having gone through the entire row in the prescribed posture, the messenger haggles over a goose: — Over the plank or the ladder? — and, depending on the answer, drags it out by the legs or by the head and sets it aside. Having redeemed all the geese from Lady Rose in this way, he invites her for coffee. She excuses herself, saying that dogs or wolves will bite her 1, etc.); finally, she agrees. Then he sets all the geese upon her; the caught Lady Rose replaces the messenger in the next game.

title: Golden Ball
body:
A game widespread in Poland (other names: Ring, Hide and Don’t Show, Chatterbox, etc.); application as above. Children divide into two teams (equal in number and strength) and simultaneously grasp (each team from one end) a long pole or rope. The team that pulls the opponents to their side wins. Then both teams stand opposite each other in two rows. The winners become the owners of the "golden ball" (a coin, ring, pebble 1, etc.) and pass it quickly from hand to hand. The defeated team, when asked by the winners: — *Guess, guesser, where is my golden ball? Is it with me, or with my brother?* — sends one person at a time (who, in some regions, hops on one foot) to find the ball. Their response: — *I would gladly tell, if only I knew.* — And then: — *Joe (Kate, etc.) has it.* — The named person opens their hands. If the "ball" is in them, the game starts anew with tugging. If not, the defeated team sends another, and so on.

body:
A game for rural and urban children, known in various regions of Poland (other names: Hell and Heaven, The Tempter, Little Devil, Drying Salt). Application as above. Children form a circle, in the center of which stands the leader, who tries to make all companions laugh in turn with various jokes and cheerful faces. Whoever laughs goes to the side as a "devil," while those who do not remain "angels." Finally, the leader arranges the angels in a line ("key"), where each holds the hips of the one in front. The "devils" line up opposite them in the same way. The first from each line grab each other's hands and, with the help of their team, try to pull the opposing side to their own. publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Pebbles
body:
A game widespread throughout Poland (other names: blirki, birki, bones, hens); suitable for children in early school grades. Five pebbles the size of hazelnuts (bean seeds, shells, etc.) are placed on the palm, then tossed upward and caught on the back of the same hand, quickly turned over. In this, either the rule of catching (on the back of the hand) applies consistently until the end, or a specific number of pebbles must be caught. In the latter case, the number for the first throw is 5, for the second 4, and so on, up to 1. In both types of the game, after an unsuccessful catch (when nothing is caught, or not in pairs, or not the specified number), the pebbles pass to the next player, according to a previously established order. The player whose turn comes again begins by repeating the move that failed the previous time. After completing the described throws, various variations are also used, such as the reverse throw (from the back of the hand to the palm), and so on. The winner is the one who, in a set number of rounds, has correctly caught the most pebbles.

author: Eugeniusz Piasecki

publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Bierki (Knucklebones)
body:
An ancient Polish game, best preserved to this day among rural boys in the Lubartów district, also known in Podlasie and Podhale; suitable for older primary school classes and younger secondary school classes. Considerably more refined than the previous game (shaped not without the influence of chess), it provides little physical activity but many opportunities to develop eye measurement and precision in hand movements. It is well-suited, for example, during rain in a camp or in a sports pavilion. Bierki are flat figures carved from wood, 1½—8 cm in length and ½—2 cm in width. All the bierki used in a given game form a "sypa" (set). The set includes: one each of a "king," "queen," "under-king," and "under-queen"—and for each player, one "priest," one "priestess," and 4 "cattle" (or "foxes"¹). Players (numbering 2—10) take turns in a predetermined order. Each places the entire set (or as many as fit) on their palm, tosses it into the air, and catches some of the bierki on the back of their hand. After tossing them again, they catch one or more figures in their palm. However, they may not catch figures of different types together (e.g., a king with a queen, a priest with a king, etc.), and foxes may only be caught in even numbers. After each correct catch, the player has the right to repeat their turn, setting aside the caught bierki. If, however, they catch nothing or break the rules, the next player in turn takes their place. When calculating the winnings, the king and queen count as 12 each, the under-king and under-queen as 7 each, the priest and priestess as 4 each, and the foxes as 1 each.

1) The technique of catching is threefold: either, after catching several bierki, the palm is tilted so that unnecessary figures slide off; 2) or the chosen figure is caught in mid-air with the fingers; or finally, 3) it is caught in the "peak," i.e., a funnel formed by the fingers.

¹) In Gołębiowski’s work, these figures are called king, steward, lord, village headman, farmer, farmhand, etc.

title: For the Fates
body:
A game of village boys from the Bukowski district (Greater Poland), suitable for older boys in elementary schools, especially rural ones. A game for 5—6 boys. On a larger, flat field stone, they place a smaller one. Having stepped back 20 paces from the stone, they draw a line on the ground which must not be crossed. Each boy selects a pebble with which he throws, as if unintentionally, beyond the line. The player whose pebble lands closest to the larger stone becomes the "guard" and positions himself nearby. The rest of the players stand behind the line with pebbles in hand. The boy whose pebble landed farthest from the large stone begins. He tries to knock the smaller stone off the larger one with an accurate throw. If he succeeds, he runs to retrieve his projectile. Meanwhile, the guard replaces the smaller stone on the larger one and also runs to retrieve the boy’s projectile. Whoever reaches it first takes the pebble and stands behind the line, while the other becomes the guard. If a player fails to knock off the top stone with his projectile, he usually does not rush to retrieve it, as the guard would outrun him. (The guard is only allowed to go for the projectile at the same time as its owner.) Therefore, the boys approach this task stealthily, crawling through byways to the spot with the projectile. If the guard spots this, he also rushes for the projectile.

title: Stone Rolling
body:
Popularity and application as previously described. Two boys choose a target (a tree, a stump, a ditch) and place a roughly spherical field stone near it. Then, from a distance of about 20 steps, they take turns throwing small stones, aiming to hit the spherical stone so that it rolls toward the target. Each player has two projectile stones. Whoever misses loses a projectile; when both projectiles are lost, the player loses the game.

title: Ducza
body:
A game from the gentry enclaves of Podlasie, suitable for older boys in elementary schools, particularly rural ones. Each player has a palant (club) of equal size; the length of ten palants marks the distance from a firmly planted post, which the boys then throw their palants at, aiming to knock it down or at least hit it. Whoever hits it earns the right to shorten the target distance by the length of one palant and throw again from that new point; whoever misses must step back as far as they overshot or fell short of the target. The one who knocks down the post wins.

¹) A similar game is described by Gołębiowski under the name "G r e l e" or "K r e l e".

title: Pikier
body:
A game played by urban and rural boys from various regions of Mazovia, Podlasie, and the Vilnius area (other names: Piekarz, Palant, Pałki, Djabeł, Pop). Its application is similar to the previous one, but the throwing distance to the goal is 20 steps, and a player who, during the palant draw, threw closest to the post driven into the ground stands by it (called the pikier, piekarz, etc.). Each player takes turns throwing once until someone knocks over the post. Then the pikier sets the post upright, and all the boys who have already thrown run to retrieve their palants. If the pikier, after setting up the post, touches a boy with his palant, that boy becomes the new pikier. Each knockdown is counted as a point.

title: The Barrel Organ
body:
A game played by village boys in the Bukowski region (Greater Poland), similar in application to the previous one. The boys stick a willow branch, roughly 24 cm long with three offshoots, into the ground. Right in front of this "barrel organ," they cross two meter-long sticks. Players stand at a distance of 20—30 steps and mark a line they must not cross. From there, they throw sticks 60 cm long at the barrel organ. If someone strikes it skillfully, the three-pronged branch springs back far. The distance from there to its original position is measured with the thrown sticks. If it equals or exceeds the distance from the throwing line to the barrel organ, the boy who knocked it over wins and leaves the game. The contest continues among the remaining players. If a player does not immediately achieve the desired distance, he remembers the number of "cubits" and "adds" the remainder when his turn comes again. The last player, lacking the required number of cubits, lifts his right leg and receives as many strikes from the first winner as the cubits he is short.

publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Polish Skittles
body:
A game widespread in Polish manors in Livonia, also known here and there in Lesser Poland. Suitable for secondary schools. Old Polish authors mention skittles (e.g., Rej in *Wizerunek*), while school regulations (e.g., the Chełmno Academy) recommend it alongside ball games during leisure time from study. The game described here, in terms of the richness of its combinations, deserves a place among the best alongside Palant, Pliń, and Nożna; it lags behind them only in the quantity and variety of movement and is therefore best suited for hot days. German skittles cannot compare with it in any respect. The pitch must be level, approximately 60 in length and 25 meters in width. Otherwise, depending on the skill of the players, the length of the pitch may be increased. The pitch is divided into three fields by two transverse lines, enclosing between them a "no-man’s land" 10 meters wide. The lines serve as the front boundary for each camp. Each camp has 12 skittles, shaped like a truncated cone 30 cm high, with a base diameter of 6 cm and a top diameter of 1 cm; the skittles of one side are marked with a colored band or a shallow groove (a "neck"). The game uses 8 wooden balls with a diameter of 18 cm. In competitions, each camp consists of 8 participants; in practice games, the number is arbitrary, as the measure of equality between camps is the number of balls, each of which is thrown only once per turn. Each camp sets up its skittles on its own field as it wishes, ensuring only that: 1) at least one, but no more than 6 skittles stand on the boundary line, 2) the entire arrangement is nowhere wider than 3 meters or deeper than 6,60 meters, and 3) the distance between skittles does not exceed 60 cm (twice the height of a skittle). Depending on the skill and throwing style of the opponents, different setups may be advisable. In each camp, the order of players is strictly marked to prevent one player from gaining an advantage in more difficult positions. One side begins and throws all the balls in turn (one player after another, one ball each), trying to knock down as many of the opponent’s skittles as possible. Throws can be made from behind one’s own skittles or from the side, from one’s own boundary line. For the continuation of the game, the position of the closest skittle to the boundary line determines the throwing point; thus, knocking down the opponent’s closest skittles moves their boundary line back. Next, the other side plays. Before throwing the balls, however, they throw the skittles that were knocked down from the distance where the given "corpse" fell, trying to knock down as many of the opponent’s skittles as possible (a flat, sweeping throw). Skittles hit in this way by other skittles are removed from the game along with those that struck them. If a skittle misses, however, it is placed where it stopped; it becomes the property of the opponent and is called a "Cossack." In further play, "Cossacks" are no longer thrown back. Throwing back the "corpses" is called "driving" or "pairing" the skittles (because the hit and the hitter are removed from the game in pairs). If a thrown skittle does not reach the opponent’s boundary line, the next player from the opposing team kicks it with their heel toward their own boundary line as far as they deem advantageous; a strong kick protects the "Cossack" from being hit but, in the absence of other skittles—usually at the end of the game—also moves the boundary line back for ball throws. The same consideration requires moderating the force of the skittle throw: if successful, a strong throw will sweep away more skittles; if it misses, however, a strongly thrown skittle will fly so far that hitting it with a ball becomes difficult; moreover, at the end of the game, such a throw may move the opponent’s boundary line back. (It is also possible to agree to throw back "Cossacks," but this excessively prolongs the game, as only skittles knocked down by skittles are removed.) After all the "corpses" have been thrown back, the side throws the balls, with the order of players counted separately for skittle throws, ball throws, and "kicking." The game ends when one field is empty and the opposing side has no more corpses to throw back. Toward the end of the game, one must try to throw the balls as strongly as possible to finish the game with as few throws as possible, which affects the calculation of the degree of victory. Balls are not thrown onto an empty field, but a "corpse" is thrown back even onto empty fields: it can be knocked down by another corpse in turn, saving balls. However, from an empty field, balls are still thrown at the opponent’s standing skittles from the end of the pitch, if balls remain. The victory is calculated by counting: one point for a "Cossack" standing on the winning side’s field, two points for one’s own skittle still standing, and one point for a ball not yet thrown. If both fields are empty (e.g., the last skittles were knocked down by "Cossacks" and removed from the game without being thrown back), the side that is to throw wins by as many points as they still have balls. Thus, if the last skittle (a "Cossack") was knocked down by the very first ball, the victory is 7; if only by the eighth, it is 0, and the game is a draw. If the winning side still has skittles and the opponent knocks down their last skittle with the very first ball, then the opponent’s last throw has only one ball at their disposal; if they also knock down the last skittle of the winning side with it, that victory counts as 8: the winning side, with an empty field, is to throw but has nothing to throw at, yet still has all 8 balls. If one side (the whites) still has one skittle and knocks down the opponent’s last non-"Cossack" skittle not with the last ball, but the thrown-back skittle clears their field in return, then the side with more balls wins, by as many points as they have more; if the whites threw the last ball, the side that is to throw (the reds) wins.

title: Kolbiki (Little Sheaves)
body:
A game played by rural boys in the Międzyrzecz district (Podlasie region), suitable for older pupils of elementary schools, especially in rural areas. Each boy constructs his own "kolbik" (little sheaf), consisting of 5 small sticks, each 30 centimeters long, arranged in 3 tiers. The first 2 sticks lie on the ground parallel to each other, the second pair is placed crosswise on the ends of the first, and the fifth is placed on top, perpendicular to the sticks of the second tier. All kolbiki form a row, spaced 3 meters apart from one another; each is surrounded by a small trench. The boys stand at a distance of 5½ meters from their kolbik and attempt, by throwing a stick ("pałka" or bat), to knock all the sticks beyond the trench surrounding the kolbik. Whoever succeeds gains the right to ride on the back of the loser from one kolbik to another.

title: The Skylark (Canary)
body:
The game is as widespread and applied as previously described. On the upper, wedge-shaped cut end of a stick vertically stuck into the ground, a fork-shaped piece of wood called the skylark is placed. Then, a groove is made around the stick, forming a "cage." The boys then take turns throwing their clubs from a distance of 5 half a metre, and a successful hit on the stick knocks the skylark off. The distance the skylark falls, measured by the club, earns points for the thrower. 100 points constitute a win, and the victor becomes the skylark (canary) and collects all the nuts, pumpkin seeds, or sometimes even money from the pot. The remaining players must hop on one leg around the cage at his command.

publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Snowballs
body:
Snowball fights have been a beloved pastime of children and youth for ages in all countries within the temperate and cold zones. Here, we will focus solely on their more refined form, suitable as a game for secondary schools. The ideal time for snowball fights is during moderately frosty days or the beginning of a thaw (when the snow is slightly sticky but does not harden into ice when pressed in the hands). A snowball should be about the size of a palant ball, not too hard, and under no circumstances should it contain foreign additives (sand, stones, mud, etc.).

**a) Snowballs in the Field.** Players, numbering 20—50, divide into two equal camps under the command of leaders. Two goals are marked (with flags, etc.) at a distance of 10 meters from each other, with lengths of 20—50 meters (depending on the number of participants). It is forbidden to step beyond these goals, either forward (toward the opponents) or sideways. Before the game, a certain amount of time (e.g., 10 minutes) is allotted for gathering a supply of snowballs. At the signal given by the referee, both camps begin throwing snowballs at their opponents. A hit player retreats as "wounded" and may only supply their teammates with snowballs. If the number of wounded on both sides becomes too great, the referee pauses the game and allows an equal number of "healed" wounded to return to the battle lines. The camp with the fewest wounded after a predetermined time (e.g., 15—20 minutes) wins.

**b) Snowballs in Trenches.** If the snow is sufficiently sticky, the above game can be enhanced by building embankments at both goals, behind which players can take cover from the opponents' snowballs.

**c) Snow Fortress.** A quarter of the participants build a fortress from snow embankments (for which a quarter of an hour is allotted) and occupy it, while the remaining three-quarters serve as the besieging army. The leaders of both sides agree before the game on what constitutes victory, e.g., the fortress is captured if, within 20 minutes, half of the defenders are "wounded," or if as many attackers as there are unwounded defenders enter its center. Otherwise, victory is awarded to the defenders. The rules regarding the wounded are as above. Attackers who enter the fortress must cease fighting and not hinder the defense, and in turn, defenders may not attack them. For rule violations, the referee adds a mark ("wounded") to the offenders, and particularly unruly players may be excluded. This applies to all three variations of the game. **Tactics** resemble those of warfare. When firing at opponents, the leader pays special attention to sequentially concentrating "fire" on individual players, especially the best ones. In capturing the fortress, demonstrations (a feigned attack from one side, followed by the real assault from another when the defenders' attention is focused) and diversions (drawing part of the enemy's forces away with an attack from another side to ensure the success of the main assault) play a significant role. The formation should be as dispersed as possible, for when aiming at a "cluster," even the worst player may wound someone.

title: The Shooter
body:
A game from rural boys in the Kraków region, suitable for elementary schools and the lowest grades of secondary schools. The children line up in a row and receive names of various birds from the leader ("the host"). Then a player who has been standing aside comes forward and begins bargaining. — Knock, knock! — Who’s there? — It’s me, the devil with a scorched pot. — What do you need? — Birds. — Which ones do you want? — Orioles (jays, storks, etc.). — There are none (if he did not guess correctly). Moreover, if he pointed to the wrong boy, that boy aims a ball at him. If the devil guessed correctly, he himself throws the ball at the chosen bird. If he hits, he takes the bird for himself; if he misses, he again exposes himself to a shot from the bird’s side. The bird that misses goes into devilish captivity. The game ends when all the birds are captured.

author: Eugeniusz Piasecki
sourceTitle: Zabawy i gry ruchowe dzieci i młodzieży
publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: Meta (Forging)
body:
A game described by Gołębiowski, still known today in Mazovia and Lesser Poland. Suitable for higher grades of primary schools and lower grades of secondary schools.

**a) Meta in Pairs.** Players stand opposite each other at a distance of 10—12 steps, each marking their position with a small stone pressed into the ground, which they must touch with their right foot (the left foot may move freely). One of them (chosen by lot) tries to hit the other with a ball ("to forge," "to strike"); the other (standing, if possible, near a wall) attempts to dodge the blows. Both begin the game with an agreed number of "lives" (5, 10, 1, etc.), of which the forger loses one for each missed strike, while the forged loses one for each hit. The game continues until one of them loses all their lives. Additionally, if the forger misses, the positions and roles of both players are swapped.

**b) Meta in Threes.** Three players stand in a straight line at intervals as in (a); the middle one, chosen by lot, is the target of the projectiles alternately from one or the other of the outer players. Otherwise, the rules are as above. In Podolia, this variant is called *kwasek*.

**c) Meta with Mothers (Forging).** This is a game played by village boys in the Rzeszów region (Lesser Poland). On an oblong playing field, two small stones are pressed into the ground at a distance of 1–0 to 1–2 steps from each other to mark the positions. The group of children divides into two teams led by "mothers," who stand in rows opposite each other. Lots decide which team throws first; the other team chooses its position. The first two players stand opposite each other, keeping their right foot on the pressed-in stone, while the others stand at a distance to catch the thrown ball and pass it to the player on the position. The team that throws first tries to hit the opponent with the ball. The next throw belongs to the other team, and so the opponents take turns throwing the ball at each other. A player who is hit, i.e., "forged," steps aside, and the next in line takes their place. The team that eliminates (forges) more opponents wins. The thrower is allowed to use feints, or "tricks," similarly to all subsequent games involving "forging." The player standing on the stone must not lift their right foot from it, though the left foot may move and dodge.

title: Kasha (Porridge)
body:
A game described by Gołębiowski; application as in the previous one. Participants, numbering 5—20, choose one among themselves to stand in the center with a ball in hand, while the others arrange themselves in a circle, spaced several steps apart. The one in the center throws the ball to the ground so that it bounces toward the circle’s edge. Whoever catches the ball in flight or picks it up aims it at the center player. If the hitter misses or the center player catches the ball, they switch places, and the new center player serves as above. If the hitter hits, the player toward whom the ball bounced catches or picks it up and again aims at the center player. The winner is the one who, in the agreed time, was not in the center at all, or (if everyone was) received the fewest hits. Rules: 1) The center player may move only within the circle; if they dodge the ball outside the circle, they are considered hit. 2) The outer players mark their positions (with chalk on the floor, a furrow in the ground): a hit where the player does not touch this mark with at least one foot is considered a miss.

3) A hit above the shoulders or below the knees is also counted as a miss. 4) If the ball falls to the ground after a serve or a hit, the center player picks it up, or one of the outer players returns it to them for another serve.

title: Sparzak (Wall Ball)
body:
A game for school-aged youth in the Kingdom of Poland (also known as Zbijak, Żydek, or Sparzony), suitable for lower secondary school classes. One player (chosen by tossing, a fee of 1, etc.) stands by the wall as the "sparzony" ("żydek"); the others position themselves at various distances from it. The player at the wall throws the ball against the wall so that it rebounds as far as possible, then turns to face the opponents. If no one catches the rebounded ball, it is returned to the "sparzony." If someone does catch it, they aim at the "sparzony" from the spot where they caught it. The "sparzony" is determined by: 1) whoever misses when striking, or

2) whoever is hit on the fingers by the ball and fails to catch it. A ball caught with both hands grants the right to one throw, with the right hand to two throws, and with the left hand to three throws. The winner is the one who, within the agreed time, was never the "sparzony" or (if everyone was) received the fewest hits.

title: The Blacksmith
body:
A game described by Gołębiowski (under the name *żydka*), still common today among urban children (most often called *Klas*); in the Tarnobrzeg and Nisko counties (Lesser Poland), rural youth also play it. Suitable for primary schools and lower secondary school grades. Here is Gołębiowski’s description: "This was a game of higher perfection, demonstrating the skill of the players and convincing spectators of what they could achieve with themselves and the equipment of this pastime. The aforementioned game consisted of various feats; the first six were, in a way, a necessity and an entry into the further ones. Whoever did not perform them with complete precision had to start from the beginning; whoever passed them successfully, even if they made a mistake later, only repeated from the unfinished feat and proceeded further in this scope until they reached the highest level of perfection.

1) A test of skill was to throw the ball against the floor so that it bounced off the wall and only then catch it. 2) The same under the leg. 3) The player leans their hand against the wall and throws the ball under it against the wall and catches it. 4) The *S a d ł o* (lard) is let go: to do this, the youth leans back slightly, resting their head against the wall, throws the ball above themselves, and catches it before it falls to the ground. 5) The *P i e c z ą t k a* (seal) is placed on a cupped hand, that is, on the thumb and the next finger joined in a circle; the ball strikes it, then the hand moves away, and the bounced ball is caught. However, each of these feats must not be performed just once, but thrice, similarly to the following ones, except where a smaller number is specified by the rules; for hitting once could be a matter of chance, but repeating thrice without error is proof of skill. Whoever failed yielded their turn to another and was last among the players to make new attempts. Whoever completed the entry feats rested until others succeeded, then everyone took turns with the further feats. 7) A new challenge: throwing the ball as if into a *k a s z a* (bowl) and catching it from above. 8) Catching from below. 9) The *B o c h e n e k c h l e b a* (loaf of bread): the ball is struck on the fist and caught. 10) The *P ó ł m i s e k* (plate), on an open palm. However, these two feats must also be repeated in reverse, that is, holding the fist and palm on top and turning them to the other side. 11) The *W a z a* (vase), on fingers raised in the shape of a vase. 12) The *N ó ż* (knife), on one finger. 13) The *W i d e l e c* (fork), double, triple, quadruple on as many spread fingers. 14) *L i c z e n i e p a l c ó w* (counting fingers) of one hand, that is, placing the ball on each. 15) *P u s z c z a n i e k r w i* (letting blood): on a bent elbow, the ball is squeezed from the bent palm and caught from above, or 16) bounced off the ground from below.

17) The ball is struck against the wall with the palm from above, and from below 24 times. 18) The ball is tossed straight up and struck once with the palm, then a second time turning the hand 48 times. 19) The player *dresses*, *washes*, *puts on shoes, trousers, a vest, a frock coat*, *combs their hair*, that is, before the ball bounces off the ground, they must pretend to do all this and catch the ball, repeating the same thrice. 30) *S p u s z c z a n i e w o d y* (letting water) single, double, up to sixfold; for this, the ball is thrown against the wall, bounces off the ground, and is caught. 21) *K l a s k a n k a* (clapping): the ball is thrown upwards, three claps are made—front, back, and front again. 22) *O b r ó t k a* (turn) upper and lower: throw against the wall, turn around, and catch from above or below. 23) *R a c z k a* (crawling): turning away from the wall and bending, the ball is thrown between the legs against the wall, bounces off the ground, and is caught from above and below. 24) The ball is thrown against the wall so that it falls on the head and is then caught—whoever accomplished all this was proclaimed king, and a privilege was sealed for them, that is, they were burned in the palm in turn by the others; if someone missed, the king struck them thrice with their royal hand. It was rare for someone to become king, for what skill it required, and even the most dexterous found it difficult to perform each of these feats."

title: Ball Relay in Two Rows
body:
A game introduced to our schools relatively recently; application as in the previous one. Children divide into two teams, which line up side by side in two rows, as in a relay race, except here the distance between the two rows does not exceed several meters. Players, designated as "ones" in both the "white" and "red" teams, simultaneously (on a given signal) begin play by throwing their twos a ball—white for the first team, red for the second. The twos throw to the threes, the threes to the fours, and so on. Catching the ball is only allowed while standing in the designated spot. Whoever fails to catch it must pick it up and throw it to the next player from the spot where it was retrieved. The team whose ball reaches the last player first wins; that player raises it high and calls out: white! (or red!) b. Throwing-Running Games

title: Stójka (Freeze Tag with a Ball)
body:
A game of rural boys from the Tarnobrzeg and Nisko counties (Lesser Poland), suitable for upper primary school grades and lower secondary school grades. The children form a circle; in its center stands the leader and throws the ball high into the air. During the throw, all others scatter; however, they must freeze on the command "Freeze!" shouted by the leader once he has caught the ball. He then aims the ball at the nearest player. If he hits ("tags" or "freezes" the player, the tagged player catches the ball or stops it), everyone scatters again to freeze on the command "Freeze!" when the ball is in the hands of the tagged player. If he misses, he must do the same until he hits someone.

title: Wokatus
body:
A game for school-age youth in Mazovia, suitable for elementary schools and the lower grades of secondary schools. (Local names include *Ball to the Hole*, *Battle of Nations*, and the like.) The children stand closely in a circle; in the center is a hole dug in the ground, containing a ball. Each child adopts the name of a nation (Pole, German, French, English, etc.). To the side stands the "referee," who calls out one of these names, saying: — Wokatur — for example, French! Then the "French" player quickly grabs the ball and aims at one of the companions, who scatter. If the throw hits someone, that player receives a mark from the referee; if the throw misses, the thrower receives the mark. The game then begins anew. The game is played until an agreed-upon number of marks, for example, to *10*. The first to reach this number undergoes "coronation," or "execution by firing squad," receiving as many hits from the ball by each player as the number of marks the given player lacks to reach *10* (see General Part).

title: Dotki (Dibs)
body:
A game played by schoolchildren in some towns of Mazovia; its application is as in the previous game. Children dig as many holes in the ground (spaced half a step apart) as there are participants. These holes lie in a straight line, and each can fit a ball. Then, each player chooses one of the holes and stands beside it. The best players ("mothers") stand at both ends, selecting the outermost holes. One of the mothers starts the game by rolling the ball along the holes toward the other mother. If the ball does not stop in any hole, the other mother takes it and rolls it back similarly! If, however, the ball stops in a hole, its owner grabs the ball and aims at the fleeing companions running in all directions. If they miss everyone, a small stone (shaving 1, etc.) called an "egg" or "child" is placed in their hole. If they hit someone, the hit player takes the ball and tries to hit someone else, and so on, until someone misses. Then, one of the mothers restarts the game. The game continues until one of the players accumulates the agreed-upon number (e.g., 10) of "eggs"; then, the "execution" follows (as in the previous game).

title: Ekstra (Extra Goal)
body:
A game described by Gołębiowski, still beloved by school youth in Mazovia to this day. Suitable for secondary schools. Players divide into two camps, each led by a "mother." Lot decides which camp goes to the center and which to the perimeter of the circle. Those on the perimeter pass the ball over the heads of the central players and, at an opportune moment, try to tag one of them. If they miss, a change of positions occurs. If they hit, the tagged player catches or picks up the ball and aims at the perimeter players, who scatter. If successful, there is also a change of positions; if they miss, the game continues with the original arrangement. The camp that achieves more marks (for tagging opponents) within the agreed time wins.

title: Knock-Down
body:
Distribution and application as previously described. It serves as preparation for Palant and is especially recommended for the lowest grades of secondary schools when children still lack skill in batting the ball. However, it can also be useful for older students (e.g., in camp or on an excursion, when Palant equipment is unavailable, 1, etc.). The playing field, game progression, rules, technique, and tactics are the same as in "Palant with Bases, Without Elimination" (see the next chapter). The only changes are as follows: 1) instead of batting, throws with the ball are used; 2) each player (including the "base" and the "ransomer") has the right to only one throw; 3) younger students ransom themselves by running to the halfway mark instead of the finish line.

title: Ball Relay in Double Rank
body:
A game recently introduced to our schools; suitable for elementary schools and lower grades of secondary schools. The children divide into two teams, which stand side by side, forming a double rank together. The first members of both ranks (the "white" and "red" teams) each receive a ball (a football). At a given signal, both simultaneously pass the balls backward (with arms stretched upward) to their teammates, who then pass them further. When the ball reaches the end of the rank (if someone drops it, they must pick it up, return to their place, and pass it further), the last person runs along the outside of the rank to the front, stands before the first, and passes it backward again. This is repeated until everyone has run. The team that completes this faster wins.

title: Basketball
body:
An American game introduced to our girls' secondary schools some dozen years ago. G a m e: On each side, 5, 6, or 9 participants stand, depending on the size of the court (room). The aim of each team is to throw the ball into their own basket while simultaneously preventing the opponents from achieving victory in the same manner. A basket scored from the field counts as 2 points, while a free throw counts as one. C o u r t, e q u i p m e n t: The court (outdoors or indoors) is a rectangle 15—30 meters long and 6—15 meters wide, marked by lines beyond which lies a free space, clear of any obstacles, at least 1 meters wide. The shorter lines are called the end boundaries, and the longer ones the side boundaries. In the center of the court, a c e n t r a l c i r c l e with a radius of half a meter is drawn. The court is divided into three equal parts by d i v i s i o n l i n e s parallel to the end boundaries. (Courts 15 meters or less in length are divided into two halves instead.) F r e e - t h r o w l i n e s, half a meter long, are drawn parallel to both end boundaries and at a distance of 3 meters from them, opposite both baskets. From the center of each free-throw line, an arc with a radius of 2 meters is marked, connecting toward the baskets with two lines running 2 meters apart, perpendicular to the end boundaries. The space thus enclosed is the f r e e - t h r o w l a n e. B a s k e t s are made of cord netting hanging from metal rings with an inner diameter of 45 cm. The baskets narrow downward so that the ball, once dropped from above, pauses momentarily before falling through the bottom opening. They are positioned so that the plane of the rings is 3 meters above the ground, and their outer edge is fixed 15 cm from the post, placed at the center of the end boundary. It is advisable to attach a backboard 2 meters long and 1'20 meters high to this post, behind the basket. B a l l s used are ordinary footballs. P a r t i c i p a n t s of each team, led by a c a p t a i n, take positions previously designated by her and communicated to the referee (and scorer). For this purpose, the captain divides her team into g u a r d s, c e n t e r s, and f o r w a r d s (see illustration J). None of these categories may cross into another third of the court during play. On shorter courts divided into two halves, the 'center' has the privilege of moving from one half to the other. On no court may the center participants attempt a shot at the basket. The r e f e r e e, belonging to neither team, ensures the game proceeds correctly and resolves disputes. For assistance, they choose a s c o r e r (recording points and fouls) and, for more important matches, several assistants. T i m e consists of two halves of 15 minutes each, separated by a 10-minute break. If a foul is committed simultaneously with or just before the end-of-game or break signal, the referee extends play to allow a free throw. The visiting team has the right to choose the basket in the first half. If both teams are playing at home, the captains draw lots for the baskets. In the second half, the baskets are switched. The ball may only be caught with both hands; holding and throwing may also be done with one hand. It is a foul to place a hand on the ball held by an opponent. Until the referee decides which opponent touched the ball first, no more than one player from each team may touch it. T h e t i p - o f f in the center circle occurs: a) at the start of each half; b) after a basket is scored; c) after an incorrect free throw; d) after the last free throw due to a double foul. Method of execution: Both c e n t e r s stand with both feet in their half of the center circle, one hand placed behind their back; this hand must remain in position until one or both opponents tap the ball. The remaining participants must not interfere with the referee or the centers. The referee tosses the ball in a plane perpendicular to the side boundaries, between the two centers, higher than both can reach by jumping, so that it falls between them. When the ball reaches its highest point, the referee signals with a whistle, after which both opponents jump and attempt to tap the ball. If the ball falls to the ground untouched, the tip-off is repeated. Neither opponent involved in the tip-off may catch the ball until another participant touches it. When the b a l l g o e s o u t o f p l a y (i.e., touches the ground or any object outside the court boundary, or a participant who is out of play), the referee orders it to be put back into play. The opponent of the player who caused the ball to go out stands behind the boundary at the point where the ball left the court and throws or bounces the ball to one of her teammates. If the referee cannot determine who caused the ball to go out, they put it back into play at a point approximately 1 meters from the boundary on the court, opposite the exit point, in the same manner as the tip-off in the center circle. T i m e - o u t s in the game may be called by the referee for up to 5 minutes, at the request of one of the captains or in case of player injury. After such a break, the ball is put back into play at the spot where it was when the timeout was called, otherwise as in the tip-off in the center circle. When two opponents simultaneously have both hands on the ball, the referee declares it a j u m p b a l l and puts it back into play between them at the same spot, as in the tip-off in the center circle. F o u l s a n d p e n a l t i e s. 1) If the free-throw shooter touches or crosses the free-throw line before the ball touches the basket (or backboard) — the basket, if made, does not count, and in any case, a tip-off in the center circle follows.

2) If the ball is thrown 'dead' into the basket, or

3) If more than 10 seconds are taken to execute a free throw — the basket, if made, does not count.

4) When a participant causes the ball to go out of play.

5) Brings the ball onto the court from out of bounds.

6) Touches the ball after it is put into play from out of bounds before another participant touches it.

7) Illegally interferes with an opponent putting the ball into play from out of bounds.

8) Holds the ball longer than 10 seconds out of bounds before putting it into play — the ball passes to the opponent out of bounds.

9) If a participant touches the ground beyond the division line with any part of her body or clothing — the opposing team gains the right to an unguarded throw (but not a basket). If the violation is committed by the team in possession of the ball, the throw is made by the player holding it; otherwise, the ball is taken by the nearest opponent to the violation.

10) When during a free throw anyone enters the free-throw lane, touches the free-throw line, or

i) The ball is 'dead': a) after a basket is scored, b) after going out of bounds, c) after being declared a jump ball, d) during a timeout, e) after a foul, f) after either of two free throws due to a double foul, g) after the game ends, h) when the ball rests on the basket supports, i) after one of the free throws due to two fouls by the same team, j) after an incorrect free throw, attempts to interfere with the shooter before the ball touches the basket (or backboard) —

a) if the offending team is the shooting team, the basket, if made, does not count, and in any case, a tip-off in the center circle follows;

b) if the offending team is the opposing team, the basket, if made, counts, and if missed, a repeat free throw is awarded.

11) When someone throws the ball into the basket from out of bounds — the basket, if made, does not count; if missed, the ball is considered still in play. T e c h n i c a l f o u l s a n d p e n a l t i e s: A free throw is awarded to the opposing team of the participant who

1) Runs with the ball (i.e., takes steps with the ball in hand; a single pivot step does not count, nor do a few steps after catching the ball while running), snatches or knocks the ball from an opponent's hands, kicks the ball, strikes it with a fist, rolls it, bounces it more than once, or passes it to a teammate.

2) Delays the game by touching the ball after it has been awarded to an opponent, by leaving the court, by removing a hand from behind the back during the tip-off before the ball is tapped, or by other violations of tip-off rules, by not getting up quickly enough after falling, or by any other unnecessary delay.

3) Holds the ball in hand longer than three seconds.

4) Passes the ball to a teammate while executing a free throw.

5) Enters the court as a substitute without the referee's knowledge.

6) Illegally 'guards' an opponent not shooting at the basket. (This means crossing with hands or torso the vertical plane passing through both hips or touching the opponent.) A point is awarded to the team executing the free throw.

7) If their opponents touch the ball or basket when the ball is on the rim or inside it. Two free throws are awarded to the team whose opponent:

8) Illegally guards (see above under

6) a participant shooting at the basket. A player who commits five technical fouls is disqualified from the game. P e r s o n a l f o u l s. A free throw for the opposing side, counting a personal foul against the offender (and, at the referee's discretion, disqualification), is awarded for:

11) Holding an opponent, impeding her movement when she does not have the ball, bumping or pushing her.

12) Unnecessary roughness in conduct. Two free throws, a personal foul for the offender (and, at the referee's discretion, disqualification), are awarded for:

13) Pushing or holding an opponent who is shooting at the basket. A player who commits four personal fouls is disqualified from the game. In all cases not covered by the rules, the referee (and their assistants) shall act according to their own judgment, in accordance with the general spirit of the rules.

¹) As seen in the illustration, participants line up in pairs, each consisting of two opponents, e.g.: defense of the reds (at their own basket) and offense of the whites, center of the reds and whites, offense of the reds and defense of the whites. Opponents in each pair 'guard' each other, impeding shots with movements of hands and torso.

publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: The Piglet
body:
A rural boys' game, widespread throughout Poland; suitable for older pupils of elementary schools, especially rural ones. All children except one (the "shepherd") stand in a circle, spaced 2 or more steps apart. Each digs a small hole in front of themselves and hides the end of the stick (palant) they are holding in it. In the center, a larger hole (the "sty," "brewery," or "kettle") is made, so that the "piglet"—a ball or small wooden disc—can fit inside it. The shepherd, standing behind the circle, tries to drive the piglet into the brewery by striking it with his palant; all the others hinder him by deflecting it in the opposite direction. However, each must be careful not to step too far away from their (small) hole, for if they do, the shepherd can reach the hole and place his palant inside it, and then the careless one takes the shepherd's place. Such a change can also occur if the shepherd succeeds in driving the piglet into the brewery. Then, everyone rushes to the center and "slaughters" the piglet, that is, they lift it with their palants. This is a favorable moment for the shepherd to occupy a hole whose owner does not notice in time and does not return.

publisher: Książnica Polska Towarzystwa Nauczycieli Szkół Wyższych
title: The Ring
body:
A game for boys and young men from various rural regions of Poland, suitable for male secondary schools. The boys divide into two teams, which stand opposite each other at a distance of 40—50 metres on level ground (or an unused road). Each player has a "stick" ("spyniaczka"), a sturdy club slightly curved at the bottom. A player from the team chosen by lot begins the game by throwing ("rolling") a wooden ring (most often beechwood; a thick plank is cut into a circle with a diameter of about S0 centimetres) so that it rolls as far as possible toward the opposing team. If one of the opponents manages to strike the ring with their stick so that it rolls back toward the starting team, this counts as one "rebound." If, however, the ring is struck forcefully and bounces upward before returning to the starting point, this is called a "hill"; a hill equals three rebounds. After the first rebound, the next throw follows (by the team that began the game), and so on, until a mistake occurs—that is, either the ring does not reach the goal or is not rebounded. In both cases, the opposing team takes possession of the ring and throws it. Besides playing for rebounds and hills, the game can also be played as "chasers." In this version, the game takes place over a larger area on a straight road and involves driving the opposing team as far back as possible. The ring can not only be rebounded but also stopped. However, if the ring falls without being stopped, those who threw it last must throw it again from that spot in the same direction, while the clumsy opponents must quickly retreat to stop it this time. The team that has advanced the farthest after a set time wins.

title: Simple Tip-Cat
body:
A Christian has not done his duty if... on Easter Tuesday he does not strike Mikołaj Rej on the head with a tip-cat until an eye pops out. This game is widespread in Poland (as is the next one) among rural and urban boys. It is suitable for older pupils of elementary schools, especially rural ones. It is played in numerous variations under different names (Kiczka, Kot, Pliszka, or Cyrka in Lesser Poland; Pchła in Kashubia; Stręk in Greater Poland; Czyż, Krypa, or Klipa in Mazovia; Szpak in Volhynia). We will consider only the **2** fundamental variations:

**a) Tip-Cat with Markers (Central Lesser Poland)**
A boy chosen by casting or measuring stands by an oblong hole dug in the ground and places the tip-cat (a stick of soft wood, 20 cm long and 2 cm in diameter) across the hole; this place is called the "win," "home," or "kingdom." The rest of the boys stand at the "loss" (or go "to tend the pigs") at various distances, having first measured out straight-line intervals from the hole: 10, 15, 20... 50 steps, marked with pebbles. The first marker is 10 steps from the hole, the second 5 steps from the first, the third 5 steps from the second. The player at the win starts by placing the bat under the tip-cat and flinging it toward his companions. If one of them catches the tip-cat in the air, he goes to the win. If not, the striker places the bat across the hole, and one of the opponents "releases" the tip-cat (rolls it along the ground) toward the bat. If it hits the bat, the striker is "shackled" and yields his place to the thrower. If it misses, the striker begins the proper game. He places the tip-cat in the hole so that one end protrudes above the edge, facing the opponents. He then strikes this protruding end so that the tip-cat leaps up, and while it is in the air, he strikes it with the bat. If someone now catches it in flight ("catches a champ"), he scores 100 and goes to strike. If the uncaught tip-cat falls to the ground, the striker scores as many marks ("tips") as the number of steps from the hole where it fell. The striker is also considered "shackled" if he fails to strike the tip-cat 3 times in a row or strikes it closer than marker 1 (10 steps). The game continues until one of the players reaches the agreed-upon number (e.g., 1000 or 3000).

**b) Tip-Cat without Markers (Kraków region, Mazovia)**
The difference from variation a) is that the "released" tip-cat, if it misses the bat, is struck from where it stopped. Since there is no hole there, either the tip-cat is whittled to a point at both ends (so that when struck on one end, it leaps up), or (in the Łomża region) the boys know how to "drag" it with the bat along the ground, and when it rolls, "pick it up" (place the end of the bat under it and toss it into the air) and strike it. If the struck tip-cat falls uncaught, the striker measures the distance from the hole with the bat and scores as many marks as bat-lengths measured. (Variation a) fascinates boys with its scoring method; variation b) provides more movement, as the tip-cat can be struck in any direction, and players must run a lot to catch it).

title: Kiczka with Mothers
body:
The dissemination and application are as previously described. Both variant a) and b) of the previous game can also be treated as a game between two camps under the command of mothers. After "measuring" with the bat (see General Part, V a), one of the camps stands on the "winning" side, and its players serve and volley 3 times in a predetermined order (the weakest first). For the safety of those catching, the very tips of these cones should be left blunt (cut off). The change of goals (i.e., the transition of the volleyers to the "losing" side and vice versa) occurs: 1) after the kiczka is caught by a player from the opposing camp; 2) after "knocking out" a l l volleyers (by failing to volley 3 times, or by hitting the bat with the kiczka, see the previous game). Points ("kiczki") are, of course, counted not for individual players, but for the camps.

title: Stręk (The Bat-and-Ball Game)
body:
A rural boys' game from the Bukowsko district (Greater Poland), similar in application to the previous one. Played by four boys. Two of them, armed with bats (palanty), hold them with the ends resting in small pits dug in the ground opposite each other at a distance of 20 paces. The other two stand at the sides. One of these side players has the *stręk* (a small ball or stick) and throws it at one of the boys standing by the pits, who tries to hit the *stręk* in mid-air with his bat. After hitting it, both boys with bats run to switch places, crossing their bats as they meet and continuing to run. One of the side players, standing closer to where the *stręk* fell, runs to retrieve it and then has the right to occupy one of the now-vacant pits if he reaches it first. In that case, the other two boys hand over their bats and take the side positions, and the game continues. If, however, the targeted player fails to hit the *stręk*, there is no mandatory change of places—only if the *stręk* flies far do the boys switch pits. Each correct occupation of a pit counts as a point.

title: Mother and Daughter
body:
A game played by village boys in the Międzyrzecz district (Podlasie); application as in the previous. The boys (usually numbering 2, less often more) decide (by "measuring" with a bat or throwing it from the foot) who will stand by the "mother." The mother consists of a stick 1 meters 20 centimeters long, planted vertically in the ground, with its top cut evenly across. On top of it, the "daughter" is placed—a small stick 15 centimeters long, 21/a centimeters thick, whittled lengthwise into stripes on four sides. The game begins with the player standing by the mother striking the end of the daughter from above or below with the bat. The daughter arcs through the air toward the opponent, tumbling, and the opponent tries to hit it back before it falls, as close to the mother as possible. From where the rebounded daughter lands, the hitter is allowed to toss it back to the mother: if they succeed (despite the efforts of the player by the mother, who tries to hit the daughter away) within a distance no greater than the length of the stick that can fit in their throat, they take the place by the mother. If, on the contrary, the rebound yields a worse result, the distance of the daughter from the mother is measured with the bat, and each bat-length counts as 1 point against the rebounder. 100 such points decide the loss, after which the winner strikes the daughter with the bat and, from where it lands, rides on the back of the opponent to the mother.

title: The Lid
body:
A game of rural boys in the Rzeszów and Brody regions (Lesser Poland); application as in the previous one. For this game, a "palerka" (bat) or "pałka śmigła" (swinging stick), a small board about 80 cm long, is driven into the ground at a half-right angle, and a "wiko" (the lid), a small piece of wood, is knocked off the board with the bat. The lid is a stick 10 cm long, with a diameter of 2 cm, whittled flat on one side along 3/4 of its length down to the axis. It is placed with this flat side on the slanted surface of the board, facing upward, resting the angle between the thicker and thinner parts of the lid against the end of the board. When struck, the bat slides from below along the board and hits the lower end of the lid. Two players compete; the opponent catches the knocked-off stick, and if successful, takes the "field" ("victory"). If they fail to catch it, they throw the stick toward the board, trying to land it as close as possible. The player on the field attempts to hit it in mid-air as far away as possible. From where the stick lands, the distance to the board is measured by the length of the bat, counting 10 for each measurement. If the stick (the lid) hits the board, the player goes "to the pigs" (to defeat).

title: Simple Palant
body:
Palant, in its numerous variations—of which we present only the most important here under 130—132—has a very ancient tradition in Poland and has always been the favorite pastime of our school youth. It is described by Gołębiowski and Kitowicz. Poles and Silesians particularly excelled in it at the Prague court, according to Guarinoni’s account (1610), who also considered palant a Polish game. The modern name of the game likely dates back to the era of Italian influences (XVI century); however, the game itself is much older in our lands. In the XIV century, a stick for striking a ball (piłatyk, from Latin *pilaticus*) is mentioned in the *Album of the Kraków Academy*. The ball, however, was even earlier called a *gałka* (knob), as evidenced by the word *galić* (to toss the ball for striking). The Old Polish language abounds in phrases, comparisons, and proverbs derived from this game. It is widespread among urban boys and, in many regions, also in villages; suitable for lower secondary school classes (as preparation for *Palant with Mothers*, or when there are too few players for the latter).

**a) Without Ransom.** The chosen player (by "measuring," see General Part, V a) takes the "kingdom" ("winning goal"); the others go to the "field" ("losing goal," "to tend pigs") and stand at various distances from the striker. The latter gently tosses the ball upward with the left hand toward the front and, in mid-air, strikes it with the end of the palant, held in the right hand. The striker loses the kingdom:
- 1) if 3 times in a row they fail to strike the ball, or strike it so that it rolls on the ground as a "szęzur" (grounder);
- 2) if one of the opponents catches the ball in flight (a "kampa"), with both hands for younger players, or with one hand for older ones. In the second case, the catcher replaces the striker; in the first, the next player in the prearranged order does so.

**b) With Ransom.** As in a), but at a distance of 20 steps from the kingdom, a "goal" is marked (with a pebble, flag, etc.). The striker, to earn the right to three more strikes, must at least once strike the ball far enough to safely "ransom" themselves—that is, run to the goal, touch it with a hand or foot (in some places, strike it 3 times with the palant), and return to the kingdom. During this run, opponents may either "strike" ("shackle") them with the ball or throw it back to the kingdom so that the ball reaches it before the returning striker. In both cases (aside from those mentioned in a), the striker loses the kingdom and goes to the field, and the player who struck them or outran them with the ball takes their place.

title: Palant with Mothers, Without Burning
body:
They strike themselves, they burn themselves. A proverb from the century XIV. As widespread as the previous. Suitable for secondary schools.

Rules

1) The g a m e f i e l d is a rectangle whose shorter side measures 25 m., and the longer side 60 m. The space bounded at the front by one of the shorter sides of the game field and its extensions on both sides is called the k i n g d o m. The kingdom is unbounded at the rear. At a distance of 25 m from the center of the kingdom’s boundary and the game field lies the h a l f - m a r k, and at a distance of 50 m, the g o a l. These are marked by posts at least 1½ m. high, firmly dug into the ground. C B o u n d a r y f l a g s must be planted at the 4 corners of the game field and on the side lines at a distance of 25 m. from the kingdom. The boundaries should also be marked on the ground with a transverse line running through the half-mark.

2) The p a l a n t (bat) must be 89—100 cm. long, made of strong wood. Its cross-section is either round with a diameter of 3½ cm., or rectangular (with well-rounded edges) of 3×4 cm. The b a l l must have a diameter of 7 cm. and a weight of 80 g.

3) The L n u m b e r o f p l a y e r s is 11 on each side, unless otherwise agreed. By ¹) casting lots with the palant, it is decided which side begins the game with the strike.

4) Among the players of each side, one distinguishes the m o t h e r, the ransomer, and 9 c h i l d p l a y e r s. When a side is in the kingdom, the child players strike first in turn, according to a fixed order predetermined by the mother; then the ransomer 2 times; finally, the mother 3 times. Additionally, the ransomer strikes out of turn if there is not a single player in the kingdom with the right to strike. If, despite this, no one ransoms themselves, the side loses the kingdom. After each new conquest of the kingdom, striking begins again with the player whose turn it was at the moment of losing the kingdom. A side loses the kingdom: a) when a player drops the palant from their hand while striking; b) when, holding the palant, they step or run outside the kingdom.

5) S k e w s t r i k e s, from which the ball, without touching the ground or any of the opponents, passes beyond the side line, are invalid; likewise invalid are strikes from which the ball, without touching an opponent, falls to the ground before the half-mark line or on it (s h o r t s t r i k e s). Invalid, too, are strikes in which the striker has even part of their foot outside the kingdom’s boundary.

6) The right to the next strike (for the ransomer: 2 strikes, for the mother: 3) belongs to a player only if they have r a n s o m e d t h e m s e l v e s by running within the boundaries of the game field to the goal and back before their turn to strike comes around again. The run may be freely interrupted and the player may return to the kingdom or the goal. However, starting or continuing the run is only permitted from the moment of a valid strike until the ball returns to the kingdom. It is not permitted to ransom oneself: a) for a player who is already ransomed, and b) when the ball is lost. When the ball returns to the kingdom or is lost, the player may not move further in their run than the place where they were at the moment the ball returned to the kingdom or was lost. For the run to be valid, the player must touch the goal post with their hand. If a player crosses the side or rear boundary of the game field during the run, the run is invalid and must be repeated. However, the runner may be “shackled” during such an invalid run. If a player encounters deliberate obstruction from an opponent during the run, the run is considered completed.

7) If any of the opponents hits ("s h a c k l e s") a victorious player (i.e., the striking side) with the ball when that player is outside the kingdom and not touching the goal post, the entire side loses the kingdom. Shackling is invalid: a) if the ball bounces off anything before hitting the player; b) if the opponents deliberately obstructed the player during the run; c) if the shackler previously ran with the ball in hand or held it longer than 2 seconds. Moreover, shackling a child player is invalid if, at the time of shackling, they were touching the half-mark post, having stopped on their way to the goal. A victorious player who deliberately touches the ball with any part of their body outside the kingdom’s boundaries is also considered shackled.

8) If any of the losing players catches the ball struck by the victorious side with one hand before it touches the ground, it counts as a c a t c h. Three catches made during one stay on the field result in a change of goal. If a player encounters deliberate obstruction from an opponent while catching, the ball is counted as caught.

9) The duration of the competition is one hour. If the camp that was randomly assigned the kingdom at the start of the game holds it until half of this time has elapsed, a change of *met* is ordered. Victory goes to the camp that, during the competition, has earned the most *kreski* (marks), calculated as follows. When all players of a given camp have *podbijali* (struck) and redeemed themselves, the camp has captured a *metę* (goal), for which one *kreska* (mark) is counted. If, however, the *meta* is *suchą* (dry), meaning it was captured in one continuous sequence without losing the kingdom, two *kreski* (marks) are counted. The competition is overseen by an impartial *sędzia* (referee), who ensures strict adherence to the rules. He resolves all disputes irrevocably. If necessary, the referee selects two assistant referees to aid him: one to monitor the game on the kingdom, count strikes and runs, and the other to pay attention to the rear part of the playing field.

Technical instructions
When **striking**, the player stands with their left side toward the playing field, legs apart, ensuring the left foot does not cross the kingdom’s boundary. The ball is tossed with the left hand so the palant can strike it with the **tip**, as this sends the ball the farthest. The right arm, wielding the palant, executes the broadest possible backward and slightly upward swing, with the elbow extended, accompanied by an energetic twist of the torso. Then the arm returns downward and forward, while the torso twists to the left; the palant strikes the ball slightly below its center. The trajectory given to the ball should be intermediate between a “candle,” flying high and too easily caught by opponents, and an ineffective “rat,” rolling along the ground. A skilled player sends the ball with such force that it flies just over the heads of opponents, making it difficult to catch, as it “burns” the hand. Moreover, they aim to direct it through momentarily unoccupied areas of the field, so no one can intercept it. When reaching for a ball returned from the field, the striker avoids extending their hand beyond the kingdom; if they catch the ball this way, they are “shackled” (see 7). During **redemption**, the player must pay attention not only to speed. They must keep their eyes on the ball and be ready at any moment to interrupt their run, retreat, or dodge the projectile. The latter (often called “gintasowanie” by our boys) requires great skill. If the ball is aimed at the feet or shins, the player jumps; if at the upper torso or head, they lean or crouch; if at the lower torso, they dodge to the side, drop to the ground, or the like. Sometimes a twist of the torso suffices. Among the actions of the “losing” team, **catches** are performed one-handed only when required by the rules, i.e., for a struck ball. A ball passed by a teammate is **always** caught with both hands to avoid dropping it (not “spitting” it). The palm of the hand, e.g., the right (if the ball comes from that side), is turned toward the ball’s flight, while the left hand assists. For catching struck balls, training both hands equally is essential, as the ball often flies more conveniently toward the left hand. **Stopping** a ball rolling on the ground (“rat”) should always be done with the hand (not the foot, which is less reliable and takes more time, as the ball must still be picked up). Immediately after lifting the ball (without straightening up), it should be passed to a teammate (for striking) or returned to the kingdom. **Passing** the ball is never taken literally: it means throwing the ball into a teammate’s hands. (A self-respecting player, even when standing quite close, will never accept or hand over the ball or palant except by catching or throwing.) The pass must be quick (but not so forceful as to “burn” the hand and hinder the catch); catching a ball arcing through the air takes too much time. The second condition is accuracy. The ball should arrive where it is most convenient to catch; the best target is the teammate’s chest. When the distance does not exceed 3—4 m., the ball is **thrown** with the arm extended downward. For greater distances, it is **hurled** from shoulder height with a bent arm. When **returning** the ball to the kingdom, accuracy is less important, but speed is sometimes crucial: a ball outpacing the runner forces them to interrupt their run. Here, a throw with a backward and upward arm swing, strong and nearly horizontal, is appropriate. **Striking** leads to victory if accurate; if missed, it can cause a significant loss of time and advantage for opponents. Thus, a skilled player will strike from a distance only when aiming at a runner returning from behind, so that if the ball misses, it goes to the kingdom and at least outpaces the runner. In all other cases, it is better to pass the ball to a teammate standing closer to the runner. Even the most accurate long throw gives the runner time to dodge. Aim should be at the runner’s torso when striking from the front or back; when striking from the side, aim slightly **ahead** of their torso. Tactical instructions
The **running order**, established by the mother, should primarily consider the ability to strike well and dodge skillfully. The mother ensures that none of the “kids” strikes too weakly and that their redemption does not rely solely on the redeemer and mother. The weakest kid strikes first, then generally the more skilled, with the rule that a stronger player is always placed between two weaker ones. The mother encourages runs when they are safe, so that not too many runners remain at the end. Not all strikes that the redeemer and mother can perform are used to their full extent. If the first strike is so far that the waiting runners can safely redeem themselves, they run, and once redeemed, the remaining strikes are skipped. To avoid accidents, the ugly habit of beginners throwing the palant behind them after striking must be combated; it should be gently placed on the ground. For the same reason, the area in the kingdom behind and to the sides of the striker, within a width of 3 m., should be clear. **Runners** should be sent, if possible, along the sides of the field, as it is harder to strike them there (only a kid redeeming themselves after a not-too-strong strike and using the privilege of stopping at the halfway point on the way to the goal must run down the center). It is also good to end runs so that several runners move simultaneously in different directions and on both sides of the field: this distracts opponents and makes striking harder. However, group runs should be avoided, as opponents can easily strike by aiming at the “cluster” of runners. The tactics of the “losing” team are more complex. Among other things, the mother must acquire the difficult skill of properly **positioning** players on the field. The formation shown in the illustration (p. 214) is typical but cannot be an absolute rule. It must adapt to the strength of the strikes and the opponents’ general playing style, and sometimes it must be changed when the palant passes to another player. Generally, however, it will be rational (as in the illustration) to position several (weaker) players around the halfway point. These will return the struck ball from nearby and sometimes strike a “kid” running to the halfway point. Stronger players are stationed near the goal (for striking) and the sides and back of the field (mainly for catches). The overall arrangement resembles an irregular checkerboard, with larger clusters near the goal and halfway point. Players should hold their positions, only running for the ball when necessary, etc., but never getting in their teammates’ way. Regarding **striking**, we have already mentioned that the safest direction is toward the kingdom. If, however, we must strike to the side or back, it can only be done with the **protection** of a teammate, who stands on the other side of the runner and catches the ball if it misses. Without this precaution, the ball flies far beyond the field, where no one can stop it; this gives time for redemption not only for the missed runner but sometimes for many others. Occasionally, **surrounding** the runner with several players, who skillfully pass the ball to each other until one finds the right moment to strike, can be effective. This requires great “coordination,” i.e., harmonious cooperation, by which the most experienced players are best recognized. When playing against weak strikers, one can also try the “starvation” tactic. The goal is not to capture the kingdom through catches or strikes but to return the ball to the kingdom as quickly as possible each time, which, by shortening or preventing runs, quickly leads weak strikers to “starvation” (i.e., coming onto the field due to a lack of players entitled to strike).

¹) See General Part, V a.

title: Fist Ball
body:
A game introduced into our schools approximately 30 years ago; suitable for upper classes of boys' secondary schools. It requires a level playing field in the shape of a rectangle with dimensions of approximately 20 by 40 metres. At the midpoint of the longer sides, posts are driven in, between which a coloured tape is stretched at a height of 2 metres, dividing the field into 2 halves. Participants divide into 2 teams of 5—11 players each and arrange themselves in a checkerboard pattern, the white team on one side of the tape and the red team on the other. The team chosen by lot, for example the white team, serves by having one player stand in the centre of their half of the field, toss the ball (like a football, only with a thinner leather cover) to head height, and as it falls, strike it with a fist or forearm so that it passes over the tape into the red team's area. The red team attempts to return the ball (also with a fist or forearm) either on the volley or after the first bounce (rebound from the ground) back over the tape into the opposing field, which counts as a point. The return is valid even if the ball was struck several times on the same side before the return, provided that after each strike the ball does not bounce more than once. If the return is successful, the white team attempts to strike the ball back again, and so on, until one of the teams makes a mistake. A mistake is: 1) when a player strikes the ball from above or with both hands, uses the palm instead of the fist, or kicks it with the foot, 2) when a player catches the ball, 3) when a player steps into the opponents' field, 4) when the ball, during the serve, falls onto the same field, 5) when the ball touches any part of the body other than the player's hand or forearm, 6) when the ball bounces twice or rolls on the same field, 7) when the ball passes under the tape or touches it, 8) when the ball passes beyond the boundaries of the field. The team at fault serves. The ball is passed for the serve underhand; it may not be struck. The team that scores the most points within a set time (half to 1 hours) wins.
